title: Maine Tech Week Comes to Aura
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine Tech Week returns to Portland, highlighting innovation across industries
Hundreds of people are gathering in Portland this week to brainstorm about technology, as the second annual Maine Tech Week got underway on Monday.
"We're actually building the tech community in real time. Maine Tech Week is a gathering of anyone and everyone who is involved in technology," said Torie Delisle, Maine Tech Week's founding director. "Our theme this year is intersections because we want to talk about when technology is found in unexpected places."
One of Monday morning's sessions at Aura, titled "Where Ocean Meets Innovation," focused on blue tech, the advanced technology sector of the maritime industry. Andrew Thompson, CEO of Maine-based Bluesonde, was on stage talking about his two-year-old company's innovative technologies.
"At Bluesonde, we developed water-monitoring tools to monitor the health of our coastlines, our lakes, our rivers," Thompson said. "Our flagship product is a basketball-sized monitoring buoy that can be deployed in minutes and collects water quality data and relays that to a web-based dashboard."
Recently, Bluesonde used its buoys in Harpswell to provide real-time data to scientists and others who were monitoring conditions of a harmful algal bloom that has led to massive shellfish die-offs in Casco Bay.
"About a half a dozen of our systems were able to capture a clear signal as that harmful algal bloom went through, and so that was helpful in the response and understanding where that water was moving," Thompson said. "Over time, as we gain more data sets in this, the goal is to have this help be an early warning tool to get a quicker jump when problems come up."
No tech week would be complete without sessions on artificial intelligence, or AI. Several sessions related to AI are being held Thursday afternoon between Aura and Mechanics' Hall.

title: In response to Lt. Dakota Dupuis
text:
We are writing with a correction to our previous opinion piece endorsing Det. Corey Bagley (R) over Lt. Dakota Dupuis (D) to be Hancock County’s next sheriff, as well as to provide clarifications about Dupuis’s rebuttal. We continue to support Bagley for sheriff and appreciate that our colleague, Rep. Holly Eaton (D-Deer Isle), has joined us in supporting Bagley, as reported in the Quietside Journal.
Our original letter incorrectly stated the sheriff’s budget increase between 2024 and 2025, based on numbers reported in the Ellsworth American. Dupuis is correct that the increase was approximately $430,000, which was an 18.7% increase — still pretty steep. Dupuis said the first budget he “helped develop from the outset” was the 2025 budget, so we compared the 2024 budget (pre-Dupuis) to the 2027 budget number Dupuis recently proposed to the County Commissioners. The 2024 budget was approved at $2,295,962, and the 2027 proposed budget is $3,311,829 — a more than $1 million, or 44%, increase in just three years.

title: Maine's forest acres are an essential dual economic engine
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WRITTEN BY WANDA CURTIS
According to the Maine Forest Service (MFS), the state of Maine boasts the highest percentage of forested land of any state in the nation. Approximately 17.5 million acres of forest land cover upwards of 89 percent of the land area.
Director of the Center for Research on Sustainable Forests Aaron Weiskittel said recently that Maine is not only the most heavily forested state in the nation, but that Maine’s history, culture, and economy are defined by trees. For centuries, he said, the working forest has shaped Maine’s character, rural communities, and way of life.
“Maine ranks among the states most dependent on its forest sector, generating roughly $1 out of every $29 in state GDP and leading the country in the forest share of its exports,” Weiskittel said. “As we celebrate Maine Forest Products Week (Oct. 18-24), these unique 17.5 million working forest acres remain an essential dual economic engine, powering an $8.3 billion manufacturing base alongside a $3.4 billion outdoor recreation industry.”
According to Weiskittel, Maine’s forest products industry contributes $8.3 billion in total annual economic output, supports over 29,000 jobs, and accounts for 3.45% of state GDP. Outdoor recreation generates another $3.4 billion in value-added GDP through woods-dependent activities like hunting, fishing, guided outfitting, snowmobiling, camping, and leaf peeping across the state, he said. That’s a total of about $11 billion in total economic output generated through Maine’s forest industry.
“Maine’s 17.5 million acres of working forests, particularly the Maine North Woods, provide the land base and infrastructure like trail networks, access roads, and managed open space that make outdoor recreation possible,” Weiskittel said. “Outdoor recreation fits alongside the forest products industry because private working forest owners maintain open access for recreation, making the forest a dual economic engine for both wood manufacturing and tourism/recreation.”
Maine Exports Millions of Dollars in Wood Products Annually
According to the Census USA Trade Online for 2022, Maine shipped $577 million worth of forest products to 49 countries in 2022. The exports included $287 million worth of paper and paperboard, $171 million worth of wood and articles of wood, $119 worth of pulp and recovered paper, and about $9 million worth of furniture. About $385 million of those products went to Canada, $40 million to China, $36 million to Belgium, $28 million to Italy, $22 million to Germany, and $20 million to Mexico.
U.S. Census Bureau and Department of Transportation 2022 statistics show that Maine also sent $20 million worth of forest products to Connecticut, $28 million to Rhode Island, $47 million to New Jersey, $119 million to Vermont, $130 million to Pennsylvania, $178 million to Massachusetts, $204 million to New Hampshire, and $1.3 billion to New York that year.
“Covering 17.5 million acres, Maine’s working forests anchor the rural economy and municipal tax base,” Weiskittel said.
Aroostook County Leads the Way
According to the 2023 Maine Forest Service Wood Processing Report, the largest Maine supplier of wood was Aroostook County. Roughly 839,000 green tons of pulpwood and 235 million board feet of saw logs were harvested there in 2023. Penobscot, Somerset, Washington, Piscataquis, Franklin, and Oxford counties also supply a large amount of wood. Southern and coastal counties contribute only a small amount, Weiskittel said.
Most Popular Species
The most popular species in Maine used for wood products, in recent years, have been spruce and fir. Those accounted for a little over half of its 890 million board feet of sawlogs in 2023, Weiskittel said. The next most popular species are red and white pine, he said. Those accounted for 172 million board feet of the sawlogs harvested that year.
Maine Also Imports Wood
Interesting to note is the fact that Maine not only exports wood, but we also import wood from other New England states and Canada. The 2023 MFS Wood Processor Report shows that in 2023 Maine imported about 2.7 million tons of wood from New Hampshire, Vermont, New York, New Brunswick, Quebec, and Ontario during that year.
“Maine’s mills take in slightly more than Maine landowners send out,” Weiskittel said. “Canadian timber is often significantly closer to northern/eastern Maine mills than southern/western Maine timber, reducing freight costs. Paper and packaging mills require softwood/hardwood blends, importing roundwood or chips when local supply of a specific species falls short. Maine mills process 11 million green tons annually against 10 million tons of local harvest (2 million of which are exported), requiring imports to maintain full capacity.”

title: Sheriff’s race: Vote leadership over hypocrisy
text:
To the Editor:
A sheriff’s race should be decided by experience, integrity, maturity, and commitment to the community — not political labels or campaign rhetoric.
Corey Bagley brings over 34 years of experience, professionalism, sound judgment, and a genuine commitment to Hancock County. His community involvement and longstanding personal and professional relationships reflect the respect he has earned through years of service. These are qualities voters should prioritize when choosing their sheriff.
A troubling issue in this race is the contradiction between the Democratic campaign’s request for a clean election with no mudslinging and the reported conduct of its supporters. Reports of intimidation directed at people supporting another candidate should concern every voter. These are not issues I have seen with Corey’s campaign. Political disagreement is a normal, but intimidation has no place in any election.
Understandably, a candidate’s political affiliation is a personal choice, but voters have every right to question what that choice represents. When someone changes party affiliation before pursuing an elected office, voters should look beyond the label and examine their history, values, and record of service. A party designation alone doesn’t establish the character, competence or leadership required.
Voters need to examine the department’s record under the opposing candidate’s claimed leadership. Budget increases, lost contracts, loss of health insurance, and significant employee turnover deserve clear explanations and accountability. These are legitimate concerns, not inconvenient details to dismiss or deflect. Hancock County deserves a sheriff who answers difficult questions with facts, accepts responsibility, and leads the department forward. The truth matters.
Ultimately, this election is about experience, accountability, integrity, and the ability to unite our community. No campaign can credibly demand clean elections while tolerating conduct that contradicts that message. Candidates should be judged by their actions, not promises.
Our sheriff should represent the best of our community. This choice deserves careful thought — not blind allegiance to a party. I believe Corey Bagley is the stronger choice for Hancock County.
Jamie Phillips Trader
Ellsworth

title: More than a rink: What makes Alfond Arena unique
text:
The Alfond Arena is home to the University of Maine Black Bears ice hockey teams and has been declared one of the best environments to watch college hockey. This year, the arena is celebrating 50 years of being an iconic venue since it opened in 1977. Since then, the Harold Alfond Foundation has donated $320 million to the University of Maine System, and $50 million of that portion went toward renovating the Alfond Arena, changes that were completed Sept. 27, 2025. The added state-of-the-art facilities provide the student-athletes a first-class, modern experience. For the best fans in college hockey, it has an enhanced experience on game days, which only adds to the electric atmosphere.
The arena has a compact seating capacity of about 5,000 fans. Maine found a way to use this to its advantage by having one of the most intimidating home environments in college hockey. Rather than having a massive arena, passionate fans are close to the ice, creating an environment where the crowd can directly influence the energy of a game by having an intimate atmosphere. The compact seating helps fans feel connected to every save, hit and goal, which the players benefit from for fuel. The Alfond Arena has become much more than a venue to watch ice hockey; it is a gathering place for students, families, alumni and longtime fans to connect the different generations of the Black Bear community. Fans feel like they are a part of something bigger than themselves.
“I feel like everyone knows each other when they’re in here, even when we’re on the bench,” said head coach Ben Barr of the UMaine men’s ice hockey team. “A lot of people have been coming here for decades and it’s a really special thing.”
Another layer added to what makes the Alfond so different is the unique rituals like having the “Naked 5” run a lap around the arena whenever Maine scores a goal, or having the UMaine band perform in the boisterous student section overlooking the ice whenever a play is dead. This student section also gives Maine an edge when competing against an opponent because of the constant chants, cheers and excitement that spreads throughout the building from the opening faceoff to the final buzzer. This support can make a big difference, especially when the game is close because a loud student section can build momentum after a big save or crucial goal, creating a clear home-ice advantage.
“We definitely get a lift every time we come on the ice here,” said Barr. “It’s the best place to play in college hockey.”
The student section also represents the connection between the team and the wider university community because it is the students who help create the identity and traditions like “The Naked 5” that make attending a game at Alfond so memorable. Their passion reflects the pride they have for representing UMaine, and they make it known every time they fill the arena.
What defines the Alfond Arena is the connection between the building, the team and the small-town community who fill its seats. There is a mix of tradition, student energy and community pride that makes it more than an arena; it makes it a defining part of what it means to be a Black Bear.

title: Politicians have a rich history of telling each other to zip it
text:
According to a 1922 edition of an internal company newspaper of JC Penney (The Dynamo), a husband or wife has “good grounds for divorce” if one tells the other to shut up. Political rivalry, though, is nothing like a marriage.
Given how ugly campaigning has become, I’m not at all perturbed that Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Troy Jackson told Sen. Susan Collins to “shut up” during last week’s Senate debate. It came after a student in the audience yelled out.
Collins could be heard saying over the shouts, “This must be a Troy Jackson supporter.”
Jackson told CNN that Collins “accused me of setting that up. I had no idea who it was. I mean, I was surprised whenever he jumped up out of there. … I just think that was another situation where she was talking down to me.”
Collins told Fox News that Jackson’s response “seemed like such an automatic quick reply” that it struck her as a “very telling” example of his mistreatment of women.
Oh, come on. Sen. Collins has put up with President Donald Trump’s incessant insults toward women with barely a peep. Furthermore, she didn’t seem to register Jackson’s rejoinder as an insult to women on the night it happened.
A glance at history shows this shouldn’t be an issue. In 1969 at the University of Edinburgh, Queen Elizabeth’s patrician husband Prince Philip presided over a meeting that a 22-year-old student disrupted with unwanted questions. The prince wasn’t having it.
“Shut up and grow up,” Philip shouted. Cheers and laughter followed, according to the Associated Press.
Back in 1982, a Republican congressional candidate from California, Gary Arnold, kept interrupting President Ronald Reagan. Fed up, the normally avuncular president pointed at him and told Arnold, “Shut up!”
The GOP audience applauded.
A couple of years later, when Walter Mondale gave a speech during his bid to oust Reagan that a group of GOP backers disrupted. Mondale turned to them and said, “Shut up, will ya!” The place erupted in cheers.
When angry relatives of American military personnel listed as missing in action confronted President George H.W. Bush in 1992, Bush had a quick response to them: “Shut up!”
“I didn’t blow my cool. I just made an emphatic point,” the president later said.
Even as august a figure as Winston Churchill once got so fed up with the heckling of a communist member of Parliament, William Gallagher, that he turned to the Scotsman with a lion’s glare in 1947 and told Gallagher, “Shut up, Moscow!”
Almost nobody criticized Reagan, Mondale, Bush or Churchill for their words.
Honestly, is there anyone who hasn’t wanted to tell a politician: oh, shut up? I’ve certainly had that desire on many occasions. I wouldn’t be surprised to find out I did it a time or two.
My best advice to Jackson? Stop talking about this, stop taking questions about it — and start telling Mainers who you are and what you stand for.

title: Maine women’s basketball team returns for new season
text:
ORONO, Maine (WABI) - The Maine women’s basketball team is back on Skip Chappelle Court.
They’re preparing for a new season that tips off at home on Thurs. Nov. 5 at 6 p.m. against Siena in the America East-Metro Basketball Challenge.
The Black Bears spoke about how this year’s lineup can contend without two-time America East Player of the Year Adrianna Smith.
“I knew (with) Addi leaving last year, someone needs to step into this role. I’m really honored to be able to work for that every day. We have two other post players working really hard as well. Bailey (Breen) and Zeina (Haleem), they’re young, but they’re feisty. We have a really, really tall team this year, so it’s nice,” said Lizzy Gruber, senior center.
“It’s definitely going to be a lot different. Addi is an unstoppable force on the offensive end, so we’ve been trying different things. We’re playing a lot different this year, a lot quicker, trying to push the pace, and I think it’s going to be a little more balanced. We have a lot of people that can do a lot of different things,” said Maddie Fitzpatrick, redshirt sophomore guard.
Notable non-conference games include Oregon’s visit to ‘The Pit’ on Nov. 13 before Maine faces Kentucky in Daytona, Fla. on Nov. 27.
The Black Bears visit Michigan State on Dec. 3 before America East play begins with a home date against Vermont on New Year’s Eve.

title: The Lincoln County News
text:
Tony Gallace passed away Oct. 13, 2026. He was born Jan. 26, 1976 in Camden, a son of Sherry Gallace and the late Peter Gallace.
He is survived by his son, Andrew and his wife, Abbey, along with their son, Odin; his mother, Sherry Gallace; sister, Susie Pease and her husband, Pete; brother, Pete Gallace and his wife, Kim; nieces and nephews, Nicolas Pease and his wife, Vivian, Emily Heal and her husband, Cody, Isabella Gallace, and Julia Gallace; and his girlfriend, Kat Read and her children Kaelyn, Gavin, and Stella. He was an amazing father to his son Andrew and father-in-law as well. He had a special place in his heart for his grandson, Odin, who he loved taking on adventures and spending time with.
Tony was a true Waldoboro legend (often referred to as “the mayor”) and knew almost everyone in town through his father’s former plumbing and heating business, delivering mail through the postal service, and his various endeavors giving back to the community. He had a passion for the ocean and a contagious laugh that we all loved to hear. He also loved the simple life and always talked about wanting to slow down so he could spend more time hunting and fishing.
A pillar of the Waldoboro community, Tony long dedicated his time and energy to ensuring his neighbors are fed, supported, and connected. As the driving force behind the local Feed the Need program, Tony turned community service into an art form, helping individuals give back to their town through meaningful local projects.
His vision for a stronger, more self-sufficient Waldoboro came to life through the Edible Waldoboro initiative. For over a decade, Tony could be found tending the community garden on Depot Street or working tirelessly to build a greenhouse at the historic Otis Benner Farm & Forgery on Route 1 to grow fresh vegetables for those facing food insecurity. His goal was simple yet profound: to show by example how much a small community can grow when everyone works together.
Beyond his agricultural initiatives, Tony was known as a man who brought people together through the simple comfort of good food and a warm grill. Whether he was supplying and cooking food for local celebrations of life or setting up a massive barbecue under the tent for the Waldoboro Business Association’s Business After Hours events, Tony’s generosity and legendary grilling skills defined countless community gatherings. Some may be happy to know that traffic in Waldoboro may speed up a little considering he will not be driving slowly in the breakdown lane with his truck freighted with supplies for his next endeavor.
His resilience, unwavering work ethic, and massive heart will leave a lasting footprint on the landscape of Waldoboro and the lives of its residents. He will be greatly missed and forever remembered.
A celebration of life will be held in the spring.
Arrangements are under the care and direction of Hall Funeral Home of Waldoboro. To extend a condolence or share a story with the Gallace family, please visit Tony’s book of memories at hallfuneralhomes.com.

title: New plans for Trump's arch don't mention the 'military complex' he said it would host
text:
New plans for Trump's arch don't mention the 'military complex' he said it would host
New Interior Department documents on President Donald Trump's proposed Triumphal Arch don't mention the "military complex" he has said it would host, but the agency said Monday the plan could accommodate such a feature.
The latest batch of planning documents are part of a meeting set for two days after the midterm election on Nov. 3 and reflect the Republican president's push to leave a lasting mark on Washington.
The documents include site maps and renderings of the arch. One response to questions from the National Capital Planning Commission asked for a justification for the structure's size — it's planned to be 250 feet tall. The National Park Service, part of the Interior Department, cited the 250th anniversary of the nation's founding.
"The proposed Triumphal Arch is the celebratory contribution of the semiquincentennial generation of Americans," the agency wrote.
The documents do not detail a military complex at the structure.
Trump said in September that he agreed, at the military's request, to convert the structure into a "top grade Military Complex/Triumphal Arch" and that it would store drones and ammunition, as well as accommodate snipers.
A spokesperson for the Interior Department said in an emailed statement that the structure could host those features, even though they were not specified in the plans.
"The current design of the Triumphal Arch is capable of accommodating the national security functions — and more — highlighted in the President's Truth Social post," the unidentified spokesperson said in an emailed statement.
The arch is proposed for a circle adjacent to the Memorial Bridge connecting the nation's capital with northern Virginia. Like other projects around the capital Trump is pushing, it faces legal challenges.
Among the others are the White House ballroom, renaming and renovating the Kennedy Center, and rebuilding a golf course in East Potomac Park, which could significantly reduce the public's access to running and biking paths.
The arch's opponents say it's too big and would disrupt the view between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery, meant to symbolize the reunification of the North and the South after the Civil War.

title: U.S. Supreme Court declines to hear appeal of Maine’s gun sale waiting period
text:
The U.S. Supreme Court has declined to hear a challenge to Maine’s 72-hour waiting period for firearm purchases.
Justices on Monday denied a petition for a writ of certiorari in the case, one of dozens they declined to take up. The court, as is its standard practice, did not explain its reasoning for declining to hear the appeal.
The 1st U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled in April that the law is likely constitutional.
The law requires a 72-hour waiting period for a gun buyer to take possession of a firearm after purchasing it.
The law, as well as one expanding background check requirements, was enacted in 2024, six months after a gunman killed 18 people in the Lewiston mass shooting. Lawmakers designed the “cooling off” period to reduce suicides and homicides sparked by impulsive firearm purchases. It took effect without the signature of Gov. Janet Mills, who faced pressure from both gun owners and safety advocates.
The lawsuit was brought by a gun buyer, a firearms training business and three firearms dealers who argued that the law interfered with the rights of victims of domestic violence to immediately protect themselves and that it caused significant business losses for firearms dealers.
In February 2025, a federal judge granted a preliminary injunction, blocking enforcement of the law. That spring, a federal appeals court upheld the pause pending the state’s appeal.
The 1st Circuit concluded in April that the plaintiffs were unlikely to succeed in their constitutional challenge to the law and vacated the injunction. The Supreme Court’s decision leaves that ruling in place, allowing the law to be enforced while the lawsuit continues in federal court.
“We know from reporting from the Department of Public Safety that Maine’s 72-hour waiting period has already worked to save lives from preventable gun deaths in our state,” Nacole Palmer, executive director of the Maine Gun Safety Coalition, said in a written statement Monday. “Despite the gun lobby’s best efforts, our waiting period law will continue to save lives and we expect and hope that it will continue to be upheld.”
The Office of the Maine Attorney General declined to comment on Monday. Attorney General Aaron Frey is the defendant in the lawsuit, which was filed by Andrea Beckwith, who runs self-defense classes for victims of domestic violence, state Rep. James White, who owns J. White Gunsmithing, and other Maine gun stores and gun owners.
Joshua Raines, president of Gun Owners of Maine, said that while the Second Amendment group disagrees with the justices’ decision not to hear the appeal, “it wasn’t a surprise that they declined to take this on as it is only an injunction.”
“The lawyers will now take the main case back to the Maine court system, and we 100% expect the courts to overturn and nullify the Maine law based on previous federal case law,” Raines said in an emailed statement Monday.

title: Police hope new picture will help them solve nearly 50-year-old murder in Portsmouth
text:
Police hope new picture will help them solve nearly 50-year-old cold case in Portsmouth, New Hampshire
The New Hampshire Cold Case Unit has shared a previously unreleased picture of a woman who was killed in 1982 in Portsmouth, New Hampshire, hoping the picture will help produce new tips in the unsolved case.
Tammy Little was a 20-year-old nursing student attending the Portsmouth Beauty School in 1982 when she was murdered inside her apartment on Maplewood Avenue in Portsmouth.
She was last seen alive in the early morning hours of Oct. 16, 1982. Her body was found inside her apartment three days later. An autopsy found she died of massive head injuries.
"Tammy was the most joyful person," her family said in a statement shared over the weekend, marking the anniversary of when Little's body was found. "She was everyone’s friend. If you were hurting or needed someone to talk to, she would be there and know what to say. She was the one you called to lift you up, and she was the one to share your happiness with. Her light was so bright. Today, her light lives on with me; she is my guardian angel and lives within my heart. There is not a day that I do not think about her and the more days we could have had together.”
The New Hampshire Cold Case Unit is working with detectives from the Portsmouth Police Department to actively investigate this case. Investigators say they continue to review case files, evaluate physical evidence for modern forensic testing, and pursue all available leads.
“Tammy was a young woman with a bright future ahead of her, and her life was taken in a brutal and senseless act of violence,” said Senior Assistant Attorney General R. Christopher Knowles, Chief of the Cold Case Unit. “Our unit, alongside the Portsmouth Police Department, remains steadfast in our commitment to finding answers for Tammy and her loved ones. We are releasing these new photographs today with the hope that someone who knew her, perhaps a former classmate at the Portsmouth Beauty School or a resident of the Maplewood Avenue neighborhood, will remember a detail they have not previously shared. No matter how much time has passed, we believe there are people who hold information critical to solving this case.”
Investigators say they want to hear from anyone who attended the Portsmouth Beauty School with Little in 1982, who lived in or around 315 Maplewood Avenue, or who frequented the area in October 1982, or who may have seen or spoken to Tammy between the early morning hours of October 16, 1982, and the discovery of her body on October 19, 1982.
Anyone with information should reach out:
- Cold Case Unit Tip Line: (603) 271-2663
- Email: coldcaseunit@dos.nh.gov
- Submit a tip at www.doj.nh.gov/criminal/cold-case
- Victim Page: www.doj.nh.gov/bureaus/cold-case-unit/victim-list/tammy-little

title: Kennebunk, Windham girls soccer show Class A South’s competitiveness
text:
KENNEBUNK — It was dark and chilly as Kennebunk senior Alina Auriemma dribbled down the sideline past her cheering teammates as the final seconds ticked off the clock. In the corner of Windham’s defensive zone, the regular season ended with a 2-1 Kennebunk win.
It’s time for the playoffs, and in Class A South, the most competitive tournament in the state will get underway.
The game Monday at Kennebunk High featured two of the best teams in this deep region. Both Kennbunk and Windham are 10-3-1. Windham will hold on to the No. 2 seed even with the loss. The Rams secured the No. 3 seed and a bye to the regional quarterfinals.
It’s been a season of close games in the league. This was Kennebunk’s fourth one-goal victory, and flipped the result of the Rams’ season-opening 2-1 loss at Windham.
“This could’ve easily been 2-1 them again,” Kennebunk coach Josh Viola said. “Two pretty even teams.”
This was Windham’s seventh one-goal game this season, and second one-goal loss in a row (the Eagles fell to Cheverus, 1-0, last Thursday). Even top-seeded and unbeaten Scarborough, winner of the last four regional championships, hasn’t run roughshod over the league. Six of the Red Storms’ 12 wins going into their regular-season finale against Sanford on Tuesday were decided by a single goal.
“Scarborough, we held them to one in double OT,” Viola said. “Unfortunately, that was one more than we scored.”
Last season, Viola’s Rams might have been the surprise of the league, winning 12 games and advancing to the Class A South semifinals. Nobody is surprised Kennebunk is among the top teams in the region this season, especially not the Rams.
Senior Ava McCourt scored the winning goal with 28:46 left in the second half, her sharp low shot from the left side finding the right corner of the net to give the Rams the 2-1 lead that held up. McCourt missed most of last season with a leg injury. A captain, she sees a team with a positive culture as it heads to the postseason.
“Everyone on this team, we’re one giant fun group,” McCourt said. “We all care. We come to practice ready to go.”
Viola didn’t hold back his praise for McCourt, calling her the best midfielder in the league. Auriemma is a returning all-conference player. Keeper Teagan Hanson rounds out Kennebunk’s trio of seniors, and is a steadying presence at the back of the Rams defense, Viola said. She doesn’t get rattled, and makes quiet saves.
If you’re looking for the dark horse in this season’s Class A South playoff race, the team that Kennebunk was a year ago, you have two choices. There’s Bonny Eagle, which won five games last season and snuck into the playoffs as the 11 seed in Class A South. The Scots, fifth in the Heal point standings, enter their regular-season finale against Portland on Tuesday with eight wins and an impressive 0-0 tie with Scarborough.
There’s also South Portland. The Red Riots, currently fourth in the Heals, missed the tournament a year ago with a 3-9-2 record. South Portland earned its 10th win Monday, beating Falmouth 4-1, and has chance to earn a bye out of the preliminary round.
Kennebunk and Windham know they have a little time to catch their breath and wait for a quarterfinals opponent. They also know they had a strong playoff-like test when they faced each other Monday night. As the No. 2 and No. 3 seeds, respectively, they could face off in a rubber match in the playoffs.
Don’t assume it will happen, though. In the SMAA, no win is guaranteed.

title: Supreme Court declines to hear appeal in disputed Afghan adoption case
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Supreme Court declined Monday to hear an appeal in a disputed adoption case involving an Afghan child orphaned in a U.S. Army raid.
The child’s relatives appealed to the high court after a U.S. Marine who helped evacuate them from Afghanistan took custody of the girl despite State Department efforts to reunite her with her Afghan family.
A 2022 Associated Press report about the case raised alarms at the highest levels of government, from the Taliban to the White House.
The child’s parents were killed in September 2019 when U.S. Army Rangers, along with Afghan forces, raided a rural compound.
The baby was found in the rubble and hospitalized at Bagram Air Base near Kabul, where military lawyer Joshua Mast decided with his wife to adopt her.
But the State Department during President Donald Trump’s first administration worked with the Afghan government to track down surviving relatives, identified as a cousin and his wife.
The Afghan couple raised her for 18 months, but during that time the Masts also obtained a final adoption order from a Virginia court without notifying them. The Masts have insisted they acted honorably to save a child and give her a loving home.
In 2021, Joshua Mast helped the family leave Afghanistan during the U.S. military’s chaotic withdrawal from the country.
Once they were in the U.S., Mast took the child at a refugee resettlement center over her relatives’ objections.
The Afghan couple went to court, asking judges to undo the adoption they said was deeply flawed from the start. Lower courts in Virginia agreed. But the state’s highest court decided in the Masts’ favor, citing a six-month deadline in state law.
Their Supreme Court appeal was backed by a former U.S. ambassador to Afghanistan as well as groups that support veterans and international adoptees.
The Masts dispute the family’s kinship and argue that reopening the adoption now would be a significant disruption for the girl, who is now 7 and has been living with their family for years.
___
Galofaro reported from Louisville, Kentucky.

title: Hidden meanings behind emojis raise safety concerns for parents
text:
(Aging Untold) — Emojis such as tears of joy, hearts and thumbs-up are used daily. For Jill Story’s three daughters, emojis represent a different language.
“They have a whole language they use that I’m constantly having to figure out,” Story said.
Moms try to crack the code
A group of mothers sat down to see if they could decode common phrases and symbols used by kids.
When asked about “Code9” or “CD9,” the moms said they didn’t know what it meant.
It means: “parents are around.”
“This is going to be really good to know,” one mom said.
The group was also asked about “GNOC.”
The term: “get naked on camera.”
“Oh, dang. Oh!” the moms responded.
Emojis carry secret meanings
The moms were then shown emojis to decode. One mom was asked about the noodles emoji.
“Nudes, send nudes,” she said, explaining she guessed based on the similarity between “noodles” and “nudes.”
The scissors emoji prompted different guesses among the group. One mom, Kathy, guessed it meant to cut clothes off, while Story guessed it referred to cutting. The scissors emoji refers to self-harm.
Expert advice for parents
Aging Untold expert Amy O’Rourke said the use of coded language among kids reflects a pattern seen across generations.
“So I think about all the generations that have gone before us and how we created our own little world that was separate from the one ahead of us because we wanted to have our own thing. The emojis are the same thing,” O’Rourke said.
O’Rourke said these digital codes often lead to real-world consequences. She said parents should ask questions about what the terms mean.
“Ask a lot of questions, get really curious. What does this mean? What should I know? And make it really fun and interesting, not intrusive to the younger person,” O’Rourke said.
Experts say parents should know who their kids follow on social media and consider following them back to learn the latest slang.
“You think your kids, my kids at home, they’re safe, but there’s a whole world in their hands that is not safe,” one mom said.

title: Marine life dramatically declined in Gulf of Mexico in years after BP oil spill, study finds
text:
Marine life dramatically declined in Gulf of Mexico in years after BP oil spill, study finds
In a deep, dark part of the Gulf of Mexico, the number of marine animals plummeted by about 60% in the years following the 2010 Deepwater Horizon explosion, a new study found.
In a crucial part of the Gulf between the light surface and the darkest depths, where the BP-operated well failed and dumped 134 million gallons of oil, the number of fish found dropped by 63.5% from the year after the spill to 2015.
Crustaceans, including shrimp and krill, a key food for whales, went down 62%, and larger animals like squid and octopuses fell 59.7%, according to a study published Monday in the journal PNAS.
And those populations haven't come close to recovering, the study found.
Researchers focused on the ocean's "twilight zone," a vast area above the seafloor, where much of the surface marine life, including dolphins and whales, feast on creatures. Yet little is known about this gigantic ecosystem, and this region of the Gulf had not been studied before the 2010 spill, said study lead author Tracey Sutton, a biological oceanographer at Nova Southeastern University.
A 2011 post-spill exploration cited in the research, which used six sets of nets at different depths and acoustic sonar, gave scientists a good sense of how much sea life was in the area between the surface and 5,000 feet deep (1,500 meters). They returned to the same place with the same equipment three-and-a-half years later and found sea life was between one-third and one-quarter of what it was in 2011.
"We saw this big decline," Sutton said. "The question was then why? So we looked at all of the natural variables we thought could account for it, namely temperature, oxygen supply and food. None of those vary with the decline. The event that did was the oil spill. So we think that's the most likely cause of the decline."
Researchers kept on sampling since 2015, and the low populations remained, with a slight rise in 2022 and 2023 that did not prove statistically significant or lasting, Sutton said.
Sutton's team documented the population declines with three different lines of evidence: what they caught in the nets, what their acoustic sonar found and genetic studies showing the species losing genetic diversity because of inbreeding.
A lot of marine life died instantly after the explosion, which killed 11 workers, and from nearly five months of leaking oil and gas. Those pollutants got stored in the eggs of survivors and subsequent generations of critters got more compromised and weaker, Sutton said.
BP spokesperson Paul Takahashi said the accident "forever changed" the company: "We have made many changes intended to help prevent an event like this from ever happening again."
Both the oil and the dispersants used to clean the spill hurt fish, but in different ways, said study co-author Isabel Romero, a chemical oceanographer at the University of South Carolina. Oil is more toxic and an overall threat, but the dispersant breaks the oil into smaller droplets, increasing the exposure of animals that live in the deeper water column, she said.
Dispersants caused many problems, and new studies show that in future accidents, it would be better to avoid those chemicals and instead add agents that increase oil-munching microbes, said former National Science Foundation Director Rita Colwell, a University of Maryland environmental microbiologist who headed a 10-year, $500 million BP-funded program to study spill effects.
Sutton said his team couldn't prove an exact causal link to the BP oil spill, but by eliminating the other possibilities and looking at the timing, it's logically clear that the spill caused the problem.
The krill population dropped 72%. Lanternfish — odd fish with blue-green lights embedded over their bodies — are a third of what they used to be, Sutton said. The stunning but scary dragonfish — with sharp teeth, light organs and a lure attached to its head — also had big losses, he said.
"These are foundational species," Sutton said. "They're the things most things eat. So it's no wonder that we had wholesale changes across the community."
Scientists learned much about this unexplored area of the Gulf.
"One of our biggest findings from the whole thing is how connected the whole oceanic Gulf is from top to bottom because the animals move up and down," Sutton said. "There are predators at the top that dive deep. Lots of things that are deep that come up at night. So the system is one very large pulsing system, rather than just a layered system like people might have thought beforehand."
Outside scientists were especially bothered by where the spill damaged.
"We know more about space in some ways than we do about the inner ocean. Because we can't see these regions, there is a tendency to assume everything is fine, but here we have a clear result showing that something went very wrong," Scripps Institution of Oceanography marine scientist Kaitlin Frasier said in an email.
Frasier, who wasn't part of the study released Monday, published a post-spill study in 2024 looking at Gulf of Mexico whales and dolphins, finding population drops as high as 83%.
"It's shocking how a single failure in a drilling rig can have this vast and sustained impact over thousands of square kilometers, with little visible recovery over 13 years after the spill," said Dalhousie University marine scientist Boris Worm, who wasn't part of the study. "It is important that we see this, because for the longest time these consequences were completely out of sight and out of mind."
Worm and Colwell said this damage should be kept in mind as the world talks about deep-sea mining and increased oil drilling in deep waters.

title: General Dynamics Bath Iron Works
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
General Dynamics Bath Iron Works is a leader in designing and building U.S. Navy ships. The company also provides maintenance, modernization and lifecycle support services for Navy ships and maintains the most sophisticated marine engineering expertise in the world to support future capabilities. Part of General Dynamics Marine Systems, the ability to design, build and maintain our nation’s most advanced warships is a critical element of the U.S. defense industrial base.
People have been building ships on the Kennebec River for more than 400 years, and maritime construction has dominated the economy of Bath since the 1800s.
General Dynamics Bath Iron Works is now the sole bearer of that legacy, and its impact continues to be felt in the Mid-Coast region and throughout the state of Maine.
Bath Iron Works was the name of a brass and iron foundry established in 1826. Brigadier General Thomas W. Hyde took over the foundry in 1865, following service with the 20th Maine Regiment during the Civil War. Nearly two decades later, he incorporated his diversified marine business interests as Bath Iron Works, Limited in 1884 before expanding into shipbuilding with the acquisition of the Goss Marine Iron Works in 1888. After having several different owners in the 20th century, BIW became a wholly owned subsidiary of General Dynamics in 1995.
Since the completion of Hull No. 1 in 1890, BIW has been awarded more than 430 shipbuilding contracts, including 260 military ships and more than 160 private yachts and commercial vessels.
In 1985, BIW won the competition for detail design and construction of USS Arleigh Burke (DDG 51), the lead ship for the Navy’s class of AEGIS guided missile destroyers, which has become the “Workhorse of the Navy.” Still going strong more than 40 years later, the DDG 51 program has become the longest-running surface combatant shipbuilding program in U.S. Navy history.
A major driver of Maine’s economy, BIW paid $508 million in wages and salaries in 2025, making it one of the state’s largest private-sector employers. Accounting for supplier spending, worker household expenditures and the on-site presence of the Navy’s Supervisor of Shipbuilding, BIW supported more than 15,100 jobs, $921 million in wages and salaries, approximately $1.4 billion in value-added (GDP), and $2.7 billion in total economic output statewide in 2025.
Through a national supplier network spanning 920 organizations across 47 states, BIW’s operations represent a critical node in the U.S. defense industrial base. Between 2021 and 2025, BIW directed approximately $2.9 billion in supplier spending to businesses across the country, supporting jobs and wages in states with major defense, maritime, engineering and manufacturing capabilities.
The key to BIW’s success is its people. The complexity of a DDG 51 requires experts in marine design and engineering as well as skilled tradespeople. BIW partners with the Maine Community College System, the University of Maine and Maine Maritime Academy to provide basic and advanced training for people who want to embark on a shipbuilding career, then provides on-site shipbuilder-specific training to new employees. Its acclaimed apprenticeship program allows employees to earn while they learn, leading to an associate’s degree, and the company offers tuition reimbursement for degrees and certifications related to shipbuilding and business, a professional development program for early-career individuals looking for a future in management, and paid internships that include high-value experience doing meaningful work.
At BIW, we strive to be an exceptional maritime company that safely provides shipbuilding, component manufacturing and specialized services with a world-class team and facilities. Our mission is to design, build and support the highest-quality surface combatants for the United States.

title: National Guard member is shot while breaking up a fight in Washington, suspect is hit in return fire
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — A National Guard member was shot and injured while trying to break up a fight in the nation’s capital, and the person suspected of firing the gun also was shot in an exchange with guard members, police said Monday.
The shooting happened at about 11:10 p.m. Sunday as seven or eight guard members in a parked van were monitoring the fight on a sidewalk in southeast Washington, in the Eastern Market neighborhood, said Jeffery Carroll, interim chief of the Metropolitan Police Department of Washington.
“They exited their vehicle to try to intervene to try to stop the fight from occurring when they heard gunshots,” Carroll told reporters. “An individual that had been involved in the fight had pulled out a firearm and began shooting.”
The person ran into an alley, Carroll said, and guard members immediately told the person to drop the gun.
“The individual then pointed the weapon toward National Guard members, who returned fire,” Carroll said.
He said one guard member was struck in the leg and the suspect was shot in the abdomen. Both were taken to hospitals for treatment for non-life-threatening injuries, he said.
Three guard members discharged their guns in the encounter, Carroll said. He said the suspect was arrested.
President Donald Trump deployed the guard to Washington in August 2025 as part of what he said was a crime-fighting mission. The force, which rose to a peak of about 5,000 troops over the summer, has supported arrest operations, patrolled city streets and neighborhoods and participated in cleanup efforts.
Trump’s Republican administration says the deployment has contributed to a decrease in crime in the city, where crime was already on the decline before the guard arrived. Officials, activists and residents in the overwhelmingly Democratic city say the deployment is a waste of taxpayer money and has normalized the militarization of a major American city.
The police department is investigating the Sunday night shooting. Carroll said there were no further threats to the community and asked for anyone with information on the shooting to contact police.

title: Lyle H. Dever | Obituaries
text:
Lyle H. Dever, LCDR, USCG, Ret., 94, died on Oct. 12, 2026, in a Dedham healthcare facility. He was born Oct. 1, 1932, on the family farm in the Ozark Mountains near Ava, Mo., the son of Joseph L. and L. Hattie (Givans) Dever.
He graduated from Ava High School in the class of 1950 and attended Southwest Missouri State University prior to his enlistment in the U.S. Coast Gard during the Korean War. Following his first enlistment he opted to make the Coast Guard a career and served 25 years through all the enlisted ranks and Warrant Officer Ranks and was promoted to Commission Status in 1969 and retired as a Lt. Commander in 1977.

title: What Trump has done to health
text:
To the Editor:
The Trump administration is not making America healthy again. The mission statement of the National Institutes of Health includes: “NIH’s mission is to … enhance health, lengthen life, and reduce illness and disability.” As noted by the Brennan Center, a nonpartisan law and policy organization, the Trump Administration froze or cut $2.3 billion in previously approved NIH grants in 2025.These cuts not only disrupted research progress but also had serious consequences for patients, as trials of potential new medical treatments were delayed or halted. The effects of these cuts will be felt for decades — advances in biomedical research rely on consistent funding over the years, and interruptions to funding now will result in fewer new drugs in the future. These disruptions also threaten to shrink the scientific workforce across the country, including Maine.

title: Apu Returned to ‘The Simpsons,’ Voiced By a New Actor
text:
Apu Returned to ‘The Simpsons’ With a New Voice Actor
On tonight’s new episode of The Simpsons — the 812th episode of the show to date, if you can believe it — one of the oldest characters on the series made their first major appearance in almost a decade.
That would be Apu Nahasapeemapetilon, the famed (and later notorious) manager of the Kwik-E-Mart. Originally voiced by Hank Azaria, Apu — and Azaria’s voice work as the character — became the subject of controversy and even an entire documentary by comedian Hari Kondabolu called The Problem With Apu, because of his embodiment of certain South Asian stereotypes (to say nothing of his being performed by a white actor).
Azaria stopped performing the character on the show not long after the documentary was released, and by 2020 The Simpsons announced it would stop its long-standing practice of having non-white characters voiced by white actors. Soon Harry Shearer was replaced as the voice of Dr. Hibbert and Azaria was replaced as the voice of Homer’s buddy Carl, two name just two of the more notable examples.
But Apu never got a new voice — he was essentially retired from all but background cameos from 2017 to 2026, when Apu finally returned as a character in the episode “The Revengening.” Apu is now performed by actor Sunil Malhotra.
You can hear a little of Malhotra’s work as Apu in the clip below. In the episode, a spoof of slasher movies, a mysterious figure in a Halloween costume keeps getting killed by residents of Springfield. He’s eventually revealed to be none other than Apu.
READ MORE: Every Simpsons Chalkboard Gag Ranked From Worst to Best
Malhotra said in an interview that his feelings about playing the character were somewhat complicated...
When my agent called me about a Simpsons audition, I knew exactly what role it was for, and the idea actually made my stomach sink ... But admittedly, part of me was also curious. It had been eight years since Apu had spoken on the show, and it got me thinking. Did the writers room look different now? Could they bring him back in a way that acknowledged and apologized for past mistakes?
He added that as part of agreeing to the role he met with The Simpsons producers to discuss his concerns. The result, he said, was a “deeply collaborative experience” in bringing Apu back to Springfield.
New episodes of The Simpsons continue to air, as they have since time immemorial, on Sunday nights on Fox. The show is already renewed for several more seasons beyond the current one, so the new Apu could get plenty more air time in the years ahead. In fact, The Simpsons executive producer Matt Selman told Variety “We’re excited by what Sunil has already brought to the role, and look forward to seeing more of Apu in the future.”

title: Reelect Michael Morris as Waterville mayor
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
As a resident and councilman of Waterville, I am proud to voice my strong support for Michael Morris in his upcoming reelection for mayor.
Our community needs a leader who listens to everyday people, who listens to our business owners and knows how to bridge those connections to build a more cohesive Waterville. He has worked hard to bring businesses and jobs to our city, and many of the businesses that have recently opened their doors are in part due to his willingness to meet them at the table and convince them that Waterville is the best place to be. His dedication and integrity make him the right choice to represent our values and continue to help make Waterville the best version of itself.
In my experience, Mayor Morris delivers meaningful results for Waterville. He has consistently demonstrated a deep commitment to the people of our city. Whether helping residents during the winter when they may be without heat or responding when part of our community faces a shared challenge, he is ready to step up, bring people together and help find solutions.
I encourage my neighbors and fellow citizens to join me in supporting Michael Morris for mayor on Election Day.
Spencer Krigbaum
Waterville

title: Untangling the massive outside money web behind Susan Collins
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Politics
Our political journalists are based in the Maine State House and have deep source networks across the partisan spectrum in communities all over the state. Their coverage aims to cut through major debates and probe how officials make decisions. Read more Politics coverage here.
An intertwined Republican network of super PACs and nonprofits has booked about $126 million in ads to reelect U.S. Sen. Susan Collins, with much of it traced to billionaires and donors who will never be named.
That is nearly all of the ad time booked by Republican outside groups in the five-term senator’s toss-up race against former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson, according to AdImpact data counting time aired and reserved through year’s end.
The dizzying network is throwing huge sums at a seat that could decide control of the U.S. Senate. Campaign finance reports filed Thursday showed how tightly the groups behind Collins are bound together. Billionaires and donor-shielding nonprofits fund several of them at once. Some groups seem to exist mostly to pass money to others.
Both parties have used these tactics since the U.S. Supreme Court struck down limits on independent spending in 2010. Collins was targeted early in her 2020 campaign by a Democratic dark-money operation and was heavily outspent. This time, Republicans rallied around her early, amid the chaos after Democratic nominee Graham Platner dropped out in July following a rape allegation he denied.
The Senate Leadership Fund, the super PAC tied to Senate Republican leaders, began a scorched-earth series of ads against Jackson over the weekend, including one calling him “a crook and a creep.” Along with an offshoot, SLF is the biggest outside spender in the race, having booked nearly $50 million in Maine ads.
Its top donor is One Nation, a nonprofit sister group that doesn’t reveal its funders. One Nation gave the fund $132.9 million through September and has booked nearly $35 million in its own pro-Collins ads. Billionaires supply much of the rest, led by Miriam Adelson and Blackstone CEO Stephen Schwarzman. Elon Musk gave $10 million.
Collins’ closest ties to the network run through Pine Tree Results PAC, which has booked $29.1 million in ads. It is run by Scott Reed, a Republican operative and friend of Collins’ husband, Tom Daffron, who was paid as a consultant by Reed’s lobbying firm last year. Pine Tree and her campaign also share limited fundraising functions, something federal regulators allow.
Reed ran a different super PAC backing Collins in 2020 that took an illegal $150,000 donation from a defense contractor, the focus of a ProPublica report last month. She denies wrongdoing and has defended Reed’s character.
Pine Tree’s donors also include Schwarzman, Ken Griffin and two nonprofits that don’t disclose their donors: Stronger America and the Lexington Fund, part of a network linked to conservative legal activist Leonard Leo. Stronger America has booked nearly $12 million in Maine ads. Collins attended a July dinner the group hosted in Washington, The New York Times reported.
At Thursday’s final debate in Bangor, Collins said dark money groups shouldn’t exist. Asked Sunday about the dinner and Collins’ ties to Pine Tree, campaign spokesperson Blake Kernen did not address either. She noted that Collins has been a major target of dark money and backs “balanced reforms” protecting speech rights.
“But our campaign is unwilling to continue to be subjected to lies paid for by dark money without fighting back,” Kernen said.
Smaller groups pass money among themselves. Nearly all of the money raised by the Eighteen Fifty-Four Fund, which sent $1 million to another pro-Collins group, came from Ardleigh Impact Corp. and another Delaware nonprofit with the same treasurer, Staci Goede. Groups that list her as treasurer have also given millions to SLF and Pine Tree.
Goede and Les Williamson, treasurer of the Eighteen Fifty-Four Fund, did not respond to questions about who is behind the groups.
The Campaign Legal Center alleged in a 2024 FEC complaint that Ardleigh was used to hide the true sources of money given to super PACs. The complaint is still pending before a Federal Election Commission that lacks enough commissioners to fully operate, noted Saurav Ghosh, the group’s director of federal campaign finance reform.
Dark money is also flowing through the Democratic side. WinSenate, a super PAC aligned with the party’s Senate campaign arm, has booked $38.6 million in Maine. It ran one of the most inflammatory ads of the cycle, which misleadingly tied Collins to Jeffrey Epstein. Its funder, Senate Majority PAC, got about a third of its money through June from Majority Forward, a nonprofit that doesn’t disclose donors, according to Issue One.
Campaign finance has been a sticking point between the candidates. When Collins noted at Tuesday’s debate that Jackson had not yet filed his first fundraising report, he promised to produce it the next morning, saying there were “no billionaires funding me.”
He filed it minutes before Thursday’s debate. Seven billionaires had given his campaign a combined $24,500, according to a BDN review of the report and Forbes billionaire lists. Nearly 100 billionaires and spouses gave $9.8 million to Collins’ campaign and other groups working on her behalf from January 2025 through May, The Maine Monitor found.
On Thursday, Collins pressed Jackson over his joint ads with Senate Democrats’ campaign arm, which takes money from billionaires and corporate PACs that he and many Democrats rejects. Jackson conceded he has billionaire support but said he owes them nothing. His campaign said he would push to require disclosure of dark money “regardless of which party benefits.”
“Billionaires have bought Congress, and everyday people can’t afford to buy them back,” Jackson said at Thursday’s debate.

title: Hearts of Pine midfielder Mikey Lopez announces retirement
text:
Hearts of Pine midfielder Mikey Lopez announced on Instagram that Portland’s season finale Saturday will be the final game of his 14-year career.
Lopez, 33, has played 47 games in two seasons with the Hearts of Pine, including 31 last season. He was named the USL League One Comeback Player of the Year in 2025 after Achilles surgery wiped out his 2024 season.
The Hearts of Pine’s captain has played 16 games this season with eight starts.
“I think Saturday will close the circle on my career,” Lopez said in a video posted to Instagram. “Being able to play in front of my family, a sold-out crowd at Fitzpatrick Stadium and playing for (Hearts of Pine coach) Bobby (Murphy) one last time I think is the perfect way to end my career.”
Lopez played for Murphy at a Texas development academy in grades 8-12. He played at the University of North Carolina and was a first-round pick in the 2011 MLS SuperDraft by Sporting Kansas City. He spent three seasons in Kansas City, followed by two with New York City FC. He also played seven seasons in USL Championship, the last six with Birmingham, where he was the franchise’s first captain.
Portland will host Charlotte Independence at 5 p.m. Saturday at Fitzpatrick Stadium. The Hearts of Pine, who reached the USL League One semifinals in their first season, are 7-14-10 and have failed to qualify for the playoffs in their second campaign.

title: Firefighter injured battling fire that heavily damaged home in China, Maine
text:
Firefighter injured battling fire that heavily damaged home in China, Maine
Three horses escaped during the fire but were recovered, according to the State Fire Marshal's Office
Firefighter injured battling fire that heavily damaged home in China, Maine
Three horses escaped during the fire but were recovered, according to the State Fire Marshal's Office
A firefighter was injured while fighting a fire that caused significant damage to a home in China on Sunday night, according to the Maine State Fire Marshal's Office.
Firefighters responded to a home at 19 41st Fire Road around 11:13 p.m. Sunday and encountered heavy flames with a garage or workshop fully involved adjacent to the two-story home.
Officials say the garage was nearly destroyed, and flames spread to the residence, ultimately damaging walls, windows and portions of the upper level.
During the firefight, an Albion firefighter suffered a leg injury involving a fire department vehicle. The firefighter was taken to a local hospital for treatment.
Investigators say the fire may have originated in the garage. A wood stove operating inside the garage is being considered as a possible ignition source, but officials say electrical equipment and e-bikes stored inside have not been ruled out.
The exact cause remains under investigation.
During the fire, three horses escaped from an enclosure on the property, and all three were safely located and returned several hours later.
The China Fire Department was assisted by Albion, Winslow, Waterville, Sidney, Palermo and Windsor fire departments.
The Fire Marshal's Office reminded residents to ensure that wood stoves and heating appliances are properly installed as heating season begins.

title: What to know about Rangeley’s four ordinance votes on Nov. 3
text:
Residents in Rangeley will decide on updates to the town lighting, signs and administrative ordinances on Nov. 3.
Before you head to the town office to vote on Election Day, make sure you know the details on the four ordinance updates and what approval would mean for the town.
Lighting code
Voting “yes” to the lighting ordinance would approve restrictions on outdoor lights to fall in line with Dark Sky community standards. Outdoor lighting would be required to be shielded by an overhang. Searchlights and lasers would be prohibited.
Sign code
The sign ordinance updates seek to preserve the dark skies as well. A “yes” vote would mean restricting internally lit blinking signs. Under the new code, an LED message board could only change once every five minutes. Existing message boards would be permitted to stay in use until they break.
Both the sign and lighting updates need to pass in order for the town to meet the criteria needed to become a Dark Sky community.
Transfer station code
A “yes” vote on the transfer station code would update licensing requirements for commercial waste haulers.
Administrative code
A “yes” vote for the administrative code would change the name of the planning department to the code enforcement, community development and planning department. It would also update language in the code.

title: US citizen injured during California ICE incident, officials say
text:
US citizen injured during California ICE incident, officials say
Video above may be disturbing. Viewer discretion advised.
A former Long Beach city employee was injured during an incident involving Immigration and Customs Enforcement on Saturday, officials said, with an unmarked SUV driving the wrong way down a one-way street before the scene escalated, according to surveillance footage and witnesses.
Ricardo Gonzalez was found by Long Beach police after he and other community members called 911 to report concerns about unmarked vehicles, Long Beach Mayor Rex Richardson said Sunday.
Surveillance video obtained by KTLA shows an unmarked SUV driving the wrong way down a one-way street as a man on an e-bike makes a turn into the intersection down the same street.
The camera angle does not show whether the e-bike and SUV collide, but the footage shows the SUV coming to a quick stop and several agents exiting the car. Two other witnesses also told CNN they saw the SUV driving the wrong way.
A verified GoFundMe created by Gonzalez’s daughter, Leslie Gonzalez, said he was injured while riding his e-bike, and video from the incident shows the e-bike next to Gonzalez as he is held down by a federal agent on the street.
ICE personnel had requested emergency assistance from the Long Beach Police Department in response to vehicle vandalism and a person in need of medical aid, Long Beach police said in a statement Saturday.
When local officers arrived, they found a man handcuffed and bleeding while being detained by ICE, police said, adding a “large group disturbance” involving the agents was taking place.
“(Gonzalez) called 911 when he saw a circumstance escalating, and so he called and asked for assistance,” Richardson said. “When the police arrived, we know that he was detained. He was on a curb. He was injured.”
CNN has reached out to the Department of Homeland Security, the city of Long Beach and Long Beach police for more information.
Videos shared by a witness, Sherman Austin, showed Gonzalez handcuffed and lying on the ground while being held down by an agent wearing a “Police ICE” vest. In one video, the man can be heard yelling repeatedly, “Help me, my arm is broken” and “Call a paramedic.”
Austin told CNN that he saw Gonzalez being struck by the unmarked vehicle and afterwards federal agents stepped out, “Tasered him, broke his arm and pinned him to the ground.” He began recording the video as more agents arrived and restrained Gonzalez as he screamed in pain and pleaded for help.
Long Beach police officers took Gonzalez to a nearby fire station, where his handcuffs were removed, police said. Fire department personnel then took him to a hospital for medical attention. Richardson declined to comment on Gonzalez’s current condition, citing his privacy.
Meanwhile, officers remained at the scene in an attempt to de-escalate the situation, police said. When Long Beach police left the scene, some ICE agents followed officers to the station’s parking lot, where the federal agents were asked to leave and told they could contact the department to file a vandalism report.
Incident leaves more questions than answers, mayor says
Gonzalez is receiving treatment for his injuries, his daughter said. She created the GoFundMe to pay his medical bills.
“My Dad is one of the hardest working men out there,” she wrote on the GoFundMe. “Because of him I have a roof over my head and I have all the opportunities around me. Our family is everything because of him.”
Richardson, who said he was “outraged” over the incident, spoke with Gonzalez, who told him he is a U.S. citizen, and his family following the incident.
The incident is among several involving ICE agents that have left people injured, including U.S. citizens, against the backdrop of the Trump administration’s sweeping immigration crackdown.
Earlier this month, a man in Texas was hospitalized with both of his legs broken after he was struck by an ICE vehicle near Houston. Days before, federal immigration agents in New York City shot and injured a driver while his 5-year-old child was in the back seat during a targeted enforcement operation.
In September, an ICE agent shot a Venezuelan man in the back in Austin, Texas, while he was delivering orders for DoorDash.
U.S. Rep. Robert Garcia, a Democrat from California, said in a post on X: “ICE agents brutally attacked and broke the arm of a North Long Beach resident and U.S. citizen,” calling the videos “horrific.”
Long Beach’s mayor said he attempted to contact ICE through its complaint hotline, but has yet to speak with someone at the agency.
What would have been a safe weekend in North Long Beach “turned into a violent incident with no transparency or accountability, and a lot more questions than answers,” Richardson said.

title: The Key to Understanding ‘You Can See Everything’ Is a Single Word
text:
The Brilliance of ‘You Can See Everything’ All Comes Down to a Single Word
The following post contains SPOILERS for You Can See Everything. It really is best to go into the film knowing nothing about it. You don’t want to know everything before you see You Can See Everything.
The title of Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s You Can See Everything is taken from a text message sent to Fielder by one of the documentary’s subjects: Disgraced entrepreneur, former billionaire, and current inmate of the Federal Prison Camp in Bryan, Texas Elizabeth Holmes. In the days prior to Holmes’ incarceration, she and her partner, Billy Evans, invited Fielder and Oppenheim to document every aspect of their lives.
Fielder is understandably skeptical of Holmes, who was convicted of multiple counts of fraud as a result of her actions as the founder of Theranos, which claimed to have created a groundbreaking device that could perform countless tests on a single drop of blood. Holmes continues to insist she is innocent, and tells Fielder she has nothing to hide. She invites him to live in her guest house for the duration of the documentary. He remains wary. While she’s walking on the beach with Evans and their children, she texts Fielder “You can totally see everything.”
Fielder and Oppenheim removed the ‘totally’ to create the name of their documentary, which is already one of the most-discussed films of 2026. The title carries layers of meaning; among other things, it’s a very dry joke about the fact that Fielder and Oppenheim’s all-access approach yields footage that includes full frontal nudity of Evans while he’s in the shower. More importantly, Holmes’ text to Fielder contains the single most important word in the entire film, the one that’s central to understanding her and this strange and fascinating movie: Can.
READ MORE: Hollywood, Please Bring Back Making-Of Documentaries
That becomes clear when Holmes digs out the remains of the notorious Edison, Theranos’ all-in-one blood testing device, and tries to explain to Fielder why she is not guilty of defrauding investors and deceiving the public. Holmes’ defense largely comes down to a matter of semantics. She said that the Edison “can” perform all manner of blood tests. “Can” — as in the device was programmable to do all kinds of test. Was it capable of performing all the tests it could theoretically do? No. It was not capable — yet. But it could be capable, eventually, with further advancements in chemistry and technology.
It seems entirely reasonable for someone who heard the sentence “This device can perform many different blood tests” to assume that it works — not that it is technically capable with more time and development. Viewers (and Theranos investors) might see Holmes’ argument as an evasion; an attempt to locate a legal loophole in her sworn testimony akin to when Bill Clinton told a grand jury “it depends on what the meaning of the word is is” when trying to claim he did not have “sexual relations” with Monica Lewinsky.
But Fielder’s footage of Holmes — in which she permits him to totally see everything about her life — invites at least the possibility that Holmes’ brain works so differently than other people that maybe she really did believe that these seemingly very false statements were, from her perspective, accurate. In one of You Can See Everything’s most spellbinding scenes, Fielder shows Holmes Abbott and Costello’s famous “Who’s on First?” comedy routine. Holmes doesn’t laugh.
Afterwards, Fielder asks Holmes to explain why the routine is funny. She can’t. (Or maybe she would say she can, she’s just not capable of explaining at this exact moment why it is funny.) She claims not to comprehend the confusion at the heart of the joke. She can’t even tell Fielder the name of the guy on first base. (“I didn’t catch it,” she says.) If someone could miss the point of “Who’s on First?” this badly, could they also miscommunicate their intentions with a medical device so badly they wound up in prison for 11 years?
It’s a stretch — but Fielder’s film at least leaves open the possibility that’s what transpired. And that possibility is what You Can See Everything is all about. After Holmes surrenders to authorities in Texas, them film resumes two years later, with Fielder still lost in a fog of uncertainty about his elusive subject. He begins following Evans again, and discovers he’s trying to resurrect the Edison in her absence.
He’s also aligned himself with some seemingly shady people, and frequently tweets from Holmes’ verified X account without her knowledge, and in ways that sound nothing like her. When Fielder questions Evans’ decisions, he insists he knows Holmes well enough to make decisions on her behalf — and anyway he has full power of attorney to do whatever he wants in Holmes’ name.
Holmes’ other defense during her trial was that she was deceived and manipulated herself by Theranos’ president Sunny Balwani, who was also her romantic partner at the time. (She also alleged that he sexually abused her, something Balwani denied.) If Holmes could be manipulated by one powerful man, is it possible that same cycle is repeating itself all over again? Fielder tries to maneuver around Evans to speak directly to Holmes in prison — not an easy task, given Evans’ protective attitude towards her, and the strict rules governing interactions with federal prisoners.
Fielder also enlists actress Amanda Seyfried to recreate her Emmy Award-winning performance as Holmes from the Hulu series The Dropout in new reenactments for his film; Seyfried plays Holmes in scenes between her and Fielder where cameras are not able to be present. (Seyfrield also plays herself reacting to Holmes’ statements about her case — and about Seyfried’s portrayal of her — in meta scenes interspersed with the reenactments.) Fielder wants a smoking gun that will prove one way or another whether Holmes is a master manipulator or a victim of manipulative men. He finds only vapor, and even more enigmatic statements from Holmes. (When Seyfried joins Fielder on a visit to Evans, and Holmes from prison, Seyfried asks her if she knew that she’d be there when she called. Her enigmatic response is something along the lines of “I'm not sure if I knew.”)
The ultimate futility of Fielder’s quest reinforces the brilliance of the title, along with the central thesis of You Can See Everything. The movie is about how even when a documentarian can see everything, even when their subject claims to offer complete transparency, the filmmakers are still not capable of getting to the absolute truth of anything — if such a thing exists at all.
