title: China house fire destroys garage, barn; 3 donkeys escape
text:
A house fire in China late Sunday night destroyed a garage and barn, and left a firefighter with a foot injury after a vehicle ran over it. Three donkeys escaped the property.
The fire damaged a house on 41st Fire Road, destroying an attached garage and a barn. Flames also spread to the residence, causing partial damage, according to a news release from Chief Joel Nelson, China Village Volunteer Fire Department. While the garage and barn were a total loss, some belongings in a daylight basement were salvageable, Nelson said.
The homeowner had minor injuries and was not hospitalized, while one firefighter suffered a foot injury after a fire apparatus ran over their foot, Nelson wrote. The firefighter was taken to the hospital, treated and released.
The homeowners planned to search for the escaped donkeys Monday morning, Nelson wrote.
A woodstove in the garage was a potential ignition source, but electrical equipment stored in the garage could not be ruled out, the Office of State Fire Marshal said in a news release Monday evening. The official cause remains under investigation.
China’s volunteer firefighters responded to the scene, assisted by departments from Albion, Winslow, Waterville, Sidney, Windsor, Vassalboro and Palermo. South China Fire, Weeks Mills Fire and China Rescue also responded at the scene, alongside China Public Works, the Office of State Fire Marshal, the Maine State Police and the Maine Forest Service.
Staff Writer Drew Johnson contributed to this story.

title: Understanding ALICE: The Workforce You Can’t Afford to Overlook
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Every day, Maine business leaders make decisions that shape hiring, compensation, benefits, and growth. Yet one segment of the workforce, essential to nearly every industry, is often misunderstood.
That workforce is ALICE.
ALICE stands for Asset Limited, Income Constrained, Employed. These are individuals who work, sometimes in multiple jobs, yet still struggle to afford basic necessities such as housing, child care, transportation, food, and healthcare.
According to research from United Way’s ALICE initiative, 40% of Maine households live below the ALICE Threshold, meaning they struggle to consistently afford the basic cost of living.
They include educators, retail associates, hospitality workers, healthcare support staff, manufacturing workers, and administrative professionals whose incomes often fall short of the cost of living in Maine.
The ALICE Household Survival Budget reflects the actual local cost of essentials such as housing, child care, transportation, and healthcare. For many Maine households, full-time employment still does not produce enough income to cover those expenses.
For example, the ALICE Household Survival Budget estimates that a Maine family of four with an infant and a preschooler needs approximately $90,636 annually to cover only the essentials, nearly three times the federal poverty level used to determine eligibility for many assistance programs.
For employers, this isn’t simply a social issue. It is a workforce issue. When employees face ongoing financial strain, businesses often experience higher turnover, increased absenteeism, and reduced engagement. Recruitment and retention challenges are often influenced by the rising cost of living, which is outpacing what many working households can afford. For example, home prices in Maine have nearly doubled since 2018, contributing to housing costs that have outpaced many household budgets.
For employers already struggling to attract talent, rising housing, child care, and transportation costs can undermine recruitment and retention efforts despite significant hiring investments.
Understanding ALICE helps employers evaluate workforce strategies and the economic pressures influencing employee performance and retention.
Employer Spotlight: Allagash Brewing Company
When employee feedback revealed that child care costs were creating financial stress for working families, Allagash Brewing Company responded with a $750 annual child care stipend per child. The stipend is contributed tax-free through employees’ dependent care flexible spending accounts, increasing its value for families while reducing payroll tax costs for the company. The company recognized that child care challenges can affect employees’ ability to manage work and family responsibilities, making it an important workforce consideration.
Rather than assuming what employees needed most, Allagash started by listening. Employee feedback helped identify child care as a serious pressure point, allowing the company to focus resources on a benefit that addressed a real and immediate need. Using an existing tax-advantaged benefit allowed employees to receive more value than a traditional bonus while also reducing payroll taxes.
Lesson Learned: Effective workforce solutions do not always require sweeping changes. By listening to employees and addressing specific barriers, employers can create targeted benefits that support working families, strengthen workplace culture, and improve employee engagement.
As Allagash’s experience demonstrates:
“We have found that benefits and programs we originally put into effect to help lower-wage earners actually help with retention for everyone at the company, and it has definitely made a difference in our culture.”
— Celine Frueh, Allagash Brewing Company
As Maine employers navigate workforce shortages and changing employee expectations, understanding ALICE provides an important lens for decision-making.
Through this series, United Way will explore ALICE’s impact on Maine’s workforce, highlight employer-led solutions, and share practical strategies businesses can use to strengthen workforce stability.
For Maine’s business community, understanding ALICE is more than an exercise in awareness. It’s a critical step toward building a resilient workforce, a stronger economy, and a thriving future for Maine.

title: Monday Five and Five: Tournament Time Is Almost Here
text:
Monday Five and Five: Big Performances and Tournament Time
We’ve reached that point of the fall season where everything starts moving pretty quickly.
There are only a few regular-season soccer games left, the tournament picture is almost set, and our cross country teams are getting ready for regional championship weekend.
Before we get there, though, there were plenty of performances from the past week worth another look.
Here are my five from last week, followed by five things I’ll be keeping an eye on this week.
Five From Last Week
5. Drew Lamoreau Scores Four for Easton
Drew Lamoreau had himself an afternoon Saturday.
Lamoreau scored four times as Easton picked up a 7-1 win over Southern Aroostook. Mason Pelletier added two goals, Aaden Tibbetts scored once and Josiah Ellis finished with two assists.
Four goals in one game is more than enough to earn a spot in this week’s Five and Five.
4. Fort Kent Gets It Done in Overtime
Fort Kent and Madawaska needed a little extra time Thursday before the Warriors came away with a 2-1 overtime win.
Madawaska has been one of the strongest teams in Class D North throughout the fall, making this a particularly good late-season win for Fort Kent.
With tournament soccer right around the corner, it was also the kind of game both teams should benefit from having played.
3. Two Hat Tricks and an Overtime Winner
If you like offense and close soccer games, Van Buren and Ashland gave us a good one.
Emily Lapierre scored three times for Van Buren, including the game-winner just 2:35 into overtime, as the Lady Crusaders pulled out a 4-3 victory.
Ashland’s Sadie Trams matched her with a hat trick of her own.
Seven goals, two hat tricks and overtime. That one pretty much had everything.
2. Ava Ezell Passes 150 Career Goals
Another week, another major milestone for Houlton’s Ava Ezell.
Ezell scored five goals and added three assists in Houlton’s 9-1 win over Schenck/Stearns, pushing her past 150 career goals.
Five goals and three assists would have been a huge afternoon by itself. Adding another career milestone makes it an easy choice for this week’s countdown.
1. Conor Schmidt Keeps Scoring
At this point, Conor Schmidt has become a regular part of the conversation.
The Katahdin standout scored five goals in a 6-1 win over Southern Aroostook, then scored both goals in a 2-0 victory over Wisdom.
Gage Phillips deserves some attention from that Wisdom game as well, finishing with 18 saves in the shutout.
For Schmidt, that’s seven more goals in two games after the huge numbers he put up the week before.
That earns him the No. 1 spot this week.
Five to Watch This Week
5. The Last Few Regular-Season Soccer Games
We’ve finally reached the end of the regular season.
There are still some important County matchups on the schedule Monday through Wednesday, and at this point every goal and every result can have an effect on where teams land when tournament play begins.
Fort Fairfield and Madawaska, Southern Aroostook and Central Aroostook, Van Buren and Easton, Ashland and Schenck/Stearns, and Presque Isle and Fort Kent are among the matchups worth following as teams put the finishing touches on their regular seasons.
4. Van Buren and Katahdin Meet Again
Here’s another game that could be interesting heading into tournament time.
Van Buren and Katahdin meet Monday on the boys side, with both teams looking to finish strong.
Van Buren has spent the season hanging around the middle of the North 8-Person tournament picture, while Katahdin has put together an 11-win season despite sitting lower in the standings than that record might suggest.
And with Schmidt scoring the way he has lately, Katahdin certainly isn’t a team anyone will want to overlook.
3. Fort Fairfield and Madawaska Close Things Out
Fort Fairfield and Madawaska meet Monday in what should be another good Class D doubleheader.
Both programs have been part of the tournament conversation throughout the season, and this gives them one more good test before everything becomes win-or-go-home.
At this point in October, that makes games like this worth paying attention to.
2. The Soccer Brackets Are Almost Here
This might be what I’m looking forward to most once the final whistles blow Wednesday.
We’ve spent the entire fall watching teams move up and down the standings, and now we’re about to find out where everyone actually lands.
Seeds, prelim matchups and possible tournament paths should all become much clearer this week.
That also means we’re getting very close to the part of the season where one goal, one save or one overtime winner can keep a season alive.
1. County Runners Head to the North Regionals
Soccer might be winding down, but cross country is moving right into championship season.
County runners head to Belfast Saturday for the North Regional Championships after another big showing at the PVC Championships.
Caribou’s boys, Presque Isle’s girls and Houlton/GHCA’s boys all head into the weekend after winning PVC team championships.
Pierce Gorneault and Emma Graves also arrive after earning individual PVC titles for Caribou.
Saturday is the next big test, with spots at the state championships on the line.
Here We Go
This is one of my favorite parts of the fall season.
The regular season is almost behind us, the brackets are coming, and championship meets are here.
We’ll have plenty to follow over the next several days as teams and athletes from across The County start chasing postseason hardware.

title: Wardens, police seek information about Maine man missing for more than two months
text:
Wardens, police seek information about Maine man missing for more than two months
The Maine Warden Service and Oxford County Sheriff's Office are looking for a man who hasn't been seen in more than two months.
John Larson, 34, of Waterford, walked away from George Allen Acres in Waterford at about 4 p.m. on Aug. 3 and was last seen at about 4:30 p.m. that day sitting next to the road near the intersection of Just Right Acres and Route 118 in Waterford.
That is along the Crooked River and not far from the intersection of Routes 118 and 37 in East Waterford.
Wardens say it is believed that Larson was wearing a dark-colored T-shirt and shorts at the time.
Anyone who has seen Larson since Aug. 3 or knows where he might be should call the Augusta Department of Public Safety Communication Center at 207-624-7076 or the Oxford County Sheriff’s Office at 207-743-9554.

title: Supreme Court rejects effort to revive Khalid Sheikh Mohammed plea deal
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Supreme Court on Monday rejected an effort to revive a plea deal for Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, the accused mastermind of the attacks on Sept. 11, 2001.
The agreement would have spared Mohammed the risk of execution in exchange for his guilty plea and a sentence of life in prison without parole.
Mohammed is accused of developing and directing the plot to crash hijacked airliners into the World Trade Center and the Pentagon 25 years ago. Another of the hijacked planes crashed into a field in Pennsylvania.
The plea agreement was approved by military prosecutors and the Pentagon’s senior official for Guantanamo Bay, Cuba, before then-Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin stepped in.
Austin threw out the deal in 2024, saying a decision on the death penalty in an attack as grave as Sept. 11 should only be made by the defense secretary.
Relatives of the Sept. 11 victims were split on the agreements for Mohammed and two co-defendants. Some said a trial is the best path to justice, while others saw it as the best hope for bringing the long, painful case to a conclusion.
Defense attorneys had argued that Austin, who served under President Joe Biden, acted too late. But a divided appeals court panel found Austin acted within his authority.
A trial date has been set for 2028.

title: Dog dies after man allegedly attacks it with machete, tries to strike woman
text:
BAYOU L’OURSE, La. (WAFB/Gray News) - A dog has died after a man allegedly attacked the animal with a machete during a domestic disturbance in Louisiana, during which he also tried to strike a woman, authorities said.
Assumption Parish Sheriff Leland Falcon said deputies arrested 29-year-old Kevin Lightell of Bayou L’Ourse following the incident Saturday, Oct. 17.
The woman called authorities and reported that Lightell was armed with a machete and had attacked her dog. Deputies detained Lightell when they arrived and found the dog had severe injuries.
According to the sheriff’s office, the woman told investigators she was asleep in her bedroom when she woke up to find Lightell standing over her with a machete.
She said Lightell attempted to strike her with the weapon as she fled the bedroom.
Lightell then allegedly attacked her dog with the machete. The dog died Sunday evening, Oct. 18.
Lightell was arrested and booked into the Assumption Parish Detention Center on the following charges:
- Aggravated cruelty to animals
- Domestic abuse aggravated assault
- Simple escape
Lightell remains in custody pending a bond hearing, according to the sheriff’s office.

Police: Car hits Australian lawmaker, critically injuring her; driver arrested
text:
Police: Car hits Australian lawmaker, critically injuring her; driver arrested
A car hit an Australian federal independent lawmaker on Monday, critically injuring her in a potentially deliberate act, police said. The driver was arrested.
Helen Haines, 65, was struck by a Toyota Land Cruiser SUV outside her electoral district office in the city of Wangaratta in Victoria state, a police statement said.
Police did not identify the victim, in accordance with privacy policy, but Haines’ family confirmed her identity in a media statement.
The 43-year-old driver was arrested at the scene by a passerby. He will be interviewed in relation to the incident, police said.
“A knife was located by police and seized from inside the Toyota,” police said.
“At this stage, police are investigating as to whether this was an intentional act,” police added.
Haines, who was first elected to the Parliament in 2019, was taken to a hospital with critical injuries, police said.
The episode has renewed safety concerns for Australian lawmakers, in a country where politicians have historically been highly accessible to the public and usually go about their business without security officers present. But public incitement against officials is growing.
Australian Federal Police Commissioner Krissy Barrett said in 2025 that threats against parliamentarians had doubled over the past three years. Police data showed more than 1,000 such threats against politicians in the 2025-2026 financial year, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said Monday.
In Britain, murders of politicians have prompted bolstered security. Labour lawmaker Jo Cox was shot and stabbed in 2016 by a far-right extremist, and Conservative David Amess was stabbed in 2021 by an attacker inspired by the Islamic State group.
In July, the former politician and reality TV contestant Ann Widdecombe was found slain with a hammer at her home. A man has been charged with murder and terrorism-related offenses.
___
Graham-McClay contributed from Wellington, New Zealand

title: Troy Jackson endorsed by Houlton Band of Maliseets
text:
The Bangor Daily News was the first to report this story. What you’re reading here would likely not be made public without the efforts of professional journalists asking questions, interviewing sources and obtaining documents.
Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Troy Jackson was endorsed Monday by the Houlton Band of Maliseets Tribal Council, the latest tribal endorsement in the high-stakes race.
The support from the tribe comes a week after the chief of the Passamaquoddy Tribe at Sipayik wrote a letter endorsing Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins, the first tribal backing she’s received during her five terms.
The endorsement for Jackson, a former Maine Senate president who along with other state and federal Democrats has supported tribal sovereignty, also came a week after he celebrated Indigenous People’s Day with tribal members and held a virtual roundtable with Wabanaki leaders.
Tribal issues have been a major political issue in the State House for years but have not arisen much during the increasingly heated race that could determine which party controls the Senate. The back-to-back endorsements, with more expected in the coming days and weeks, mark another contrast in the pair’s positions and pitches to Mainers.
Collins has built much of her campaign on her ability to bring federal dollars home, including for tribal projects, while Jackson has touted his record in Augusta and says he’d press in Washington to address long-term wrongs against Maine tribes.
“From championing clean drinking water initiatives to his role in creating the commission to reexamine the 1980 Maine Indian Claims Settlement Act, Troy has consistently proven that he listens to indigenous voices and stands with the Wabanaki people,” Chief Clarissa Sabattis said in a statement.
Jackson, who has lamented that one of Gov. Janet Mills’ vetoes of bills he supported included tribal sovereignty, said in a statement that he was proud to earn the council’s support and pledged to fight for tribal rights on Capitol Hill if elected.
“Representing a rural community, I understand that when the Wabanaki Nations have a vibrant economy, health care, infrastructure and educational opportunities, all of rural Maine benefits,” he said.
Collins’ endorsement last week came after she met Pleasant Point reservation leaders last year and helped secure $5 million to construct a new wastewater treatment plant and collection system, according to Chief Pos Bassett.
The senator has not yet supported federal efforts, such as a bill from Democratic U.S. Reps. Jared Golden and Chellie Pingree, to counteract the Maine Indian Claims Settlement Act of 1980. The law gave the tribes more than $80 million but let the state regulate them like towns and cities without the rights of most tribes in other parts of the country.
Collins’ team has said she supports tribes having governmental authority to manage their own affairs, and also has backed extension of federal programs to the tribes such as the Violence Against Women Act. Collins’ office said she would examine impacts to Maine tribes if any state regulations require amendments to federal law.

title: Hearts of Pine midfielder Mikey Lopez announces retirement
text:
Hearts of Pine midfielder Mikey Lopez announced on Instagram that Portland’s season finale Saturday will be the final game of his 14-year career.
Lopez, 33, has played 47 games in two seasons with the Hearts of Pine, including 31 last season. He was named the USL League One Comeback Player of the Year in 2025 after Achilles surgery wiped out his 2024 season.
The Hearts of Pine’s captain has played 16 games this season with eight starts.
“I think Saturday will close the circle on my career,” Lopez said in a video posted to Instagram. “Being able to play in front of my family, a sold-out crowd at Fitzpatrick Stadium and playing for (Hearts of Pine coach) Bobby (Murphy) one last time I think is the perfect way to end my career.”
Lopez played for Murphy at a Texas development academy in grades 8-12. He played at the University of North Carolina and was a first-round pick in the 2011 MLS SuperDraft by Sporting Kansas City. He spent three seasons in Kansas City, followed by two with New York City FC. He also played seven seasons in USL Championship, the last six with Birmingham, where he was the franchise’s first captain.
Portland will host Charlotte Independence at 5 p.m. Saturday at Fitzpatrick Stadium. The Hearts of Pine, who reached the USL League One semifinals in their first season, are 7-14-10 and have failed to qualify for the playoffs in their second campaign.

title: Developer who wants to convert Bangor Mall into housing just lost key investor
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The developer who wants to convert part of the Bangor Mall into housing just lost a key investor.
Michael Cole, whose Bangor Marketplace and Residences LLC is behind the bid to redevelop the mall, told CBS affiliate WABI that the departure of a key investor delivered a “gut punch” to the plan.
Attempts to reach Cole for comment weren’t immediately successful Monday morning.
Earlier this year, Cole went public with a plan to buy the mall and redevelop it into an assisted living facility, housing and stores.
That news was met with excitement after a yearslong decline at the mall, which has lost key retailers such as Macy’s and Sears and by one estimate has a 30% occupancy. The mall’s current owner, Namdar Realty, has been embroiled in a legal fight with the city over code violations.
Cole had hoped to close the sale back in June, but that got delayed by months. Now it’s uncertain how this latest development may affect the sale of and redevelopment prospects for the aging retail hub.

title: Mountain Valley field hockey knocks off Lisbon in overtime
text:
LISBON — Sometimes all it takes is a little reset.
That was the case for Mountain Valley on Monday in its 3-2 overtime win over Lisbon in a Class C field hockey clash.
After surrendering a 2-0 lead in the fourth quarter, the Falcons regrouped and struck first in the extra eight-minute period, notching their 10th win in the team’s penultimate game of the season.
“I thought they played a little flat, a lot of ‘Monday flat’ going on,” said coach Melissa Forbes. “And then when they got in overtime, they’re like, ‘OK, this is embarrassing. We were up 2-0. It never should have gotten to be tied.’ So I think they did their own self-regrouping, which is good.”
Mountain Valley forward Addison Libby scored the winner — her second goal of the game.
The junior had a goal and an assist when the Falcons defeated the Greyhounds 4-1 last Monday, so it was fitting that she picked up where she left off in the teams’ second meeting.
“7v7, full field, so everybody’s just breathing so heavy. … I got in the circle and (shot) the ball, and it went in and everybody went crazy,” Libby said of her overtime goal. “I didn’t expect it to go in, honestly. It was a very bad angle, but it did, so happy about that.”
HOW IT HAPPENED
The Falcons found the back of the cage first with under a minute to go in the first quarter, when Melina Byam scored off a pass from Emma Williamson. Libby then extended Mountain Valley’s lead in the second quarter, and by halftime it looked as if it was going to be another commanding win over Lisbon.
The Greyhounds had different plans, however, scoring twice in the fourth quarter — the second goal, by Julia Quagliaroli, coming with under 30 seconds to play in regulation. All of a sudden the game was tied and headed to overtime.
Late in the bonus period, Libby notched her second score, clinching Mountain Valley’s sixth consecutive victory.
WHAT THIS MEANS
Mountain Valley (10-3) will play Oak Hill (4-9) in its regular-season finale Tuesday — a game originally set for last Friday but was postponed.
Regardless of Tuesday’s result, the Falcons seem destined to hold the third seed in the Class C North tournament.
Lisbon (10-4), playing its final regular-season game, is likely locked into the third seed in C South.
“My guess right now is we’re probably going to stay third, so we get home-field advantage, which is always nice,” Lisbon coach Kayla Royer said. “Like I just told the girls, ‘It’s a clean slate coming into playoffs. So it doesn’t matter what your record is. It’s do or die.’”
UNSUNG HERO
Mountain Valley goalkeeper Isabella Dupuis was a brick wall in the cage. She tallied double-digit saves and until the fourth quarter, held Lisbon scoreless.
STATISTICAL LEADERS
• Mountain Valley: Addison Libby (two goals), Melina Byam (goal), Emma Williamson (assist), Isabella Dupuis (11 saves)
• Lisbon: Julia Quagliaroli (goal, assist), Melanie Simmons (goal), Hayley Melvin (assist)

title: InvestigateTV+: A rise in Lyme disease cases
text:
(InvestigateTV) — InvestigateTV+ heads to a state where Lyme disease cases have more than quadrupled to examine a rise in cases nationwide and the effort to prevent future infections.
Plus, a drop in test results during and after the COVID-19 pandemic underscores its impact on education. We uncover the age groups experts say are missing more milestones and strategies to reverse the trend.
How Lyme disease cases are rising in the Midwest
Michigan health leaders say everyone needs to think about Lyme disease now.
“Our state’s Lyme disease rates have been increasing over the past 10 years pretty dramatically. And we are actually now a high incidence state based on CDC’s definition of Lyme disease incidence,” said Rachel Burkholder, with the Michigan Department of Health and Human Services.
Burkholder said the state has seen a more than 350% increase in Lyme disease cases in five years, from 471 cases in 2020 to more than 2,000 in 2025.
What we’ve learned about pandemic learning loss
Schools are seeing the first wave of children born during the COVID-19 pandemic. Many teachers are reporting seeing speech and vocabulary delays in their classrooms.
Dog-like robot acting as security
A high-tech robot is adding an extra layer of security at businesses across the country, combining AI technology and human expertise to track down security threats.
The robot, covered in sensors and about the size of a dog, conducts automated patrols at locations. The device checks gates, doors, locks and looks for people in places where they shouldn’t be.

A group of Trine University engineering students spent months designing a device to help a Navy veteran regain the ability to shoot a bow, after injuries left him without the use of his left arm.

title: I oppose the school consolidation proposal before you this November
text:
I have long served on our school boards. I write this as an individual, albeit one with that experience. I respect the hard work and good faith efforts of my colleagues who have served on the Reorganization Planning Committee (RPC) — the author of the proposal. I do not oppose their work lightly.
I support true regionalization of our educational system. Demographics, including declining school enrollment, the unaffordability of life here for young families and those on fixed incomes, the rising complexity, demands and opportunities of a modern educational system, and our finite resources combine to incentivize us to regionalize our educational efforts.
The difference between regionalization and the reorganization proposed is that regionalization would be driven by a vision and a proposed model for providing a combined educational system, whereas the changes on offer focus only on administrative and budget consolidation. Those things should happen, but proposing them now is putting the cart before the horse with negative consequences for true consolidation.
Streamlining the administration, an effort that can continue in our current structure, is not ever going to be a sufficient reason to substantially shift costs, curtail local control, remove town meetings from budgetary oversight and cede ownership of school properties to a centralized school administration.
Regionalization needs to be rooted in a community conversation about how we structure our schools to support the best education we can provide in the coming decades.
We need to openly consider the drawbacks to having so many small schools with single small classes per grade. How does that impact teaching effectiveness or the depth and breadth of opportunities for students?
Can combining grades across town lines enhance equality and enrichment of opportunity without sacrificing essential community identities?
We need to ask ourselves why Bar Harbor’s cost per pupil has long been lower than smaller schools. Are they short-changing their children or are we paying the price for refusing to consider economies of scale? Could we possibly be providing more for our kids with the money we spend?
A problem with the current proposal is that without centering their work on the search for a commonly provided educational structure, the RPC has had to tailor their message to each town. They have repeatedly altered the plan in the hopes of getting something passed regardless of the final shape of the plan.
Their proposal to group middle school students in Southwest Harbor, which was predicated on the currently unmet social and educational needs of that age group, was quickly scrubbed from the plan when some Southwest residents voiced opposition.
The RPC then voiced support for a future school board figuring out how to provide a middle school while leaving the only likely remaining option the building of a new middle school. But still there is pushback to the idea of the need to assess the effectiveness of so many elementary schools with even smaller remaining enrollments.
Some argue that not having their school as is/where is isn’t negotiable so the topic was never seriously explored. I suggest that resistance is not entirely for educational reasons. It’s for more complex community reasons that deserves respect but also deeper discussion.
Originally the plan excluded cost sharing of the bond payments for the new Connors Emerson school. Bar Harbor objected so that was added into the combined cost. That has a major impact on the cost shifting in the proposed funding formula.
Then we come to Mount Desert whose taxpayers would be required to shoulder a major increase in property taxes for no meaningful change in the educational opportunities it would provide. It’s like asking us to pay a lot of money for nothing. Based on the current system budget, that shift would result in a tax increase of around $144 dollars per $100,000 in property valuation before factoring in inevitable additional increases, including needed capital improvements in several existing schools. (I am a Mount Desert taxpayer.)
Some on the RPC have suggested to me that if we form the new school structure that new board can and should work on further school consolidation efforts. But RPC members have been telling people in many towns they’d never do anything to change the “special nature” of each of our small schools, making the possibility of productive regionalization hard to imagine.
We have been combining educational efforts for more than a century. Small schools all over this island have been successfully re-purposed. In so doing we have slowly but surely gotten better at delivering for our students.
Our predecessors faced these sorts of discussions over the high school. We had three small, outmoded schools. It took time and several rounds of losing votes before each town on MDI gave up its small high school for one regional school. In the process, Mount Desert agreed to shoulder a greater burden for its ongoing financing, a duty we still meet. Who would argue today that the benefits of truly combined efforts to educate our high schoolers was a bad idea?
Similar forces are at work today for every grade and building in our school system. If we want to shift tax burdens for the entire system, we need to put more on the table than just rearranging school boards, budgets and the central administrative duties. The plan needs to be focused on how to ensure the ability to provide ongoing educational excellence efficiently and effectively. It needs to be a win-win for students, communities and taxpayers in every town.
I do not urge we stop talking about reorganizing our school system. I urge we defeat this proposal and see that not as a loss, but as a data point that tells us we need to focus on future educational needs and opportunities first, then figure out how to structure and finance the system to better provide them.
Our public schools are the most important thing our towns do. We are blessed to have consistent and strong support for our schools. Our schools provide lots of good reasons for that support, but to retain that support we must not remain static in the face of seemingly inevitable shifts in the needs of our students and our communities.
Voting no is not a failure to support our schools. It is a message that we support continuous improvements in our schools where they matter most: in the classrooms.
Gail Marshall is a resident of Mount Desert.

title: Couple celebrates 30 years on airline where they first met
text:
Love at first flight: Couple celebrates 30 years on airline where they first met
Jeffrey Larson drove more than 400 miles from Minneapolis to catch a flight in Kansas City in October of 1996. His friend Rob had bought him a ticket to visit Phoenix.
"It was a standby flight, and he can check, you know, whether or not flights are available," Jeffrey said. "He said Chicago looks full; go to Omaha or Kansas City."
Jeffrey chose to drive straight through Omaha to Kansas City. That choice changed the rest of his life.
"I noticed her right away because she was this beautiful, cute little redhead," Jeffrey said.
A five-hour delay brought him face to face with Salesia. They were both flying Southwest back when they had open seating.
"My plan was to get next to her so that I could sit next to her on the plane, and that's exactly what happened," Jeffrey said.
"I was definitely right away after that three-hour trip like, 'I want to see him again,'" Salesia said.
That three-hour flight turned into a first date in Phoenix. Salesia still has the note Jeffrey wrote her on a napkin, a poem complimenting her smile.
"After that day that we spent together, I actually called my mom and said, 'I found the man I'm going to marry,'" Salesia said.
That first date turned into traveling home together. The two changed their flights so they could fly back. When another delay stuck Salesia at Kansas City International Airport, Jeffrey came to the rescue.
"I was driving home to Minneapolis, and I said, 'Why don't I just drive you home?'" Jeffrey said. "It was kind of on my way, a little bit out of the way, and she's like, 'OK!'"
That drive home turned into a 30-year relationship. A blizzard stranded Jeffrey in Omaha and left him with no other option than to stay with Salesia in her parents' house.
Want more content like this? Subscribe to our News We Love newsletter here.
"Six months after that flight, after visiting each other on the weekend to Minnesota, he packed up his life in Minnesota, left his family, and moved here," Salesia said.
A year later they were engaged, and a year after that, the couple got married. Now, Jeff and Salesia have six kids, a painting company and a lifetime of memories.
"Just seeing how he has grown so much over the last 30 years and the father he's become and the amazing husband," Salesia said.
Their daughter Gracie said the relationship has never been turbulent. She said she grew up in a home full of love and patience.
"They were always making time for each other and showing us what it was like to really be in love," Gracie said.
She said those qualities are now prevalent in her own life.
"I think that they just really influence what I want to look for in a person," Gracie said. "Kindness and the effort that they put into one another."
Now, the Larsons are celebrating their 30th anniversary on the same airline that brought them together. The couple hopped on another Southwest flight Thursday to remember how it all started.
"They should've kept that open seating so that people can meet randomly like that," Salesia said.

title: Masardis woman accused of trying to burn 2 homes with a lighter
text:
A Masardis woman allegedly stormed out of a house after fighting with her ex-partner and tried to burn it and another nearby home with a lighter.
Brooke Robinson, 26, set fires at the home of her ex-partner and at a vacant building, according to an affidavit filed Thursday at Aroostook District Court in Presque Isle.
Investigators ruled the fires were purposely set. Arson, a Class A or felony crime in Maine, carries a penalty of up to 30 years in prison and up to a $50,000 fine.
Ashland police received a complaint on Oct. 10 that Robinson had broken windows and entered an unoccupied house at 1158 Frenchville Road, state fire marshal’s office investigator Cody Fenderson stated in court documents obtained by the Bangor Daily News.
The property owner, Nelson Hafford, reported the broken windows and found an area that looked like someone had tried to burn the structure, Fenderson said.
The home’s former occupants, Jasmine Wentworth and Brandon McPherson, had recently moved across the street, according to court records. They reported seeing Robinson breaking the windows, arguing with a man outside an adjacent property and doing something near the home’s exterior with her hands.
Fenderson’s investigation revealed that Robinson was living with her ex-boyfriend, Christopher Bowring, and his father, Robert Bowring, in a nearby mobile home at 1164 Frenchville Road. Christopher Bowring said he and Robinson had argued on Oct. 10, according to court records.
Robinson allegedly stormed outside, and Robert Bowring followed her because he was afraid of what she would do. He noted smoke and flames in an outside corner of his home and found Robinson holding a torch lighter to another area, Fenderson reported. Robert Bowring put out the fires.
Robinson next ran to the unoccupied home, one side of which faces the Bowrings’ residence. Robert Bowring noted the red torch-style lighter in her hand when she ran, but neither he, Wentworth nor McPherson saw her attempt to burn the vacant building, according to court documents.
Fenderson described the damage at the vacant home as a roughly 2-by-3.5-inch charred space in a corner of the mobile home’s entryway.
Damage to the Bowring home included a large area of charring where blue foam insulation burned, and another area along the bottom where skirting material was consumed by fire.
Fenderson ruled that both fires were “consistent with ignition by an open flame applied to exterior building materials,” records stated.
Ashland police arrested Robinson, who was taken to Northern Light A.R. Gould Hospital in Presque Isle for treatment, court records stated.
Ashland police did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Robinson’s rap sheet includes several charges for disorderly conduct, criminal trespass and theft, according to court documents.
She was charged in 2021 in Orono with theft and violating conditions of release, and was incarcerated for 55 days. A charge of eluding an officer was dismissed.
She was charged with operating under the influence and theft in 2022 in Presque Isle, and received seven days’ incarceration, a $500 fine and 150-day license suspension.
Bail was set at $1,000 cash, with the conditions that Robinson cannot possess any incendiary devices and must not have any contact with Christopher Bowring, Robert Bowring, Hafford, Wentworth or McPherson.
No court date has been set.

title: Our votes demonstrate our values
text:
The decisions voters are now facing are much more about their personal values than any policy (political) views they have. Many have come to terms with their own party’s “demonstrated values” and now must cast their ballots.
Each political party has demonstrated their values through their own actions or inaction. A total of 147 Republicans voted to approve Trump’s efforts to overturn a fair election in 2021. Meanwhile, the Democratic Party has tried to pass legislation to guarantee healthcare for U.S. citizens and make the wealthiest Americans pay their fair share of taxes.
The divergence of our citizens’ values will not be solved by any election. Our votes to select a governor, a U.S. representative and a U.S. senator, however, will demonstrate our values to our families and fellow citizens.
Tom Turner
Augusta

title: Search ends for more survivors from boat that sank off Mexico’s Baja California coast
text:
The U.S. Coast Guard has called off the search for 11 people believed missing after a boat thought to be carrying more than two dozen people sank off Mexico’s Baja California coast.
Rescuers saved 16 of those who were on board, including several who had suspected shark bites, the Coast Guard said. Crews spent nearly four days looking for survivors before ending the search late Sunday.
The boat capsized in an area frequented by smugglers outside of U.S. waters, according to the Coast Guard. Survivors pulled from the water early Friday told officials there were 27 people on board.
A mayday call came from someone on the boat around 1 a.m. Friday, said Coast Guard Lt. Santiago Tamburini. A helicopter reached the site two hours later, and it took about 90 minutes to rescue the 16 people, Tamburini said.
The Mexican consulate in San Diego said all those rescued were Mexican nationals. The Coast Guard has said Customs and Border Protection was investigating and interviewing the survivors.
Both the Coast Guard and the U.S. Navy along with the Mexican Navy searched the waters with helicopters, planes and multiple boats.
The boat went down about 140 miles (225 kilometers) west of Ensenada, Mexico. The boat’s origin and destination were not clear.
The region is popular with fishing and leisure boats, but some attempts to transport migrants from Mexico to the U.S. have turned deadly in past years.
In May 2025, at least three people died when a boat flipped off the coast north of the U.S.-Mexico border. In 2023, eight people were killed in one of the deadliest maritime smuggling accidents off the U.S. coast, when two boats approached a San Diego beach in heavy fog and one capsized in the surf.

title: Kennebunk, Windham girls soccer show Class A South’s competitiveness
text:
KENNEBUNK — It was dark and chilly as Kennebunk senior Alina Auriemma dribbled down the sideline past her cheering teammates as the final seconds ticked off the clock. In the corner of Windham’s defensive zone, the regular season ended with a 2-1 Kennebunk win.
It’s time for the playoffs, and in Class A South, the most competitive tournament in the state will get underway.
The game Monday at Kennebunk High featured two of the best teams in this deep region. Both Kennbunk and Windham are 10-3-1. Windham will hold on to the No. 2 seed even with the loss. The Rams secured the No. 3 seed and a bye to the regional quarterfinals.
It’s been a season of close games in the league. This was Kennebunk’s fourth one-goal victory, and flipped the result of the Rams’ season-opening 2-1 loss at Windham.
“This could’ve easily been 2-1 them again,” Kennebunk coach Josh Viola said. “Two pretty even teams.”
This was Windham’s seventh one-goal game this season, and second one-goal loss in a row (the Eagles fell to Cheverus, 1-0, last Thursday). Even top-seeded and unbeaten Scarborough, winner of the last four regional championships, hasn’t run roughshod over the league. Six of the Red Storms’ 12 wins going into their regular-season finale against Sanford on Tuesday were decided by a single goal.
“Scarborough, we held them to one in double OT,” Viola said. “Unfortunately, that was one more than we scored.”
Last season, Viola’s Rams might have been the surprise of the league, winning 12 games and advancing to the Class A South semifinals. Nobody is surprised Kennebunk is among the top teams in the region this season, especially not the Rams.
Senior Ava McCourt scored the winning goal with 28:46 left in the second half, her sharp low shot from the left side finding the right corner of the net to give the Rams the 2-1 lead that held up. McCourt missed most of last season with a leg injury. A captain, she sees a team with a positive culture as it heads to the postseason.
“Everyone on this team, we’re one giant fun group,” McCourt said. “We all care. We come to practice ready to go.”
Viola didn’t hold back his praise for McCourt, calling her the best midfielder in the league. Auriemma is a returning all-conference player. Keeper Teagan Hanson rounds out Kennebunk’s trio of seniors, and is a steadying presence at the back of the Rams defense, Viola said. She doesn’t get rattled, and makes quiet saves.
If you’re looking for the dark horse in this season’s Class A South playoff race, the team that Kennebunk was a year ago, you have two choices. There’s Bonny Eagle, which won five games last season and snuck into the playoffs as the 11 seed in Class A South. The Scots, fifth in the Heal point standings, enter their regular-season finale against Portland on Tuesday with eight wins and an impressive 0-0 tie with Scarborough.
There’s also South Portland. The Red Riots, currently fourth in the Heals, missed the tournament a year ago with a 3-9-2 record. South Portland earned its 10th win Monday, beating Falmouth 4-1, and has chance to earn a bye out of the preliminary round.
Kennebunk and Windham know they have a little time to catch their breath and wait for a quarterfinals opponent. They also know they had a strong playoff-like test when they faced each other Monday night. As the No. 2 and No. 3 seeds, respectively, they could face off in a rubber match in the playoffs.
Don’t assume it will happen, though. In the SMAA, no win is guaranteed.

title: Driver in deadly Kansas soccer field crash released while investigation continues
text:
Driver in deadly Kansas soccer field crash released while investigation continues
A woman who drove a pickup truck onto a soccer field during a weekend youth game in Kansas, killing two people and injuring 10 others, has been released without charges as the investigation continues, police said Sunday.
Previous video: Officials speak after two were killed when a vehicle drove through a youth soccer game
The 34-year-old woman was released, pending results of toxicology tests and a mechanical examination of the vehicle in the aftermath of Saturday's crash. Her name hasn't been made public.
"Our officers and investigators will continue working to understand exactly what happened," Wichita Police Chief Joe Sullivan said, noting that no charges have been filed to date.
The woman had one child playing soccer on another field at the Stryker Sports Complex in northeast Wichita when Saturday's crash occurred, a police statement said. The statement said two of her other children were with her in the pickup truck when it struck multiple children and adults.
According to a preliminary investigation, the Chevrolet pickup was parked in a parking space near the soccer fields before it drove onto one of the fields.
Police identified those killed at the scene as Cole Adrian, 6, and Nicholas Schafer, 35, both of McPherson, Kansas. They were not related.
Ten others ranging from 5 years old to 68 were taken to area hospitals with injuries described as non-serious.
Investigators said they have interviewed more than 30 witnesses, including the driver and her two children who were her inside the pickup at the time of the crash.

title: 'Spa-inspired' dental hygiene practice to open at Rock Row
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A registered dental hygienist with 25 years in the industry is opening her first independent practice in Maine, at the Rock Row development in Westbrook.
Josering Alobwede said build-out for the dental hygiene practice, Blue Bliss Dental Wellness, is underway. The practice’s approach will be to connect oral health and overall well-being.
“More than two and a half decades in the dental profession inspired me to create a practice built around what patients want and need: excellent care, time to ask questions and an environment where they feel at ease,” said Alobwede.
Alobwede leased 2,225 square feet in Suite 420 at 11 Rock Row, at the Rock Row Health Campus.
Mark Malone and Nick Malone of Malone Commercial Brokers facilitated the lease.
In addition to the health campus, Rock Row has retailers Market Basket, REI Co-op, Chick-fil-A, Starbucks, Crumbl Cookies, the Paper Store. The developer is Needham, Mass.-based Waterstone Properties Group Inc.
Aromatherapy
A graduate of the University of Medicine and Dentistry of New Jersey — now Rutgers School of Dental Medicine — Alobwede has practiced in New Jersey, New York and Texas in private and corporate dentistry.
Blue Bliss will combine preventive and aesthetic oral wellness services with a spa-inspired setting that includes an aromatherapy lounge. Services will include preventive dental hygiene care, advanced periodontal care, professional laser whitening and patient education.
It’s expected the practice will open in early November with three employees, she said. The build-out is being performed by Optimum Construction Inc., headquartered in Danvers, Mass., with an office in Portland.

title: 🎃 HALLOWEEN WARNING! Don’t Visit Stephen King’s Bangor House on October 31! 👻
text:
Stephen King’s Bangor, Maine House Is Off-Limits On Halloween
Halloween is almost here! Come to Bangor, but don't stop on West Broadway!
You really can't drive down West Broadway in Bangor without spotting someone gawking at Stephen King's famous house. Trust me, I know...I live right in the neighborhood!
Just about every day, when I drive past the street, there's at least one car parked along the side of the road, with people snapping pictures, trying to get a better look at the property, or simply soaking in the excitement of being there.
It's all pretty normal to me, but Stephen King's house draws fans from all over the world who want to see where the master of horror lives.
With the spookiest night of the year arriving soon, plenty of people are making the trip to Bangor to catch a glimpse of the iconic home belonging to the city's most famous resident.
Read More: CP Holiday Train Returns To Hermon & Greenville, Maine Next Month
Here's a helpful hint: If you're thinking about stopping by Stephen King's West Broadway home to trick-or-treat, you'll be out of luck.
In fact, the master of horror himself has made it clear: Don't come to my house on Halloween.
It's a lot of people to accommodate, and the Halloween tradition at the house is no longer happening. Besides, Stephen and his wife, Tabitha, spend much of their time at their second home in Florida.
But don't worry, there are other ways to celebrate Halloween Stephen King-style!
As any hardcore Stephen King fan knows, Bangor helped inspire the fictional town of Derry, Maine, which has appeared in several of his novels and short stories.
No Stephen King sightseeing trip is complete without a few classic stops, including Mount Hope Cemetery, the Paul Bunyan statue, the corner of Jackson and Union streets, the Thomas Hill Standpipe, and, of course, the famous West Broadway house.
Just remember to be respectful of the neighborhood and the people who live there. You can admire the property from a distance without trespassing or disturbing the residents.
If you're planning a visit, Sk-Tours offers a unique experience for Stephen King fans right here in Bangor.
The people behind the tour — Penney, Jamie, and Stu — are perfect guides for the job. They spent two decades owning and operating a bookstore specializing in King's books and memorabilia. You can learn more about their story here.
So, if you're heading to Bangor for a little Halloween horror, there's plenty to explore. Just remember: enjoy the Stephen King sights, but leave the trick-or-treating at his house off your itinerary!
Happy Halloween!

title: Seeing red trees?
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
COURTESY OF THE MAINE FOREST SERVICE FOREST HEALTH & MONITORING
Spruce and fir trees that turn reddish brown in summer may be showing signs of feeding damage from the native spruce budworm. The caterpillars primarily eat developing buds and needles of spruce and fir, causing the damaged foliage to die and turn reddish brown. In communities around Fort Kent, spruce budworm has caused extensive defoliation in recent years, raising concerns about forest health and long-term impacts.
Spruce budworm is always present in Maine’s forests, but populations can occasionally overwhelm their natural enemies and build to outbreak levels. Repeated heavy feeding can cause a significant decline of spruce and fir trees and may eventually lead to tree mortality. Dead and declining trees are more than just a change in color. Healthy trees can withstand stressors such as drought, disease, and insect damage. Widespread spruce budworm outbreaks can alter this balance, affecting wildlife habitat, forest resources, and the Maine communities that depend on healthy forests.
A management approach that includes small woodlots.
Spruce budworm populations are tracked by washing out and counting the small second-instar caterpillars (L2) from collected tree branches. These L2 counts approximate population density and show where spruce budworm populations are growing and poised to reach outbreak levels.
To help maintain the health and resilience of Maine’s forests, the Early Intervention Strategy (EIS) uses targeted aerial insecticide applications in woodlands with rising spruce budworm populations to prevent an outbreak. When EIS reduces budworm populations, natural enemies of spruce budworm can keep them low and stable, maintaining forest health.
In 2026, 38 owners of small woodlands participated in EIS management with 127 woodlots enrolled. Another 62,249 acres were treated on large woodland ownerships and public lands across Northern Aroostook County.
Early results are encouraging.
The goal of EIS isn’t to eliminate spruce budworm – success in the EIS approach across the landscape is defined as stabilized budworm populations, reduced host damage, and the presence of natural enemies helping keep populations in check. In treated areas, post-treatment monitoring samples documented a ~90% reduction in spruce budworm populations. In both treated and untreated areas, evidence of spruce budworm mortality from parasitoids, insect natural enemies of spruce budworm, was also documented. Fewer budworm caterpillars across the landscape meant fewer caterpillars feeding on host foliage throughout the season. As a result, spruce and fir trees remained green this summer.
Don’t see red in your woodlot!
The Maine Forest Service is organizing another voluntary EIS program for small woodland owners in areas with rising spruce budworm populations in 2027. Landowners with spruce-fir woodlots in Northern Aroostook County may qualify to enroll their forests in the EIS program for free and are invited to submit a landowner interest form with information about the woodlots they would like considered for inclusion.
We encourage landowners to talk to their neighbors with adjoining woods that may also be eligible for treatments. Encourage them to submit a landowner interest form by going to the Maine Forest Service website at www.maine.gov/sbw. Maine Forest Service District Foresters and Forest Health staff can also provide free woodlot visits if you have further questions.
Spruce budworm outbreaks are regional. Given the populations in the region, we expect several more years of potential damage from feeding budworm larvae. Early intervention can prevent budworm health impacts on your forest. Join the effort to prevent a larger outbreak of this pest and fill out the landowner interest form on our website today!
Submission Deadline: December 1

title: Letter to the Editor: Old phone poles
Facebook Marketplace deal turns into robbery. Tips to protect yourself
text:
MARTINEZ, Ga. (WRDW/WAGT/Gray News) — Three Augusta residents are facing robbery charges after deputies said they stole a PlayStation 5 during a Facebook Marketplace meetup.
Columbia County Sheriff’s Office deputies were called Friday afternoon to Fierce Fitness for a reported “robbery by sudden snatch.”
Investigators said a 23-year-old man arranged online to sell a PlayStation 5 for $500 and agreed to meet three buyers in the parking lot.
When they arrived, the victim walked to the vehicle with the console and power cord so the buyers could plug it in and test it.
After he handed the game console through a door, the man in the backseat slammed the door, and the driver sped away without paying.
As deputies headed to the scene, license plate readers picked up the Ford Escape traveling into Richmond County.
Deputies stopped the SUV a short time later and detained all three occupants.
The stolen PlayStation was recovered in the vehicle, and deputies said they also seized marijuana and a firearm.
The three occupants − a 22-year-old man, a 20-year-old man and a 24-year-old woman − were arrested, charged with robbery and booked into the Columbia County jail.
Don’t let it happen to you
Here are some tips to help keep you safe:
- Choose a safe meeting spot. Whenever possible, meet at a law enforcement “exchange zone,” such as a police station lobby or a camera-monitored parking lot, instead of a random parking lot.
- Don’t meet at anyone’s home. Avoid inviting strangers to your house, and don’t agree to meet at their residence or in a secluded area.
- Stick to daylight hours. Schedule exchanges during the day in a busy, well-lit public place.
- Bring another adult. Take a friend or family member with you so you’re not alone during the transaction.
- Stay aware of your surroundings. Keep your eyes up instead of on your phone, and park in a spot where you can leave quickly if something doesn’t feel right.
- Keep communication on the platform. Use Facebook Messenger for all messages and avoid sharing your personal phone number, home address or email when possible.
- Be cautious with cash and payments. Don’t carry large amounts of cash. If you’re using digital payments, make sure you fully inspect the item before sending money.
- Check who you’re dealing with. Look at the buyer or seller’s profile for friends, photos and previous Marketplace activity. Be extra careful with brand-new or nearly empty accounts.
- Don’t ignore red flags. If the other person repeatedly tries to change the time or location at the last minute, or if the deal seems too good to be true, cancel the meetup and walk away.

title: ‘We’re going to die’: Couple recount terrifying emergency landing during American flight
text:
ST. LOUIS (KMOV/Gray News) - A couple on board an American Airlines flight that had to make an emergency landing about 15 minutes after takeoff feared they wouldn’t make it home to their kids.
Tessa and Mark Springer, a couple from Waterloo, Illinois, were flying from St. Louis to Pennsylvania for work. Their flight took off Saturday morning from St. Louis Lambert International Airport, but trouble started before the plane even left the ground.
“We heard just this really horrible noise coming from the back of the plane. It was like... real loud buzzing, kind of grinding sound,” Mark Springer said.
Before takeoff, the pilot came over the intercom.
“The pilot comes back on and says, ‘Uh, there’s a problem with the engine on the airplane,’” Mark Springer said. “‘We can’t get it started.’”
The Springers say the plane took off roughly two hours later.
‘We’re going to die’
About 15 minutes into the flight, Mark Springer says conditions suddenly changed.
“All of a sudden, the plane just felt like it hit... like in a car, when you slam on your brakes... and everybody kind of lunges forward. Then, maybe a minute later, the plane just kind of goes boom and drops. All of the oxygen masks fall, and we just kind of looked at each other like, ‘Is this serious? Is this real?’” Mark Springer said.
He says the cabin filled with haze, and the flight attendant started shouting emergency orders.
Tessa Springer says she texted her children, “Problem on our plane, we love you guys.”
“I was like, ‘We’re going to die,’” she said.
However, the plane turned back to Lambert and was able to land safely.
Evacuation on the runway
The Springers say they evacuated the plane by jumping from the wing, with strangers catching each other on the way down. Tessa Springer took photos while they waited next to the runway for transportation back to the terminal.
The couple are now home – grateful but shaken up.
“I just kept closing my eyes and seeing my kids and thinking about them losing both of us at the same time,” Tessa Springer said. “I don’t think I’ll ever be able to get on another airplane ever again.”
American Airlines said in a statement that the flight returned to Lambert after an odor was reported on board. The plane was pulled from service for inspection.

title: Trump signs an order aimed at boosting women’s health research, a plan backed by the first lady
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump on Monday directed the federal government to bolster federal research into women’s health, a move pushed by his wife, first lady Melania Trump.
The Republican president signed an executive order that creates a new women’s health division at the National Institutes of Health and a White House task force to focus on the issue. That panel was set to hold its first meeting Monday after the Trumps held a Rose Garden signing ceremony.
“Beginning today we will change the reality of women’s health,” Melania Trump said. “Previous generations fought for women’s rights. Our generation will fight to discover the cures that will ensure a woman can live her life in health and to the fullest.”
The president, who spoke after his wife, said the order will “promote new research and really go after the understudied diseases affecting women.” The order is also intended to promote diagnostic technology and improve treatment.
White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, who recently completed treatment for breast cancer, and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. will lead the White House task force. Donald Trump said the task force will coordinate with various federal agencies and programs. The order does not include specific funding goals.
The initiative comes after a series of meetings the first lady had with federal health officials.
The president called it a “historic action” and praised the first lady’s work.
“She’s accomplished so much,” he said before pivoting into unscripted commentary on White House renovations, including the patio stone that now covers what was once the Rose Garden lawn.
Shifting back to women’s health, the president expressed surprise that some of the order’s requirements had not already been imposed.
“Who the hell wouldn’t have a women’s health division?” he said, after recalling that he’d asked Melania Trump, “Are you sure they don’t have that?”
The executive order calls for targeting maternal health, mental health and endometriosis. It also mentions other health concerns and diseases, including Alzheimer’s, osteoporosis, heart disease and stroke.
Melania Trump helped shape the order and the task force in consultation with physicians, White House officials, Kennedy and the Republican president. The initiative adds a new dimension to her policy portfolio as first lady.
In Donald Trump’s second term, the first lady has focused on improving foster care systems and expanding technology and artificial-intelligence access in education. In Trump’s first presidency, the first lady’s signature initiative, Be Best, focused on child well-being, safe social media use and reducing drug abuse.
The White House ceremony comes weeks before Nov. 3 elections and as Donald Trump’s job approval ratings have declined, including among women.
About 4 in 10 independent women supported Trump during the 2024 election against Democrat Kamala Harris and in the pre-presidency period, according to AP-NORC polls. That dropped to around a quarter in the opening months of this midterm election year, the period marked by Trump’s hard-line immigration crackdown in U.S. cities and the opening weeks of the Iran war.

Dagmar Boggs, The Coca-Cola Company’s North America president of foodservice and on-premise, also shared her excitement.

title: Man admits he shot, ran over several goats with a 4-wheeler in property dispute with neighbor, deputies say
text:
EAU PLEINE, Wis. (WSAW/Gray News) — Deputies in Wisconsin said a man admitted to killing his neighbor’s goats in 2024 over a property dispute.
Dean Ress, a farmer, said he found some of his goats shot and killed in October 2024. He said the goats are like his family.
“I’ve been suffering with this emotionally for over two years now,” Ress said.
Court records show some of the goats were shot in the hips and head. Others had been run over with a four-wheeler.
Ress said a total of 13 goats died.
Investigators said they have enough evidence to charge Ress’ neighbor, Eric Seelow, with four of the deaths.
According to court documents, Seelow admitted to investigators in August that he killed the goats. He is facing felony and misdemeanor charges.
Deputies said Seelow told them he needed to “confess his sins” following a conversation with his pastor this summer.
Court documents show that Seelow admitted taking a rifle from his grandfather’s home without permission in October 2024, shooting one goat, and using an ATV to run over others that had crossed onto his property.
Dispute over shared fence
Ress and Seelow’s dispute stems from a shared fence on the property. Both have pointed blame at the other for who is responsible for maintaining the fence.
Deputy Zachary Ruesch with the Marathon County Sheriff’s Office Animal Investigations Unit said these types of issues need to be addressed in civil court.
“This is generally a civil issue that we try not to get involved in, because we don’t have the authority to say, ‘this is your fence, this is your fence, and this person needs to fix this portion of it,’” Ruesch said.
Ress lives on a farm that used to be Seelow’s property. Both Ress and the Seelows said the Seelows did not want to give up that property.
Seelow declined an interview but said that he told Ress many times to keep his animals contained. The Seelows said the goats were wrecking their crops.
Seelow has an initial appearance on Nov. 18. If convicted, he will face a maximum sentence of 14 years in prison.
Ress is currently on house arrest. He said there was a physical conflict with Seelow after the goats died.

title: 7K students have left Maine's public school system since elimination of nonmedical vaccine exemptions
text:
It’s been five years since the state of Maine repealed philosophical and religious exemptions to the vaccine requirement to attend public schools. Since then, the Department of Education says 200 students have been dropped because of their vaccination status. Another 7,000 have voluntarily left the system and started homeschooling, although it’s unclear to what extent vaccine policy played a role.
Rebecca Brugman knew after the vaccine changes were made in 2021 that her unvaccinated kids wouldn’t be allowed to attend public school. Brugman said she trusted her children’s immune systems to protect them from disease. So, she withdrew her son, Isaiah, from the eighth grade and decided to homeschool him. But the decision came with consequences.
“We lost a lot of the school community, and I was really angry about that, and tried to get him even to after-school things, and it was basically like he was ostracized,” Brugman said.
Isaiah, now 18, remembers his mom telling him that he couldn’t go to school because he was unvaccinated.
“What the heck? Why can’t I go to school anymore? I was just kind of bummed that I wasn’t gonna get to see my friends as much. I was worried, you know, I’d fall behind in general, but it was rough,” he said.
Isaiah said there were a lot of extracurricular activities that he wasn’t able to do after leaving the public school system.
“I got to do band and wood shop, and they even had, like, a robotics club. So, I think I definitely loved those parts a lot more, being able to hang out with other people outside of the usual classes,” Isaiah said.
“When your world is consumed by the public school, you know your kids are in sports, your kids are in theater, all your friends go to your school, and you’re ripped away from that. Those families went through all the stages of grief,” said Brooke Thompson, the co-founder of the Maine Home Education Alliance.
Thompson said it was challenging for some families who felt abandoned by the state.
“When you don’t have time to prepare, when it’s unexpected, you know, that’s not the best way to start off your home education journey,” Thompson said.
When she purchased a home in Kennebunk in 2022, Jennifer Parke didn’t realize the new vaccine requirement was in place. Parke vaccinated her children when they were young but decided to stop during COVID. She didn’t want to homeschool her kids, so instead packed up and moved to Philadelphia.
“We called Maine our home. I bought a home, I wanted to settle there, and I thought that I would have the right to choose what I want for my children, right, until they’re 18 years old, and to be so forced out because of this really leaves such a bad taste in my mouth. Because every other experience I had in Maine was wonderful,” Parke said.
Among other things, Parke said she worries about a link between the measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine and autism despite extensive scientific research that shows one does not exist.
“I don’t want to inject my children with it. I just don’t. I feel like the diseases are sort of already eradicated, and I’m just like, why, why would I just keep pumping my kids with these?” Parke said.
The National Medical Association said vaccination remains one of the safest and most effective tools to protect children and communities, but so far this year more than 4,000 Measles cases have been confirmed around the country, the highest number in three decades. At least two measles-related deaths have been reported in Pennsylvania. Despite this trend, vaccine hesitancy continues to climb, driven in part by misinformation online. And as it grows, so does the number of children being homeschooled.
“When you have a large group of people who are denied access to a public system, they will take their business elsewhere,” Trish Hutchins at Homeschoolers of Maine said.
Hutchins said the surge in homeschoolers in the last five years has radically changed the public school system.
“It’s kind of like introducing an element of competition to the school market that’s never been there before. But this does impact state and national funding for our local schools,” Hutchins said.
The Maine Department of Education was unable to provide anyone for comment for this story. But Hutchins believes the vaccine mandate has sped up the rate of school consolidation and closure across the state.
Vaccination rates among Maine kindergartners have steadily increased since 2019, but growing vaccine hesitancy is recognized by the World Health Organization as one of the most pressing threats to public health.
This story appears through a media partnership with Maine Public.

title: Minnesota teen accused of plotting terror attack at Mall of America to remain jailed
text:
MINNEAPOLIS (AP) — An 18-year-old from Minnesota who prosecutors say planned a terror attack at the Mall of America and who was arrested after buying an AK-47 from an undercover FBI employee must remain in custody, a federal judge ruled Monday.
Sheikhdoon Abdullahi Mohamud, an American-born U.S. citizen of Somali descent, won’t be released because he’s a risk to the community and a flight risk, U.S. Magistrate Judge Dulce Foster said.
Mohamud had been on the FBI’s radar since December 2024, when he began trading messages with a confidential informant. He was arrested Oct. 6 after meeting with an FBI employee posing as a member of the Islamic State group and paying $600 for the rifle, 200 rounds of ammunition and four 30-round magazines, authorities said.
“This was as close to committing a terrorist attack as he could have gotten,” Assistant U.S. Attorney Benjamin Bejar said during the hearing. “He was 100% committed to doing this crime and he was 100% committed to doing it on behalf of ISIS.”
Mohamud’s attorney, Manny Atwal, said during Monday’s hearing that he was just 16 when the confidential informant began speaking to him, and that his only access to weapons was through those supplied by the FBI. She had asked that he be held in a halfway house where he would be monitored by GPS and have no access to the internet.
Mohamud was arrested at a public park in Richfield, the Minneapolis suburb where he lived, several miles northwest of the mall. Authorities said Mohamud said he planned to attack the mall on Oct. 24, when there was a scheduled arts celebration by the Hmong community, Minnesota’s largest Asian ethnic group.
“He wanted to harm as many people as possible,” FBI Special Agent Keegan Rupenthal testified at Monday’s hearing. The teen’s “ultimate goal was to become a martyr,” and during his arrest he pledged allegiance to the Islamic State group’s leader, Rupenthal said.
Mohamud initially expressed interest in messages about traveling to Somalia to fight for al-Shabab militants, according to Rupenthal’s affidavit in support of the criminal complaint. But Mohamud, who expressed admiration for terror attacks that had happened in the U.S., eventually said he didn’t have enough money to travel overseas and decided to carry out an attack in Minnesota, according to the affidavit.
Rupenthal said during the hearing that on multiple occasions, the confidential informant told Mohamud that the attack was a serious thing, and that he could back out. “He said that he was 100% committed to doing it and that he wasn’t being pressured,” Rupenthal testified.
The FBI has foiled several alleged attacks through sting operations in which agents posed as terror supporters, supplying advice or equipment. Critics say the strategy can amount to entrapment.
In May 2025, FBI agents were concerned enough that they went to Mohamud’s home. His mother told them he wasn’t home from school yet and called the boy’s father, who declined to speak with them and said he would give their contact information to his lawyer, the complaint said.
Tens of thousands of people of Somali descent live in Minnesota, dating back to when refugees began arriving in the 1990s. Over the years several have been charged with attempting to join militant groups.
___
Schmidt is a corps member for The Associated Press/Report for America Statehouse News Initiative. Report for America is a nonprofit national service program that places journalists in local newsrooms to report on undercovered issues.
___
Associated Press reporter Jamie Stengle in Dallas contributed to this report.
