title: Homeland Security grants temporary deportation reprieve for more than 100K Ukrainians and Sudanese
text:
MIAMI (AP) — More than 100,000 people from Ukraine and Sudan can stay in the United States without immediate risk of deportation, the Department of Homeland Security said, in what amounts to a temporary reprieve after their right to stay in the country was set to expire Monday.
Temporary Protected Status was set to end Oct. 19 for about 101,000 Ukrainians and 1,800 Sudanese. But DHS said an announcement “will be made at the appropriate time.” Until then, the department said in a written statement, Ukrainians and Sudanese in the U.S. covered by those temporary measures “retain protection.” The Department did not indicate how long they could stay or when a final announcement would be made on their status.
DHS did not respond to a question about whether they can keep their work permits, but TPS generally allows people to work while their protections remain in effect.
The decision Monday marks another incident where the Trump administration, which has previously sought to end these temporary protections from deportation and send people back to their home countries, has allowed people covered by the temporary status to stay in the country but without giving any guidance as to how long.
The context of the decisions to keep the protections
The Trump administration has already terminated TPS for more than 1 million people from 13 countries, including Venezuela, Haiti, Honduras, Nicaragua, Afghanistan and Syria.
But in a change in practice roughly a month ago, the administration kept protections in place for nearly 200,000 Salvadorans whose TPS was set to expire Sept. 9. In that case they also said that they were going to make a decision at the appropriate time and that in the meantime, people from El Salvador could continue to work and live in the U.S.
Activists and a bipartisan group of lawmakers have been raising the alarm over the upcoming deadline for TPS to expire for Ukrainians, arguing that conditions remain unsafe for them to return home amid the war with Russia.
Ukraine was first designated for TPS in April 2022, following Russia’s full-scale invasion two months earlier. The Biden administration subsequently extended the designation, most recently in January 2025, when DHS authorized an additional 18 months of protection through October 2026.
The TPS program for Sudan was established in 1997, and since then, successive U.S. administrations have extended it due to the armed conflict and political instability that have plagued the African nation.
The decision Monday comes two weeks before the Nov. 3 midterm elections, when Trump’s hard line immigration policies will face a test at the ballot box.
The TPS program has offered protections for decades but is controversial
The U.S. Congress created TPS in 1990 to prevent deportations to countries suffering from natural disasters or civil strife.
It allows people already in the country to remain and work, for renewable periods if the homeland security secretary determines conditions are unsafe for their return. But it doesn’t give them a pathway to permanent residency.
Supporters say that using this tool protects people from being returned to dangerous situations and that uprooting people covered by TPS after years of living in the U.S. is cruel. Critics, especially in the Trump administration, say successive administrations have extended these protections for years regardless of what has happened in the home countries.
Federal rules say TPS is automatically extended for six months if the secretary doesn’t make a determination at least 60 days before the designation expires.
Advocates are grateful for DHS decision, warn about the war
“We’re grateful for an extension, however temporary, for TPS holders from Ukraine and Sudan,” said Myal Greene, president and CEO of World Relief, an organization that has provided humanitarian assistance in both countries. “We encourage the administration and Congress to consider longer term relief for women, men and children trying to carve out stability while their countries of origin remain in upheaval.”
Krish O’Mara Vignarajah, president and CEO of Global Refuge, noted Ukraine and Sudan are not safe and meet the legal conditions for TPS to be extended.
“Russia’s war on Ukraine is nearing its fifth year, and Ukrainians are bracing for another winter under drone and missile strikes, driving civilian casualties and devastating critical infrastructure. Sudan remains locked in a brutal civil war marked by famine, widespread human rights abuses and the hallmarks of genocide,” Vignarajah said. “It is not safe for these families to go home.”
——-
Associated Press reporter Rebecca Santana contributed from Washington.

title: These US high school seniors teach older adults around the world how to use technology
text:
These Florida high school students teach older adults around the world how to use technology
Inside Brookdale Senior Living, seniors share their wealth of knowledge.
"Do unto others as what you want done to you," said Jeanne McCafferty, a resident of the facility in Lee County, Florida.
Despite their years of wisdom, there's one realm of understanding that's a little more limited.
"I don't do any of it," said Bob Bockman. "It never interested me."
What never interested Bob was learning how iPhones, computers, and this "tech stuff" work.
Thankfully, every week, a team of high-tech titans steps in to help.
Six years ago, a group of students at Canterbury High School noticed a problem they were confident they could help seniors fix. It's why they started CLEO, which stands for Computer Literacy Education Outreach. It's a program that teaches seniors how to use technology.
"It's very meaningful," said Canterbury senior Bradley Laquis, who is also the Executive Director of CLEO. The initiative started as a way for him and his brother to stay in touch with their grandparents.
What started as helping seniors in one city has grown into helping seniors throughout the country and internationally.
"Seeing the smile on the senior citizens' faces truly just means a lot," said Bradley.
Week after week, these students come back to help seniors stay connected to the world around them, but most importantly, to each other.

title: CSD trustees investigate reserve fund transaction history
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
On Oct. 15, Community School District (CSD) trustees voted to proceed with a proposed capital and facilities assessment by Dirigo Strategist Advisors, at a cost not to exceed $21,000. According to the document, the scope includes capital accounts and reserves, facilities and the physical plant, debt and capital financing, and governance and policy.
This was spurred by trustees requesting more information about the capital reserve fund's transaction history, from fiscal year (FY) 2019, when the balance was $12,500, to today. The request also asked how the district arrived at the $140,000 figure in 2019, what the charter obligates the district to set aside and why the budget code for the fund changed over the years, per the document.
As reported in the Register, Alternative Organizational Structure (AOS) 98 Superintendent Robert Kahler said that, historically, only $12,500 was set aside for minor capital projects from 1953 to 2019, but the amount increased to $140,000 after the 2019 charter change. These reserves were drained during the flood at Boothbay Region Elementary School (BRES), leaving about $2,500; $140,000 was transferred in FY 2024, FY 2025 and FY 2026 (unaudited), leaving a balance of $422,585 available for capital projects. The funds can be accessed only for designated purposes (capital projects) and only with the trustees' permission.
According to Kahler, there has not been enough time to generate a transaction history report because expenditure details before 2024 are not readily available electronically due to changes in accounting services and financial systems.
Members Paul Roberts and Steve Lorrain abstained from the vote. While both supported the proposal, they felt the timing was off.
"I think we got bigger fish to fry right now. I can see going forward with an audit ... I don't know if this is the particular right time to do it, is all. There's just so much coming at us here," explained Lorrain.
Roberts added, "My feeling lately has been that we're spending a lot of time on things that are important, but aren't as important as things that we're supposed to be spending some time on ... I can't remember the last time, other than (about the) oil tank, we discussed anything about the building we're sitting in right now."
In other business, the future of AOS 98 remains questionable. Formed in 2010, AOS 98 combines the Community School District (CSD), Southport, Edgecomb and Georgetown for the purpose of sharing central office services, such as the superintendent. However, many AOS systems are dissolving, with only seven remaining out of Maine's original 19.
"Essentially it's the lack of efficiency. It is incredibly difficult for central office staff to get to five board meetings a month, five collective bargaining agreements, and five different budgets, and all the rest of the level of work that is required of that," said AOS 98 Board Chair Heather Sinclair.
Four options are being explored. 1) Stay as an AOS but work towards improvements. Sinclair said there were original documents that outlined sharing policies, collective bargaining agreements, standardized testing procedures and other things that were not successfully implemented in the past.
2) All the schools go their separate ways. 3). Reorganize into a Regional School Unit (RSU). While this option has higher efficiency by creating a single board, budget, contracts and policies, it also gives up a level of town control. Maintaining local identity was a main driver behind the creation of the AOS.
4) Explore whether an Educational Service Center (ESC) can exist without an AOS. An ESC is a state-created system designed to promote central office efficiency where, in exchange for towns sharing services, the schools receive a fund reimbursement. Because the schools were already sharing services, AOS 98 added the ESC as an additional layer.
"One of the questions we're trying to examine is whether the ESC could exist without the level of AOS. Is that the best option for us?" Sinclair said.
On BRES's about $30 million renovation, trustees hired Senior Vice President Joseph P. Cuetara of Moors & Cabot’s Capital Markets Division as their municipal advisor for the bond process. They are still seeking bond council, which deals with the legal aspects of bond acquisition.
The school has also received $2.48 million in donations for the renovations: $848,334 in cash and $1.64 million in signed letters of intent.
CSD School Committee member Abigail Jones of Boothbay discussed increasing communication between boards, as well as efforts to share more information with the public. Earlier this month, they published a press release through the Register, and plan to continue to do so.
High school senior Kale Rogers is the new student representative for the trustees.

title: Kennebunk, Windham girls soccer show Class A South’s competitiveness
text:
KENNEBUNK — It was dark and chilly as Kennebunk senior Alina Auriemma dribbled down the sideline past her cheering teammates as the final seconds ticked off the clock. In the corner of Windham’s defensive zone, the regular season ended with a 2-1 Kennebunk win.
It’s time for the playoffs, and in Class A South, the most competitive tournament in the state will get underway.
The game Monday at Kennebunk High featured two of the best teams in this deep region. Both Kennbunk and Windham are 10-3-1. Windham will hold on to the No. 2 seed even with the loss. The Rams secured the No. 3 seed and a bye to the regional quarterfinals.
It’s been a season of close games in the league. This was Kennebunk’s fourth one-goal victory, and flipped the result of the Rams’ season-opening 2-1 loss at Windham.
“This could’ve easily been 2-1 them again,” Kennebunk coach Josh Viola said. “Two pretty even teams.”
This was Windham’s seventh one-goal game this season, and second one-goal loss in a row (the Eagles fell to Cheverus, 1-0, last Thursday). Even top-seeded and unbeaten Scarborough, winner of the last four regional championships, hasn’t run roughshod over the league. Six of the Red Storms’ 12 wins going into their regular-season finale against Sanford on Tuesday were decided by a single goal.
“Scarborough, we held them to one in double OT,” Viola said. “Unfortunately, that was one more than we scored.”
Last season, Viola’s Rams might have been the surprise of the league, winning 12 games and advancing to the Class A South semifinals. Nobody is surprised Kennebunk is among the top teams in the region this season, especially not the Rams.
Senior Ava McCourt scored the winning goal with 28:46 left in the second half, her sharp low shot from the left side finding the right corner of the net to give the Rams the 2-1 lead that held up. McCourt missed most of last season with a leg injury. A captain, she sees a team with a positive culture as it heads to the postseason.
“Everyone on this team, we’re one giant fun group,” McCourt said. “We all care. We come to practice ready to go.”
Viola didn’t hold back his praise for McCourt, calling her the best midfielder in the league. Auriemma is a returning all-conference player. Keeper Teagan Hanson rounds out Kennebunk’s trio of seniors, and is a steadying presence at the back of the Rams defense, Viola said. She doesn’t get rattled, and makes quiet saves.
If you’re looking for the dark horse in this season’s Class A South playoff race, the team that Kennebunk was a year ago, you have two choices. There’s Bonny Eagle, which won five games last season and snuck into the playoffs as the 11 seed in Class A South. The Scots, fifth in the Heal point standings, enter their regular-season finale against Portland on Tuesday with eight wins and an impressive 0-0 tie with Scarborough.
There’s also South Portland. The Red Riots, currently fourth in the Heals, missed the tournament a year ago with a 3-9-2 record. South Portland earned its 10th win Monday, beating Falmouth 4-1, and has chance to earn a bye out of the preliminary round.
Kennebunk and Windham know they have a little time to catch their breath and wait for a quarterfinals opponent. They also know they had a strong playoff-like test when they faced each other Monday night. As the No. 2 and No. 3 seeds, respectively, they could face off in a rubber match in the playoffs.
Don’t assume it will happen, though. In the SMAA, no win is guaranteed.

title: Maine voters must choose between listener and lecturer
text:
Brenda Power is a retired educator who lives in Ellsworth. She received the UMaine Distinguished Professor award in 1999.
I attended a town hall meeting of Troy Jackson’s in Ellsworth and witnessed a remarkable exchange.
A young woman stood up and said to Troy, “I want to support you. But I am an immigrant. I watch your campaign ads. You talk about the logging blockade in the 1990s, and how you worked so hard to keep foreigners from taking Maine jobs. How do I know you will support and help people like me, and not see me as a foreigner taking a Maine job?”
Her voice was shaky and lightly accented. Everyone could see how much courage it took for her to stand up and ask her question.
Troy paused. You could tell he was as moved as the audience by the question. He responded, “Thank you for speaking up. I’m sorry.”
He then explained how it was never his intention to castigate the Canadian workers. He saw the problem at that time as the same one we face today throughout Maine and the U.S. — large, wealthy corporations in Canada were using their workers as pawns.
He said he would have supported those Canadian workers immigrating to Maine for a better life, and was dedicated to finding pathways for immigrants in Maine, because we desperately need and want immigrants here. He vowed to look at the ad and improve his message, and thanked her for identifying a problem he needed to address.
After the session ended and most everyone left to partake in the pizza provided, Troy made a beeline to that woman for a private conversation. I noticed Troy mostly listened. At the end, he pulled out a contact card and wrote down a personal cellphone number, urging the woman to call if she wanted to continue the dialogue.
I couldn’t help but contrast that exchange with another I read about recently.
The last conversation Sen. Susan Collins had with Maine Planned Parenthood representatives was reportedly almost eight years ago, just weeks before the Kavanaugh vote. Nicole Clegg, the head of the Maine Planned Parenthood Action Fund, flew down with a small group of Maine women to D.C. in early August 2018, all of whom either worked with Planned Parenthood, or had received abortion care.
When they sat down to talk with Collins, they were stunned when she gave them little time to share their stories. As Clegg explained, “Before we could even have these women share their experiences, Senator Collins wanted to share her displeasure at the fact that during Colby [College’s] graduation ceremony, where she was the speaker, many Colby students wore ‘I Stand with Planned Parenthood’ stickers. That set the tone for the meeting. I left deeply regretful that I had asked these women to come down and do this. Because it was clear to me it did not have an impact. I actually communicated to their office to say ‘I can’t bring constituents into this space if I don’t think they are going to be respected.’”
Planned Parenthood of Maine has not had a conversation with Collins since.
These Maine women all showed great courage. One is an immigrant who worries any step outside her Maine home might bring her face to face with ICE. Yet she comes to a town hall to confront a candidate because she wants to understand his views and share her experience. The others flew to D.C. to share deeply personal trauma with a powerful legislator who was supposed to be their voice in Congress. One person listened. The other lectured.
It’s no wonder Troy Jackson has evolved in his views over the past 15 years, leading the Maine Legislature to pass one of the most thoughtful abortion rights laws in the country. And it’s also no wonder Susan Collins has “evolved” to support militant anti-abortion judges.
I hope Maine voters will also show some courage in the coming weeks. We have a choice to vote for someone who shows up and welcomes those who challenge him so that he can become a better representative. Or we can vote for the senator who hasn’t held a town hall in 25 years, preferring to lecture those who challenge her in private. The choice couldn’t be more clear.

title: Husson basketball programs set to tip off new campaigns
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - The Husson basketball programs have started preseason practice.
The women’s team is coming off a NAC semifinal appearance.
They spoke about building toward a deeper run at the conference title this season.
“To win (the NAC Championship) is definitely the main goal, but I think we’re all really determined. We know what we want. It’s kind of nice this year because I feel like we don’t have as much pressure on us this year. We’re kind of the underdogs to some people, so I think we’ll really play into that,” said Saige Evans, junior forward.
“It’s just been really good to meet everyone. I knew a lot of the freshmen coming in. I knew a few of the upperclassmen, but all the freshmen, we clicked instantly. We met all the upperclassmen, everyone’s just clicked, and it’s been really good,” said Addison Cyr, freshman forward.
The Eagles start with Gallaudet on Fri. Nov. 6 at 7 p.m. at the Brandeis Tip-Off Tournament in Massachusetts.
Husson’s home opener is on Sat. Nov. 21 at 1 p.m. against Southern Maine.
The men’s team also bowed out in the NAC semis last season.
The Eagles are a young group that is building to compete again.
“The biggest part is just setting the standard. Here at Husson, we have a standard that we always want to set. It’s good to get those young guys, obviously, the guys who have been here who know it, we make sure that we keep that standard and set it for them,” said Dylan Burpee, junior guard, forward.
“Every day we’ve been playing, getting used to each other, and the energy’s built up. Everyone’s starting to get to know each other, and now it looks amazing,” said Jayeson VanBeveren, senior forward, center.

title: This dog-like robot adds security layer to businesses nationwide
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WADDELL, Ariz. (InvestigateTV) — A high-tech robot is adding an extra layer of security at businesses across the country, combining AI technology and human expertise to track down security threats.
The robot, covered in sensors and about the size of a dog, conducts automated patrols at locations including a warehouse in Waddell, Arizona. The device checks gates, doors, locks and looks for people in places where they shouldn’t be.
“This robot has patrolled thousands of miles just in this yard,” said Ryan Hodgens of Asylon, the company behind the technology.
Robots patrol facilities nationwide
Hodgens said robots like this patrol distribution centers and manufacturing plants across the country. When on patrol, they provide live video feeds to a monitoring center in Pennsylvania where people are watching.
“We can stop the robot in one place, move the camera over, zoom in 40x to a door to inspect it,” Hodgens said. “We can, if we’re operating at night, switch over to thermal as well, to easily detect heat signatures.”
The technology is also used at large events including the DNC and RNC.
At the Indianapolis 500, the robot operates with a chemical gas detection sensor integrated on board underneath the tunnel system, Hodgens said.
Advanced navigation capabilities
The robot can navigate obstacles from tunnels to stairs thanks to about 20 sensors that are built in. Every single joint moves independently.
“There’s a lot of engineering work that’s gone into the stability piece,” Hodgens said. “In terms of its ability to stay upright, around curves, up and over gravel, uneven terrain here, the stability is truly unmatched.”
The movements sometimes mimic an animal so well that operators almost forget it’s a robot.
“Each one kind of has their own personality,” Hodgens said.
Privacy and operational details
On potential privacy concerns, Hodgens compared DroneDog to other closed circuit cameras.
“This camera happens to have four legs,” Hodgens said. “It’s the same exact kind of architecture on the back-end, in terms of privacy as all these other closed circuit cameras that we’re seeing around.”
The robot has a 90-minute battery life before returning to its charging station to recharge and rest up for the next patrol.
It includes a speaker that can communicate with people in its path using either pre-recorded messages or live communication.

title: How to avoid getting stuck with two mortgages during a move
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — Buying a new home before selling a current one can leave homeowners juggling two mortgages, or without a place to move into right away. A current home could sell quickly, while finding and closing on the next one may take longer in a competitive market.
Kate Wood, with NerdWallet, said lining up a sale and purchase perfectly is difficult in an imbalanced market, but there are ways to manage the overlap.
One option is a sale contingency, which ties the purchase of a new home to the successful sale of the current one.
“A sale contingency basically states some aspect of the purchase is contingent on, relies on you having successfully sold your home,” Wood said. “So when you are approaching a seller with this, saying, ‘Hey, in order for me to buy your home, I need to have sold my home,’ it’s a good idea to be working with a real estate agent that’s going to help you craft a really compelling offer.”
Wood noted that a sale contingency can make it harder to compete against cash buyers or those who are already pre-approved.
Another option is a bridge loan, which provides short-term financing to cover the gap between buying and selling.
“A bridge loan basically gives you a loan for 12 months or so that allows you to have the cash to make that next home purchase,” Wood said. “So you’re buying your next home, and then when you sell your previous home, you use proceeds from that sale to pay off the bridge loan.”
A home equity line of credit, or HELOC, is another option, though Wood said it needs to be set up before a home is listed for sale. A HELOC allows a homeowner to borrow against the equity in their current home to fund the purchase of a new one, then repay the loan using proceeds from the sale.

title: Jared Golden sends campaign cash to fellow Democrats around the country
text:
Outgoing U.S. Rep. Jared Golden of Maine may not be running for reelection this year, but he is deploying his campaign’s unspent war chest to boost fellow Democratic House candidates across the country.
From July through September, Golden’s campaign committee spent nearly $300,000, much of it in the form of campaign contributions.
Filings with the Federal Election Commission show Golden gave at least $1,000 each to Democratic candidates in Montana, Kentucky, Florida and elsewhere.
His largest contribution, $150,000, went to the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, the fundraising arm of House Democrats. He also made smaller donations to local candidates in Maine.
Golden has held Maine’s conservative-leaning 2nd Congressional District since 2018, but decided not to seek reelection this year.
Republican former governor Paul LePage and Democratic State Auditor Matt Dunlap are vying to succeed him in a race that has drawn national attention for its potential to determine which party controls Congress next year.
This story appears through a media partnership with Maine Public.

title: Longtime CNN anchor Christiane Amanpour leaving network after a storied career of 43 years
text:
(AP) - Longtime CNN anchor Christiane Amanpour will be leaving CNN after 43 years at the network.
The network’s chief international anchor will scale back her daily show, “Amanpour,” on CNN International to once a week at the beginning of 2027, and end the show at the end of May, leaving the network the following month. She said in a statement that she looks forward to “interesting new projects down the line.”
Amanpour, 68, also will end her PBS show, “Amanpour and Company,” at the end of the year, she said in her statement, shared by CNN. She will continue her podcast, “The Ex Files,” with her ex-husband, Jamie Rubin, a former U.S. diplomat.
“After many months of thought and a few sleepless nights, I have decided to separate from CNN, my partner of 43 fantastic years!” Amanpour said in the statement.
Amanpour also said she would “always be rooting for CNN and maintaining its history of independent journalism. Remember: always be truthful, not neutral.”
Amanpour’s exit coincides with a new era at CNN as it comes under a new owner, Skydance. After a yearlong process, Skydance-owned Paramount closed its $81 billion buyout of Warner Bros. Discovery on Oct. 6. The merger unites under one roof two giants in TV news — CBS and CNN.
On a personal front. Amanpour has spoken openly about her 2021 diagnosis of ovarian cancer and its later recurrence, calling it “the invisible killer.” She has urged others to “get all the scans that you can.”

title: Maine Launch Summit to put state's space industry in focus
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Aiming to pick up where the Maine Space Conference of 2024 left off, the Maine Space Corp. plans to convene the two-day Maine Launch summit next month.
The event is scheduled for Nov. 5-6 at Northeastern University’s Roux Institute at 100 Fore St. in Portland.
The summit is part of the Maine Space Corp.’s effort to expand Maine’s role in the growing global space economy. More than 90 Maine companies have some role in the space supply chain.
“By unifying these various companies, Maine will better position itself to compete in the rapidly expanding national and international space economy,” said John Karp, executive director of Maine Space Corp. “I am excited to gather our state’s space-focused manufacturers, entrepreneurs and industry leaders in one room where we will identify opportunities to advance Maine’s position in this industry.”
The Thursday, Nov. 5, sessions are by invitation only. Sessions on Friday, Nov. 6, are open to the public. For the full agenda and to register, visit the Maine Space Corp.’s website.
Development paths
The conference will showcase Maine’s space industry. Nov. 5 sessions will evaluate three possible launch concepts: from land, sea, or air.
The objective is to identify not only where launches occur but also the ecosystem that could generate the greatest long-term economic value, workforce opportunities, strategic partnerships and commercial competitiveness for Maine, according to a news release.
Supply chain
The Nov. 6 sessions will address the space supply chain. Participants will include existing Maine space supply chain manufacturers, manufacturers wishing to join the Maine space supply chain and out-of-state manufacturers considering moving to Maine to join the space supply chain.
An additional aim of the conference is to inform manufacturers and businesses in the state but not yet in the space business on ways they might participate by collaborating on contracts, workforce development and marketing.
The nonprofit Maine Space Corp. was created by Maine statute to develop a Maine Space Complex by leveraging the state’s geographic, rocketry, manufacturing and higher education assets and capabilities to establish the state as a destination for launching small launch vehicles and small satellites into polar orbit.

title: Rural Maine emergency services face more calls and fewer volunteers, study finds
text:
Rising call volume paired with limited volunteer availability are key issues facing rural Maine fire departments, according to a study released Friday by the Office of State Fire Marshal and the University of Maine.
For years Maine has heard dire warnings about the state of fire departments, but never had firm numbers to assess where things stand. The surveys, sent to fire departments in 2025, create a first-of-its-kind look at where the state’s fire services stand.
“It gives us this good snapshot of where we are now and we honestly need this information ongoing every year,” Sen. Chip Curry, D-Belfast, said. He worked two stints on the state’s Maine Emergency Medical Services Commission.
The survey was designed to count every firefighter in the state, as well as look at other issues facing the fire service. But only 219 of 347 departments, or 63%, responded to the survey.
A total of 5,611 firefighters are rostered for departments who took the survey, while the state has an estimated 9,087 firefighters.
“These are critical services, fire and EMS that we’re talking about,” Sen. Mike Tipping, D-Orono, said. “When they fail or when they’re late the results can be devastating.”
Maine has already seen the system fail. A woman died in rural Aroostook County after 10 ambulance services refused to respond in January 2025. The study released Friday has been touted as a step toward addressing the state’s coverage gaps.
Only 6% of the departments in the survey are fully career firefighters. The other 205 departments have volunteers with more than half operating fully volunteer. The number of volunteer firefighters has plummeted nationwide, with the service losing a quarter of its members in 15 years, according to the National Fire Protection Association.
Some level of emergency medical service is provided by 66% of the fire departments, the study found. They’ve seen a 42% increase in calls from 2014 to 2024. That change comes as Maine’s population ages, and people 65 and older call 911, for a variety of reasons, more often than their younger counterparts, according to a study published in Prehospital Emergency Care.
About 50% of Maine’s firefighters are younger than 40, but volunteer departments heavily rely on firefighters who are 50 and older, the study found. Those volunteers are starting to age out of service.
A Down East ambulance service will close in November because it cannot find enough volunteers to continue. Two of the four volunteers who are in their 80s are retiring.
The state needs to ensure volunteer firefighting is sustainable for the next 30 years, Curry said. He said there will be a package of legislation presented next year to modernize fire service and help volunteer services.
Full-time, paid career firefighting is not financially possible for the state, he said. It would cost $654.5 million a year, according to the study. That cost would result in property taxes no one could afford or fire fighting deserts, he said.
Training isn’t easily accessible for volunteers, especially those in western Maine, the study found. Staff have to drive a long way to reach a training facility. Oxford County has the fewest people certified to enter into a building fire, the study found.
It can be difficult to get interior teams into a fire until mutual aid arrives because of staffing, a department said in the survey.
The training distance can be a deterrent, especially because volunteers either need to take time off from day jobs or sacrifice time on their weekends, Curry said. He said he plans to propose a volunteer reimbursement program to the Legislature.
“We’ve got to invest in the volunteer fire service because the state can’t afford a career service all over the state,” Curry said.
The state has seen growing acceptance of regionalizing fire departments, as well as some departments taking their own initiative, the study found. Some areas share equipment and fire apparatus.
There are also more mutual aid activations, the study said. Kennebunk Fire Department has 20 mutual aid relationships, while Hermon fire has 21. The study maps all mutual aid responses, showing a tangled web of who responds where.
Moving forward there needs to be more support to meet minimum training, the study found.
Regionalization, where towns and departments work as a combined agency, is a way to save money in local budgets, the study said. There currently is no funding at the county level, the way a sheriff’s office is funded.
A centralized fire department means there isn’t a need to buy duplicates of expensive equipment and can make it easier for departments to submit grants and do fundraising, the study said.
The study created more breathing room for the state to look at longer term fixes, Tipping said. The state can help by supporting, but not mandating, regionalization, he said.
A comprehensive report is expected in early 2027.

title: Maine heating oil prices remain 80% higher than a year ago
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine’s heating oil prices remain 80% higher than a year ago.
The average cost for a gallon of heating oil is $5.97, unchanged since the week before, according to the Maine Department of Energy Resources.
That’s also lower than last month’s record high of $6.02.
Still, this time last year the average cost for a gallon of heating oil was $3.31, meaning the price is 80% higher.
That means it will cost Mainers an additional $731.50 to fill a standard 275-gallon tank.
In eastern and Down East Maine, prices range from a low of $5.50 to a high of $6.30.
The skyrocketing cost of heating oil has been fueled by President Donald Trump’s ongoing war against Iran, which effectively halted fuel shipments out of the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of the world’s natural gas and oil passes. The ongoing war between Russia and Ukraine also has strained global fuel supplies.
Maine is particularly vulnerable to such price shocks, because the state is heavily reliant on heating oil to keep warm during the winter.
This month, the Trump administration released about $37 million in low-income heating assistance to help Mainers stay warm during the coming winter. An additional $1.4 million was awarded to the state’s four federally recognized tribes.

title: No time for banged-up Patriots to recover
text:
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. — The Patriots are testing the boundaries of the “next man up” mentality that is preached across a league in which injuries are guaranteed every week.
New England has just three days to recover coming off a 26-19 win over the New York Jets, during which it lost three offensive linemen to injuries.
Right tackle Morgan Moses (ankle) and left guard Alijah Vera-Tucker (hamstring) were Week 1 starters, while Ben Brown (knee) was starting at right guard for the second straight week. Brown was in the lineup after Mike Onwenu (ankle) was placed on injured reserve after two games and Greg Van Roten, his original replacement, went on IR the following week.
“As bad as it is and as unfortunate as it is, that’s just the way this game goes,” left tackle Will Campbell said. “I feel like some guys stepped up big for us.”
The Patriots, who play at Chicago on Thursday night, are banged up at other spots. Wide receiver Romeo Doubs exited in the first quarter with a shoulder issue following his touchdown catch and was placed on injured reserve Monday. Coach Mike Vrabel acknowledged the injuries will require everyone to remain fluid this week.
“We’ll just have to figure out who we have available and find 48 to put out there,” Vrabel said.
Rookie Caleb Lomu, a week after coming in for Campbell, jumped in at right tackle for Moses, with Walter Rouse subbing in at right tackle and Matt Pryor at left guard.
Lomu, Rouse and Pryor helped open lanes that allowed the Patriots to eventually run out the clock in the fourth quarter.
“Everybody prepares as a starter. I can’t wait to watch those guys that prepare all week without knowing whether they’re going to get an opportunity to play,” Vrabel said. “And then when they do, take advantage of it, and that’s a testament to those players.”
What’s working
Despite the offensive line injuries, the group kept Drake Maye off the turf. The quarterback wasn’t sacked Sunday, the first time that’s happened this season. He has been sacked only twice over the past three games after being taken down nine times in the first three.
What needs help
Ball security. The Patriots are second in the NFL this season with 13 turnovers (six lost fumbles, seven interceptions), behind the Los Angeles Chargers with 15 (seven fumbles, eight INTs).
Fixing that is a top priority.
“We’ll rep it more. We’ll put more time into it, I guess. I don’t know how you can put any more time into the amount of ball security drills we do,” Vrabel said. “I’m certainly cognizant. You can put it on me. That’s probably the easiest thing.”
Stock up
Lomu and Pryor. They allowed zero pressures on Maye during their combined 106 snaps.
Stock down
WR DeMario Douglas. He caught a 9-yard touchdown in the second quarter, but also had a 39-yard catch that ended with him getting the ball ball punched out from behind by Jamien Sherwood. The fumble led to a Jets field goal.
Injuries
The Patriots have moved quickly to replenish the backup depth on the offensive line, adding Andrew Rupcich and Jacob Rizy to the practice squad.
Key number
2 — The number of consecutive games Maye has gone without a turnover.
Next steps
The Patriots have a short turnaround before heading to Chicago for Thursday’s primetime matchup.

title: Gov. Mills attends Blue Ambition conference in Ireland
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine Gov. Janet Mills attends Blue Ambition conference in Ireland
Gov. Janet Mills has begun a four-day trip to Ireland by speaking at Blue Ambition, a global gathering of policymakers, industry leaders and researchers with a focus on innovation, investment and growth in the blue bioeconomy.
Mills spoke to Blue Ambition attendees Monday, highlighting Maine as a great place for investment. She also met with economic and government leaders from across the world.
"Maine and Ireland share more than our rocky coasts and rolling green hills; we are united in our common values of resilience, community, and respect for our traditions — especially our maritime heritage which continues to drive innovation and opportunity across our blue economies," Mills said in a statement. "I'm grateful to visit Ireland to explore new ways to strengthen our ties and to meet with government and business officials to expand opportunities for collaboration on everything from oyster farming to education. I look forward to building on our great partnership to create a more sustainable future for generations to come."
Blue Ambition was held during the first day of the fifth Global Bioeconomy Summit, which is a four-day gathering of world leaders who are focused on advancing bio-based economic opportunities.
Mills said that over the coming days, she will discuss trade and investment opportunities with Irish businesses and hold bilateral meetings with Irish government leaders on trade, renewable energy and educational initiatives.
The governor has already met with Irish Senate President Mark Daly, who launched the American Irish State Legislatures Caucus in 2021. Daly visited the Maine State House in Augusta in 2024 as part of his extensive travels across the United States.
Mills also met with Irish Agriculture, Food, and Marine Minister Timmy Dooley to discuss opportunities for trade and collaboration.

title: "A clear danger": Maine school district bans e-bikes from district property
text:
"A clear danger": Turner, Maine school district bans e-bikes from district property
A school district in Maine announced on Monday that it is banning e-bikes from all district property, effective immediately.
Cari Medd, Superintendent for MSAD 52, which includes Leavitt Area High School in Turner, posted a letter on Monday saying there have been numerous incidents on school grounds this school year involving dangerous riding and near-miss accidents.
"We have been growing increasingly concerned for the safety and well-being of our students and those who are sharing our roads and parking lots," Medd wrote.
She said, given the volume of reports and complaints, the district had to act immediately to prevent a serious accident from happening.
"We support students being active and outside. We support the use of regular, human-powered bicycles and will continue to welcome them on our property. However, E-bikes, many of which are illegal for any operator under 16 years old, present a clear danger to those coming to our campuses to work, attend school, and visit," Medd wrote.
She said the School Board is working to update district policy concerning recreational vehicles on school property.
Just last month, police in Farmington shared some safety reminders regarding the use of e-bikes and e-motos as their popularity grows in Maine.
Statewide data has shown a significant increase in the number of crashes involving e-bikes since 2021, mirroring a similar trend across the country, with dozens reported in both 2025 and 2026.
If you ride an e-bike (or any bike)
- Follow all traffic laws, signs, and signals
- Ride predictably and maintain control
- Wear a properly fitted helmet
- Use lights and reflectors when visibility is reduced
- Be especially cautious at intersections, driveways, and when crossing roadways
- Never assume a driver sees you—even if you have the right-of-way.
If you are driving a motor vehicle
- Stay alert and actively look for bicycles and e-bikes
- Check carefully before turning, changing lanes, or entering a roadway
- Yield to bicyclists when required
- Give bicyclists adequate space when passing
- Slow down and eliminate distractions
Police said drivers need to remember that bicycles and e-bikes are legitimate roadway users who deserve the same attention and consideration as everyone else.

title: Two Hancock County lawyers vie to replace controversial probate judge
text:
Hancock County has effectively not had its own sitting probate judge for more than a year, but that will change following the November election contest between two local lawyers.
One of them, Matt Foster, is a former local district attorney who lost reelection in 2022 after he was caught lying during a candidates forum.
Foster, a Republican, is competing against Democrat Brian Thomas, a former archaeologist and current Lamoine land trust lawyer, to fill a seat that’s been largely in limbo since April 2025.
The county’s current probate judge, William B. Blaisdell IV, has been suspended both from his part-time job presiding in probate court and from working as a lawyer after facing a string of contempt orders in neighboring Waldo County for repeated overdue child support payments to his ex-wife. He also admitted to a judge to not paying state or federal income taxes for at least three years, according to court records.
Blaisdell, who turned himself in at Hancock County jail in mid-March after he failed to appear in court, is barred from practicing law for the next three years or from presiding on the bench. He is listed as Hancock County’s elected probate judge on the county’s website, but did not seek to run for re-election.
Thomas decided to run in June as a write-in candidate after learning that no Democrat — or any candidate — was planning to challenge Foster for the seat.
“I didn’t think that was a good approach to finding a judge,” Thomas recently told the Bangor Daily News, adding he didn’t think judges should be partisan elected officials in the first place. “The system is what it is, so we live with that. There is a candidate on the Republican ticket, and I don’t feel like that is somebody I have a lot of confidence in to be handling a position like that.”
Foster was investigated by state officials in 2017 and 2018 — while he was the district attorney for Hancock and Washington counties — for allegedly inappropriately touching a 13-year-old child living with him at the time. He later denied the allegations and was never charged with a crime.
Foster lost his 2022 reelection bid as the two counties’ top prosecutor post after lying during a candidates forum about whether he had ever been investigated by the state attorney general’s office. He lost his re-election bid to current District Attorney Bob Granger.
“What strikes me about that is that this was a person whose first instinct was to lie, and I just don’t think that’s the right temperament for being a judge,” Thomas said of Foster.
Also, in 2020 when he was district attorney, Foster was accused of posting a racist meme on Facebook that mocked looters who pillaged stores during protests over the death of George Floyd, the Ellsworth American reported at the time. Foster denied being responsible for the post and said that his account may have been hacked.
Foster did not respond to multiple interview requests this past week from the BDN.
The former prosecutor, who now runs Downeast Legal Services on State Street in Ellsworth, hung up on a BDN reporter in mid-March after filing to run for the seat. The reporter did not have time to ask about the race before Foster terminated the call.
Thomas received 1,300 votes in the Democratic primary in June, well surpassing the 300 needed to qualify as the Democratic nominee for the November ballot.
Thomas has never served as a judge, but he has had a wide range of jobs in the past. He was a state representative in Georgia for nine years after serving in the U.S. Army, and has spent much of his professional career as an archeologist focused on environmental permitting. He’s also worked as a newspaper copy editor and UPS driver, he said.
“I’ve been in a lot of parts of the economy, and I think I have a much better connection to the range of people that are going to be before the court,” Thomas said. “I didn’t grow up rich — I’ve lived under the poverty line and I’m the first person in my family to ever go to college — so I’ve got a background that will lend itself well to being able to talk to people, evaluate things and make good decisions. I’ll make mistakes, everybody does, but they won’t be mistakes of ego.”
Thomas described Blaisdell’s tenure as a “complete embarrassment” and a “horrible state of affairs,” noting the troubled lawyer hasn’t been able to serve for more than a year and still has refused to resign his position.
During Blasidell’s absence, the county’s probate cases — many of which involve sensitive family matters like estates, guardianships and name changes — have been handled by other probate judges from nearby counties.
“What’s really necessary is somebody to actually show up and do the job — the bar is set so low right now, it’s just sad,” Thomas said. “Presumably, there’s going to be quite a backlog of cases.”

title: Organization is trying to help healers amid Oregon nursing shortage
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
PORTLAND, Ore. (Aging Untold)— Oregon faces a nursing crisis that experts say stems not from a lack of licensed nurses, but from workplace conditions that drive healthcare workers away from frontline positions.
The U.S. will see nearly 200,000 job openings for registered nurses each year until 2032, according to the American Association of Colleges of Nursing. Higher nurse-to-patient ratios can increase the likelihood of errors and decrease patient satisfaction, researchers at Ohio University found.
Oregon has more licensed nurses than ever before, but 30% of new nurses leave their first jobs within their first year out of nursing school, according to the Oregon Center for Nursing.
“My belief is that in Oregon, we don’t actually have a nursing shortage. What we have is a vacancy crisis, and that’s because of persistent, unhealthy work environment, increased stress, increased workplace violence,” Christy Simila, director of professional practice at the Oregon Nurses Association, said.
Nurses seek healing after pandemic trauma
Registered nurse Heather Sweeney and therapist Amy Ponteri started “Helping Healthcare Heal” to address what they saw as insufficient resources for healthcare workers in intense settings like emergency rooms.
“We never healed from that — they just give you a pizza party and say, ‘It’s time to move on, COVID’s over, here we go.’ Nobody gave us an opportunity to heal,” Sweeney said.
The organization offers retreats, support groups and continuing education for healthcare workers. Sweeney described the pressure many nurses feel to work extra shifts.
“And then you get all these text messages every day of open shifts, and you feel like you should go pick it up because you don’t want to leave your teammate down. But, then all of a sudden, you’ve worked 60 hours in the week,” Sweeney said.
Nurses find alternative roles
Simila said many nurses are taking jobs adjacent to frontline healthcare settings, such as nurse coaches, consultants or working in call centers doing triage.
Susan Ashenfelter, a nurse who participated in the healing programs, said the retreats helped her process intense experiences.
“I realized I had time to process some really, intense things that I’ve gone through in the last year or two that I had not had time to do,” Ashenfelter said.
Penny Haggerty, another participating nurse, said the experience was transformative.
“It was just like something new happened to me inside myself,” Haggerty said. “Just being with the other women, hearing their stories, learning from the ladies. Just came back empowered.”
New laws address working conditions
A law in Oregon is meant to address nurse-to-patient ratios in hospitals.
“I think hospitals can really start by listening to their nurses and what the nurses need, and really working to create a more healthy work environment, working to create a safer work environment, or where nurses aren’t showing up and potentially being subject to workplace violence as often,” Simila said.

title: Jackson doesn't regret telling Collins to 'shut up' after protester interrupted Senate debate
text:
Troy Jackson doesn't regret telling Sen. Susan Collins to 'shut up' after protester interrupted Maine debate
Maine Democrat Troy Jackson says he does not regret telling Sen. Susan Collins that she should “shut up” after the Republican suggested a protester who interrupted their recent debate was one of his campaign's backers.
"She said that it was a Troy supporter. She accused me of setting that up. I had no idea who it was,” said Jackson, a former president of the state Senate who is trying to deny Collins, the longest-serving Republican woman in Senate history, a sixth term. He spoke in an interview with CNN’s “State of the Union” that aired Sunday.
During their final debate Thursday night in the closely contested race, as the Nov. 3 election nears, a protester opposing data centers began yelling as Collins spoke. While moderators asked for that person to be removed, the senator said the demonstrator was “obviously one of Troy’s supporters.”
Jackson responded: “Oh, shut up. I don’t even know that kid.”
The Sunrise Movement group posted on its Instagram page that the outburst came from one of its members. In a caption of an Instagram post, the group's page said: “We’re proud of this Sunrise volunteer who took action yesterday.”
The New York Times said the protester, Henry Elgie, a 19-year-old student at Bowdoin College in Maine, told the newspaper in an interview Saturday that he had “zero coordination” with Jackson's campaign. "I do not know Troy Jackson personally or at all,” he was quoted as saying.
The Sunrise Movement is a left-wing political advocacy organization that champions the Green New Deal, aimed at transitioning the U.S. economy to 100% renewable energy. The group, which has local arms around the country, regularly organizes protests, sit-ins and climate strikes.
Jackson told CNN that he shook hands with Collins after each of their debates.
“But what I’m not going to be is talked down to by Sen. Collins,” he said. He added: "I’m fighting for Mainers and I just think that was another situation where she was talking down to me and I’m not going to apologize for that.”
Collins told Fox News’ Sean Hannity on Friday that she was “struck by how reflexive the response, ‘Oh, shut up,’ was.” Collins said, "the fact that it seemed like such an automatic, quick reply was very telling.”
She cited what she said was “the reputation” that Jackson had in the Legislature “particularly when he’s dealing with women with whom he disagrees. So in some ways it didn’t surprise me.”
Some state lawmakers who worked with Jackson have criticized him as having a temper, including once throwing a plastic water bottle on the ground in frustration while disagreeing with a female lawmaker. Asked by reporters during the campaign about the confrontations, Jackson said, "I wear my heart on my sleeve.” He took responsibility for his outburst and apologized to those he had confrontations with at the time.
Jackson was asked on CNN about some Republicans who are saying there were stories that he was aggressive in his tone to women from his time in the Legislature and that his remark Thursday night was another example of that.
Jackson said some Republicans have been spending millions “attacking me and my family, making untrue claims. … So it doesn’t surprise me."

title: Van Buren to Vote on Funds for New Playground
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
VAN BUREN, Maine (WAGM) - Families in Van Buren could soon have a new place for children to play.
The Town of Van Buren is holding a Special Town Meeting tomorrow night, Tuesday, October 20th at 6:00 PM in the Town Council Chambers at 320 Main Street. Residents will be asked to consider and vote on the purchase and installation of new playground equipment at the Champlain Street Recreation Park. The proposed $160,000 project would be funded through $60,000 from the Town’s undesignated funds and $100,000 through a 10-year bank loan. According to town documents, the original playground, built in 1971, deteriorated and no longer met safety standards. Documents say the playground was no longer able be insured, and the town had to remove it due to safety and liability concerns. The Champlain Street Recreation Park has been without playground equipment for three years now. The proposal for new equipment has received the recommendation of both the Town Council and Budget Committee. Town officials say residents are encouraged to attend and participate in this important community decision.

title: Future of Bangor Mall redevelopment uncertain after investor group loses lead backer
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - The local investor group working to buy and redevelop the Bangor Mall says it has lost its lead investor in what the group’s leader calls an 11th-hour setback.
Mike Cole, who leads Bangor Marketplace and Residences LLC, told WABI Monday the loss was a “gut punch” to the effort.
He said the party stepped away for personal reasons. He declined to say who the party was or what those reasons were.
Cole said the group is now looking for someone to step in to help move the project forward. He says they need between $4 and $6 million to close the deal.
“If I didn’t do this, and it failed, just because we needed one person that was sitting out there that didn’t hear this, that would be horrible,” Cole said. “That is the elite piece of real estate in Bangor. It’s kind of a no brainer. When you look at this top to bottom, when you see what we have and you see the numbers that we have, it’s definitely, we have to do this.”
In April, Cole told WABI the group had signed an agreement to buy the struggling mall, then estimated at about 30% occupied, from Namdar Realty Group. The vision, called Bangor Marketplace & Residences, called for tens of millions of dollars in investment for 200-plus condominiums, assisted living, medical offices, and outlet-style retail.
The city rezoned the mall’s commercial area several years ago to allow housing to support such a redevelopment.
Cole said through this process the plans haven’t changed, but development priorities have shifted.
“The whole condo and assisted living idea, those have been tabled. First, we need to stabilize the property,” Cole said. “So, the big focus is, yes, it’s always going to be the Bangor Mall and it’s going to have retail, but the entertainment side of things and things to do is really what’s going to stabilize the whole thing. So, we have signed some exciting new things that’s coming in. I can’t say what it is, but it’s exciting.”
Cole said there are non-disclosure agreements that prevent him from saying what the entertainment-style businesses would be.
We will continue to follow this story as it develops.

title: National Guard member is shot while breaking up a fight in Washington, suspect is hit in return fire
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — A National Guard member was shot and injured while trying to break up a fight in the nation’s capital, and the person suspected of firing the gun also was shot in an exchange with guard members, police said Monday.
The shooting happened at about 11:10 p.m. Sunday as seven or eight guard members in a parked van were monitoring the fight on a sidewalk in southeast Washington, in the Eastern Market neighborhood, said Jeffery Carroll, interim chief of the Metropolitan Police Department of Washington.
“They exited their vehicle to try to intervene to try to stop the fight from occurring when they heard gunshots,” Carroll told reporters. “An individual that had been involved in the fight had pulled out a firearm and began shooting.”
The person ran into an alley, Carroll said, and guard members immediately told the person to drop the gun.
“The individual then pointed the weapon toward National Guard members, who returned fire,” Carroll said.
He said one guard member was struck in the leg and the suspect was shot in the abdomen. Both were taken to hospitals for treatment for non-life-threatening injuries, he said.
Three guard members discharged their guns in the encounter, Carroll said. He said the suspect was arrested.
President Donald Trump deployed the guard to Washington in August 2025 as part of what he said was a crime-fighting mission. The force, which rose to a peak of about 5,000 troops over the summer, has supported arrest operations, patrolled city streets and neighborhoods and participated in cleanup efforts.
Trump’s Republican administration says the deployment has contributed to a decrease in crime in the city, where crime was already on the decline before the guard arrived. Officials, activists and residents in the overwhelmingly Democratic city say the deployment is a waste of taxpayer money and has normalized the militarization of a major American city.
The police department is investigating the Sunday night shooting. Carroll said there were no further threats to the community and asked for anyone with information on the shooting to contact police.

title: ‘Mister Miracle’ Series Reveals First Look and Voice Cast
text:
‘Mister Miracle’ Animated Series Reveals First Look and Voice Cast
The animated Mister Miracle series from DC (and set within the DCU) has its two stars.
“Welcoming Josh Hutcherson as Mister Miracle and Mackenzie Davis as Big Barda in [Tom King]’s forthcoming animated DCU series,” wrote DC’s James Gunn, along with an image from the series, which is based on King’s Mister Miracle comic.
READ MORE: The Worst Performances in DC Comics Movies
Mitch Gerads, who illustrated King’s Mister Miracle comic series commented on Gunn’s post, writing “and let me tell you, Josh and Mackenzie’s performances are PERFECT. Get those veggie trays ready, DCU fans!”
King and Gerads’ Miracle Miracle was published by DC from 2017 to 2019, and won multiple Eisner Awards. In the 12-part series, Mister Miracle and Big Barda are caught up in the eternal war between Apokalips and New Genesis, while Miracle also grapples with his trauma from a lifetime fighting the forces of darkness.
The Mister Miracle character, a superhuman escape artist, was created by legendary comic creator Jack Kirby in 1971 as part of Kirby’s “Fourth World” of interconnected series at DC, which also included New Gods and Forever People. Mister Miracle and Big Barda (a Fourth World warrior and Mister Miracle’s love interest, also created by Kirby) have remained DC fixtures ever since, and have occasionally served as members of the Justice League of America.
King’s DC work is clearly a favorite of DC Studios co-CEO James Gunn; King’s Supergirl: Woman of Tomorrow was adapted to last summer’s Supergirl movie and King was also a co-creator and producer and writer on the recent HBO Max series Lanterns.

title: J. Edward Knight Insurance welcomes Kristy Cromwell to Boothbay Harbor team
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
J. Edward Knight Insurance, a leading provider of insurance solutions in Midcoast Maine since 1898, is pleased to announce the addition of Kristy Cromwell to its Boothbay Harbor team. Cromwell recently joined the agency and has successfully earned her license to sell personal lines insurance, bringing a strong foundation of administrative expertise, customer care, and deep ties to the local community.
Cromwell comes to J. Edward Knight Insurance with nearly two decades of professional experience across healthcare administration and client services. Her background includes serving as an advanced medical support assistant at Togus Primary Care in Augusta, as well as an administrative technician at Bath Iron Works. Over her career, she has held administrative and care roles at several Midcoast Maine organizations, including Midcoast Medical Group Nephrology in Bath, Martin’s Point Health Care in Brunswick, Wiscasset Family Medicine, and Lincoln Medical Partners in Boothbay Harbor.
"We are thrilled to welcome Kristy to our Boothbay Harbor team," said Robert Wheeler, president of J. Edward Knight Insurance. "Her extensive background in client-focused administration and deep familiarity with the local Midcoast community make her a fantastic addition. Earning her personal lines insurance license is a great accomplishment, and we are excited to see her bring that same dedication and care to helping our clients protect what matters most."
A graduate of Wiscasset High School, Cromwell’s extensive experience in customer service, scheduling, accurate documentation, and administrative operations positions her well to help personal lines insurance clients protect what matters most.
" I have never joined a company or organization that has made me feel so welcome and supported from day one. J. Edward Knight is the greatest group of individuals that combined, make up the best work family," Kristy said.
Outside of her professional work, Cromwell resides in Windsor with her husband and child. Above all, she treasures family time, shares a passion for stock car racing, hockey, and football, and is an avid reader whenever time permits.
In her new role at the Boothbay Harbor office, Cromwell will assist clients with personal insurance solutions, including home, auto, and personal liability coverage.

title: Why Troy Jackson says he doesn’t regret telling Susan Collins to ‘shut up’ during Maine Senate debate
text:
WASHINGTON — Maine Democrat Troy Jackson says he does not regret telling Sen. Susan Collins that she should “shut up” after the Republican suggested a protester who interrupted their recent debate was one of his campaign’s backers.
“She said that it was a Troy supporter. She accused me of setting that up. I had no idea who it was,” said Jackson, a former president of the state Senate who is trying to deny Collins, the longest-serving Republican woman in Senate history, a sixth-term. He spoke in an interview with CNN’s “State of the Union” that aired Sunday.
During their final debate Thursday night in the closely contested race as the Nov. 3 election nears, a protester opposing data centers began yelling as Collins spoke. While moderators asked for that person to be removed, the senator said the demonstrator was “obviously one of Troy’s supporters.”
Jackson responded: “Oh, shut up. I don’t even know that kid.”
The Sunrise Movement group posted on its Instagram page that the outburst came from one of its members. In a caption of an Instagram post, the group’s page said: “We’re proud of this Sunrise volunteer who took action yesterday.”
The New York Times said the protester, Henry Elgie, a 19-year-old student at Bowdoin College in Brunswick, told the newspaper in an interview Saturday that he had “zero coordination” with Jackson’s campaign. “I do not know Troy Jackson personally or at all,” he was quoted as saying.
Jackson told CNN that he shook hands with Collins after each of their debates.
“But what I’m not going to be is talked down to by Sen. Collins,” he said. He added: “I’m fighting for Mainers and I just think that was another situation where she was talking down to me and I’m not going to apologize for that.”
Collins told Fox News’ Sean Hannity on Friday that she was “struck by how reflective the response, ‘Oh, shut up,’ was.” Collins said “the fact that it seemed like such an automatic, quick reply was very telling.”
She cited what she said was “the reputation” that Jackson had in the Maine Legislature “particularly when he’s dealing with women with whom he disagrees. So in some ways it didn’t surprise me.”
Some state lawmakers who worked with Jackson have criticized him as having a temper, including once throwing a plastic water bottle on the ground in frustration while disagreeing with a female lawmaker. Asked by reporters during the campaign about the confrontations, Jackson said, “I wear my heart on my sleeve.” He took responsibility for his outburst and apologized to those he had confrontations with at the time.
Jackson said some Republicans have been spending millions “attacking me and my family, making untrue claims. … So it doesn’t surprise me.”

title: Medway man arrested on arson charges after two fires, authorities say
text:
MEDWAY, Maine (WABI) - A man was arrested for arson in connection with two separate fires - one in Medway and another Woodville.
Paul York, 41, of Medway is also charged with criminal mischief and violating conditions of release.
The first fire happened at a camper on Turnpike Road in Medway on September 30th.
The Fire Marshal’s Office says the camper was destroyed and a nearby mobile home and storage shelter were damaged.
The next day, investigators were called to a gravel pit in Woodville for a vehicle fire.
Authorities determined the camper and vehicle were both owned by York.
