title: 'Office Space' actor Richard Riehle dies at 78
text:
Longtime actor Richard Riehle, known for roles in 'Office Space,' and 'The Fugitive,' dies at 78
Longtime actor Richard Riehle, known for roles in "Office Space," "Casino," and "The Fugitive," has died at 78.
TMZ was the first to report his death.
Wright Entertainment Inc. said Monday that Riehle had died Oct. 15 but disclosed no cause or details. "Our industry has lost an exceptional talent, and our community has lost a truly wonderful man," said a statement.
In "Office Space," Riehle appeared as Tom Smykowski, an Initech staffer whose job was to communicate with clients and relay their concerns to the company's technical team.
Riehle had over 400 credits as an actor, per his IMDB page. Notably, he portrayed Santa Claus in eight different projects.
During his career, Riehle became a prolific character actor in TV and film, often playing authority figures but equally skilled at comedy.
"If a casting director has found themselves in need of a burly, blustery, mustachioed man for their project, Richard Riehle has likely been near the top of their list," The AV Club said in 2017.
He fell into acting as a senior at the University of Notre Dame. He couldn't really afford to stay another year but was told he could take all the credits he needed in speech and drama in one semester. He stayed.
"I spent a semester doing anything and everything that you do in the theater — acting, directing, building sets, etc. — and then for some reason they liked what I did enough that they got me a teaching assistantship at the University of Minnesota. So I went on and got my MFA (Masters of Fine Arts). I figured, 'What the heck? If they're gonna pay me to do it, I'm gonna do it!'" he told the AV Club.
He had his first lines in the 1977 movie "Joyride" alongside Desi Arnaz Jr., Anne Lockhart, Robert Carradine and Melanie Griffith. He'd go on to appear in the broad comedy "Bridesmaids," the comedy-mystery "Shadows and Fog" for Woody Allen, "Black Rain" with Michael Douglas and the sitcom "Grounded For Life."
Riehle's almost five-decade career also included playing a quartermaster in the Civil War drama "Glory," a prison guard in "The Fugitive," an air marshal in "Executive Decision," a police officer in a guest spot on "The West Wing" and a principal on the TV adaptation of "Ferris Bueller's Day Off."
He had an affinity for the "Star Trek" world, landing parts in three franchises — "Star Trek: The Next Generation" in 1992, "Star Trek: Voyager" in 2000 and "Star Trek: Enterprise" in 2004. He was on Broadway three times, including with Paul Giamatti in a 1999 revival of "The Iceman Cometh."
"Beyond his immense talent, he will be remembered for his genuine goodness, boundless kindness, and unwavering generosity, particularly toward emerging actors and filmmakers, whom he encouraged and supported at every opportunity," Wright Entertainment said.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: Safety system can stop planes that overshoot runways, but most airports don’t have it
text:
Miami, Florida (InvestigateTV) — In the hours after an Amazon cargo plane overshot the runway at Miami International Airport in September, crashing through a fence and hitting two vehicles on a road bordering the facility, investigators from the National Transportation Safety Board swarmed the scene.
Their leader, NTSB Chair Jennifer Homendy, used three words to describe the aftermath of the crash, “Devastating. Utter devastation.”
Aerial video of the scene shows deep black scars cut into the earth at the edge of the airport property, where charred, twisted metal sits scattered well beyond the tarmac — pieces of a cargo jet thrown where a plane was never meant to go.
“You can see on the paved surface, tire marks that continues in the grass. There’s debris everywhere,” Homendy said.
The plane, a Boeing 767, had overrun the airport runway by 1,200 feet according to the NTSB — killing five people riding in its path. The accident is what the agency calls an “excursion”, where a plane goes off the runway.
Since 2008, more than 3,000 have been investigated by the NTSB.
InvestigateTV analyzed NTSB accident data and found nearly one-fifth of those excursions involved planes that went beyond the end of the runway, with some leading to deaths.
Lives lost in accidents like this raise an inevitable question: Could specific safety technology have prevented tragedy?
A system that’s designed to slow planes and save lives in overruns is available and has already prevented serious crashes involving commercial airliners and smaller private jets across the country. Yet, InvestigateTV discovered most American airports don’t have it installed.
Renewed focus on runway overrun solutions
As investigators sort through the pieces of the Amazon crash, there’s renewed interest in technology that some believe could have been a potential difference maker in a situation like Miami. It’s called EMAS: engineered material arresting system.
“Should EMAS be everywhere at every airport? That will be a key part of our investigation,” Homendy said.
It’s a valid question as regulators look for potential solutions to deal with overruns. Since the 1980s, federal regulations have required commercial airports to have Runway Safety Areas that extend 1,000 feet beyond the end of the runway.
But many airports built before those regulations were implemented simply don’t have enough space to provide that buffer, so they need an alternative in the event of an overrun. That’s where EMAS comes in.
EMAS is made up of crushable concrete pads constructed with individual blocks stacked like stair steps at the end of a runway. The technology was developed by the Federal Aviation Administration in the 1990s with several partners, including a company called ESCO, now Runway Safe — the sole manufacturer of EMAS approved for use in the United States.
“When it engages with the tires - it just crumbles. It crumbles right down to a dust. That is what absorbs the kinetic energy, believe it or not, from the whole aircraft with all of its landing gear,” said Trip Thomas, Runway Safe’s director of commercialization.
InvestigateTV was given an exclusive look inside Runway Safe’s New Jersey facility, where hundreds of pallets of EMAS blocks were being prepped for delivery. To construct an entire bed for an arresting system, Thomas said an average of about 3,000-3,500 blocks is needed to provide the cushion that ultimately slows a plane in crisis.
“His wheel will be just crushing down most of the way. And he’s got this wall of material in front of him. And it’s just the effort, the energy he uses to crush the blocks is what decelerates the aircraft,” he said.
EMAS has saved lives, yet most airports lack the technology
InvestigateTV’s examination of FAA data shows EMAS has been involved in stopping aircraft in 26 overruns to date, including Boeing 737s carrying dozens of travelers and crew as well as smaller Cessnas carrying just a pilot and passenger. Yet the system is not found at many airports across the United States.
In fact, the FAA says just 70 domestic facilities have EMAS installed. Twelve of those facilities are at major airports including John F. Kennedy International Airport in New York, O’Hare International Airport in Chicago and Logan International Airport in Boston.
Some smaller airports with commercial traffic have also put EMAS onto their runways including Hilton Head, South Carolina, DeKalb Airport near Atlanta, Baton Rouge, Louisiana and Telluride, Colorado.
OTD in 2018, a passenger plane overran a runway during landing at @fly_BUR in Burbank, California. Thanks to the crushable concrete of the Engineered Materials Arresting System, none of the 117 people onboard were injured. Read more about EMAS at https://t.co/SDIpgeKUFc. https://t.co/HLOZxbGObw
— The FAA ✈️ (@FAANews) December 6, 2021
To be clear, EMAS is not required, even if airports do not have the 1,000-foot buffer laid out in that federal Runway Safety Area requirement, but it is a strongly-recommended option for airports facing limited space.
Ultimately it is airports and local governments that are the ones weighing the multi-million dollar cost versus the risk.
“Some airports do look at it strictly very much like an insurance policy which I think is a bit simplistic, but I can understand the basic thinking to it,” Thomas said. “With the Miami situation we are hoping here and we’re planning to go talk to some people about is maybe we should really be looking at these runway ends from a risk reduction potential.”
Safety zones and limitations
It’s a critical consideration.
Using FAA data, InvestigateTV mapped the areas of highest risk at the end of runways located at the more than 500 commercial airports across the U.S. that accept scheduled passenger service.
These defacto “danger zones” included a trapezoidal area extending 1,000 feet beyond each physical runway end, widening with distance from 500 feet to 1,000 feet, and were modeled to bridge FAA standards for a Runway Safety Area, Runway Object Free Area and Runway Protection Zone for each runway.
Based on published FAA guidelines and agency-funded external research, the shape captures the potential for an aircraft to deviate from the centerline during an overrun.
Comparing these “danger zones” with U.S. Census street data, InvestigateTV’s analysis found hundreds of commercial airports where at least one runway had an active public road running through the mapped area.
After a 2005 crash at Midway in Chicago, the FAA worked for more than a decade to bring airports into compliance with its Runway Safety Area standards, with facilities having three main options: retooling the airport’s layout through land purchases and relocating structures and roads, installing an EMAS, or functionally shortening runways to allow for the needed space.
Most of the facilities InvestigateTV identified as having roads encroaching into areas at risk of an overrun do not have EMAS beds to slow planes — including large, busy passenger airports such as Baltimore/Washington International Thurgood Marshall Airport (BWI), Nashville International Airport (BNA) and Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport (PHX).
FAA data and airport records show all three of those airports utilize a “displaced threshold” where the official takeoff or landing distances available to aircraft are reduced, shifting the functional end of the runway back and creating the additional space needed to fit into the FAA’s requirements.
InvestigateTV reached out to the airports about the data findings and to ask if there has been any consideration of adding an EMAS, either in the past or in the wake of the crash in Miami.
“At Phoenix Sky Harbor, safety is the top priority. The airport meets or exceeds all Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) runway safety design standards,” a spokesperson said in an emailed response. The spokesperson did not directly address the use of EMAS, but said that any future runway development at the airport “will also meet FAA runway safety design standards.”
A spokesperson for the Metropolitan Nashville Airport Authority said EMAS was used to meet FAA standards at the body’s smaller facility, John C. Tune Airport (JWN) but that requirements at the larger airport were otherwise accomplished.
“At BNA, we were able to provide the full 1,000-foot-long by 500-foot-wide safety areas beyond the runway ends. At JWN, we were able to accommodate a 1,000-foot safety area at the north end of the runway. At the south end, the nearby road, park and floodplain limited the available space, requiring the use of EMAS,” the spokesperson said. “MNAA is required to comply with all applicable federal aviation regulations and FAA requirements. These safety measures reflect our ongoing commitment to safe operations at both airports.”
The runway at Miami the doomed cargo jet utilized was also flagged by InvestigateTV’s analysis, but at the opposite end — the end the aircraft overran has a Runway Safety Area that is completely clear.
But that 1,000-foot buffer was ultimately not enough, as the plane went 1200 feet beyond the end of the pavement, according to the preliminary NTSB report.
Whether EMAS could have helped slow the plane is still unknown, although the NTSB has said it’s evaluating that question as part of its investigation.
Thomas said the Miami aircraft left the runway at 112 knots, while its systems to date are designed to a maximum of 70 knots.
“I hope it opens up the conversation that just because somebody has 1000 feet doesn’t mean it’s an ironclad answer, and it’s the only answer,” Thomas said. “We absorb energy. What I heard is it left the runway at 112 knots. Our systems are, to date, designed to a max of 70 knots, so obviously we would not have stopped that aircraft. But if you think about it in terms of energy, we would have absorbed a lot of the energy that aircraft was carrying as it left the 1,000 feet,” Thomas said.
Aircraft speed, weight create limitations for EMAS
Despite its benefits, EMAS does have limitations.
As Thomas indicated in relation to the Miami crash, arresting systems can only slow planes moving up to a certain speed and common, light general aviation planes don’t weigh enough to crush the material, so many smaller, private airports that don’t see commercial traffic haven’t installed it.
There was no EMAS at the end of the runway when the plane Michael Garrah was flying in aborted its takeoff, broke through a fence and slid across a crowded Maryland highway at rush hour, clipping a car.
“You could hear the landing gear collapsing and you could hear metal bending and just making all these sounds,” Garrah said.
Garrah and the pilot escaped the 2019 incident with only minor injuries. Evidence photos from the investigation show the wing of the small plane they were flying, crushed by a cement barrier. EMAS technology couldn’t have prevented their crash given the weight of the aircraft. But Garrah, a pilot, still believes the blocks can be lifesavers in the right situation.
“If there’s houses and there’s a heavily traveled road, then that’s more reason to implement something like that and protect, right? You want to protect the people all around. That’s important,” he said.

title: Officer’s use of force was justified in shooting death of 1-year-old Kohen Wiley at a Walmart, AG says
text:
SENATOBIA, Miss. (WMC/Gray News) — A police officer’s use of force that resulted in the death of a 1-year-old child was justified, the Mississippi Office of the Attorney General announced Monday.
The announcement marks the conclusion of the state’s investigation into the death of 1-year-old Kohen Wiley, who was shot and killed June 14 in the parking lot of a Walmart in Senatobia.
On that day, Senatobia police responded to the Walmart for a call about someone trying to steal diapers.
Officials said the call involved Wiley’s mother and great aunt.
Wiley was inside a car with his mother, who was holding him, and his great-aunt, who was driving, when an officer fired toward the vehicle. Wiley and his great-aunt were shot. Wiley died from his injuries.
The officer who fired his gun was placed on administrative leave, which city leaders said was standard practice after deadly police shootings.
The Mississippi Bureau of Investigation assigned five agents to the case to gather statements and reviewed witness accounts, body-camera and dashcam video and Walmart surveillance video.
In an initial account of the shooting, state investigators said: “Officers attempted to stop the vehicle, but the driver drove in the direction of the officers, almost striking one. An officer then discharged their weapon and the vehicle fled the scene.”
The killing has drawn comparisons to other instances where Black people lost their lives over accusations of petty criminal offenses, such as the murder of George Floyd.
Attorney Ben Crump, who rose to prominence representing the families of Floyd and other Black people killed by police, emphasized that the officers’ own report says they saw two women and a child get into the car. He questioned why the officer would shoot, knowing there was a kid inside.
“They want us to believe that it was a life-or-death situation,” Crump said at the time of the shooting. “They told us that, but they have not showed us that.”

title: Kenduskeag Stream retaining wall will be rebuilt
text:
A retaining wall along Kenduskeag Stream in downtown Bangor will be rebuilt.
The City Council on Wednesday authorized the city manager to enter into a contract with Sangerville-based Gordon Contracting Inc. to rebuild the south-facing retaining wall at Hamlin Park.
A site evaluation report earlier this year found that multiple granite blocks have been dislodged from the lower portion of the wall between Central and Hammond streets and that plant growth is widening gaps between the stones. Grout used to protect the steel and rebar pins has largely washed away.
All those factors have come together to make the retaining wall, built nearly a century ago, more vulnerable to tides.
Gordon Contracting was one of three companies to bid for the project and submitted the lowest bid at $3.8 million.
The project will replace about 115 feet of wall with an average height of 26 feet.
The timeline for the project wasn’t immediately available. On Thursday, Gordon Contracting said in a social media post that it will strive to reduce the length of construction to minimize impact on nearby businesses and residents.
It’s the second retaining wall along Kenduskeag Stream to require repair in recent years. The stretch of retaining wall west of Franklin Street was replaced after segments of the concrete wall fell into the stream.

title: UMaine students weigh in on Maine candidates ahead of November election
text:
University of Maine students are weighing their choices in several closely watched races ahead of the Nov. 3 election, including those for governor and U.S. Senate. In interviews with the Maine Campus, students expressed concerns about political influence, immigration enforcement and an increase in negative campaign advertising.
Robert Glover, an associate professor of political science and honors and co-leader of UMaine UVote, also offered his general perspective on the significance of the upcoming election via email.
“This is an incredibly important election,” wrote Glover. “We have an open seat for the Governor’s race and in the second Congressional district. And our Senate race is extremely close. Senator Collins is a uniquely powerful and well-established Senator to be facing a credible electoral challenge. Races like these could determine who controls each house in Washington. But it’s not all just D.C. politics. An individual vote can often have the greatest impact in municipal races, who is in the State House, etc.”
Glover also articulated that this election was unique relative to 2022 in that, as midterm elections reflect voters’ assessment of the president’s actions, the particular impacts that the Trump administration has had on people’s daily lives would factor into their decisions in the Congressional and Senate races.
“This race also puts Senator Collins in a challenging position. She’s always positioned herself as a moderate Republican. Opponents are trying to portray her as someone who has not been forceful enough in standing up to Donald Trump, while some Republicans would actually like to see her be more in the mold of a MAGA Republican,” wrote Glover. “I think Collins and her proximity to Trump are going to be top of mind for a lot of voters.”
The Maine Campus also interviewed Samuel Landry, a fourth-year ecology and environmental sciences student and executive officer at Alpha Tau Omega.
“Troy Jackson’s a regular working-class American, compared to Susan Collins who’s been in politics for years,” Landry said. “He has a lot more connection to the community with how he operates. He’s done a massive amount of town halls; Susan Collins hasn’t done any, to my knowledge.”
Landry emphasized his belief in the importance of separating corporate influence from the political sphere, and also said affordable housing and corruption are key issues.
“I think people taking favors for money in the Senate is absolutely abysmal and abhorrent,” said Landry. “It shouldn’t be happening. There should be no room for money in our politics.”
The Maine Campus also reached out to fourth-year ecology and environmental sciences student Gordon Young.
“I prefer Troy Jackson by virtue of him not rolling over to Trump… I don’t have a strong allegiance to him, but he’s what we’ve got,” said Young.
Young underlined his central issues for this election cycle being government transparency, as well as stronger protections for MaineCare and immigrants. When asked about reporting by New York Magazine that Jackson’s campaign had distanced itself from some grassroots supporters and a ProPublica investigation into allegations linking federal contracts and political contributions benefiting Collins, Young expressed doubts about both candidates.
“To me it just sounds like business as usual for both parties… I wasn’t aware of these accusations about Jackson, but that does check out, and it kinda makes me sad. This is behavior that I expected from Susan Collins. She’s done it before, she’ll do it again,” said Young.
When asked about Republican gubernatorial candidate Bobby Charles, both Landry and Young raised concerns about his remarks at an Aug. 20 event, where he said he planned to ask border czar Tom Homan to send Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents and U.S. marshals to Maine polling places, according to the Bangor Daily News. Charles’ campaign said the proposal was intended to prevent illegal voting.
“It sounds like voter disenfranchisement to me,” Young said. “As far as I know, having ICE there would have no purpose considering that the average immigrant knows that they can’t vote and is gently informed as such by the people who do voter registration in Maine.”
“While I do believe illegal immigration is a problem, the solution is not getting rid of every immigrant in Maine,” Landry said. “Immigrants have built America and they continue to do so to this day. We shouldn’t have masked agents in the street who can operate with impunity with their actions, and I don’t think we need any more of that in Maine.”
The frequency and intensity of negative political advertisements was also a concern Young raised. He said that the high influx of negative ads surrounding each candidate had negatively influenced his view of all candidates.
“The content attacking each other instead of actually talking about the problems you want to take care of irks me,” Young said.

title: New Gloucester’s Shaker Village receives $1.4M in NPS grants for renovations, preservation
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Sabbathday Lake Shaker Village received roughly $1.4 million in grants from the National Park Service last week, capping off years of uncertainty around federal funding.
The grants include a $750,000 Save America’s Treasures grant to fund the renovation of the village’s herb house into a community center, as well as a $667,000 History of Equal Rights grant to preserve the village’s historic meetinghouse.
Shaker Village Director Michael Graham said the herb house project first applied for federal funding in 2022, and received $750,000 from the National Endowment for the Humanities. In 2025, shortly after President Donald Trump’s return to the White House, funding for the project was cut, leading to the herb house community center project losing momentum.
Graham said the project has since gotten back on track. A judge deemed the Trump administration’s mass cancellation of National Endowment for the Humanities grants illegal in May and the grant was reinstated. The village was eligible to continue its fundraising efforts toward the grant and collect the undistributed award balance. He said $148,000 of the grant is uncollected, and the village has until the end of February to raise $600,000 to fully optimize the remaining award.
Graham said the Save America’s Treasures grant, which is not eligible to be used as a match for the national endowment grant, is vital to the herb house project, and will help with structural repairs, building the arts and culinary classrooms in the building’s lower level, and get the building in order and allow it to open within the next two years.
This is not the first Save America’s Treasures grant the village has received. In 2022, Graham, said, the village received a $500,000 grant to restore the village’s nearly 200-year-old barn, which serves as the center of the village’s operation, as well as housing sheep and cattle.
The History of Equal Rights grant will protect the Shaker Village’s meetinghouse, which, according to a news release, is the fourth oldest in the United States. The grant was funded as part of a program to preserve and protect historic sites related to the development of equal rights in the United States.
Graham also talked about an impending congressional vote on legislation that would substantially weaken Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act. The federal grants the village has received in recent years require a review through Section 106, in which federal and state agencies meet with an affected local site or group to make sure a project does not have any adverse impact on a site’s historical value. The legislation would “dramatically narrow the historic and cultural properties and projects that are subject to review,” according to the National Trust for Historic Preservation.
Currently, the Shaker Village is protected as a national historic landmark, with both the buildings and surrounding landscape deemed historically significant. Without Section 106 and its protective standards in place, Graham said the village would be subject to “potentially destructive” alteration.
“I hope that our leaders remember (the importance of Section 106 for historic preservation) and vote accordingly,” said Graham, “because sites like ours benefit immensely from the protective policies in place and standards that have been established.”

title: Middle school principal arrested on public intoxication, child neglect charges
text:
LOGAN COUNTY, W.Va (WSAZ/Gray News) - A middle school principal was arrested Tuesday on charges including public intoxication and child neglect, authorities said.
The Logan Police Department said Michael Bryan Kidd, 41, was charged with public intoxication and child neglect creating risk.
Officers said Kidd was arrested at the school after police met with a member of the Logan County Board of Education.
Kidd was arraigned in Logan County Magistrate Court.
A statement from Logan County Schools confirmed Kidd as the same employee they said was “removed from their duties” due to the criminal charges.
The district said it became aware of allegations involving the conduct of a school district employee “while on duty.” Upon receiving information concerning the matter, school district officials responded promptly and took immediate action to address the situation, the school system said.
The employee has been removed from their duties “pending further review and consideration of appropriate action.” The school system did not release any information about the accusations.

title: New tennis courts in Maine community dedicated to man who died in El Faro sinking
text:
New tennis courts for Spruce Mountain community dedicated to Mainer who died in El Faro sinking
The Spruce Mountain School District's new tennis courts were dedicated Monday to Michael Holland, who was one of four people from Maine who died in the sinking of the SS El Faro more than a decade ago.
Holland, who was from Wilton, was an assistant engineer aboard the El Faro when the cargo ship sank off the coast of the Bahamas on Oct. 1, 2015, during Hurricane Joaquin.
The tennis courts are located in Jay but are open to the greater Spruce Mountain community, which includes the neighboring towns of Livermore and Livermore Falls.
The Holland Strong Community Foundation worked to raise money for the new courts. Deb Roberts, Holland's mother, said solidifying her son's legacy in the community has been something she and her family have been working on for a decade.
"These courts are more than just a place to play tennis. They are a place for our students and our community to gather, to compete, to make friendships, to create memories and to build a future. And for me and my family, they are also a lasting way to honor Michael," Roberts said.
The Holland Strong Community Foundation has raised money for a scholarship fund for local high school students. During the 10th, and likely final, Holland Strong Ice Fishing Derby, Roberts said the scholarship fund should be able to last for decades. Roberts also hosts a toy drive in her son's name.
Holland was a graduate of Maine Maritime Academy, as were the other three Maine residents who died in the sinking of El Faro: Captain Michael Davidson, of Windham; Danielle Randolph, of Rockland; and Dylan Meklin, of Rockland. A fifth Maine Maritime Academy graduate, Mitchell Kuflik, of Brooklyn, New York, also died.
The sinking of El Faro has been described as one of the worst maritime disasters in recent history, as all 33 people who were on board the cargo ship were killed.

title: Three concerts added to Portland Ovations season
text:
PORTLAND, Maine — Amazing melodies, thrilling jazz, and groundbreaking Korean rock fusion have been added to Portland Ovations’ dynamic 2026-2027 season. All three concerts will perform at Portland’s newest music venue, Live at Madrid’s, this spring. Tickets are on sale exclusively to Ovations Members, with public ticket sales beginning Friday, Oct. 23. Thank you to Coffee By Design for sponsoring all three of these vibrant concerts.
“We are so excited to kick off our first three concerts at Live at Madrid’s,” says Portland Ovations Executive & Artistic Director Aimée M. Petrin. “Several years ago, after our presentation of the Iranian-Canadian duo Niyaz at Port City, audience member Adele Masengo Ngoy came up to me and said: ‘It doesn’t need to be my language sung on stage or my culture represented. What I care about is being part of a global community in which we all feel connected, welcome, and safe.’ Those thoughtful words best describe the ethos behind this series. The vision is one of cosmopolitan artists, of the world, but not “world music.” Eclectic, free of boundaries and prejudices, each of the bands crosses traditions and spans the contemporary. All have great energy, and all promise the unexpected. Come curious, leave connected.”
Barrut, Thursday, March 25 at 7 p.m. – Hailing from the Occitania region of southern France, Barrut is a powerhouse ensemble of seven singers and one percussionist whose voices collide, soar, and intertwine in thrilling polyphonic song. Rooted in the language and musical traditions of their homeland, Barrut transforms centuries-old sounds into something visceral and unmistakably alive, driven by pounding rhythms, extraordinary harmonies, and an infectious energy that can quite literally shake the room. No translation required: this is music you feel as much as hear.
Insun Park & Generals, Wednesday, April 7 at 7 p.m. – Presented in partnership with Maine Asian American Community Center. Ancient traditions meet the electric energy of today with Insun Park & Generals, a groundbreaking ensemble blending Korean traditional music, the propulsive rhythms of mask dance, and the raw power of rock. Drawing from ancestral sounds while fearlessly pushing them into new territory, the group creates music that feels both deeply rooted and exhilaratingly contemporary—a vibrant collision of rhythm, movement, tradition, and amplification.
Jamie Saft Trio, Thursday, April 15 at 7 p.m. – Maine-based pianist, keyboardist, and composer Jamie Saft has built a luminous career at the intersections of jazz, rock, experimental music, and improvisation, collaborating with artists ranging from Iggy Pop, Beastie Boys, and Bad Brains to Dave Liebman, Wadada Leo Smith, and Marshall Allen. Stay tuned to hear which of his extraordinary fellow musicians this voracious collaborator invites to join him in Maine for this concert. It’s a rare Maine appearance from a musician’s musician—extraordinary improvisers finding new possibilities in music both iconic and unexpected.
“Live music is about bringing people together, and that starts with the people working behind the scenes,” says Meg Shorette, Live at Madrid’s Talent Buyer and Event Manager. “When venues and promoters support each other, we create more opportunities for music to happen and for people to feel connected to their community. No one venue or promoter can do it alone, and working together makes that community stronger. I feel incredibly honored to be one of the people who gets to help bring these artists and audiences together and grateful to work alongside others who care deeply about keeping live music thriving in Portland. I think that spirit of collaboration is what makes this music community of ours special, and the team at Portland Ovations are some of the best doing this work. I hope you’ll come out to experience one of these shows.”
To become an Ovations Member and view the full season of events, visit portlandovations.org.
All tickets may be purchased through PortTIX, the trusted box office for purchasing Portland Ovations tickets. You can purchase tickets by phone at (207) 842-0800, in person at the PortTIX Box Office (Monday through Friday, 11 a.m. to 3 p.m.), or online anytime at PortTIX.com
Portland Ovations is a nonprofit cultural organization based in Southern Maine dedicated to gathering communities to share in the power of live performance. Ovations connects artists and audiences both onstage and off — making the arts an integral part of community life. Learn more at portlandovations.org.
Portland’s newest venue on the peninsula, Live at Madrid’s is forged by generations of live music and community in Portland, Maine. With space for up to 800, the former warehouse at 144 Fore Street transforms each night, creating memorable concert experiences. liveatmadrids.com/

title: Gail Joseph Bowden | Obituaries
text:
Gail Joseph Bowden, 98, passed away peacefully on Oct. 7, 2026. He was born on Oct. 23, 1927, in Salisbury Cove, Maine, to Lewis and Jennie Bowden.
His life was deeply rooted in his hometown of Salisbury Cove, where the family business, Edgewater Motel & Cottages, was central to his life and legacy. In his formative years, Gail attended a one-room schoolhouse in Salisbury Cove before graduating from Bar Harbor High School in 1944. He went on to earn a degree in Electrical Engineering from Northeastern University, taking a two-year leave during his studies to serve in the United States Navy. After graduation, Gail moved to upstate New York and began his career with General Electric in the turbine industry. This work provided him opportunities to travel internationally while building a rewarding career in engineering. In 1958, Gail and his late wife, Ann K. Bowden, settled in Reading, Mass., where they raised their five children.

title: Susan Collins’ math doesn’t add up
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Need some straight data on why it’s time to vote Sen. Susan Collins out? The senator takes credit for bringing money to Maine, but the math doesn’t work.
Her one vote allowing the “big, beautiful bill” is estimated to cost Maine a projected $4.125 billion in cuts over 10 years. Compare that to the $3.45 billion she claims to have brought in over 10 years and we get a loss of $675 million. She could have stopped it. She’s playing us, and it’s costing lives. The real costs of that legislation start in January.
Add on the rising costs of the Iran war, heating oil, gasoline, groceries, health insurance, tariffs and devastating hospital closures from her Trump support, and Troy Jackson is the common- sense choice.
Martha White
Rockport

title: If not this November, when?
text:
This upcoming Senate race should be about replacing Sen. Susan Collins.
Has she done good things for Maine? Absolutely. She’s brought a lot of money to Maine and has been very helpful to many individuals and should be commended for that work. However, her voting record has nearly supported all of Trump policies with the exceptions of the few token opposition votes. Her SCOTUS votes have proven disastrous to women. How many other Mainers have been negatively affected due to her voting?
Reality is, because of age and possible health concerns, she will need to be replaced anyway. Why wait? Why not this year?
We voters will have serious choices to make in November: Listen to and believe the negative ad campaigns and reelect Collins; give the new guy a chance for six years; or don’t vote for either one — which is legal. Not telling folks how we voted is also legal.
Joseph Mailey
Auburn

title: More than 1.5 million pounds of meat including hot dogs, bacon and deli meat recalled
text:
(Gray News) - More than 1.5 million pounds of meat, including hot dogs, kielbasa, deli meat, cocktail franks, bologna, bacon and chicken sausage, have been recalled because the products might have been stored at the wrong temperature, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Food Safety and Inspection Service.
The recalled products were sold under names including Kayem, Specialty Products, Al Fresco, Triple M, McKenzie, Deutschmacher, Jordan’s, Essem and Winnisimmet. The recalled items were produced between March 31 and Oct. 7.

title: A Waterford man has been missing since August
text:
A Waterford man has been missing since August.
John Larson, 34, left George Allen Acres about 4 p.m. on Aug. 3 and was last seen sitting near the intersection of Just Right Acres and Route 118 about 4:30 p.m., according to the Maine Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife.
He may have been wearing a dark-colored T-shirt and shorts, the department said Monday.
Anyone with information about Larson’s whereabouts can call the Maine Warden Service through the Augusta dispatch center at 207-624-7076 or the Oxford County Sheriff’s Office at 207-743-9554.

title: Former Maine writer John Gould’s Lisbon home destroyed by fire Sunday
text:
A fire early Sunday morning in Lisbon destroyed well-known author John Gould’s hand-built house, which was soon to be a renovated into a recovery home.
According to the Maine Department of Public Safety, a fire broke out at 51 Gould Road around 3 a.m. Firefighters found the residence fully engulfed and beginning to collapse when they arrived. The home was unoccupied and no one was inside, according to authorities.
The property had been recently sold to Lewiston-based An Angel’s Wing Inc., which posted on Facebook Sunday morning the property was planned as a recovery house for those struggling with alcohol and substance abuse disorder.
“This property represented so much hope, hard work, and planning for the future, and seeing it damaged this way is heartbreaking,” the group posted. “We are still processing the loss and determining what comes next.”
The home was built by Maine author and columnist John Gould in 1940. In his book “The House That Jacob Built,” Gould mentions that his great-grandfather, Jacob Gould, built the original house on the lot in the 1780s before it burned down. John rebuilt the house himself.
Gould died in 2003 at the age of 94. He was the author of numerous books and columns on Maine life, including writing a weekly column for The Christian Science Monitor for more than 60 years.
Debra York, executive director of An Angel’s Wing Inc., said that last Friday members of her team brought over three carloads of furnishings to the house such as bedding and cookware, donated by community members, and left it in the home’s livingroom area.
York said she’s waiting to see what their insurance company tells them before making any decisions about the property.
York said the organization was still in the planning process for the home. Leaders were considering using it as a recovery home for eight veterans providing 24/7 care, but nothing was finalized.
An investigation into the fire is ongoing.

title: Saudi Arabia executes 2 Bangladeshis over ‘indecent acts,’ and other Mideast news
text:
(AP) - Saudi Arabia says it has executed 2 Bangladeshi nationals over “indecent acts” inside a mosque in Mecca. Bangladesh said that it hadn’t been informed of the executions beforehand.
Meanwhile, Israeli police have arrested 10 suspects in connection with a wave of settler violence, including against a U.S. journalist and European diplomats in the occupied West Bank over the weekend.
Here’s the latest news from the Middle East on Monday. Read our full coverage here.
Saudi Arabia executes 2 Bangladeshis over ‘indecent acts’
Saudi Arabia has executed two Bangladeshi nationals after they were convicted of committing “indecent acts” in a mosque in the Muslim holy city of Mecca.
Bangladesh said that it wasn’t informed before the sentences were carried out and has sought information from Saudi Arabia.
The Bangladeshis, a man and a woman, were executed on Wednesday after their death sentences were upheld by the highest court and a royal decree authorized their executions, the Saudi Interior Ministry said.
The statement said that they were executed because of “the gravity and seriousness of their actions in violating the sanctity of both time and place.” The ministry didn’t elaborate.
Bangladeshi Foreign Ministry official Shama Obaed said that her ministry sent a letter to the Saudi government seeking “detailed information.”
Saudi authorities on Saturday also executed five Saudi nationals who were convicted of terrorism-related charges, the ministry said.
Saudi Arabia is one of the world’s most prolific users of the death penalty, with 356 executions in 2025, behind only China and Iran, according to human rights group Amnesty International.
So far this year, the kingdom has executed more than 170 people, according to the Interior Ministry.
Israel arrests 10 suspects following settler violence
Ten suspects were arrested on Monday following a string of violent attacks by Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank, police said, after the attacks led to heavy international criticism against Israel.
Israeli police didn’t identify the suspects or their roles in the attacks, which also targeted Washington Post photographer Heidi Levine and European diplomats. The attacks came during a spike of settler violence during the annual olive harvest.
Levine was beaten Friday by a crowd of young male settlers in the village of Abu Falah, leaving her with several broken ribs and vertebrae. A day later, masked settlers attacked a group of European diplomats and others visiting the Christian village of Taybeh.
Settler violence has surged in recent years, and rights groups say that attackers are rarely arrested or punished for attacks on Palestinians.
Houthi attack on military camp kills 53 soldiers
Iran-backed Houthi rebels struck a military camp for government forces in southern Yemen, killing at least 53 soldiers, provincial authorities said, making it one of the deadliest attacks in the recent surge in fighting.
The rebels fired three ballistic missiles on the al-Alam military camp in the southern province of Shabwa in an attack that also wounded 200 recruits, the Shabwa provincial government said. The recruits were receiving training to be part of the internal security forces, it said.
The rebels have acknowledged targeting the camp in Shabwa.
The attack was part of a recent escalation in fighting, which began months ago as tensions spiked in the wider Iran war. The escalation between the Houthis and forces of the Saudi-backed government shattered a 2022 ceasefire deal that largely stopped fighting in Yemen’s civil war.
U.K. warns companies against helping to build Israeli settlements
The United Kingdom’s top diplomat has urged companies not to help build new Israeli settlements in the West Bank, saying they could breach international law if they do.
Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said that the E1 settlement project approved by Israel “is a direct threat to the prospect of a two-state solution” to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict.
Israel’s top diplomat responded by saying his country wouldn’t be “intimidated by threats.”
“The days when Israel would quietly accept threats, sanctions and attempts to dictate its policies are over,” Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar said in a statement.
“Judea and Samaria are not foreign lands to the Jewish people,” he said, using the biblical name of the West Bank. “Our historical rights are not subject to approval from London.”
In September, the U.K. government, along with France and Canada, banned trade with Israeli settlements. The U.K. also gave itself power to sanction companies that provide services for the settlements, including financing, construction, infrastructure, real estate and advertising.
U.S. calls for release of ex-embassy staff in Yemen
The United States has called for the “immediate and unconditional release” of former U.S. Embassy staff who were detained by the Houthis five years ago.
“For five years, these innocent people and their families have endured separation, intimidation, and abuse,” a U.S. State Department statement said Monday in reference to the former employees of the embassy in Sanaa, which closed down in 2015.
“The Houthis’ continued detention of their fellow Yemenis stands as further evidence that the group relies on fear and violence against their own people to sustain their hold on territory,” the statement said.
Houthis seized the headquarters of the U.S. Embassy in October 2021, detaining dozens of former staffers, many of whom were later released.
Iran will respond forcefully to new U.S. attacks, official says
An adviser to Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei says that Iran will respond forcefully to any renewed U.S. attack.
Conservative politician Mohammad Mokhber said that Iran would strike “nine countries” if Iranian bases or “petrochemical” facilities were struck again.
“If they want to hit a base, we have to hit the bases of nine countries,” he said Monday in recorded comments posted by Tasnim, a semiofficial news agency close with the Revolutionary Guard.
The report didn’t name the nine countries.
Mojtaba Khamenei was named Iran’s supreme leader after his father and predecessor, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, was killed by Israel on the first day of the war. The younger Khamenei hasn’t been seen or heard publicly since his appointment.

title: Maine women’s hockey aims to make history with Alfond Attendance Challenge
text:
The University of Maine women’s ice hockey team is challenging its community to help make history this winter, setting its sights on filling Alfond Arena. The goal is to break the Hockey East single-game attendance record when the Black Bears host the University of New Hampshire on Friday, Dec. 4.
Alfond Arena will provide a stage for one of the biggest crowds in women’s college hockey, with the building holding a capacity of 5,125. The conference record Maine will be aiming to break is 3,965 fans, set on Nov. 14, 2025, when Boston University faced Boston College.
Maine held a similar event last season, when the Black Bears broke their program attendance record on Valentine’s Day. A crowd of 1,730 attended the Senior Day matchup against New Hampshire as part of the “Fill the Steins” promotion. Maine went on to lose the game 3-0, but the turnout demonstrated the potential for increased interest and visibility for the program.
Maine’s most-attended home game so far this season was its preseason matchup against the University of New Hampshire, which drew 998 fans. The upcoming December Border Battle offers another opportunity to bring the community to Orono, this time with an even more ambitious goal.
The effort comes during a period of transition for the Black Bears and growth in women’s sports. Molly Engstrom stepped down as head coach to take an assistant coaching position with Professional Women’s Hockey League Detroit. Alex Gettens was named the eighth head coach in program history, returning to Maine after serving as an assistant coach during the 2017-18 season. During that campaign, Maine won its first Hockey East playoff game and recorded a program-best 19 wins.
Gettens sees the attendance challenge as an opportunity for the community to take ownership of a major achievement.
“It’s a record that they own,” Gettens said. “It’s a record that they can take pride in. The community can take pride in it, and they can say, like, yes, legitimately we’re number one.”
The potential impact of the attendance challenge extends beyond Orono, with colleges across the country using special events to draw attention to women’s sports. In August, the University of Georgia held its “Soccer in Sanford” event, playing in Georgia’s football stadium and drawing 25,433 fans for a 6-0 victory over James Madison University. The crowd set NCAA Division I attendance records for soccer, demonstrating the scale of support women’s sports can attract when universities and their communities rally around them.
For Maine, a successful attendance challenge could offer similar opportunities to grow interest in the team and connect the university with the surrounding community. A packed arena would give players the chance to compete in front of a large audience while allowing students, families and young hockey players to experience the program firsthand.
Third-year forward Gracie Hanson said the event could also help inspire the next generation of hockey players.
“I think it also helps grow the game for the next generation,” Hanson said. “It’s really cool to see all the younger girls come out to watch us play and see the opportunities that are out there for them in hockey.”
Gettens also believes a large crowd could leave a lasting impression on younger players who are watching women’s hockey grow.
“When you walk into an environment like that, it just captivates you in every way,” Gettens said. “It sparks your imagination, and it ignites a passion of saying, like, this is what I want to do. This is what I want to be.”
The challenge would also build on the success of women’s sports at Maine. The women’s basketball team has drawn strong crowds while competing at a high level, and women’s soccer has won the past three America East titles while playing at its new stadium. The women’s cross-country team also won the America East championship last fall.
Maine women’s hockey is currently 2-5 and will finish off its weekend set with RPI before returning to Orono to host Providence and open conference play. The Black Bears have several weeks to build momentum before the December attendance challenge.
The goal is bigger than simply getting people through the door. Maine hopes to strengthen its connection with the community and help grow women’s hockey.
On Dec. 4, the Black Bears will have an opportunity to turn that goal into reality. With a conference attendance record in reach, the team is inviting the community to help make history at the Alfond.

title: Maine's Stunning Fall Colors Are Almost Gone for Another Year
text:
Maine’s Stunning Fall Colors Are Almost Gone for Another Year
The days are shortening and the colors are fading. Oh, how time sadly flies.
We’re wrapping up the 2026 fall foliage season, and let’s be honest, it’s always a bit of a bummer. It’s just never long enough.
When Does the Maine Fall Foliage Season End?
The foliage season has cruised by, with reports dropping weekly. According to Maine.gov, we’ve already passed peak season in the majority of the state, with peak foliage typically arriving around the end of October in Southern Maine.
Comfortable daytime temperatures and cool nights early in the season were a huge help. They also created a wonderful atmosphere for folks to enjoy the leaves while taking part in other fall activities.
So, how do things look on the trusty fall foliage map? Thanks to the Maine Department of Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry's Maine Foliage Report, we can see exactly where things stand.
Welp, that’s just about a wrap, folks. The last few regions are riding out their final days of peak foliage before the entire state goes purple on the map. It was a fun run, but I guess we now have snow to look forward to?
How Great was the 2026 Maine Fall Foliage Season?
While it’s sad to see the season coming to an end, we can at least look back at what was a very solid foliage year. Those comfortable daytime temperatures were certainly a big bonus for everyone out enjoying the colors. I mean, who didn’t love a little apple cider and beautiful foliage while basking in 70-degree temperatures?

Now comes the worst part of the entire year: picking up all those leaves. The absolute worst. I can already feel my back aching.
Happy cleanup, everyone!

title: Wood stove sparked N.H. fire that killed man and two dogs, officials say
text:
Wood stove sparked Stark house fire that killed man and two dogs, New Hampshire officials say
Woman seriously injured in fire was airlifted to Massachusetts General Hospital in Boston
Wood stove sparked Stark house fire that killed man and two dogs, New Hampshire officials say
Woman seriously injured in fire was airlifted to Massachusetts General Hospital in Boston
A fire in a northern New Hampshire home that killed a man and two dogs and left a woman seriously injured was sparked by a wood stove, according to officials.
The State Fire Marshal's Office said the fire at 37 Montgomery Road in Stark, which is near Pike Pond, started shortly before 1:30 a.m. Sunday.
Officials said a woman who lives at the home reported the fire to a neighbor, who then called 911. Dispatchers were told that a man was still inside the burning house and that flames were spreading.
According to the Fire Marshal's Office, a neighbor tried to rescue the man who was inside, but they were unable to do so due to the growing fire.
Officials said that by the time firefighters arrived a few minutes later, the house was fully engulfed in flames, which were coming out of the doors and windows. Firefighters were unable to immediately enter the home due to the worsening conditions, and additional crews from Milan and Groveton responded to the scene.
The Fire Marshal's Office said the fire was ultimately brought under control around 4:30 a.m.
The man who was inside the home was found dead, along with two dogs. Officials said the man's identity is being withheld pending an autopsy, which was scheduled for Monday at the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner.
The woman was seriously injured and flown to Massachusetts General Hospital in Boston, according to officials.
The Fire Marshal's Office said the fire is not considered suspicious. Investigators believe a wood stove inside the home was a primary factor in the fire, which destroyed the home.
A neighbor in the area told WMTW sister station WMUR that she heard loud noises, and when she looked across the pond, she saw the camp in flames. Another neighbor said the community is tight-knit.
Authorities are asking anyone with additional information to contact investigators by calling 603-223-4289 or sending an email to fmo@dos.nh.gov.
In the news release about the fire in Stark, State Fire Marshal Sean Toomey reminded all New Hampshire residents about the importance of proper maintenance and annual cleanings of wood-burning appliances and chimneys. Toomey said combustible materials should be kept at least 3 to 5 feet away from any heating appliance. He also reminded people to always properly dispose of wood stove ash and to ensure paths inside and outside of the home are clear and maintained.

title: Ask ACE: What are Digital Product Passports and does my business need to pay attention?
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
ACE advises: If you sell products into European markets (or plan to) Digital Product Passports (DPPs) are something you need to get ahead of now. This is one of the most significant regulatory shifts affecting product-based businesses in recent years.
What is a DPP? A Digital Product Passport is a digital record linked to a physical product, containing data on its materials, origin, manufacturing process, repairability and end-of-life options. Think of it as a product’s digital identity — scannable, traceable and shareable across the entire supply chain. The EU’s Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation (ESPR) is driving this rollout.
Who needs it? Any brand or manufacturer selling into the EU needs a passport, including U.S. companies. Textiles and apparel are among the first product categories targeted. If you have European customers, wholesale partners or retail distribution channels, this affects you directly.
Benefits. DPPs aren’t just compliance boxes to check. They build consumer trust through transparency, can streamline customs and certification processes, and position your brand as a sustainability leader. This is an increasingly important competitive advantage with retail buyers and end consumers alike.
Next steps. Start by auditing what product data you currently have and identifying the gaps. Engage your supply chain partners now to improve traceability. Investing in a data management system before deadlines arrive will save significant time and cost.
Timeline. The EU is phasing in DPP requirements beginning in 2026, with textiles and apparel expected in the 2027-28 window. That timeline may feel comfortable, but supply chain data collection takes longer than most brands expect. Start the conversation now.

title: Supreme Court denies petition to hear challenge to Maine’s 72-hour gun waiting period
text:
PORTLAND, Maine (WMTW) - The U.S. Supreme Court will not take up a case that challenges Maine’s 72-hour waiting period to purchase a firearm.
The nation’s highest court denied a petition filed by gun rights groups, who asked the Supreme Court to review the Boston-based First Circuit U.S. Court of Appeals’ prior ruling that said the Maine law is likely constitutional.
The Maine law requires gun sellers to wait 72 hours before giving a firearm to a buyer. It was passed in response to the Lewiston mass shootings that killed 18 people on Oct. 25, 2023. Gun rights advocates have argued the law violates their Second Amendment rights.
The three-day waiting period went into effect in August 2024, but a U.S. District Court judge put the law on hold in February 2025 as he ruled in favor of gun rights groups who filed a federal lawsuit.
In April 2026, the First Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that the law can take effect while the case continues, as it determined that the waiting period does not block people from owning guns and only slows down the process.
“In our view, this likely renders the act a burden on, but not an infringement of, the Second Amendment right to keep and bear arms,” the federal appeals court said in its decision.
First Circuit Court of Appeals judges also pointed to evidence lawmakers relied on showing waiting periods can reduce suicides and violence.

title: Orrington breaks ground on new Penobscot River boat launch
text:
ORRINGTON, Maine (WABI) - A boat launch years in the planning process broke ground Monday at the end of McGinn Road in Orrington.
The facility, called Baker’s Landing Boat Launch, is named for Alan Baker, a longtime Orrington resident who went on to be the publisher of the Ellsworth American.
Once complete, it will be the first public access to the Penobscot River from the east side in a stretch that Baker said runs from Eddington Bend to Castine.
Planning began six years ago
The idea has been decades in the making, but efforts began in earnest about six years ago, according to Town Manager Chris Backman.
“There’s been wild dreams here for many, many years,” Backman said. “A lot of planning. A lot of design work. Can we do this? Can we do that? What’s the best option? Engineering. Dealing with the river. She has her own mindset and what she’s going to want to do.”
The facility will not be limited to boaters. Plans include a playground, pavilion, picnic area, walking trails, and more.
Funded by environmental trust grant
Backman said the project is fully funded through a $2.5 million grant from Greenfield Environmental Trust.
The trust is also responsible for cleaning up decades of mercury contamination in the Penobscot River from the former HoltraChem plant in Orrington, work that began in August.
“So the town’s very excited,” Backman said. “It’s reclaiming the river.”
Public safety benefits cited
Orrington Fire Chief Scott Stewart said the launch will also serve public safety needs.
“Currently, we have a boat landing in South Orrington that’s very tidal, which means that certain times of the day we cannot launch our boat. So, if we had an emergency on the river, we would be forced to drive to Hampden to launch, which would take 20 to 30 minutes of extra time,” Stewart said.
Officials are eyeing June 2027 for the opening of the boat launch. Baker, the project’s namesake, was among the guests at Monday’s groundbreaking.
“What a wonderful project this is. And all you need to do is look at that river and see how right it was that we should have access to it here in our community,” Baker said.
Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, who calls Baker a friend, also attended.
“I can think of no better tribute to all of your service than to have this boat launch named for you. And so many people for generations to come will enjoy using it and they’ll know your story,” Collins said.

title: Does MaineCare cover chiropractic visits?
text:
Yes.
MaineCare, Maine’s Medicaid program, covers certain chiropractic services, including spinal manipulation, examinations to diagnose spinal conditions and certain X-rays.
For adults 21 and older, coverage generally includes 12 visits per calendar year. Additional visits require prior authorization, documentation of medical necessity and a referral from a medical provider. Members younger than 21 need a referral beyond 12 visits, but not prior authorization.
MaineCare does not cover all forms of medical treatment. For example, acupuncture and massage therapy are excluded.
The federal government recently approved a plan that will allow eligible tribal health organizations to bill MaineCare for traditional Wabanaki healing services. Coverage is not yet available; Maine officials tentatively anticipate launching the benefit on Oct. 1, 2027. The state and Wabanaki Nations are still determining which healing practices will qualify, who can provide them and how the benefit will work.

title: More than 60,000 Maine college students, faculty to receive free local news subscriptions
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
More than 60,000 students, faculty and staff at Maine colleges and universities will receive free one-year digital subscriptions to Maine Trust for Local News publications this fall through a new sponsored program.
The subscriptions will provide access to the Portland Press Herald, Sun Journal, Morning Sentinel and Kennebec Journal, among other Maine Trust publications. Funded by Bangor Savings Bank, the program covers Maine’s public universities, the Maine Community College System, Husson University in Bangor and Thomas College in Waterville.
Eligible students, faculty and staff will register using a school email address through a dedicated online page and receive digital access on computers and mobile devices.
Gavin Robinson, senior vice president, community relations manager and public finance officer at Bangor Savings Bank, said in a statement that the initiative is intended to increase access to local news and encourage civic engagement.
“Strong communities depend on people who are informed, connected and engaged,” Robinson said.
The program also aims to give students access to news about communities where they attend school and, in some cases, where they may eventually work.
“Maine’s community college students tend to come from — and ultimately stay and work in — their local communities, so having free access to the local news is a real gift,” said David Daigler, president of the Maine Community College System, in a statement.
Daigler said community college graduates enter fields including healthcare, emergency response, skilled trades and business, making familiarity with current events and local issues useful as they begin their careers.
The program comes after four private colleges — Bates College in Lewiston, Colby College in Waterville, Bowdoin College and The Roux Institute at Northeastern University in Portland — are already paying for Maine Trust digital subscriptions for their school populations.

title: Mother of 8 hit and killed by train during morning run: ‘She was an angel’
text:
ELOY, Ariz. (AZFamily/Gray News) - An Arizona family is grieving after a mother of eight was hit and killed by a train while on a morning run.
Thelma Candelaria, 47, was a caregiver and mother of eight children. She had been baptized less than a week before her death in what was supposed to be the start of a new beginning.
She went out for a routine run Thursday morning in Eloy. She was recording the run on social media, and her daughter, Alaisha Candelaria, provided videos showing her smiling and in good spirits.
“She was singing along to Jessie Reyez, which is her favorite artist. She was laughing,” said Alaisha Candelaria of her mother.
Alaisha Candelaria would later use her mother’s videos, along with surveillance footage, to piece together what happened next.
She never saw the train that killed her
During her run, Thelma Candelaria stopped at a railroad crossing around 6 a.m. As she was recording one train, a separate train on another track approached her from the opposite direction, according to her daughter.
The mother didn’t see the second train, and any sound it made was muffled by her earbuds and the train she was already recording. Eloy Police say both trains sounded their horns before she was hit.
“She had her noise-canceling Beat headphones on. She was in her own world,” Alaisha Candelaria said.
Eloy Police say the train that hit Thelma Candelaria applied its emergency brake but couldn’t avoid the collision. She was pronounced dead at the scene.
“It’s a lot. It’s a lot,” Alaisha Candelaria said.
She says she wants the community to know her mother’s death was a horrible accident.
“People, continuously, they’ve always told me my whole life, ‘You are so, so lucky to have the mother that you have,’” Alaisha Candelaria said. “She was an angel.”
The family has created a GoFundMe to help with funeral costs and support for Thelma Candelaria’s children.
The Eloy Police Department’s Vehicular Crimes Unit is investigating the incident.

title: Safety system can stop planes that overshoot runways, but most airports don’t have it
text:
Miami, Florida (InvestigateTV) — In the hours after an Amazon cargo plane overshot the runway at Miami International Airport in September, crashing through a fence and hitting two vehicles on a road bordering the facility, investigators from the National Transportation Safety Board swarmed the scene.
Their leader, NTSB Chair Jennifer Homendy, used three words to describe the aftermath of the crash, “Devastating. Utter devastation.”
Aerial video of the scene shows deep black scars cut into the earth at the edge of the airport property, where charred, twisted metal sits scattered well beyond the tarmac — pieces of a cargo jet thrown where a plane was never meant to go.
“You can see on the paved surface, tire marks that continues in the grass. There’s debris everywhere,” Homendy said.
The plane, a Boeing 767, had overrun the airport runway by 1,200 feet according to the NTSB — killing five people riding in its path. The accident is what the agency calls an “excursion”, where a plane goes off the runway.
Since 2008, more than 3,000 have been investigated by the NTSB.
InvestigateTV analyzed NTSB accident data and found nearly one-fifth of those excursions involved planes that went beyond the end of the runway, with some leading to deaths.
Lives lost in accidents like this raise an inevitable question: Could specific safety technology have prevented tragedy?
A system that’s designed to slow planes and save lives in overruns is available and has already prevented serious crashes involving commercial airliners and smaller private jets across the country. Yet, InvestigateTV discovered most American airports don’t have it installed.
Renewed focus on runway overrun solutions
As investigators sort through the pieces of the Amazon crash, there’s renewed interest in technology that some believe could have been a potential difference maker in a situation like Miami. It’s called EMAS: engineered material arresting system.
“Should EMAS be everywhere at every airport? That will be a key part of our investigation,” Homendy said.
It’s a valid question as regulators look for potential solutions to deal with overruns. Since the 1980s, federal regulations have required commercial airports to have Runway Safety Areas that extend 1,000 feet beyond the end of the runway.
But many airports built before those regulations were implemented simply don’t have enough space to provide that buffer, so they need an alternative in the event of an overrun. That’s where EMAS comes in.
EMAS is made up of crushable concrete pads constructed with individual blocks stacked like stair steps at the end of a runway. The technology was developed by the Federal Aviation Administration in the 1990s with several partners, including a company called ESCO, now Runway Safe — the sole manufacturer of EMAS approved for use in the United States.
“When it engages with the tires - it just crumbles. It crumbles right down to a dust. That is what absorbs the kinetic energy, believe it or not, from the whole aircraft with all of its landing gear,” said Trip Thomas, Runway Safe’s director of commercialization.
InvestigateTV was given an exclusive look inside Runway Safe’s New Jersey facility, where hundreds of pallets of EMAS blocks were being prepped for delivery. To construct an entire bed for an arresting system, Thomas said an average of about 3,000-3,500 blocks is needed to provide the cushion that ultimately slows a plane in crisis.
“His wheel will be just crushing down most of the way. And he’s got this wall of material in front of him. And it’s just the effort, the energy he uses to crush the blocks is what decelerates the aircraft,” he said.
EMAS has saved lives, yet most airports lack the technology
InvestigateTV’s examination of FAA data shows EMAS has been involved in stopping aircraft in 26 overruns to date, including Boeing 737s carrying dozens of travelers and crew as well as smaller Cessnas carrying just a pilot and passenger. Yet the system is not found at many airports across the United States.
In fact, the FAA says just 70 domestic facilities have EMAS installed. Twelve of those facilities are at major airports including John F. Kennedy International Airport in New York, O’Hare International Airport in Chicago and Logan International Airport in Boston.
Some smaller airports with commercial traffic have also put EMAS onto their runways including Hilton Head, South Carolina, DeKalb Airport near Atlanta, Baton Rouge, Louisiana and Telluride, Colorado.
OTD in 2018, a passenger plane overran a runway during landing at @fly_BUR in Burbank, California. Thanks to the crushable concrete of the Engineered Materials Arresting System, none of the 117 people onboard were injured. Read more about EMAS at https://t.co/SDIpgeKUFc. https://t.co/HLOZxbGObw
— The FAA ✈️ (@FAANews) December 6, 2021
To be clear, EMAS is not required, even if airports do not have the 1,000-foot buffer laid out in that federal Runway Safety Area requirement, but it is a strongly-recommended option for airports facing limited space.
Ultimately it is airports and local governments that are the ones weighing the multi-million dollar cost versus the risk.
“Some airports do look at it strictly very much like an insurance policy which I think is a bit simplistic, but I can understand the basic thinking to it,” Thomas said. “With the Miami situation we are hoping here and we’re planning to go talk to some people about is maybe we should really be looking at these runway ends from a risk reduction potential.”
Safety zones and limitations
It’s a critical consideration.
Using FAA data, InvestigateTV mapped the areas of highest risk at the end of runways located at the more than 500 commercial airports across the U.S. that accept scheduled passenger service.
These defacto “danger zones” included a trapezoidal area extending 1,000 feet beyond each physical runway end, widening with distance from 500 feet to 1,000 feet, and were modeled to bridge FAA standards for a Runway Safety Area, Runway Object Free Area and Runway Protection Zone for each runway.
Based on published FAA guidelines and agency-funded external research, the shape captures the potential for an aircraft to deviate from the centerline during an overrun.
Comparing these “danger zones” with U.S. Census street data, InvestigateTV’s analysis found hundreds of commercial airports where at least one runway had an active public road running through the mapped area.
After a 2005 crash at Midway in Chicago, the FAA worked for more than a decade to bring airports into compliance with its Runway Safety Area standards, with facilities having three main options: retooling the airport’s layout through land purchases and relocating structures and roads, installing an EMAS, or functionally shortening runways to allow for the needed space.
Most of the facilities InvestigateTV identified as having roads encroaching into areas at risk of an overrun do not have EMAS beds to slow planes — including large, busy passenger airports such as Baltimore/Washington International Thurgood Marshall Airport (BWI), Nashville International Airport (BNA) and Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport (PHX).
FAA data and airport records show all three of those airports utilize a “displaced threshold” where the official takeoff or landing distances available to aircraft are reduced, shifting the functional end of the runway back and creating the additional space needed to fit into the FAA’s requirements.
InvestigateTV reached out to the airports about the data findings and to ask if there has been any consideration of adding an EMAS, either in the past or in the wake of the crash in Miami.
“At Phoenix Sky Harbor, safety is the top priority. The airport meets or exceeds all Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) runway safety design standards,” a spokesperson said in an emailed response. The spokesperson did not directly address the use of EMAS, but said that any future runway development at the airport “will also meet FAA runway safety design standards.”
A spokesperson for the Metropolitan Nashville Airport Authority said EMAS was used to meet FAA standards at the body’s smaller facility, John C. Tune Airport (JWN) but that requirements at the larger airport were otherwise accomplished.
“At BNA, we were able to provide the full 1,000-foot-long by 500-foot-wide safety areas beyond the runway ends. At JWN, we were able to accommodate a 1,000-foot safety area at the north end of the runway. At the south end, the nearby road, park and floodplain limited the available space, requiring the use of EMAS,” the spokesperson said. “MNAA is required to comply with all applicable federal aviation regulations and FAA requirements. These safety measures reflect our ongoing commitment to safe operations at both airports.”
The runway at Miami the doomed cargo jet utilized was also flagged by InvestigateTV’s analysis, but at the opposite end — the end the aircraft overran has a Runway Safety Area that is completely clear.
But that 1,000-foot buffer was ultimately not enough, as the plane went 1200 feet beyond the end of the pavement, according to the preliminary NTSB report.
Whether EMAS could have helped slow the plane is still unknown, although the NTSB has said it’s evaluating that question as part of its investigation.
Thomas said the Miami aircraft left the runway at 112 knots, while its systems to date are designed to a maximum of 70 knots.
“I hope it opens up the conversation that just because somebody has 1000 feet doesn’t mean it’s an ironclad answer, and it’s the only answer,” Thomas said. “We absorb energy. What I heard is it left the runway at 112 knots. Our systems are, to date, designed to a max of 70 knots, so obviously we would not have stopped that aircraft. But if you think about it in terms of energy, we would have absorbed a lot of the energy that aircraft was carrying as it left the 1,000 feet,” Thomas said.
Aircraft speed, weight create limitations for EMAS
Despite its benefits, EMAS does have limitations.
As Thomas indicated in relation to the Miami crash, arresting systems can only slow planes moving up to a certain speed and common, light general aviation planes don’t weigh enough to crush the material, so many smaller, private airports that don’t see commercial traffic haven’t installed it.
There was no EMAS at the end of the runway when the plane Michael Garrah was flying in aborted its takeoff, broke through a fence and slid across a crowded Maryland highway at rush hour, clipping a car.
“You could hear the landing gear collapsing and you could hear metal bending and just making all these sounds,” Garrah said.
Garrah and the pilot escaped the 2019 incident with only minor injuries. Evidence photos from the investigation show the wing of the small plane they were flying, crushed by a cement barrier. EMAS technology couldn’t have prevented their crash given the weight of the aircraft. But Garrah, a pilot, still believes the blocks can be lifesavers in the right situation.
“If there’s houses and there’s a heavily traveled road, then that’s more reason to implement something like that and protect, right? You want to protect the people all around. That’s important,” he said.
