title: Here’s what researchers found out about pandemic learning loss
text:
HARRISBURG, N.C. (InvestigateTV) — Schools are seeing the first wave of children born during the COVID-19 pandemic. Many teachers are reporting seeing speech and vocabulary delays in their classrooms.
Researchers examining how the pandemic affected child development found that children born in 2020 are not the age group facing the biggest challenges, according to a Johns Hopkins Medicine study.
First wave of pandemic-born students
September 2025 marked the first time classrooms were made up of students born in 2020, during the height of the COVID-19 pandemic.
Rahisha Clay, who has taught for more than a decade at Ace Academy in Harrisburg, North Carolina, said she noticed something different with this group of students.
Clay and other school officials said they saw students with speech and vocabulary delays.
“Babies learn by seeing your facial expression, by hearing the sound and the tone of your voice,” said Laila Minott. “And if we were isolated, or you’re only just in your home, that limited what they were able to see and learn.”
Laila Minott is executive director of Ace Academy, where Clay teaches.
“You have some kids that had a lot of educational resources and access while they were home with their parents,” Minott said. “And then you have some kids that didn’t have anything, and they barely know the ABCs.”
Only slight delays for children born in 2020
Johns Hopkins Medicine examined child development milestones on a national level, analyzing results of more than 50,000 questionnaires completed by parents of children six months to five and a half years old. Researchers found only slight delays in communication, problem solving, and personal social development.
“There are still kids who are going to struggle, just like there were kids who were going to struggle before the pandemic,” said Professor of Pediatrics Dr. Sarah Johnson, who led the study. “But overall, we’re not seeing that this is like a weight that this entire generation is going to carry.”
Johnson said babies born in 2020 were not far off track, and that older children felt the pandemic’s disruption differently. She said teachers saw kids returning to the classroom without practice negotiating and sitting. Johnson said educators were working to close not just a communication gap, but an academic one.
“It was absolutely drinking from a firehose for many teachers, whether they were in early childhood ed settings or kindergarten or later grades,” Johnson said.
Reading declines & gains
In 2024, the Nation’s Report Card showed about 40% of fourth graders were working below the basic level in reading, the largest percentage in decades.
That same year, Louisiana became one of the first states in the country to launch a state-funded tutoring initiative in direct response to pandemic learning loss.
Districts there are mandated by law to provide tutoring during school hours for eligible students in grades K through five, using high dosage tutoring.
According to Duke University, high dosage, or high impact, tutoring typically includes at least three interactions per week with a student, each at least 30 minutes, with a maximum of three students per tutor.
East Baton Rouge Parish public school administrators said they are already seeing results.
At the beginning of the 2025-2026 academic year, just 35% of kindergarten students were reading at or above their grade level. By the end of the school year, that number was up to 64%.
“It’s not only about remediation, but is also about acceleration,” said administrator Sito Narcisse. “And the more we give our kids opportunities and access to get better with their needs, the faster that they learn, the better they do overall.”
During that same time period, Louisiana students in grades K through three saw a 33% increase in literacy scores statewide. State leaders credit quality instructional materials, professional learning, coaching support and high dosage tutoring.
Tutoring support
Back in the North Carolina classroom, teachers said state dollars supporting tutoring can be the difference between a student falling further behind or finally catching up.
A bill in the Louisiana State House aims to expand the high dosage tutoring law to students through eighth grade. Other policymakers have taken notice of the impact. In Indiana, eligible families can receive a $1,000 stipend for high dosage tutoring.
At the federal level, the Department of Education announced it would prioritize grants for states and school districts that propose to implement or expand high dosage tutoring.

title: High schools Monday: Hall-Dale/Monmouth field hockey prevails
text:
Makayla Norton and Hannah Rauch scored to lead Hall-Dale/Monmouth field hockey to a 2-0 victory over Dirigo on Monday in Farmingdale.
Sidney Keleher added an assist for the Bulldogs (5-9), and Haylie Stevens stopped seven shots to earn her second straight shutout.
Samantha Searles made 10 saves for the Cougars (2-12).
WINSLOW 7, WATERVILLE 1: Delana Ferran scored three goals to lead the Black Raiders (7-6-1) past the Panthers (1-13) in Waterville.
Adriana Lombardi, Belen Farnham, Emma Fales and Clareese Jones also scored for Winslow. Emma McCaslin and Silver Picard combined for make seven saves.
Addison Thomas scored, while Zakiya Kiante and Stella Donahue-Beard combined to make nine saves for Waterville.
BOYS SOCCER
PINE TREE ACADEMY 6, VALLEY 0: Collin Verrill scored two goals and Pine Tree Academy (11-0) opened a 4-0 halftime lead on the way to defeating Valley (5-5-4) in Freeport.
Fitzroy Hakazimana, Santi Lopez, Lucky Kadeya amd Sam Cornish also scored for the Breakers, who received three saves from Abner Poland.
MONMOUTH ACADEMY 8, MOUNTAIN VALLEY 0: The Mustangs (14-0) finished off an unbeaten regular season with a dominant win over the Falcons (5-7-2) in Rumford.
Zane Foyt paced Monmouth with four goals and an assist. Bryce Fletcher scored twice, and Jake Harmon and Josh Iwanyanwu added a goal apiece. Wade Givens and Max Robitaille each had an assist. Goalie Gavin Parsons made two saves.
Gabe Hall stopped 12 shots for Mountain Valley.
GIRLS SOCCER
MARANACOOK 1, MT. ABRAM 0: Caroline Harper scored the game-deciding goal to give the Black Bears (13-1) a victory over the Roadrunners (13-1) in Salem Township.
Mt. Abram ends the regular season as the No. 1 seed in Class C South, while Maranacook is No. 2. The two teams split the regular-season series, with the Roadrunners topping the Black Bears 1-0 in Readfield on Sept. 25.

title: Coats of Kindness program returns to help Maine families stay warm
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - As Maine prepares for another season of colder temperatures, community partners are coming together once again to help ensure everyone has access to a warm winter coat. Penquis is calling on community members to help make a difference through its annual Coats of Kindness program, which collects and distributes winter coats to individuals and families facing the challenges of Maine’s cold weather.
While the official Coats of Kindness campaign kicks off on November 1, community support is already underway. New this year, coat donations are being accepted at all six Gold Star Cleaners locations throughout Penobscot County, giving donors even more time to contribute before winter arrives. Donors are encouraged to drop off gently worn coats of all sizes. Each coat will be professionally cleaned free of charge by Gold Star Cleaners before being distributed by Penquis to people in need throughout the region.
Last year, 1,000 coats were cleaned and redistributed through the program, helping provide warmth, comfort, and dignity to hundreds of Mainers. “Every year, we’re reminded that something as simple as a winter coat can have a tremendous impact on a person’s well-being,” said Chantelle Haltizer, Resource Development Coordinator at Penquis. “As heating costs rise and household budgets continue to be stretched, many families are forced to make difficult choices. Donating a coat you no longer need is a simple way to help ensure a neighbor stays warm, safe, and comfortable this winter.”
This year marks the seventh consecutive year that Gold Star Cleaners has partnered with Penquis to support the Coats of Kindness program. Through this partnership, Gold Star Cleaners donates cleaning services for every collected coat, ensuring each item is fresh and ready for its next owner. “We’re honored to be part of a program that brings our communities together to care for one another,” said Serena Lane, District Manager for Gold Star Cleaners. “Beginning collections earlier this year gives people more opportunities to donate and helps us prepare even more coats for distribution before the coldest months arrive. It’s a privilege for our team to help make sure every donated coat is ready to provide warmth to someone who needs it.”
In addition to coat donations, community members can also support the program through financial contributions. Monetary donations are stretched even further thanks to the support of community partner W.S. Emerson, which provides new coats at cost, maximizing the number of people who can be served each winter. Donations can be made online at www.penquis.org/donate by selecting Coats of Kindness, or in person at any Penquis office. Financial gifts help purchase new coats for children and adults when donated inventory falls short of community need. “Coats of Kindness is successful because of the generosity of our community and the commitment of partners like Gold Star Cleaners and W.S. Emerson,” Haltizer said. “Together, we’re making sure that no one has to face a Maine winter without the warmth they deserve.”
Gently used coats can be dropped off at the following Gold Star Cleaners locations as of October 1st:
- 220 Union Street, Bangor
- Brewer Shopping Center, Brewer
- 200 Wilson Street, Brewer
- Corner of Main & Depot, Lincoln
- University Mall, Orono
- Old Town Plaza, Old Town
For more information about the Coats of Kindness program or to make a donation, visit www.penquis.org.
A small selection of coats is currently available at Penquis’ Bangor location. Starting in November, people in need of a coat can also stop by Penquis’ offices in Dover-Foxcroft, Lincoln, and Rockland during the office’s normal business hours.

title: Arundel boatbuilding school confirms permanent closure, with property to be auctioned
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The Landing School of Boatbuilding & Design has confirmed its permanent closure after months of consideration, with the Arundel school’s property set to go up for auction.
The school, which for nearly 50 years had equipped students to work in the marine industry, initially announced its closure in May, citing enrollment declines that caused financial issues.
Soon after, school leaders said they were exploring a potential partnership with a Massachusetts maritime college. But in August, The Landing School announced that its board of trustees had determined the deal with the Northeast Maritime Institute was “not viable.“
In a letter signed by the board of trustees, the school announced this month that its leaders have been unable to find a workable solution to keeping the school open.
“The legacy of The Landing School will carry on in the boats our graduates built, the businesses they started, the skills they brought to their careers, the people they mentored, and the countless lives they touched,” the letter reads.
Landing School President John Caron said in August that 2026-27 academic programs were being canceled and that incoming students who had enrolled would have their deposits reimbursed.
Caron did not respond to a request for comment Monday.
The school will hold two auctions next month through Keenan Auction Company to sell off the school’s possessions: one for the contents of the school building, and another for the property, the board’s letter said. A live real estate auction will take place at 11 a.m. on Nov. 10 at 286 River Road.
Bidding in the online auction for the school’s equipment will open at 9 a.m. Nov. 1 and close on Nov. 16. Some of the equipment included in that auction include marine manufacturing equipment, vessels and tools.
The Landing School opened in 1978, teaching students boatbuilding and marine systems, and described itself as the oldest institution of its kind in the United States.

title: This Maine City Is No Longer Among the Country's 10 Safest Major Cities
text:
This Maine City Is No Longer Among the Country’s 10 Safest Major Cities
While we are used to hearing about how safe Maine is compared to the rest of the nation, we no longer have a city in the top 10.
👇 KEEP READING: 22 of The Oldest Bars and Restaurants in Portland, Maine 👇
WalletHub compared 182 U.S. cities using 41 metrics across three categories: home and community safety, natural disaster risk and financial safety.
Each city’s ranking was based on a weighted overall score, with the analysis limited to city boundaries and excluding surrounding metropolitan areas.
Portland ranked 11th overall in WalletHub’s safest cities report this year after placing in the top 10 in previous years.
The city ranked 41st in home and community safety, 15th in natural disaster risk, and first in financial safety.
City safety includes protection from crime, traffic fatalities and natural disasters, as well as financial risks, according to WalletHub analyst Chip Lupo.
He said financial safety involves reducing fraud and identity theft, helping residents stay employed and insured, and addressing homelessness.
And there you have it! Our Portland has slipped out of the top 10 safest major cities in the country, coming in at No. 11 in this year’s rankings.

title: Owl spotting on the Upper West Side
text:
I love modern technology. On a family trip to New York City this past weekend, a GroupMe chat announced the presence of a cooperative family of American Barn Owls on the Upper West Side. So, while my Natalie and Anouk went off to Madison Square Garden for a Harry Styles concert, I worked my way uptown for a different form of evening entertainment.
Like most owls, American Barn Owls are nocturnal, hunting with a distinctive, buoyant flight. This family of owls — mom, dad and six young — was first noticed Oct. 6, the young poking their heads out of a hole in a derelict, rooftop water tank, so very Big Apple. Like the Barred Owls of Mount Desert Island, these owls are cavity-nesters.
My evening free, combined with the fact of never having observed this species before, there was never any question about seeking out the birds.
On Central Park West, an hour’s walk north of my 26th Street hotel, I came upon a gaggle of binocular-toting people milling about. In the fading twilight, someone shouted that an owl emerged. Everyone looked up as one; binoculars, spotting scopes, and digital cameras with veritable bazookas for lenses all trained on a particular narrow slice of skyline to the rooftop water tower. I instantly saw two owls, one making a brief, wing-stretching sortie, the other perched on the edge of the artificial cavity. A life bird!
I struck up a conversation with Betsy and Chris Marshall, of Rochester, N.Y., who had trekked six hours just to see and photograph these birds. They relayed a conversation they had with a local in-the-know who stated the owlets fledged the previous night. Fledging means leaving the nest to start flying on their own. In the case of owls, young that can fly still need many additional weeks of hunting lessons. Our observation of these two juveniles may just have been their last night at the water tower before they begin roaming the city, doing their part to reduce the rat population.
American Barn Owls are so rare in Maine that the Maine Bird Records Committee has only a smattering of reports for MDI. Ralph Palmer’s 1949 book “Maine Birds” reports a pair at Great Head in about 1900. It wasn’t until 1961 for the next report, this one in Southwest Harbor. And in 2011, one was reported at Sand Beach.
Spending an evening observing these uncommon owls set me to pondering rarity. This comes in many forms: regional rarity to global rarity, naturally small populations to populations reduced by human activities, species at the edge of their range, and outright vagrants. I have been fortunate in seeing my share of vagrants here on MDI.
In science, the terms “vagrant” and “vagrancy” are unencumbered by negative connotations; instead, they are labels applied to species that find themselves outside their typical range. Northern Cardinals were once vagrants. They first bred in southern Maine in 1969. The first MDI report comes from 1960; there is a 10-year gap until the next report. Today, cardinals are common around most homes.
Perhaps MDI’s most charismatic rarity was a 2017 Great Gray Owl. Standing nearly 3 feet tall, this bird of the uninhabited boreal forests to the north comes south when food supply crashes. For nearly a week, it stuck around Schooner Head, affording incredible wildlife watching to hundreds of awed spectators. Alas, when one photographer got too close in pursuit of the “perfect photo,” the owl flew the coup and was not seen again.
In August 2007, I received a call about an unusual hummingbird. My immediate thought was juvenile Ruby-throated Hummingbird. It was described as all green (consistent with a juvenile Ruby-throat), with a decurved, or downward pointing bill and a purple patch behind the eye. That had my attention. “I’ll be there in five minutes!” Upon my arrival, I was treated to Maine’s first, and only, occurrence of a Mexican Violetear, a species you expect in the Yucatan, not Mount Desert.
Another famous vagrant was Wendell Gilley’s Ivory Gull (I wrote about this in a column last December), a bird of the edge of Arctic ice. In February 1940, Gilley called Acadia National Park ranger Maurice Sullivan reporting an unusual gull. Maurice directed Wendell to “collect” (a euphemism for shooting) the bird for the park’s collections. Somewhere along the way, the specimen was lost. Thanks to the perseverance of park archivist Marie Yarborough, the bird was refound in 2025!
There is a long list of rare-to-MDI vagrants that have visited our region, including Black-bellied Whistling Ducks (six hung out for four days at the high school ponds May 2013), Chuck-will’s-widow (reported in 1974), Red-billed Tropicbird (1986 at Mount Desert Rock), White-chinned Petrel (2010 from a Bar Harbor Whale Watch), Magnificent Frigatebird (1984 at Otter Point and 2005 at Bar Harbor town pier), Brown Booby (2021 on Mount Desert Rock), Masked Booby (2021 on Mount Desert Rock and a first state record), Swainson’s Hawk (2015 flying over the Cadillac Mountain Hawk Watch), Red-headed Woodpecker (most recently over-wintered in Southwest Harbor 2018-2019), Ash-throated Flycatcher (1975 in Bar Harbor), Violet-green Swallow (2018 over Hamilton Pond), Varied Thrush (observed twice in the same head-of-MDI yard, most recently in 2021), Northern Wheatear (2026 on Ship Island), Lark Bunting (1965 in Hulls Cove, 1968 in Southwest Harbor, 2015 in Seal Cove), Yellow-headed Blackbird (2014 on the Atlantic Oceanside lawn), Bullock’s Oriole (over-wintered 1960-1961 in Southwest Harbor), Brewer’s Blackbird (1981 in Northeast Harbor), Kentucky Warbler (1973 on MDI, 2019 and 2021 on Mount Desert Rock), Black-throated Gray Warbler (1987 on Mount Desert Rock), Black-headed Grosbeak (2020 in Mount Desert), Lazuli Bunting (1974 on MDI), and Painted Bunting (2018 in Bar Harbor).
So, what does it take to see a vagrant? It’s a combination of having an idea of what is typical for a region coupled with spending time outdoors being observant. Nearly everyone has a smartphone these days; so, when in doubt, take photos and share them with people that know about the natural world.

title: President Trump waives new sanctions on Russia
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
President Trump waives new Russia sanctions
President Trump has temporarily waived some sanctions targeting Russia's energy sector and economy as he says he's "in the process of negotiating peace."
President Trump waives new Russia sanctions
President Trump has temporarily waived some sanctions targeting Russia's energy sector and economy as he says he's "in the process of negotiating peace."
President Donald Trump has temporarily waived some key sanctions targeting Russia's economic and energy infrastructure, arguing the move will keep the country at the negotiating table and put an end to the war in Ukraine.
The sanctions, which are part of the bipartisan Lindsey Graham Act passed last month, were designed to target Russia's energy sector and economy, which have helped fund the country's ongoing war in Ukraine.
"My decision on Russia is a very simple one. I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine, and don't want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table," Trump said in a Truth Social post. "Signing that document at this time will do that, and I can sign it later, or any time that I want!"
The Trump administration said the waived sanctions would last for the next 60 days.
"The president's been clear he'd like the war in Ukraine and Russia to end," Secretary of State Marco Rubio said to reporters over the weekend. "He's done the things he's done with suspending the sanctions for 60 days because he wants to see if there's an opportunity for the talks that are going on right now with both Ukraine and Russia to lead to something positive and avoid another disastrous year of war and conflict."
But the decision drew criticism from international leaders, who argued it would be too "soft" a move on Russia.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called it "unfortunate."
"It's unbelievable. It's a tragedy. It's a historic mistake and big tragedy," Zelenskyy said. "If the United States will take officially, will take the side of Russia, of course, if the two countries will be together, of course, of course we will not prevail."
The pause drew criticism from bipartisan lawmakers, including Sen. Darline Graham, R-South Carolina, who now holds the seat of her late brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham, the very senator the law is named after.
"The president and I share the same goal, which is to end the war, to get gas and diesel prices down, and the sanctions bill is one of the tools he can use to do that," Graham said. "It's up to him whether or not he chooses to use it. Personally, I would choose to keep the pressure on Russia to end the war and get the gas prices down."
The Lindsey Graham Act also includes sanctions against Russian President Vladimir Putin, senior military leaders, Russian financial institutions, and energy projects. It targets a "shadow fleet" of oil tankers used by Russia to circumvent previous sanctions, imposes tariffs on countries buying Russian oil and gas, and expands sanctions against Iran.
Key buyers of Russian exports, including China and India, are also affected, per the bill.
The announcement comes a week after Trump revealed a deal allowing Russia to export diesel to the global market, though analysts say the deal will do little to lower global diesel prices.
Overall, fuel prices remain high. Gas prices have risen more than 34% year over year, according to the latest government inflation data.
The Get the Facts Data Team found that gas prices have risen sharply since the U.S. war with Iran that began in February.

title: Photographer captures 250 veterans’ portraits to honor service
text:
(Aging Untold) — Photographs are powerful. For photographer Mikel Conrad, they are a way to tell the story of those who put their lives on the line for the country’s future.
Ron Camillo is one of hundreds featured in Conrad’s “250 Faces of Service & Sacrifice.”
“Active duty 1950-51. I can remember like yesterday, Korea. The problem is I saw things over there I can’t talk about,” Camillo said.
Camillo is a Korean War veteran who served with the 1st Marine Division and the 5th Marines.
“Just their willingness to serve and just do what they had to do and not beat their chest about it. ... They just went out and did what they had to do,” Conrad said.
Conrad’s vision is a portfolio made for the country’s 250th birthday so the stories of these heroes can still be told long after they are gone.
Aging Untold host and gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said these portraits do more than capture a face.
“You know, so many of our veterans come back feeling unseen. And this gives them that, I see you and I hear you and I’m honoring you, and what you did mattered. What you did for all of us matters so much. And it is so dignifying and shows so much respect for our veterans,” Cradduck said.
This is about honor and respect, Cradduck said.
“And so, when we take away the vanity side and we just say, we want to honor you, not we want to capture you, we want to honor you, it gets rid of some of the apprehension of sitting in front of the lens,” she said.
The “250 Faces of Service & Sacrifice” project is a tribute to the men and women who have kept the country’s history in focus.
“We’re all tied together. We’re all brothers,” veteran Gene Acker said.

title: ‘God is going to grow something out of this’: Fire rips through church building
text:
CLEVELAND COUNTY, N.C. (WBTV/Gray News) - A fire tore through a North Carolina church Sunday morning, collapsing the roof and forcing cancellation of services.
The fire broke out shortly after 7 a.m. on Oct. 18 at Dover Baptist Church on Polkville Road in Shelby.
“No services today. Pray for our church. Our building is currently on fire,” wrote church officials in a social post.
Cleveland County Fire said crews responded to the massive fire as flames tore through the roof and the front sanctuary of the church.
Photos taken by WBTV showed the aftermath of the fire, with a large portion of the roof collapsed into the one-story building as multiple fire trucks responded.
Authorities said no one was injured and the church was reportedly unoccupied when the fire started.
The pastor, Jerry Reed, said the loss is difficult, but he remains hopeful.
“It seems like a setback. It’s heartbreaking to share this with our church members,” Reed said. “But we’ve had an outpouring of support from other churches and the community, and we just feel that God is going to grow something out of this. That this is not the end of our story.”
The cause remains under investigation, but officials said no foul play was suspected.
“Thank you to everyone who has prayed for us. Our building is gone, but the church is not!” wrote the church.

title: Man Injured in Castle Hill Fire
text:
CASTLE HILL, Maine (WAGM) - A woodstove sparked a fire that injured a Castle Hill man and badly damaged his mobile home this weekend.
According to the Maine State Police, on Saturday, October 17th at 1:09 pm, the Mapleton Fire Department responded to a report of a structure fire in Castle Hill. Upon arrival, firefighters encountered heavy fire conditions at a mobile home in the area. Fire crews were able to suppress the fire, which caused substantial damage to the residence. The sole occupant of the home, a 60-year-old man, injured his hand while attempting to put out the fire. Investigators from the State Fire Marshal’s Office responded to the scene to determine the origin and cause of the fire.
Investigators determined that the fire started near the home’s woodstove which ignited combustible wall materials behind it. This resulted in the fire spreading throughout the mobile home. Investigators ruled the fire accidental. The State Fire Marshal’s Office reminds residents of the importance of ensuring that woodstoves and other heating appliances are properly installed and maintained. Residents should verify that all heating appliances have the required clearances from combustible materials, including walls, furniture, and other nearby items. The State Fire Marshal’s Office emphasizes that maintaining proper clearances between heating appliances and combustible materials is essential to preventing residential fires and protecting lives and property.

text:

Emergency crews responded to a crash involving a semi-truck on Royalsborough Rd in Durham early Monday morning.
One person injured in semi-truck crash in Durham
Emergency crews responded to a crash involving a semi-truck on Royalsborough Rd in Durham early Monday morning.
One person was hurt after a crash between a semi-truck and a small car in Durham early Monday morning.
According to the Durham Fire Department, the person's injuries aren't considered life-threatening. The injured occupant was taken to Maine Medical Center in "serious but stable condition."

title: Service member who died in rappelling accident at college football game identified
text:
(Gray News) - The United States Air Force identified the service member who died in a rappelling accident at a college football game on Saturday.
Tech. Sgt. Ian Patterson was attempting to rappel from the rafters as part of a demonstration before the football game between the University of Texas at San Antonio and the U.S. Naval Academy when he fell. The game was the university’s annual Salute to Armed Forces and Veterans event.
He was taken to the hospital, where he later died.
GRAPHIC WARNING: The video may be disturbing to some viewers.
Patterson was a Tactical Air Control Party instructor assigned to the 6th Combat Training Squadron, Detachment 2, Joint Base San Antonio, Texas, according to Nellis Air Force Base.
He was from Fort Stewart, Georgia, and served for 15 years. His decorations included the Air and Space Commendation Medal with three oak leaf clusters; the Army Commendation Medal, Air and Space Achievement Medal and Army Achievement Medal, each with one oak leaf cluster. In 2022, Patterson was named the Air Force Special Warfare Enlisted Instructor of the Year at the Headquarters Air Force level, according to the Air Force.
“This tragedy is felt deeply across the 57th Wing,” said U.S. Air Force Brig. Gen. Scott C. Mills, 57th Wing commander. “Tech. Sgt. Patterson and his service mattered immensely to our wing, and to the family, friends, and teammates who had the privilege of knowing and serving alongside him. Our team is now focused on standing beside Ian’s family, loved ones, and fellow Airmen as we navigate this profound loss together.”
The rappelling accident is under investigation.

title: Mother of 8 hit and killed by train during morning run: ‘She was an angel’
text:
ELOY, Ariz. (AZFamily/Gray News) - An Arizona family is grieving after a mother of eight was hit and killed by a train while on a morning run.
Thelma Candelaria, 47, was a caregiver and mother of eight children. She had been baptized less than a week before her death in what was supposed to be the start of a new beginning.
She went out for a routine run Thursday morning in Eloy. She was recording the run on social media, and her daughter, Alaisha Candelaria, provided videos showing her smiling and in good spirits.
“She was singing along to Jessie Reyez, which is her favorite artist. She was laughing,” said Alaisha Candelaria of her mother.
Alaisha Candelaria would later use her mother’s videos, along with surveillance footage, to piece together what happened next.
She never saw the train that killed her
During her run, Thelma Candelaria stopped at a railroad crossing around 6 a.m. As she was recording one train, a separate train on another track approached her from the opposite direction, according to her daughter.
The mother didn’t see the second train, and any sound it made was muffled by her earbuds and the train she was already recording. Eloy Police say both trains sounded their horns before she was hit.
“She had her noise-canceling Beat headphones on. She was in her own world,” Alaisha Candelaria said.
Eloy Police say the train that hit Thelma Candelaria applied its emergency brake but couldn’t avoid the collision. She was pronounced dead at the scene.
“It’s a lot. It’s a lot,” Alaisha Candelaria said.
She says she wants the community to know her mother’s death was a horrible accident.
“People, continuously, they’ve always told me my whole life, ‘You are so, so lucky to have the mother that you have,’” Alaisha Candelaria said. “She was an angel.”
The family has created a GoFundMe to help with funeral costs and support for Thelma Candelaria’s children.
The Eloy Police Department’s Vehicular Crimes Unit is investigating the incident.

title: Chellie Pingree’s Portland office gets suspicious letter, prompting FBI response
text:
U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree’s Portland office received a suspicious letter Monday, the latest in a string of concerning packages that have been sent to members of Congress in recent days.
Starting last week, representatives and senators around the country began getting similar letters, many of which authorities said contained an unknown white powder. The Portland office of Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, received one, her staff said Friday. Sens. Pete Ricketts, R-Nebraska, Ted Cruz, R-Texas, and Chuck Schumer, D-New York, were also among the several dozen recipients, NBC News reported.
The envelope containing the letter addressed to Pingree, D-1st District, had a return address of “DSA” along with the street number for a building in New York City’s financial district. But NBC reported that authorities have yet to trace the letters’ origins.
So far, no injuries have been reported in connection with the mailings.
“We cannot accept threats and intimidation as a normal part of our politics. The people who work in congressional offices and administer our elections are public servants dedicated to helping their communities. They deserve to do that work without fear,” Pingree said in a written statement. “Political disagreement is part of a healthy democracy. Threatening the people who keep it running is unacceptable.”
The statement from Pingree noted that the FBI responded to her office’s call about the letter, as did the Portland police and fire departments.
Pingree is heavily favored to win a 10th term representing Maine’s deep-blue 1st District this fall as she faces Republican Ronald Russell for the second straight election.

title: Lewiston girls soccer knocks off Edward Little to secure 1st playoff berth since 2019
text:
LEWISTON — The Lewiston girls soccer team removed any doubt about its playoff hopes in its regular-season finale.
Goalkeeper Emily Desrosiers’ clean sheet helped the Blue Devils defeat Edward Little 2-0 at Don Roux Field on Monday, guaranteeing Lewiston its first playoff appearance since 2019.
“It’s kind of crazy because I wasn’t even close to being in high school in 2019,” Desrosiers said. “Last year, every year I’ve been here, we just kept winning and winning more. Then finally we made it to the playoffs, and I think we really deserve it because we’ve been playing our butts off this year. We’ve really been improving this whole year.”
Blue Devils coach Kevin Albert said it was extra sweet to end the seven-year drought by beating the Red Eddies (3-11).
“Well, first off, it was a great game. Both teams played well,” Albert said. “But coming in, knowing that we could really secure a spot, it meant a lot, and against our rivals. You always want to have a good game. …We really wanted to have some good momentum heading into the playoffs. So this was a big win for us for sure.”
Lewiston beat Brewer 2-1 in the preliminary round of the 2019 Class A North playoffs before losing to top-seeded Camden Hills 12-0 in the quarterfinals.
What does this mean?
Lewiston (3-9-2) will probably finish seventh in Class A North and face either Brunswick or Mt. Ararat in the quarterfinals.
“Brunswick’s a good team, but we also showed them twice that we can compete with them,” Albert said. “They did beat us the first time (4-0), but it was a pretty close game. It was on their home field. We got to get used to playing on the road, on the grass, which we’re not used to. But our girls are excited for the opportunity.”
The Blue Devils had only one victory in September, but had a strong finish to the season that included a 2-2 draw against Brunswick, a 2-1 victory over second-place Mt. Ararat and the win over Edward Little on Monday.
The Red Eddies, who beat Lewiston 5-2 on Sept. 19, will miss the postseason.
How did it happen?
Lewiston struck first in the 11th minute when Chloe Croteau’s corner kick deflected off an Edward Little defender into the goal.
“Sometimes that’s all you need (is a bounce),” Albert said. “She actually had one the first time we played EL. She scored on a corner directly into the net, which was great.”
Piper Croteau scored in the second half, finishing off a feed from Sawdah Ali.
Desrosiers was tested in the first 10 minutes, making five saves before Lewiston took the lead on the own goal. She also made a few big plays in the final five minutes, aggressively grabbing the ball in the 18-yard box after a corner kick and stopping a shot in the final seconds to preserve the shutout.
“It was really nerve-wracking because it just kept coming back to me,” Derosier said of the first half. “There weren’t any, like, hard ones to stop at the beginning, but it was just really repetitive. So I just got tired really quick. I was just getting stressed out.”
Statistical leaders
Edward Little: Aubrie Binette (eight saves)
Lewiston: Emily Desrosiers (nine saves); Piper Croteau (goal), Sawdah Ali (assist)

title: Rep. Pingree says her Portland office received a suspicious letter
text:
Rep. Chellie Pingree says her Portland office received a suspicious letter
Maine congresswoman says letter is consistent with those recently received by other congressional and election offices
Rep. Chellie Pingree says her Portland office received a suspicious letter
Maine congresswoman says letter is consistent with those recently received by other congressional and election offices
Maine Congresswoman Chellie Pingree announced that her office in Portland received a suspicious letter Monday morning that is consistent with letters that have been recently sent to other congressional and election offices.
Pingree's Portland office is located at 2 Portland Fish Pier, which is the same address as the Maine International Trade Center.
"I am grateful to the Portland Police and Fire departments and the FBI for responding quickly to the potential threat and helping keep my staff and others in the Marine Trade Center safe. U.S. Capitol Police has been notified," Pingree said in a statement shared Monday.
This news comes three days after U.S. Sen. Susan Collins' office in Portland received a letter with a suspicious substance.
Collins, a Republican, and Pingree, a Democrat who represents Maine's 1st Congressional District, are both seeking reelection to their respective offices.
"We cannot accept threats and intimidation as a normal part of our politics," Pingree said in her statement. "The people who work in congressional offices and administer our elections are public servants dedicated to helping their communities. They deserve to do that work without fear. Political disagreement is part of a healthy democracy. Threatening the people who keep it running is unacceptable."
"My team and I will not be deterred from our work," Pingree added. "We will continue showing up for the people of Maine."
Federal investigation into suspicious letters
On Thursday, Oct. 15, The Associated Press received a statement from the FBI that said the bureau and the U.S. Postal Inspection Service were "investigating a series of suspicious mailings sent to various addresses nationwide, including Secretary of State offices and their related election offices."
"Some of the letters contained an unknown substance and we are working closely with our law enforcement partners to respond to each incident," the FBI said in its statement to the AP. "We are also working with our partners to identify the individual or individuals responsible for the letters."
The office of Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester, a Delaware Democrat, said in a statement that it was sent a letter with a "suspicious substance" that was intercepted by Capitol Police. Democratic Sen. Alex Padilla of California said the Postal Service intercepted a suspicious package before it reached his office. And Democratic Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand said postal inspectors intercepted a suspicious piece of mail addressed to her New York City office.
Last week, mailed packages containing a powdery substance led to the evacuation of election offices in at least two states, Louisiana and Oklahoma. The Ohio secretary of state said the Postal Service intercepted a package containing a white powder intended for its office and noted that similar mailings had been sent to election officials in multiple states. Numerous states, from Idaho to Florida, said their election offices either received letters or had them intercepted by the Postal Service.
The Wisconsin Elections Commission said in a statement that it received a letter and the white powder enclosed in it was not hazardous, according to tests. "Let this be very clear: this incident will not shake us," Wisconsin elections administrator Meagan Wolfe said.
Information from The Associated Press was used in this report.

title: Our votes demonstrate our values
text:
The decisions voters are now facing are much more about their personal values than any policy (political) views they have. Many have come to terms with their own party’s “demonstrated values” and now must cast their ballots.
Each political party has demonstrated their values through their own actions or inaction. A total of 147 Republicans voted to approve Trump’s efforts to overturn a fair election in 2021. Meanwhile, the Democratic Party has tried to pass legislation to guarantee healthcare for U.S. citizens and make the wealthiest Americans pay their fair share of taxes.
The divergence of our citizens’ values will not be solved by any election. Our votes to select a governor, a U.S. representative and a U.S. senator, however, will demonstrate our values to our families and fellow citizens.
Tom Turner

title: Professional Logging Contractors (PLC) of the Northeast Log A Load for Kids effort raises $292,746 in 2025
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
COURTESY OF JON HUMPHREY, PROFESSIONAL LOGGING CONTRACTORS (PLC) OF THE NORTHEAST
The Professional Logging Contractors (PLC) of the Northeast raised $292,746 for Children’s Miracle Network (CMN) last year through its annual Log A Load for Kids fundraising efforts.
The total for 2025 included funds raised at the PLC’s two Log A Load golf tournaments, the Log A Load live auction at the PLC’s 2025 annual meeting, and a Log A Load half marathon fundraiser in December.
“This total represents the incredible generosity and commitment of the PLC’s Members, Supporting Members, friends, families and supporters,” said Dana Doran, Executive Director of the PLC. “In a time of unprecedented challenges and struggle for the industry, this group rallied to once again achieve an amazing result for the children and families supported by Children’s Miracle Network, and everyone involved should be very proud of this accomplishment.”
On Jan. 23 of this year, Doran presented a check for the funds to representatives from Northern Light/Eastern Maine Medical Center in Bangor and MaineHealth Barbara Bush Children’s Hospital in Portland. Both are CMN hospitals.
The check was presented at the PLC’s office in Augusta. Those accepting the check on behalf of the hospitals were Nichole Trainor, Northern Light Eastern Maine Medical Center CMN Program Director; Tracy Jameson, Philanthropy Specialist for Northern Light Eastern Maine Medical Center CMN; and Meaghan McNamara, MaineHealth Senior Philanthropy Manager.
“We want to express our deepest gratitude to the Professional Logging Contractors of the Northeast for your continued support,” Trainor said. “Because of you, our youngest patients and their families feel comforted, safe, and deeply cared for. Thank you for standing with them — and with us.”
“We can’t thank the Professional Logging Contractors of the Northeast enough for their commitment to making a difference in the lives of our patients,” McNamara said. “The PLC — and the whole logging community who rallies around these fundraising events – helps to transform the care and services that we’re able to provide. And we are so grateful for that support!”
The PLC’s Log A Load efforts had raised more than $2.9 million since 1995 by the end of last year. While the total for 2026 has not yet been fully tallied, it surpassed $3 million in May.
The PLC raises the majority of Log A Load funds each year during an auction at its annual meeting in the spring and at golf tournaments in Maine in August and September. In 2025 for the first time, additional funds were raised at the Millinocket half-marathon in Maine in December.
The PLC and the Northern Light Health Foundation (formerly Eastern Maine Health Systems Foundation) have partnered in the Log A Load fund-raising effort since 1996. Donations have gone to support research and training, purchase equipment, and pay for uncompensated care, all in support of the mission to save and improve the lives of as many children as possible. Northern Light Eastern Maine Medical Center in Bangor includes a Neonatal Intensive Care Unit that has received support for years from the PLC’s Log A Load efforts. The PLC began partnering with MaineHealth Barbara Bush Children’s Hospital in Portland for the southern tournament in 2019, and in 2024 for the first time began partnering with the University of Vermont Children’s Hospital in Burlington, Vermont as well — also a CMN hospital.
Log A Load for Kids is an annual campaign which began in 1988 when loggers and others in the forest products community began donating the value of a load of logs to their local CMN hospital. Today, Log A Load is a leader in CMN Hospitals’ fundraising, raising more than $6.5 million annually through golf tournaments, fishing events, dinners, truckloads of log donations, and other events.

title: AI agents are only as good as the personal information you share. That raises privacy concerns
text:
Matt Robb wanted to sell his computer keyboard.
So he made a listing on Facebook Marketplace — and, as an experiment late last month, he put Meta’s new artificial intelligence agent Muse in the driver’s seat.
“I kind of went into it like a guinea pig,” said Robb, a Toronto-based content creator who regularly reviews consumer tech. He had seen Muse’s plush toy-looking avatar pop up on Instagram and decided to see if the AI agent could spare him some online bargaining.
Muse got to work. But within a day, Robb got an alarming update: A buyer he didn’t know had shown up outside his house late at night. How? Muse had struck a deal on its own and shared Robb’s home address after agreeing to a pickup. It even sent an automated “Yep, I’m here!” message from his account when the buyer arrived — all without Robb’s knowledge.
“Not only did it give my address when the guy asked and it accepted the offer, but it literally was almost like teasing the guy (about me being there when I wasn’t),” said Robb, who also detailed the experience in his now widely-shared social media posts. “That really baffled me.”
Many have welcomed AI agents into their online lives, and raved about how personalized assistants like Muse can handle everyday tasks with ease — from snagging a dinner reservation or planning a trip, to organizing email inboxes. But like other AI bots, the agents are only as good as the information they have access to. They perform better the more they know about a user — and perhaps also that person’s friends, family and even colleagues. That raises privacy concerns.
Robb and the buyer eventually made amends, and Meta reached out to talk through what went wrong. But the episode showed real-world risks that can arise from sharing extensive personal information with the technology.
“Using an AI agent is similar to handing someone your keys and a to-do list,” said Veronica Rivera, assistant professor at Georgia Tech’s School of Cybersecurity and Privacy. “How helpful they are, and by extension how risky, depends on which keys you hand over.”
Companies have varied privacy policies for AI agents
Since its September launch, downloads of Meta’s Muse app have skyrocketed. And competition is only growing. OpenAI recently rolled out its own lineup of “always on” AI helpers, called dots, which can be integrated into ChatGPT and workplace platforms like Slack and Microsoft Teams.
Older generative AI chatbots, like the standard version of ChatGPT, respond to specific prompts. At the user’s request, they can write essays, generate new images or music, or even write lines of code.
Meta’s Muse and OpenAI’s dots go a step further to perform day-to-day tasks on a person’s behalf. AI agents are powered by the same large language models as chatbots, but they run in a loop. That allows an agent to take proactive steps, even when the user isn’t looking.
“One of the things that makes these AI agents really appealing is that they are unprecedentedly useful,” said Rivera, who is also a Microsoft-funded Computing Research Association Trustworthy AI Research Fellow.
But the convenience comes with the price of sharing more details about your life.
Once AI agents obtain users’ information, it’s very difficult to fully withdraw access, said Ebrahim Bagheri, a professor at the University of Toronto’s Faculty of Information.
“If you provide access to your credit card to an agent, the agent now immediately has access to all of the historical transactions … they will immediately — within less than seconds — ingest all of that data,” Bagheri said. And while users can later withdraw access, Bagheri said there’s “no taking back” data the agent has already seen, and how developers store historical data can be murky.
Both Meta and OpenAI outline privacy policies for their new AI agents, which operate on their own dedicated cloud computers. You can turn off memory sharing between dots and ChatGPT, but information the agent previously received isn’t automatically deleted. OpenAI gives users an option to request access to, delete or correct personal information, although rights can vary depending on where you live.
Meta’s Muse gives users options to delete message history and other information, too. For day-to-day use, the agent prompts users for access permissions — and Meta has said Muse learns about a user and who they interact with “based on public information and from what you’ve chosen to share.” But the company says that all stays secure for each user.
But the tech giant also notes that Muse can still “make mistakes or take unexpected actions.”
Risks of mishaps rise with AI agents’ level of access
In Robb’s case, he learned the disclosure of his address came down to “always allow” permissions he granted when he first let Muse on his Facebook Marketplace profile, where he had shared his pickup address. But he warned others could similarly misunderstand the extent of that access — and said he initially thought the AI agent would check with him before sharing that information or accepting offers, regardless.
His AI agent didn’t follow the rest of his instructions without error, either. For another item Robb was selling, Muse seemingly suggested he would accept a price $100 below the previously-set minimum. When reached by The Associated Press, Meta acknowledged the agent’s error without offering further comment.
Robb later largely disconnected Muse from his apps. In an interview earlier this month, he said it could’ve been a far worse situation, especially “if some stranger turned up to someone more vulnerable’s house.” Still, Robb said he expects these agents to be fine-tuned and he would consider re-enabling Muse in the future. He’s since been testing another AI agent — Grok Bot from Elon Musk’s X, which launched in beta in August.
Other tech companies have become wary of the influx of AI agents. Earlier this month, Apple said it would introduce new controls for its Mac operating system in response to AI agents’ broader access of apps like mail, messages and even browsing history without users’ “full knowledge and understanding.”
“As AI agents become increasingly capable and autonomous, the risks associated with this level of access will grow substantially,” Apple wrote in an Oct. 2 update.
Apple didn’t specify any developers or agents by name, but the update arrived after Inc. Magazine columnist Jason Aten reported that Muse watched notifications on his Mac — including Messages — without him giving the agent that specific access.
Meta spokesperson Andy Stone has maintained such integration is “entirely opt-in,” writing on social media last month that users would have to enable both the Apple security feature “Full Disk Access” and a Messages connector through Muse. Aten said he didn’t grant the agent those permissions.
Even those who do not join the AI agent boom aren’t necessarily shielded. Consumers who don’t download an AI agent might still interact with others who do. And beyond potential confusion when AI sends messages on behalf of a user, experts warn of ripple effects when it comes to privacy.
“When your agent reads your inbox or your texts, it’s also reading what your friends and family sent you, even if they never explicitly agreed to that,” Rivera said.

title: UMaine study finds sharp decline in baby lobster population along Midcoast
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
UMaine study finds sharp decline in Midcoast region's baby lobster population
A new study conducted by the University of Maine is sounding the alarm for the state's lobster industry.
Researchers found there was an 80% drop in the Midcoast region's baby lobster population between 2010 and 2022.
The study also revealed that since 2015, the adult population of lobster in the same waters has dropped 50%.
Researchers said the sharp decline in baby lobsters had a huge impact on the number of legal-sized adult lobsters fishermen could catch.
As for the reasons behind the population decline, the researchers cited warming temperatures and less food for baby lobsters, as well as lobsters living in deeper habitats, which complicates tracking efforts.
Robert Jarrett, the lead researcher and a recent Ph.D. graduate, said the data does not mean the lobsters are going away, but fishing might have to change with the trends.
“Because of the differences in eastern and western Maine, we're probably going to have different habitats that lobsters can continue to use into the future. But that might result in changes in what the fishery looks like," Jarrett said. "We might have more fishermen fishing offshore or have better success in, say, western Maine than eastern Maine as the Gulf of Maine changes."
The Maine Department of Marine Resources said fishermen caught nearly 79 million pounds of lobster totaling $461 million in 2025.

title: National Guard member is shot while breaking up a fight in Washington, suspect is hit in return fire
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — A National Guard member was shot and injured while trying to break up a fight in the nation’s capital, and the person suspected of firing the gun also was shot in an exchange with guard members, police said Monday.
The shooting happened at about 11:10 p.m. Sunday as seven or eight guard members in a parked van were monitoring the fight on a sidewalk in southeast Washington, in the Eastern Market neighborhood, said Jeffery Carroll, interim chief of the Metropolitan Police Department of Washington.
“They exited their vehicle to try to intervene to try to stop the fight from occurring when they heard gunshots,” Carroll told reporters. “An individual that had been involved in the fight had pulled out a firearm and began shooting.”
The person ran into an alley, Carroll said, and guard members immediately told the person to drop the gun.
“The individual then pointed the weapon toward National Guard members, who returned fire,” Carroll said.
He said one guard member was struck in the leg and the suspect was shot in the abdomen. Both were taken to hospitals for treatment for non-life-threatening injuries, he said.
Three guard members discharged their guns in the encounter, Carroll said. He said the suspect was arrested.
President Donald Trump deployed the guard to Washington in August 2025 as part of what he said was a crime-fighting mission. The force, which rose to a peak of about 5,000 troops over the summer, has supported arrest operations, patrolled city streets and neighborhoods and participated in cleanup efforts.
Trump’s Republican administration says the deployment has contributed to a decrease in crime in the city, where crime was already on the decline before the guard arrived. Officials, activists and residents in the overwhelmingly Democratic city say the deployment is a waste of taxpayer money and has normalized the militarization of a major American city.
The police department is investigating the Sunday night shooting. Carroll said there were no further threats to the community and asked for anyone with information on the shooting to contact police.

title: Maine's Stunning Fall Colors Are Almost Gone for Another Year
text:
Maine’s Stunning Fall Colors Are Almost Gone for Another Year
The days are shortening and the colors are fading. Oh, how time sadly flies.
We’re wrapping up the 2026 fall foliage season, and let’s be honest, it’s always a bit of a bummer. It’s just never long enough.
When Does the Maine Fall Foliage Season End?
The foliage season has cruised by, with reports dropping weekly. According to Maine.gov, we’ve already passed peak season in the majority of the state, with peak foliage typically arriving around the end of October in Southern Maine.
Comfortable daytime temperatures and cool nights early in the season were a huge help. They also created a wonderful atmosphere for folks to enjoy the leaves while taking part in other fall activities.
So, how do things look on the trusty fall foliage map? Thanks to the Maine Department of Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry's Maine Foliage Report, we can see exactly where things stand.
Welp, that’s just about a wrap, folks. The last few regions are riding out their final days of peak foliage before the entire state goes purple on the map. It was a fun run, but I guess we now have snow to look forward to?
How Great was the 2026 Maine Fall Foliage Season?
While it’s sad to see the season coming to an end, we can at least look back at what was a very solid foliage year. Those comfortable daytime temperatures were certainly a big bonus for everyone out enjoying the colors. I mean, who didn’t love a little apple cider and beautiful foliage while basking in 70-degree temperatures?

title: Fact check: JD Vance falsely blames Biden policy for high gas prices
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
JD Vance falsely blames Biden policy for high gas prices. Iran war is mainly to blame.
As the Trump administration faces voter pushback over high gasoline prices, Vice President JD Vance tried to shift the blame to former President Joe Biden.
This story was originally published on PolitiFact.com.
During a CBS News town hall Oct. 17, Vance said, “The biggest reason why gas prices are so high is because when Joe Biden was president, we had about 20% of American refining capacity that went offline. We’re slowly bringing that online. But it does take a little bit of time. And because we shut down so much refining capacity, we were more susceptible to the shocks that we’ve seen in the Middle Eastern energy crisis.”
Vance’s office did not respond to our questions for this article. But while California has lost 20% of its gasoline refining capacity, national refinery capacity has remained relatively stable.
Twenty percent is “not a correct statistic in terms of national refinery capacity,” said Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis for GasBuddy, which tracks U.S. gasoline prices.
What’s more, presidential policy is one of many factors that shape U.S. refining capabilities, multiple oil industry experts told PolitiFact, and that the most obvious cause of today’s high gasoline prices is the Iran war, which was launched by Trump, not Biden.
“The biggest factor influencing high gasoline prices is the elevated cost of crude oil, caused by the reduction in ship traffic through the Strait of Hormuz and damage to export and pipeline facilities in Saudi Arabia and other Gulf countries,” said Hugh Daigle, a professor with the University of Texas at Austin’s petroleum and geosystems engineering department.
How could Biden’s policies have made a difference?
Energy market experts said that some of Biden’s policies — notably efforts to combat climate change, which involve transitioning away from fossil fuels and toward cleaner, renewable energy — likely contributed to some refiners’ decisions not to greenlight new refineries or to expand existing ones.
In particular, California’s stringent environmental policies help explain why two refineries shuttered there. The timing is less clear than Vance made it sound: The closure of a Phillips 66 refinery in Los Angeles was announced two weeks before Trump won reelection in 2024. Valero announced the closure of its refinery in Benicia, California, in April 2025, when Trump was president. Both facilities closed during Trump’s second term.
How does the refining economy work?
Biden’s policies are not considered the prime culprit for today’s high gasoline prices, experts said.
The bigger factors shaping U.S. refining capacity are market-driven, experts said. They include:
The current and expected demand for fuel. The growth of electric cars — partially nudged by government policy but also driven by consumers’ decisions — has put some downward pressure on demand for gasoline, and thus the demand for refining. And as more people work from home, they have to drive less often.
Foreign refining capacity. The more foreign refining capability there is, the less pressure for oil companies to rely exclusively on U.S. refiners. “Since 2019, global refining capacity has shrunk by about 1 million barrels a day while demand has grown by about 4.5 million barrels a day,” said Skip York, a fellow at Rice University’s Center for Energy Studies.
U.S. refiners are busy right now because 3 million barrels a day are offline in Russia and the Middle East because of Ukrainian and Iranian attacks. Much of the Russian and Middle Eastern refinery capacity is geared toward producing diesel. As a result, York said, U.S. refiners have switched some of their production from gasoline to diesel — which has further hiked gasoline prices for U.S. drivers.
Refinery profitability. When Phillips 66 announced it was closing the Los Angeles refinery, the company said that in addition to concerns about California regulations, it made the decision despite the facility being profitable There were “more attractive projects in the company’s portfolio,” York said.
U.S. and world events. During recessions, there is less demand for gasoline, so refinery use tends to drop. “The big drop in U.S. refining capacity utilization happened in spring of 2020, during the initial wave of COVID shutdowns,” said Clark Williams-Derry, an energy finance analyst at the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis.
How does U.S. refinery capacity today compare with the Biden era?
Despite disruption driven by the COVID-19 pandemic, wars and market factors, U.S. refinery usage has remained relatively stable under both Biden and Trump, data from the U.S. Energy Information Agency shows.
In 2021 and 2022, deferred maintenance and supply-chain breakdowns during the pandemic undercut refinery capacity. U.S. refining capacity has been at historically normal levels ever since, Daigle said.
Williams-Derry calculated how many refineries’ last date of operation fell during Trump’s two terms and compared it with how many shut down during Biden’s term. He found that the amount of refining capacity lost from shutdowns under Trump quadrupled the amount lost under Biden.
“Personally, I don’t think that politics had much to do with any of these closures,” Williams-Derry said. He cited a Phillips 66 facility in Belle Chasse, Louisiana, that was 50 years old in 2021 when it suffered hurricane damage. “Phillips tried to sell it but couldn’t find a buyer, so it turned it into a terminal and closed the refinery,” he said.
Why are gasoline prices high now?
The most obvious cause of high gasoline prices today is the start of the Iran war. Prices spiked immediately after the war began Feb. 28 and have remained high since.
“Reduced refinery capacity would contribute somewhat to higher gasoline and diesel prices today, but this is by no means the biggest reason why gasoline prices are so high today,” said Kenneth Gillingham, a Yale University economist who specializes in energy and environmental issues.
Our ruling
Vance said, “The biggest reason why gas prices are so high is because when Joe Biden was president, we had about 20% of American refining capacity that went offline.”
Vance’s statement is inaccurate on multiple levels.
California, not the U.S., lost 20% of its refining capacity. The national outlook has been largely stable. Market forces and global realities influence refinery production more than presidential policy does, and the most obvious cause of today’s high gasoline prices is the Iran War, which was launched by Trump, not Biden.
We rate the statement False.

It is republished here as part of a reporting and fact-checking partnership between PolitiFact and Hearst Television.

title: College student dies after falling in creek during hiking trip
text:
TUCKER COUNTY, W.Va . (WXIX/Gray News) - A missing University of Cincinnati student hiking in West Virginia was found dead Monday.
Thomas Donnelly, 21, who was part of an eight-member group from the UC Mountaineering Club, went hiking in the Red Creek Trail and Fisher Springs Trail area of Tucker County on Oct. 9, according to West Virginia State Police.
The group was trying to cross a creek when they hit elevated water levels and swift currents, state police explained.
Donnelly lost his footing and was swept downstream by the swift-moving water, state police said.
A 911 call was made around 11:30 a.m. Oct. 11 to report Donnelly was missing.
Search-and-rescue efforts began but were suspended that evening because of approaching inclement weather and diminishing daylight, state police said.
The search resumed Monday. Donnelly’s body was found around 2 p.m. that day.
“This loss is incredibly heartbreaking and has had a significant impact for many members in the Bearcat community. Our thoughts are with Thomas’ family, friends, and classmates that have been impacted by this tragic news. Please keep Thomas’s family in your thoughts during this difficult time,” UC Dean of Students Shaka Sydnor said in a statement.

title: Trump signs first lady-backed order aimed at boosting women's health research
text:
Trump signs first lady-backed order aimed at boosting women's health research
President Donald Trump on Monday directed the federal government to bolster federal research into women's health through all stages of their lives, a move pushed by his wife, First Lady Melania Trump.
The Republican president signed an executive order creating a Women’s Health Division at the National Institutes of Health and a separate White House Women's Health Task Force. The panel was set to hold its first meeting on Monday.
“Beginning today we will change the reality of women’s health,” Melania Trump said. “Previous generations fought for women’s rights. Our generation will fight to discover the cures that will ensure a woman can live her life in health and to the fullest.”
The president spoke after his wife and said the order will “promote new research and really go after the understudied diseases affecting women.” The order is also intended to promote diagnostic technology and improve treatment.
White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, who recently completed treatment for breast cancer, and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. will lead the White House task force. Donald Trump said the task force will coordinate with various federal agencies and programs. The order does not include specific funding goals.
Trumps want more research into key areas of women's health
The initiative follows meetings the first lady had with the president, Kennedy and other federal health officials to help shape the order and the task force.
The president called it a "historic action” and praised her work.
“She’s accomplished so much,” he said before pivoting into unscripted commentary about White House renovations, including the patio stone now covering what used to be the Rose Garden lawn.
Shifting back to women's health, the president expressed surprise that some of the order's requirements had not already been imposed.
“Who the hell wouldn't have a women's health division?” he said, after recalling that he'd asked Melania Trump, “Are you sure they don't have that?”
The NIH has an Office of Research on Women’s Health, established in 1990 to advance understanding of the biological and social factors that influence women's health and disease, according to its website.
A goal of the new Women's Health Division is to improve the government's ability to coordinate research, according to a fact sheet distributed by the White House.
The executive order signed Monday calls for more research into key areas of women's health, including maternal health, mental health, endometriosis, infertility, fibroids and menopause. It also mentions other health concerns, including Alzheimer’s and heart disease, osteoporosis and stroke.
The executive order calls for targeting maternal health, mental health and endometriosis. It also mentions other health concerns and diseases, including Alzheimer’s, osteoporosis, heart disease and stroke.
Women more likely to focus on health issues
The White House announcement comes about two weeks before Nov. 3 elections and as Donald Trump’s job approval ratings have declined.
About one-third of women now approve of how Trump is handling the presidency, according to recent AP-NORC polling. About two-thirds of women disapproved of how Trump was handing healthcare issues in a July AP-NORC poll.
An AP-NORC poll conducted earlier in October found women more likely than men to say healthcare is “one of the most important issues” in the upcoming election.
It was unclear whether Trump's order conflicts with his earlier executive actions curtailing federal programs and policies with a focus on diversity, equity and inclusion.
The administration’s broad cuts to scientific research have included studies focusing on women as it continues to eliminate grants with a “DEI” or diversity focus. Last year, the administration announced that the long-running Women’s Health Initiative, a study of preventive health strategies, would be closed early before abruptly reversing that decision amid protest.
Trump order cancels Biden action on women's health
In 2023, the administration of Democratic President Joe Biden signed an executive order as he announced a White House initiative to improve how the federal government approaches and funds research into the health of women, who make up more than half the U.S. population. The initiative was led by First Lady Jill Biden.
Before leaving the White House, the Bidens highlighted Jill Biden’s effort and said the research initiative had attracted nearly $1 billion in federal funding, including from the Defense Department and NIH.
Trump's executive order rescinded the Biden effort.
The Trump White House said the steps announced Monday go beyond what was accomplished under Biden, citing the planned use of artificial intelligence, which Trump calls “super intelligence,” and creating a government-wide task force rather than having the first lady lead the initiative.
Melania Trump expands her portfolio
The initiative adds a new dimension to Melania Trump’s policy portfolio as first lady.
In Donald Trump's second term, Melania Trump has focused on improving foster care systems, expanding technology and artificial-intelligence access in education, and reuniting children separated from their families by Russia's war against Ukraine.
In Trump's first presidency, the first lady's signature initiative, Be Best, focused on child well-being, safe social media use and reducing drug abuse.
