title: UMaine UVote highlights early voting opportunities for students
text:
As the Nov. 3 election approaches, UMaine UVote is working to increase student participation through classroom visits, voter registration resources and information about early voting. In an Oct. 15 interview with the Maine Campus, UMaine UVote ambassador Justine Ordinario discussed the organization’s efforts to help students navigate the early voting process.
Early voting in Maine is known as in-person absentee voting. Voters can cast absentee ballots at their municipal clerk’s office through Oct. 29. Absentee ballots returned by mail or drop box must be received by 8 p.m. on Election Day. Maine residents can also register to vote in person through Election Day.
Ordinario believes that early voting is beneficial for students because Nov. 3 polls may not always be accessible for students and picking up a ballot in October can help get students involved.
“It helps students actually participate because it’s more flexible,” Ordinario stated.
One way that UMaine UVote has been preparing for early voting is by having ambassadors go into classrooms and meet with students so that students are aware of who they can go to about voting questions. In the past month, this effort has allowed voting ambassadors to reach over 2,000 students. Voting signs with QR codes provide easier access for students to make sure they are registered to vote.
“The first thing that students should do is check if they’re registered to vote. If not, they should go and get that done as soon as possible,” Ordinario said.
UMaine UVote encourages students to go online and find information about the different candidates running for different office positions. Additional social media content with voting resources will be available on their Instagram page. UMaine UVote anticipates hosting more tabling and creative events in the coming weeks as well, so students can put a face to a name on who they can ask voting questions to.
One of the most significant changes in recent years was Orono’s decision to change municipal elections from spring to fall. By shifting municipal voting in November, students are now fully present on campus and able to participate in local governance. Given that UMaine students make up a substantial portion of Orono’s population, student voter turnout has the potential to sway election results.
“The state of Maine wants us to be involved in politics that represent us, because that’s the workforce that we are going into,” said Ordinario.
Maine’s same day registration provides students easier access to voting at the polls. Students who are interested in serving as poll workers can use this form to volunteer. Oct. 27 is the last recommended day to mail in absentee ballots and Oct. 29 is the last day to cast an in-person absentee ballot. For more information, students can visit Maine voting residence fact sheet for election and voting guidelines. To stay up to date with candidates and local Maine politics, students can also review the Fogler Library election guide.

title: Why Troy Jackson says he doesn’t regret telling Susan Collins to ‘shut up’ during Maine Senate debate
text:
WASHINGTON — Maine Democrat Troy Jackson says he does not regret telling Sen. Susan Collins that she should “shut up” after the Republican suggested a protester who interrupted their recent debate was one of his campaign’s backers.
“She said that it was a Troy supporter. She accused me of setting that up. I had no idea who it was,” said Jackson, a former president of the state Senate who is trying to deny Collins, the longest-serving Republican woman in Senate history, a sixth-term. He spoke in an interview with CNN’s “State of the Union” that aired Sunday.
During their final debate Thursday night in the closely contested race as the Nov. 3 election nears, a protester opposing data centers began yelling as Collins spoke. While moderators asked for that person to be removed, the senator said the demonstrator was “obviously one of Troy’s supporters.”
Jackson responded: “Oh, shut up. I don’t even know that kid.”
The Sunrise Movement group posted on its Instagram page that the outburst came from one of its members. In a caption of an Instagram post, the group’s page said: “We’re proud of this Sunrise volunteer who took action yesterday.”
The New York Times said the protester, Henry Elgie, a 19-year-old student at Bowdoin College in Brunswick, told the newspaper in an interview Saturday that he had “zero coordination” with Jackson’s campaign. “I do not know Troy Jackson personally or at all,” he was quoted as saying.
The Sunrise Movement is a left-wing political advocacy organization that champions the Green New Deal, aimed at transitioning the U.S. economy to 100% renewable energy. The group, which has local arms around the country, regularly organizes protests, sit-ins and climate strikes.
Jackson told CNN that he shook hands with Collins after each of their debates.
“But what I’m not going to be is talked down to by Sen. Collins,” he said. He added: “I’m fighting for Mainers and I just think that was another situation where she was talking down to me and I’m not going to apologize for that.”
Collins told Fox News’ Sean Hannity on Friday that she was “struck by how reflective the response, ‘Oh, shut up,’ was.” Collins said “the fact that it seemed like such an automatic, quick reply was very telling.”
She cited what she said was “the reputation” that Jackson had in the Maine Legislature “particularly when he’s dealing with women with whom he disagrees. So in some ways it didn’t surprise me.”
Some state lawmakers who worked with Jackson have criticized him as having a temper, including once throwing a plastic water bottle on the ground in frustration while disagreeing with a female lawmaker. Asked by reporters during the campaign about the confrontations, Jackson said, “I wear my heart on my sleeve.” He took responsibility for his outburst and apologized to those he had confrontations with at the time.
Jackson was asked on CNN about some Republicans who are saying there were stories that he was aggressive in his tone to women from his time in the Legislature and that his remark Thursday night was another example of that.
Jackson said some Republicans have been spending millions “attacking me and my family, making untrue claims. … So it doesn’t surprise me.”

title: Man admits he shot, ran over several goats with a 4-wheeler in property dispute with neighbor, deputies say
text:
EAU PLEINE, Wis. (WSAW/Gray News) — Deputies in Wisconsin said a man admitted to killing his neighbor’s goats in 2024 over a property dispute.
Dean Ress, a farmer, said he found some of his goats shot and killed in October 2024. He said the goats are like his family.
“I’ve been suffering with this emotionally for over two years now,” Ress said.
Court records show some of the goats were shot in the hips and head. Others had been run over with a four-wheeler.
Ress said a total of 13 goats died.
Investigators said they have enough evidence to charge Ress’ neighbor, Eric Seelow, with four of the deaths.
According to court documents, Seelow admitted to investigators in August that he killed the goats. He is facing felony and misdemeanor charges.
Deputies said Seelow told them he needed to “confess his sins” following a conversation with his pastor this summer.
Court documents show that Seelow admitted taking a rifle from his grandfather’s home without permission in October 2024, shooting one goat, and using an ATV to run over others that had crossed onto his property.
Dispute over shared fence
Ress and Seelow’s dispute stems from a shared fence on the property. Both have pointed blame at the other for who is responsible for maintaining the fence.
Deputy Zachary Ruesch with the Marathon County Sheriff’s Office Animal Investigations Unit said these types of issues need to be addressed in civil court.
“This is generally a civil issue that we try not to get involved in, because we don’t have the authority to say, ‘this is your fence, this is your fence, and this person needs to fix this portion of it,’” Ruesch said.
Ress lives on a farm that used to be Seelow’s property. Both Ress and the Seelows said the Seelows did not want to give up that property.
Seelow declined an interview but said that he told Ress many times to keep his animals contained. The Seelows said the goats were wrecking their crops.
Seelow has an initial appearance on Nov. 18. If convicted, he will face a maximum sentence of 14 years in prison.
Ress is currently on house arrest. He said there was a physical conflict with Seelow after the goats died.

title: A modernized health plan: Supporting cost management and the employee experience.
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The Surest health plan came from a group of innovators wondering: What if health care was easier to shop for? What if care options and costs weren’t a guessing game, but available in advance?
In 2016, that concept became reality. In 2022, the Surest health plan joined UnitedHealthcare to expand its reach while retaining a consumer-centric approach.
The Surest difference.
Available nationwide, Surest is an employer-sponsored health plan built around copays rather than deductibles. In New England, employers can choose the funding approach that best fits their needs—including self-funded, fully insured, and level funded options.
In a time of rising health care costs, the Surest plan offers an approach that may appeal to employers looking for a different way to manage benefits.
What makes Surest different? For one, with access to cost, coverage, and treatment options before making an appointment, consumers can evaluate providers and compare health care services much like they do other products and services. There is no deductible to meet and no coinsurance to calculate. Instead, members see a single copay in advance and can choose what works for their budget.
The pricing structure is also different. Surest Care Ratings help members understand, real-time in the Surest experience, the link between copays and provider value. Surest starts by evaluating providers on services they offer based on their historical effectiveness and cost-efficiency performance for a service. Then, a provider who scored higher gets a higher Care Rating—and a lower copay—for that service.
And Surest members have access to a broad, national UnitedHealthcare network of more than 1.8 million physicians and health care professionals and more than 5,600 hospitals.¹
The plan works, with proven savings for both employers and members.²
Employers typically save around 7%, and members may save 20% to 40%, depending on employer geography and specific plan designs.³
The power of transparency.
Since its introduction, Surest has grown from serving 1 in 9 of UnitedHealthcare’s largest employer clients to 1 in 4 today. Employers are seeing the value, including ISG, an architecture and engineering firm with more than 600 employees.
At ISG, thinking outside the box is part of the culture, and that mindset extended to their benefits. “We’re very open to having some change,” says Aubrey, ISG’s employee experience manager. “Surest is a great fit for us … having it on an app, having it be really easy, knowing your costs upfront … is just what our employees were looking for.”
Surest works. Proven results.
Instead of digging for answers, members can find information right in the app. This design makes it more likely for members to engage with the plan:
- 90% of households with a claim registered on the app⁴
- 88% of households with a claim searched before care⁵
And—with access to care options and cost information in advance—members who use the app choose differently than they would without this information.
- Members who shopped and obtained quotes prior to care were 57% more likely to choose higher-value providers than those who did not comparison shop.⁶
This resulted in:
- 17% fewer ER visits among members who shopped for care⁷
- 2.5 times more virtual visits than members on traditional plans⁸
Today, Surest has climbed to 1.3 million members and 4,000+ clients (and counting).⁹
Looking for a new way to think about health benefits? For more details, reach out to your broker or UnitedHealthcare representative, or visit surest.care/newengland.

title: Husband left unrecognizable after breaking up fight between 2 family dogs
text:
ATLANTA (ANF/Gray News) - A Georgia man’s life changed in a split second when he tried to break up a fight between two family dogs, leaving him severely injured.
Dustin Low suffered severe facial injuries while breaking up a fight between two family dogs. Since then, he’s needed multiple surgeries.
“It was probably a matter of five minutes total action time, and then, the rest was just trying to gather myself, my breath and control the bleeding,” Dustin Low said.
His wife, Chelsea Low, recalls the night she looked at her husband and noticed his facial tissue had been badly damaged.
“He came downstairs and was like, ‘I need help with the pets.’ I’m like, ‘No, you need a hospital,’” Chelsea Low said.
Dustin Low has undergone two major facial reconstructive surgeries since the incident and needs a third to help him return to a sense of normalcy.
“It will get rid of this piece, which is the rest of my forehead flap, and it will sew that back up,” he said.
But medical bills for the surgeries have been stacking up, and the couple are asking for help to get Dustin Low into that third surgery.
“We need $12,310 just to get him on the operating table for the third surgery. They will not do the third surgery until we pay $12,310. That’s for the first two surgeries. The last surgery is $6,500,” Chelsea Low said.
As the Lows pray for a miracle, they say they don’t hold anger toward the dogs and plan to keep them.
“It was a mistake. It was a freak accident. They didn’t want to harm him,” Chelsea Low said.
A GoFundMe has been set up to help the couple.

title: Judges bristle as they are forced to decide the details of Trump's Washington makeover
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — District and federal court judges in Washington are used to handling some of the nation’s thorniest issues, from complex deportation cases to the fates of Jan. 6, 2021, Capitol riot defendants and more.
But in the nearly two years since President Donald Trump returned to office, they have been adjudicating a litany of cases challenging construction projects he initiated to remake the nation’s capital at a breakneck speed. Judges accustomed to parsing the Constitution are now being forced to decide how many trees may be cut down or whether paint tests can proceed.
Their decisions ultimately could determine how Washington is reshaped and could have a significant say on the limits of presidential power. But in reaching those conclusions, the judges appear to be growing increasingly frustrated with being thrust into what otherwise might be the purview of project managers, zoning officials or board legal counsel.
The docket of renovation projects has ballooned over the months, drawing in at least nine judges so far. Cases are now underway challenging, among others, Trump’s proposed monumental arch where he plans to place drones and snipers; the potential destruction of the iconic Kennedy Center; a White House ballroom and the renovation of a public golf course that enthusiasts fear will make it unaffordable.
Together they highlight an increasingly mistrustful third branch exasperated by the president’s behavior in pursuit of his desires. The evidence is in statements, rulings, orders and outright anger during hearings.
“The administration has created a problem where the courts are flooded with challenges to efforts that they have undertaken to satisfy one man’s ego,” said David Singleton, a law professor at the University of the District of Columbia.
The White House did not respond to a request for comment.
One judge’s frustration on display in hearing
The judicial frustration erupted into full view last week during a remote hearing over the Washington golf course that Trump wants to turn into a world-class venue. Plaintiffs argue the administration’s redevelopment would violate the congressional act that created the park.
Judge Ana Reyes excoriated a government attorney for the first 15 minutes of the hearing over what she said was the administration’s deceit after it cut down trees at the course over a holiday weekend, with little notification to plaintiffs.
Reyes, appointed by Democratic President Joe Biden, spent months telling skeptical plaintiffs that she trusted the government and did not need updates on routine work.
“I am not the Lorax, I do not speak for the trees. I am a judge,” she said at one hearing referencing a Dr. Seuss character. At another she said: “I don’t want to be the overseer of Parks and Rec. I’m no Amy Poehler.”
That reticence ended after the tree-cutting spree earlier this month.
“I trusted you all not to do precisely what you have done,” she said. “Not only have you lost credibility, now we’re dealing with this.”
In her memorandum, the incredulity continued as she summarized the hearing. “Breakneck speed to clear trees that posed no harm. The reason? Disputed. The budget? Unclear. The environmental impact? Unstudied. The urgency? None. Next steps: bulldoze hundreds more.”
The government responded to her filing and courtroom outburst by asking that she be removed from the case citing hostility toward the government and favoritism for the plaintiffs. Reyes denied the motion late Sunday, noting that before October she had rejected “about a dozen” requests from the plaintiffs that she issue formal orders against the administration. She denied them all. Despite the pending hearing, Trump announced Sunday on social media that the course will close for 15 months beginning Nov. 15 for redevelopment.
Judge protests micromanaging projects
A judge asked to decide the fate of the Kennedy Center, which Trump added his name to and then a Trump-appointed board voted to close down for renovations, has repeatedly expressed frustration over the court’s involvement in the project.
“Can it close for two weeks? Can it close for a season? Can it close for the summer while the air conditioner is being repaired?” said Judge Christopher Cooper. “You’re asking the court, arguably, to, you know, micromanage the Kennedy Center’s, you know, construction projects, which obviously I’m not in a position to do, and it’s not my role to do.”
Still, Cooper has been made to rule on those very things. He ordered the board to give 30-day notice of plans to demolish it, due in part to Trump’s public statements that it could be torn down if he is not given proper recognition for his efforts to restore it. Cooper has also blocked Trump’s name from being returned to the building.
Charles Birnbaum, founding president and CEO of The Cultural Landscape Foundation, a Washington-based advocacy organization and a plaintiff in the Kennedy Center lawsuit, said the courts, and the public, were “growing weary” of “the administration’s spurious claims of absolute authority.”
Concerns that the administration is outrunning the courts
The judges’ frustrations have also centered around the speed with which the administration is pushing ahead on the projects with little regard for the approvals needed to pursue such work.
Trump tore down the White House’s East Wing last year to make room for a ballroom, which the administration argues is needed to address national security concerns. Plaintiffs, who argued that Trump has no unilateral authority to undertake the work, accused the White House of trying to “outrun the courts” by accelerating construction.
Judge Tanya Chutkan, overseeing the case against Trump’s Washington arch, referred to the ballroom circumstances in one hearing.
“The president has said he’s getting his arch,” said Chutkan, a Barack Obama appointee. “And as we’ve seen from Judge (Richard) Leon’s case with the White House ballroom, the president tends to get what he wants even if it means that you wake up one morning and there are bulldozers demolishing part of the White House.”
Chutkan has also voiced skepticism of responses from government lawyers over her requests for details on plans for the arch, reflecting the judiciary’s growing mistrust of the executive.
She said the lawyers “come in and they say, ‘I don’t know. I’m not aware of anything.’ But that doesn’t mean it’s not happening.”
“One would expect that you would know the answers to those very, very basic questions, which is: Is there any preparation for demolition happening? Have any contracts been awarded? Because all of that goes to whether — goes to whether construction is imminent.”
The judges’ decisions could ultimately resonate far beyond the walls of the edifices and monuments they are ruling on.
Matt Dallek, a political historian at George Washington University, said the projects may seem “a little trivial.”
But, he said, they “go to the heart of the executive power and what kind of authority Trump can wield based on a whim.”
___
Associated Press reporter Michael Kunzelman contributed to this report.

title: Maine Audubon opens All Persons Trail in Falmouth
text:
FALMOUTH — Under yellow and orange foliage, a flock of turkeys crossed the smooth path at Maine Audubon’s Falmouth wildlife sanctuary. Following a ceremonial ribbon cutting, a crowd of people followed suit, wandering down the trail into the crisp fall woods.
Some visitors used wheelchairs, white canes and other mobility aids — their experience made possible by the trail’s intentional design.
“I’ve never seen anything like this before,” said John Lee, who is visually impaired and navigated the new trail using a white cane. “What they’ve done here is an excellent thing.”
Maine Audubon opened its new accessible trail at Gilsland Farm Audubon Center in Falmouth on Monday. The All Persons Trail is designed to be inclusive and is one of only a few wheelchair-accessible trails in a wildlife sanctuary in the greater Portland area.
“This project is a really great example of Maine Audubon’s commitment to being inclusive and to make sure that nature is available for everyone,” said Maine Audubon President Judy Camuso.
The trail is accessible by having a smooth tread surface, very limited slope, and three rest areas with benches along its loop. The half-mile main trail starts at the visitor center and goes through woods and along a boardwalk into a meadow before looping back to the center. An additional 300-foot spur trail in the meadow winds upward for a view of the Presumpscot River.
About $250,000 was raised for the trail, according to Maine Audubon staff, and its construction is part of a multimillion-dollar enhancement of the Gilsland Farm Audubon Center. Other projects include the construction of a native plant education center and renovations to the visitor center.
The trail was built to U.S. Forest Service trail accessibility guidelines and disabled community members were consulted in the process, according to Maine Audubon. Interpretive signs that are tactile and feature audio descriptions will be installed in the weeks ahead.
“What’s especially meaningful is that accessibility wasn’t an afterthought. This trail was thoughtfully planned, and people with disabilities were included in the process,” Portland resident Jessica Russell said during the ribbon-cutting ceremony.
Russell shared that she was active in the outdoors before a car accident left her paralyzed 27 years ago. As a wheelchair user, she said projects like this allow her to be back in nature and share in its mental, social and physical benefits.
“I feel incredibly lucky to have this beautiful, accessible trail just 10 minutes from my home now,” said Russell. “I’m excited to add one more beautiful outdoor space to my growing list of places where I’m welcome.”

title: Tourism task force to advance draft proposal next month
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BAR HARBOR — The town's Sustainable Tourism Management Task Force is closing in on the end of its mission, with a report of its findings to be presented next month. That leaves the group with only a few weeks to refine eighteen months of work into a roadmap that it hopes can help guide tourism policy in town for the future.
At the penultimate meeting of the task force, held on Oct. 14, members were shown an initial draft of the report that will, in its final form, represent the culmination of their work, in conjunction with Planning Department staff and consulting firm JE Austin Associates. During that time, the task force has attempted to quantify the current impact of tourism and to chart a more harmonious path forward for the various community stakeholders. But while the draft report, totaling around 30 pages to date, contains plenty of management strategy suggestions and a roadmap for implementation, task force members were cognizant of just how much work still needed to be done, and reiterated that there were no overnight fixes available for any of the myriad issues identified throughout the process.

title: A history lesson on healthcare in Maine
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
In 2009, Democratic Gov. John Baldacci promised a $45 million payment on Maine’s $373 million debt to Maine hospitals. That payment did not happen until three years later in 2006.
When Baldacci left the Blaine House, he left a $484 million debt, which Republican Gov. Paul LePage paid off. Prior to this payment, the Maine hospitals were on the verge of financial failure. When Gov. LePage left office in 2019, the state had a financial surplus.
Jump ahead to Democratic Gov. Janet Mills. Almost half of birthing centers are closed and a number of hospitals as well. If Mainers think for a moment that the Democratic candidate Hannah Pingree is going to save our healthcare system, they need to look at history.
If people really think that socialized medicine is the answer, they should move to Canada.
Leo Mazerall Jr.
Stockton Springs

title: If not this November, when?
text:
This upcoming Senate race should be about replacing Sen. Susan Collins.
Has she done good things for Maine? Absolutely. She’s brought a lot of money to Maine and has been very helpful to many individuals and should be commended for that work. However, her voting record has nearly supported all of Trump policies with the exceptions of the few token opposition votes. Her SCOTUS votes have proven disastrous to women. How many other Mainers have been negatively affected due to her voting?
Reality is, because of age and possible health concerns, she will need to be replaced anyway. Why wait? Why not this year?
We voters will have serious choices to make in November: Listen to and believe the negative ad campaigns and reelect Collins; give the new guy a chance for six years; or don’t vote for either one — which is legal. Not telling folks how we voted is also legal.
Joseph Mailey
Auburn

title: Examining UMaine’s student voting culture ahead of the midterms
text:
If you haven’t figured it out from the endless ads, phone calls or texts asking you to participate in a poll on voting, the midterm election is mere weeks away. For Maine, this is a hotly contested election, with national attention being placed on the 2nd Congressional District race, the governor’s race, and of course, the race for U.S. Senate. A lot of times the rhetoric around elections feels like it’s just trying to confuse you, and as college students, it feels like there is so much else going on that you need to focus on.
Moreover, it can feel a lot like these races are being forced into every type of media we consume, and with a lot of it being inherently negative, it is understandable that people want nothing to do with it. According to FairVote, about 60% of Americans vote in the presidential election cycle, which is 20% more than the midterms that fall at 40%. So what do students at the University of Maine think?
Overall, the people that I am surrounded by are very in touch with current events, and subsequently the seats that are being contested in this cycle, but I understand that this is not the norm for most students. It can feel hard to find unbiased news, or even where to start, and college can feel like a bubble where the real world doesn’t matter because we are not a part of it.
I chatted with Edgelynn Venuti, a member of UMaine UVote, and she told me there seems to be a “50/50 split between students who are super involved and have a concrete plan, and those that have no idea what’s on the ballot.” This makes sense, especially if you are in a major whose focus is not on current events, as politics often does not become a conversation topic.
While this is true, according to Tufts Center for Information and Research on Civic Learning and Engagement, “More than half [53%] of college students voted in 2024,” with 70% being registered to vote. These results are on par with what Venuti described to me, but for the students that do have a plan or are considering voting, two of the elections on the Maine ballot this cycle win out as most important.
The first race that came up a lot in a small poll of students was the gubernatorial election, which had Republican Robert Charles facing Democrat Hannah Pingree as major party candidates, with independent Rick Bennett also running for the position. For students, this race feels important because it feels that it will affect them much more than a congressional seat. For example, the governor of Maine is in charge of the budget, meaning that we as students at a public university are affected by the decision of how much funding the University of Maine System receives. The governor also appoints members to the Board of Trustees who directly make decisions about UMaine and its faculty.
While this race is on the mind of many students, the race that almost everyone deemed as “feeling the most important” was the U.S. Senate race between Republican incumbent Susan Collins and Democratic challenger Troy Jackson. This race is truthfully hard to ignore. With significant national attention and funding, these candidates’ names are ingrained in many Mainers’ minds.
The biggest reason for this race being under the microscope is because Collins is chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, which allocates federal funding and is a huge asset to the Republican Party as a whole. In this role, Collins recently secured $45 million in congressional funding to build a new health science building here on campus.
At the end of the day, while they may be hard to understand, these races have real and direct effects on students here, and they hold a lot of significance for UMaine and its current and future students. There are many resources for students to vote, such as UMaine UVote, which can help you register with proof of ID and residency. Additionally, students can vote in person at the New Balance Field House and Memorial Gym, which serves as the polling site for the town of Orono.

title: Elon Musk says he will give a SpaceX share to 'every kid in America'
text:
Elon Musk says he will give a SpaceX share to ‘every kid in America’
Elon Musk has said he will give every child in America a stake in SpaceX, his $2 trillion aerospace and artificial intelligence company, as tech firms face intensifying scrutiny over their impact on society.
“Next year, I will give one of my SpaceX shares to every kid in America,” he wrote on X on Monday. “This will be the first of many.”
SpaceX only began trading publicly in June (and after the biggest initial public offering in history). The company’s shares were trading for about $146 when the market closed on Friday.
Musk’s proposal was thin on detail. It is not clear how those shares would be distributed to the tens of millions of American children or whether all of them would even be eligible.
According to the United States Census Bureau, there are roughly 73 million people under the age of 18, making Musk’s potential giveaway worth about $10.7 billion at SpaceX’s current share price.
Offering young people a stake in the U.S. stock market isn’t a new idea. This month, the Treasury Department automatically signed up millions of under-18s to Trump Accounts, a new federal savings and investment vehicle, with children born between the start of 2025 and the end of 2028 eligible for a one-off $1,000 government contribution.
In July, SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell and her husband pledged to donate one SpaceX share to each of roughly 2 million children already signed up to an account. The couple said they will prioritize donations to children from lower-income households and in SpaceX’s home state of Texas.
Damage control?
Musk’s offer came in response to Anthropic’s announcement on Sunday that it will commit at least 5% of its shares — worth $48 billion at the private company’s latest valuation — to a “Public Benefit Fund” that will donate money to social causes.
The fund could make “large donations” to nonprofit organizations or “direct distributions to specific populations,” the company wrote on its website, adding that the money could help mitigate the impact of artificial intelligence on people’s jobs.
Musk, the world’s richest person, retorted on X: “I recommend giving the shares directly to the public… This is what I will be doing.”
Musk signed the Giving Pledge in 2012 — a commitment by the world’s richest people to donate the majority of their wealth to charitable causes during their lifetime or in their wills.
His charitable organization, the Musk Foundation, focuses on grant-giving in a handful of fields including renewable energy, space exploration and pediatric research, according to its website.
According to a New York Times analysis last year, the foundation held more than $14 billion in assets at the end of 2024, making it one of the largest in the United States. But the Times said the foundation’s donations that year went largely to organizations closely connected to Musk’s business interests.
SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the Times’ claims.
Musk has also openly questioned the effectiveness of traditional charitable giving. Speaking about philanthropy on the People by WTF podcast last year, Musk said: “We should try to do things that help our fellow human beings.”
“The biggest challenge I find with my foundation is trying to give money away in a way that is truly beneficial to people,” he said. “It’s very easy to give money away to get the appearance of goodness. It is very difficult to give money away for the reality of goodness.”
In 2021, Musk said he would sell $6 billion-worth of Tesla stock and donate it to the United Nations’ World Food Programme if the organization could demonstrate how the money would “solve world hunger.” It does not appear that Musk has yet donated the sum.
Both Musk’s and Anthropic’s offers come as AI companies face intense backlash over the safety of their products (Anthropic itself recently warned of the “existential risk to humanity” posed by the technology), the potential for AI to push humans out of their jobs en masse, as well as the social and environmental impact of the industry’s gargantuan data center buildout.
Tech titans more broadly are catching heat.
New movies like “The Social Reckoning” — about a Facebook employee blowing the whistle on unsafe company practices — and documentary “You Can See Everything” — following blood testing start-up founder and convicted fraudster Elizabeth Holmes — are helping to remind audiences of the long-running recklessness of some in Big Tech.
Musk himself is the subject of the new documentary “Musk,” charting his life and career. It is unsparing in its criticism of some of his business practices and his controversial foray into politics.

title: Trump says ‘France is burning.’ What sparked violent protests, 550K marchers and 2,400 arrests
text:
PARIS (AP) — French President Emmanuel Macron on Sunday voiced the public’s “anger” and “shame” over rioting and looting during nationwide protests against rising living costs and poor conditions in schools. At least 2,400 people were arrested.
Macron echoed other government officials in blaming much of the violence on far-left activists, accusing them of attacking police and public buildings to foment chaos.
“Those who looted will have to pay for the damage, and those who sought to bring down the Republic will be held accountable,” Macron said in a televised address to the nation.
He denounced “unrestrained violence” by “insurrectionist elements from radical far-left groups, joined by numerous criminals.”
Macron earlier held an emergency meeting with senior government officials, a day after masked groups set fires and attacked city halls in several cities. He said he had instructed prefects to work with mayors to protect public buildings and businesses in the coming weeks, including by banning protests when necessary.
Flames engulfed the 19th-century City Hall in the city of Limoges, in central France, causing its roof to collapse and nearly destroying the building.
New tensions erupted in Paris on Sunday
In Paris, hundreds of protesters gathered again on Sunday at the Place de la République amid a heavy police presence. Officers used tear gas as tensions flared sporadically in the neighborhood, with small groups of people trying to set bicycles and trash bins on fire.
“The right to protest is a fundamental right. Deliberately and collectively sowing disorder through violence is not,” Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez wrote on X, citing the looting of hundreds of businesses across the country.
Authorities estimated Saturday’s marches had a turnout of about 550,000, while organizers put it at 800,000. Demonstrators answered calls from a labor union, student organizations and activists hoping to revive the “yellow vest” movement, which emerged in 2018 to protest social injustice.
Mass protests in France are often marred by violence on the fringes of otherwise peaceful marches, leading to clashes with police. The arrest tally reported Sunday approached the nearly 2,000 recorded nationwide during a single day of yellow vest protests in December 2018.
Paris police said one person died of a heart attack, without providing details. The Paris prosecutor’s office said it was investigating.
Parisians deplore shattered shops and a damaged square
Dislodged cobblestones, shattered storefronts and broken glass littered the area around Paris’ Place de la République on Sunday. Looting and damage were also reported in other tourist and shopping districts.
Paris police said 855 people were arrested in the capital region. Prosecutors said 557 remained in police custody.
“I am actually stunned by the level of destruction and violence that was expressed,” said government employee Marie Peyreigne, 57, wondering what had led to the mayhem.
Parisians inspecting the damage photographed the partially dismantled base of the square’s central monument, a statue of Marianne, a symbol of France.
Jean Foissy, 74, said he had wanted to join the protest but encountered “a wall of riot police and fires everywhere” and returned home.
“I was very scared,” he said. “I’ve been a Parisian since I was born, so when I got here, it almost made me want to cry because I find it so bad, it hurts me.”
Margaux Eude, 26, said she supported the protest movement but “didn’t think it would escalate like this.”
“It’s the troublemakers who came, and it breaks my heart because it delegitimizes the movement,” she said.
Political leaders trade blame ahead of presidential election
Political leaders traded accusations over Saturday’s violence ahead of next spring’s presidential election.
Far-right leader and presidential hopeful Marine Le Pen criticized Macron’s centrist government as “exhausted, disoriented and seemingly incapable of doing anything other than commenting on its own powerlessness,” in a video posted on social media.
Far-left contender Jean-Luc Mélenchon accused Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu of “playing with fire,” alleging that “by banking on degradation, you have only succeeded in uniting all youths and workers’ unions.”
Mélenchon, who joined the Paris march Saturday, insisted that “my message is clear: those who share our fight have no business in looting or destruction.”
U.S. President Donald Trump posted “France is burning!” on his Truth Social platform, apparently linking the unrest to “the immigration of people from an entirely different world.”
“Close your Borders and take control, before it is too late!” he wrote.
French authorities and police have not linked immigrants to the rioting. Macron, speaking about troublemakers, asked: “How can French people do this to France?”
Hundreds of businesses looted across the country
“The scale of the damage is considerable and unprecedented,” Paris Mayor Emmanuel Grégoire wrote in an open letter. “Paris is a city of freedoms, debate and demonstrations. It must remain so. But it must also be a city where everyone can work and run a business safely.”
The mayors of Paris, Marseille and Lyon, the three largest cities, requested a meeting with the prime minister in the coming days “given the extent of the damage and the seriousness of the situation.”
In Marseille, some protesters briefly forced their way into City Hall’s lobby and a group of people wearing hoods and masks damaged a police station. In Lyon, a fire broke out inside a tourist office.
In Limoges, the City Hall was ravaged by flames after “radical troublemakers” broke in while elected officials, employees, security personnel and members of the public were inside, Haute-Vienne prefect Maurice Barate said. “They deliberately set the building on fire. It is an extremely serious and unspeakable act,” he said.
In eastern France, the Mulhouse prosecutor’s office said an investigation has been opened after a 17-year-old girl was injured during the protests and lost an eye. On Saturday, another investigation was opened after a young protester lost a hand in Saint-Etienne.
The injuries come as police have drawn sharp scrutiny over their use of grenades and other riot-control weapons during recent demonstrations.

title: Trump signs an order aimed at boosting women’s health research, a plan backed by the first lady
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump on Monday directed the federal government to bolster federal research into women’s health, a move pushed by his wife, first lady Melania Trump.
The Republican president signed an executive order that creates a new women’s health division at the National Institutes of Health and a White House task force to focus on the issue. That panel was set to hold its first meeting Monday after the Trumps held a Rose Garden signing ceremony.
“Beginning today we will change the reality of women’s health,” Melania Trump said. “Previous generations fought for women’s rights. Our generation will fight to discover the cures that will ensure a woman can live her life in health and to the fullest.”
The president, who spoke after his wife, said the order will “promote new research and really go after the understudied diseases affecting women.” The order is also intended to promote diagnostic technology and improve treatment.
White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, who recently completed treatment for breast cancer, and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. will lead the White House task force. Donald Trump said the task force will coordinate with various federal agencies and programs. The order does not include specific funding goals.
The initiative comes after a series of meetings the first lady had with federal health officials.
The president called it a “historic action” and praised the first lady’s work.
“She’s accomplished so much,” he said before pivoting into unscripted commentary on White House renovations, including the patio stone that now covers what was once the Rose Garden lawn.
Shifting back to women’s health, the president expressed surprise that some of the order’s requirements had not already been imposed.
“Who the hell wouldn’t have a women’s health division?” he said, after recalling that he’d asked Melania Trump, “Are you sure they don’t have that?”
The executive order calls for targeting maternal health, mental health and endometriosis. It also mentions other health concerns and diseases, including Alzheimer’s, osteoporosis, heart disease and stroke.
Melania Trump helped shape the order and the task force in consultation with physicians, White House officials, Kennedy and the Republican president. The initiative adds a new dimension to her policy portfolio as first lady.
In Donald Trump’s second term, the first lady has focused on improving foster care systems and expanding technology and artificial-intelligence access in education. In Trump’s first presidency, the first lady’s signature initiative, Be Best, focused on child well-being, safe social media use and reducing drug abuse.
The White House ceremony comes weeks before Nov. 3 elections and as Donald Trump’s job approval ratings have declined, including among women.
About 4 in 10 independent women supported Trump during the 2024 election against Democrat Kamala Harris and in the pre-presidency period, according to AP-NORC polls. That dropped to around a quarter in the opening months of this midterm election year, the period marked by Trump’s hard-line immigration crackdown in U.S. cities and the opening weeks of the Iran war.

title: Photographer captures 250 veterans’ portraits to honor service
text:
(Aging Untold) — Photographs are powerful. For photographer Mikel Conrad, they are a way to tell the story of those who put their lives on the line for the country’s future.
Ron Camillo is one of hundreds featured in Conrad’s “250 Faces of Service & Sacrifice.”
“Active duty 1950-51. I can remember like yesterday, Korea. The problem is I saw things over there I can’t talk about,” Camillo said.
Camillo is a Korean War veteran who served with the 1st Marine Division and the 5th Marines.
“Just their willingness to serve and just do what they had to do and not beat their chest about it. ... They just went out and did what they had to do,” Conrad said.
Conrad’s vision is a portfolio made for the country’s 250th birthday so the stories of these heroes can still be told long after they are gone.
Aging Untold host and gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said these portraits do more than capture a face.
“You know, so many of our veterans come back feeling unseen. And this gives them that, I see you and I hear you and I’m honoring you, and what you did mattered. What you did for all of us matters so much. And it is so dignifying and shows so much respect for our veterans,” Cradduck said.
This is about honor and respect, Cradduck said.
“And so, when we take away the vanity side and we just say, we want to honor you, not we want to capture you, we want to honor you, it gets rid of some of the apprehension of sitting in front of the lens,” she said.
The “250 Faces of Service & Sacrifice” project is a tribute to the men and women who have kept the country’s history in focus.
“We’re all tied together. We’re all brothers,” veteran Gene Acker said.

title: Chellie Pingree’s Portland office gets suspicious letter, prompting FBI response
text:
U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree’s Portland office received a suspicious letter Monday, the latest in a string of concerning packages that have been sent to members of Congress in recent days.
Starting last week, representatives and senators around the country began getting similar letters, many of which authorities said contained an unknown white powder. The Portland office of Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, received one, her staff said Friday. Sens. Pete Ricketts, R-Nebraska, Ted Cruz, R-Texas, and Chuck Schumer, D-New York, were also among the several dozen recipients, NBC News reported.
The envelope containing the letter addressed to Pingree, D-1st District, had a return address of “DSA” along with the street number for a building in New York City’s financial district. But NBC reported that authorities have yet to trace the letters’ origins.
So far, no injuries have been reported in connection with the mailings.
“We cannot accept threats and intimidation as a normal part of our politics. The people who work in congressional offices and administer our elections are public servants dedicated to helping their communities. They deserve to do that work without fear,” Pingree said in a written statement. “Political disagreement is part of a healthy democracy. Threatening the people who keep it running is unacceptable.”
The statement from Pingree noted that the FBI responded to her office’s call about the letter, as did the Portland police and fire departments.
Pingree is heavily favored to win a 10th term representing Maine’s deep-blue 1st District this fall as she faces Republican Ronald Russell for the second straight election.

KNOXVILLE, Tenn. (WVLT/Gray News) — A 20-year-old man has been charged after he allegedly dressed up as a security guard to sneak into the University of Tennessee’s football game against Alabama on Saturday.

title: “The Social Reckoning”: Stick it to the Zuck
text:
Some of you eagle-eyed readers may have noticed that last week I dropped the name of a film that I was looking forward to seeing, but the film for this week is not that movie. That is because I have cleverly fed you all the reddest of herrings to cover up the real movie I was eager to see this October. That’s how you know Aaron Sorkin’s “The Social Reckoning” is good; it made me bamboozle you all!
For those who don’t know, it is a sequel to the 2010 film “The Social Network,” directed by David Fincher and written by Aaron Sorkin. This dramatic biopic follows the lives of Mark Zuckerberg and Eduardo Saverin during the creation of Facebook and the lawsuits between them and the Winklevoss twins. “The Social Reckoning” takes place in the years following the publication of “The Facebook Files” by The Wall Street Journal. Investigative journalist Jeff Horwitz, with the help of Frances Haugen, a Facebook data engineer turned whistleblower, helped bring the files to light.
In the film, Haugen was compelled to approach Horwitz because of the inexplicable radicalization of her childhood friend. The two go back and forth, with Haugen feeling a great sense of loyalty to her job until finally realizing how much damage her company is doing to people. All the while, we jump between their teamwork and Mark’s inner circle dealing with the fallout of The Wall Street Journal article and the Jan. 6 crisis.
This film is very professional in its presentation; its pacing is engaging but lags behind in certain places, especially in its second act, where Horwitz tries to get information out of Haugen. I would say that the film’s stronger qualities are in Jeremy Allen White’s performance as Jeff Horwitz. It was an interesting choice for sure, especially considering his career up until this point has been films like “Movie 43.”
Yet, his performance in this film shows that he has the chops to be a very serious actor. Mikey Madison as Frances was also very interesting, and despite her looking stunning in this film, I will admit, it is an odd casting choice considering she looks nothing like Frances Haugen. I think the actor who really steals the show was Jeremy Strong’s portrayal of Mark Zuckerberg. This is both reflective of the synthetic, unfeeling man the public knows him as, and the true, straightforward and megalomaniacal businessman he is.
The film’s message is worn quite clearly on its shoulders, with it delving into a slightly surface-level analysis of Facebook’s MSI algorithms, its refusal to fact-check ads and how those practices have affected people who use Facebook every day. However, I will admit it could have been better when it came to explaining these systems. Of course, the techno-illiteracy of Jeff Horwitz is supposed to be a stand-in for the audience’s own blindness to the technical aspects. Other films, such as 2015’s “The Big Short,” have done this better. It was not only entertaining but was able to explain its frankly complicated subject simply and effectively.
All in all, the film was good, though not perfect, and it does not talk down to you. It respects your intelligence but is not really a film that you can go see to turn your brain off. Coupled with its important message and solid characters, I’d say this one is well worth the price of admission.

title: Sen. Collins looks to make history with a sixth term in Washington
text:
Sen. Susan Collins of Maine looks to make history with a sixth term in Washington
Sen. Susan Collins’ first visit to Washington came long before she stepped into the Senate chamber. As a teenager, Collins visited the nation’s capital for the U.S. Senate Youth Program, meeting people in the same position she would someday be elected to.
"I remember leaving Margaret Chase Smith's office and thinking that women could do anything, that girls could grow up to be anything," Collins said.
Aside from her high-profile job, the Caribou native loves to cook, baking her mother’s recipe for wild blueberry muffins.
"It's really terrific," Collins said. "I'd be glad to share it."
The senator hasn’t been baking as much lately since she’s been busy fighting to keep her seat in the U.S. Senate.
All eyes are on Maine's Senate race as Collins' challenger, Troy Jackson, seeks to unseat the Republican incumbent and move the Senate toward a Democratic majority.
"What I bring to the job is obviously great knowledge of the Senate, of federal issues, relationships with other senators that enabled me to be effective, to pass legislation like the Social Security Fairness Act," Collins said.
Collins is already one of the longest-serving U.S. senators from Maine, first getting elected back in 1996. She'll move to the top of that list if she completes another term.
The senator has taken more than 10,000 consecutive votes on the floor, but as chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, Collins says there’s still more she wants to do.
"We passed a temporary funding bill to ensure that government did not shut down, but when we go back, we will immediately start bringing to the Senate floor the appropriations bills that are so important for our veterans," Collins said.
With her long record comes criticism. Some voters still question the senator for voting to confirm Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh, who voted to overturn Roe v. Wade.
Collins cast that vote nearly 10 years ago.
"I'm very disappointed in his vote to overturn Roe v. Wade, but there was no way for me to anticipate that, because it's not appropriate to ask a Supreme Court nominee how he or she is going to vote," Collins said.
In more recent headlines, a report by ProPublica alleges Collins was in a pay-to-play scheme during her last reelection bid in 2020. She repeatedly denies the claims, which the FBI also called false.
"This is so frustrating to me. I have served the people of Maine with the utmost integrity," Collins said. "I'm an honest person."
Driving across the state, Collins is spending a large portion of her campaign reminding voters of the millions of dollars in federal funding she brings to the state as appropriations chair.
"That has allowed me to bring home funding for more than 670 projects in every county in this state, and it has made a real difference to so many communities and nonprofits," Collins said.
This election cycle has been anything but ordinary. Collins' initial Democratic challenger, Graham Platner, dropped out after a sexual assault allegation he denies. His departure came after other controversies that followed him throughout the campaign.
"This race has been the strangest race that I have ever had in my years running for office," Collins said.
Platner was replaced late in the process, after the primaries, with former state Senate president Troy Jackson.
Although Jackson’s campaign for Senate hasn’t been long, he’s been sparring with Collins plenty. Jackson has spent time trying to tie Collins to President Donald Trump and criticizing her voting record.
As voters decide whether the senator will keep her seat, Collins says there’s a big difference between her and Jackson.
"I believe he says that Governor Mills vetoed something like 40 of his bills, and that Governor LePage vetoed even more," Collins said. "That's not a sign of working together to get things done."
Election Day is Nov. 3.

title: Maine falls to Bryant for sixth straight loss
text:
ORONO, Maine — On Saturday, Oct. 17, the University of Maine football team lost its sixth straight game 17-14 at home against the Bryant University Bulldogs.
This game marked the return of the Black Bears following their bye week. It also marked the first game for the running backs coach, Sean Green, in his new role as the interim offensive coordinator.
The Black Bears had a solid start to the first half, with their first drive advancing 44 yards in 10 plays. The drive ended when redshirt second-year kicker Samuel Tremblay scored a field goal, putting the Black Bears up early. Following that play, Maine couldn’t get out of its own way.
The Bulldogs’ drive ended in a touchdown following a Maine holding penalty. The penalty meant a 10-yard gain for Bryant and allowed third-year quarterback Brennen Myer to complete a 30-yard pass to third-year wide receiver Jose Leon, who was already in Maine’s end zone. Second-year kicker Nicholas Stoyanovich successfully scored the extra point.
Following the Bulldogs’ touchdown, Maine didn’t have any success. Its next three drives didn’t get it very far, with the first two ending in punts and the third ending with a fumble.
That fumble led to another Bulldogs touchdown, with redshirt fourth-year running back OJ Ross rushing up the middle to Maine’s end zone. Stoyanovich again successfully scored the extra point.
After that, Maine’s next drive once again ended in a fumble, leading to another strong offensive push by the Bulldogs. This time, the Black Bears were able to have a very strong defensive line and prevented the Bulldogs from rushing for a third touchdown.
Following this show of defense, the Black Bears were able to gain some momentum and ended the first half with a solid drive.
To start the second half, the Black Bears were on offense again. Maintaining their momentum from the end of the first, Maine was able to move the ball 75 yards in eight plays. The drive ended with redshirt third-year quarterback Caden Drezek completing an 11-yard pass to redshirt second-year running back Rashawn Marshall for the touchdown. Redshirt second-year linebacker Noah Carpenter was able to rush into the end zone for an extra two points following the touchdown.
About halfway through the third quarter, the Bulldogs’ offensive line and the Black Bears’ defensive line were squared up nine yards from Maine’s end zone. The Black Bears were able to prevent a touchdown. However, Stoyanovich successfully kicked a field goal on a fourth-and-9 play.
The next few plays for each team didn’t result in very much, with all of them ending in punts and little to no movement for either team.
The Black Bears ended the scoring with a field goal by Tremblay early in the fourth quarter, following a mediocre drive of 78 yards in 20 plays.
This game didn’t end the way the Black Bears were hoping following coaching changes and a week without playing a game. While wind played a role in the game, the Black Bears were barely able to catch any passes made and couldn’t hang on to the ball. The Black Bears are now 1-6 overall and 1-3 in CAA games.
Going into their next game, the Black Bears will look to improve their offense and turn strong defensive plays into strong drives. The Black Bears play at home on Saturday, Oct. 24, against Campbell University in a conference game.

title: 3 injured after horse jumps during wagon ride at popular North Carolina drive-thru zoo
text:
MOORESVILLE, N.C. (WBTV/Gray News) - Three people were injured after a startled horse jumped while pulling a wagon at Lazy 5 Ranch, officials said.
The incident happened Saturday during a horse-drawn wagon ride at the ranch, a popular drive-thru zoo in North Carolina.
According to a social media post, a limb fell from a nearby tree and hit the side of the wagon, causing the horses to jump and three people to fall from the wagon.
All three were taken to a hospital for treatment, but their conditions were not available Sunday morning, officials said.
The other passengers were unharmed or declined treatment, and the wagon driver was uninjured, officials said. The horses were unharmed and were evaluated before returning to work.
“Our thoughts and prayers are with everyone involved in this incident, and we extend our heartfelt concern to those affected and their families,” officials said. “This is the first incident in [Lazy 5 Ranch] history resulting in hospitalizations requiring an overnight stay.”
Lazy 5 Ranch is located in Rowan County, about 36 miles northeast of Charlotte, North Carolina. More than 3 million people have experienced the ranch’s horse-drawn wagon rides, according to officials.

title: Hannaford still offline after supermarkets in France face cyberattack
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Hannaford supermarkets were still offline Monday, a week after Dutch owner Ahold Delhaize shut down its websites and apps following a “cybersecurity incident.”
The outage began the same day that cyberattacks disrupted supermarket refrigeration systems across France. A spokesperson for Hannaford, which operates 68 stores in Maine, said the company does not believe the issues are related. But some Hannaford locations have recently experienced refrigeration problems.
“The issue impacting some of our stores is specific to the refrigeration equipment itself, not other factors,” spokesperson Caitlin Cortelyou said in an email Monday.
About 700 French supermarkets experienced widespread food loss and some fires on Oct. 12, when hackers forced refrigeration units into continuous defrost cycles and set temperatures as high as 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit), according to The Associated Press.
Ahold Delhaize announced the same day that it had taken “some systems offline to help protect them” as “precautionary measures following (a) cybersecurity incident,” according to the company’s website.
The company said its stores — including Albert Heijn in the Netherlands, Delhaize in Belgium and Hannaford, Stop & Shop, Food Lion and Giant in the United States — would stay open while its websites and apps were offline.
On Monday, Ahold Delhaize announced that its European stores were back online and that e-commerce services at its U.S. stores “are expected to come back in the coming days.”
The company said it had no evidence that suggests any sensitive customer, associate or partner data was taken. It also didn’t note a connection to the cyberattacks on supermarkets in France.
“As the investigation is ongoing, we are not sharing further details that could compromise security measures or interfere with our response efforts,” the company said.
Based in Scarborough, Hannaford operates 188 stores across the Northeast and is Maine’s second-largest employer, with about 9,500 workers in stores from York to Fort Kent.
Hannaford confirmed Monday that it continued to experience a network issue affecting some services, including its website, mobile app, and Hannaford To Go pickup and delivery.
“This is related to a security issue within the network of our parent company, Ahold Delhaize,” Cortelyou said. “While we can’t comment on another company’s issue, we do not have any reason to believe the Ahold Delhaize matter is related to the issue impacting some French retailers.”
She noted that Hannaford stores remain open and continue to welcome customers, and that customers can continue to shop with the store online through Instacart, DoorDash and Uber Eats.
French Finance Minister Roland Lescure told Parliament last week that while the cyberattacks on refrigeration systems posed no risk to France’s food supplies, the attack “touches the heart of our food security,” AP reported.

title: U.S. Supreme Court declines to hear appeal of Maine’s gun sale waiting period
text:
The U.S. Supreme Court has declined to hear a challenge to Maine’s 72-hour waiting period for firearm purchases.
Justices on Monday denied a petition for a writ of certiorari in the case, one of dozens they declined to take up. The court, as is its standard practice, did not explain its reasoning for declining to hear the appeal.
The 1st U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled in April that the law is likely constitutional.
The law requires a 72-hour waiting period for a gun buyer to take possession of a firearm after purchasing it.
The law, as well as one expanding background check requirements, was enacted in 2024, six months after a gunman killed 18 people in the Lewiston mass shooting. Lawmakers designed the “cooling off” period to reduce suicides and homicides sparked by impulsive firearm purchases. It took effect without the signature of Gov. Janet Mills, who faced pressure from both gun owners and safety advocates.
The lawsuit was brought by a gun buyer, a firearms training business and three firearms dealers who argued that the law interfered with the rights of victims of domestic violence to immediately protect themselves and that it caused significant business losses for firearms dealers.
In February 2025, a federal judge granted a preliminary injunction, blocking enforcement of the law. That spring, a federal appeals court upheld the pause pending the state’s appeal.
The 1st Circuit concluded in April that the plaintiffs were unlikely to succeed in their constitutional challenge to the law and vacated the injunction. The Supreme Court’s decision leaves that ruling in place, allowing the law to be enforced while the lawsuit continues in federal court.
“We know from reporting from the Department of Public Safety that Maine’s 72-hour waiting period has already worked to save lives from preventable gun deaths in our state,” Nacole Palmer, executive director of the Maine Gun Safety Coalition, said in a written statement Monday. “Despite the gun lobby’s best efforts, our waiting period law will continue to save lives and we expect and hope that it will continue to be upheld.”
The Office of the Maine Attorney General declined to comment on Monday. Attorney General Aaron Frey is the defendant in the lawsuit, which was filed by Andrea Beckwith, who runs self-defense classes for victims of domestic violence, state Rep. James White, who owns J. White Gunsmithing, and other Maine gun stores and gun owners.
Joshua Raines, president of Gun Owners of Maine, said that while the Second Amendment group disagrees with the justices’ decision not to hear the appeal, “it wasn’t a surprise that they declined to take this on as it is only an injunction.”
“The lawyers will now take the main case back to the Maine court system, and we 100% expect the courts to overturn and nullify the Maine law based on previous federal case law,” Raines said in an emailed statement Monday.

title: Trump calls for New Mexico to change its name ‘immediately’: Here’s what he suggests
text:
(CNN) - President Donald Trump posted on social media Monday calling for New Mexico to change its name to “New America.”
The post read: “New Mexico should immediately change its name to New America. We are not Mexico, we are the United States of America!”
Trump claimed, without citing evidence, that home values and incomes would rise because of a name change.
Trump previously suggested renaming New Mexico in September.
He signed an executive order in August to change the name of Lake Ontario to “Lake America” as part of his ongoing trade war with Canada.
He took similar action last year to rename the Gulf of Mexico to “Gulf of America.”
Name predates US founding
New Mexico’s name predates the founding of the United States.
According to the Bureau of Indian Affairs, its name dates back to the 16th century.

title: For equal rights for LGBT citizens, Collins has been in the room where it happens
text:
Ken Mehlman is a businessman and former chairman of the Republican National Committee (2005-2007). Michael S.C. Soto is the co-leader of the Equality and Fairness for All Americans Coalition.
One of the most memorable songs in “Hamilton” is “The Room Where It Happens.”
It tells the story of a 1790 dinner where Alexander Hamilton, Thomas Jefferson and James Madison struck a deal. Hamilton won federal assumption of the states’ war debts. Jefferson and Madison won a capital on the Potomac. Aaron Burr, who sings the song, is left outside wondering how it all came together.
Washington still works much the same way. Debates happen in public, and public opinion shapes what is possible. But the details are usually settled in smaller rooms, among members of Congress, with the White House and with the advocates and stakeholders who will live with the results.
We have spent our careers in and around those rooms. One of us has worked in Republican politics, the other in progressive politics. We don’t agree on everything. But we have both worked to advance freedom and equal opportunity for gay and transgender Americans, and we have learned that who is in the room matters.
When it comes to gay rights, Sen. Susan Collins has been in that room for a long time.
In 2010, she and Sen. Joe Lieberman led the effort to repeal “Don’t Ask, Don’t Tell,” allowing gay and lesbian Americans to serve openly in the military. She supported federal hate crimes protections and workplace protections. She opposed amendments to ban same-sex marriage, publicly supported marriage equality and signed the Republican brief urging the Supreme Court to recognize same-sex marriages nationwide. In 2019, she joined Democratic Sens. Jeff Merkley, Tammy Baldwin and Cory Booker in introducing the Equality Act.
Some of the most important rooms in Washington are the ones where budgets get written. As chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, Collins secured more than $2.5 billion for the Ryan White HIV/AIDS Program this year, including $525 million that had been slated for cuts. Last year she stopped a proposed $400 million cut to PEPFAR, the global AIDS program that has saved an estimated 26 million lives. That work earned her the 2025 Champion Award from U.S. Business Action to End HIV.
Over time, she has become the Republican that Democratic senators call first when they want to move equality legislation forward. The Respect for Marriage Act shows why.
In 2022, many married same-sex couples worried their marriages were not fully secure under federal law. Congress had a chance to act, but only if a bill could reach 60 votes in the Senate. That meant bringing Republicans along without losing Democrats.
Collins and Baldwin led that effort, working with Sens. Rob Portman, Thom Tillis and Kyrsten Sinema. Much of the work happened quietly. They met with colleagues one at a time, listened to concerns about religious liberty and wrote language that addressed those concerns while keeping the heart of the bill intact. The final law repealed the Defense of Marriage Act and required federal and state recognition of same-sex and interracial marriages.
It passed the Senate 61-36 with support from Democrats, Republicans, equality advocates and religious organizations. President Biden signed it into law.
Some people hear the word “compromise” and worry it means supporters of equal rights must settle for less. That is not what happened here. The religious liberty language did not weaken the protections for married couples. It ensured everyone had a seat at the table and answered honest concerns so the bill could win the votes it needed and stand up in court. Sen. Collins knew the difference. She knew what could change and what could not, and people on both sides trusted her to keep her word.
That kind of legislating rarely makes headlines. It is slow, and it often happens out of view. But it is how lasting protections get written into law.
Washington is more divided today than at any point in our careers. That makes lawmakers who can work across party lines to solve our country’s biggest challenges more valuable and harder to find.
The room where it happens is less glamorous than Broadway makes it look. But for more than two decades, whenever the rights and lives of gay and transgender Americans have been on the table, Susan Collins has been in that room. And the laws that came out of it are stronger because she was there.

title: First National Bank invites communities to share warmth through Hat & Mitten Drive
text:
A warm hat or pair of mittens can make a meaningful difference during Maine's cold winter months. This fall, First National Bank is inviting community members to help keep their neighbors warm through its Warm Hands, Warm Hearts Hat & Mitten Drive, taking place now through Nov. 16.
Throughout the drive, all First National Bank branches will serve as collection locations for new hats, gloves, and mittens to benefit local children and families. Handmade items are also welcome, giving community members another meaningful way to contribute.

Every hat and pair of mittens donated is a reminder that even small acts of kindness can bring warmth to someone's day."
The initiative reflects First National Bank's ongoing commitment to strengthening the communities it serves. By encouraging customers, employees, and residents to participate, the bank hopes to bring people together around a shared goal of helping neighbors stay warm this winter.

Community members can donate new hats, gloves, and mittens, including handmade items, at any First National Bank branch from now through Nov. 16.

title: Does MaineCare cover chiropractic visits?
text:
Yes.
MaineCare, Maine’s Medicaid program, covers certain chiropractic services, including spinal manipulation, examinations to diagnose spinal conditions and certain X-rays.
For adults 21 and older, coverage generally includes 12 visits per calendar year. Additional visits require prior authorization, documentation of medical necessity and a referral from a medical provider. Members younger than 21 need a referral beyond 12 visits, but not prior authorization.
MaineCare does not cover all forms of medical treatment. For example, acupuncture and massage therapy are excluded.
The federal government recently approved a plan that will allow eligible tribal health organizations to bill MaineCare for traditional Wabanaki healing services. Coverage is not yet available; Maine officials tentatively anticipate launching the benefit on Oct. 1, 2027. The state and Wabanaki Nations are still determining which healing practices will qualify, who can provide them and how the benefit will work.
This fact brief is responsive to conversations such as this one.

title: Pres. Trump defends decision to pause sanctions
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - With a little over two weeks until Election Day, a number of high-profile Republicans are breaking with President Trump on his approach to Russia and President Vladimir Putin. In many cases, these are Republican senators in unexpectedly tight re-election races.
Before they left town, Congress passed the Lindsey Graham Sanctioning Russia Act of 2026. The provisions were supposed to go into effect late last week. However, before they could, the President signed an executive order waiving the sweeping new sanctions and tariffs against Russia before they were scheduled to take effect.
President Trump wrote on Truth Social over the weekend, “My decision on Russia is a very simple one. I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine, and don’t want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table. Great progress - he said - is being made.”
Before he departed for his latest rally in Wichita, Kansas, President Trump reiterated the message in that Truth Social, telling reporters, “I’m in the midst of negotiating a deal. When you’re negotiating a deal, you don’t do that to the people you negotiate. And the deals to Ukraine deal. Also, I’m negotiating with them on Iran because they’ve been very well behaved on Iran. Also, I’m negotiating with them on hostages. And I’m also negotiating on diesel. So when you when you, that’s my business. When you’re negotiating, you don’t do that.”
But since that decision, Mike Rogers, running to be the next Republican Senator from Michigan, has said he opposes buying Russian diesel fuel. And Senator Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska) as well as Rep. Ashley Hinson (R-Iowa) now running for the Senate- said they too are opposed to buying diesel fuel from Russia
Meanwhile, The Wall Street journal reported over the weekend that Russian President Vladimir Putin has proposed a summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping and President Donald Trump to end the Ukraine war. Ukraine president Volodymyr Zelenskyy is not a part of those plans.
Despite the President’s approach to Russia, diesel prices have remained high. And that has impacted the trucking and farming industries -creating more headwinds for Republicans trying to maintain control of both the House and the Senate.

title: Family mourns 81-year-old veteran shot, killed while leaving Walmart on mobility scooter
text:
ATLANTA (ANF/Gray News) - The family of an 81-year-old Georgia man is mourning after he was shot and killed while leaving Walmart. Police say one teenager has been arrested and charged with his murder while another suspect is still on the run.
James McDaniel, 81, was using a mobility scooter Wednesday night as he left a Walmart in Gainesville when he was shot and killed, according to Gainesville Police.
Police say the shooting stemmed from a fight inside Walmart that spilled into the parking lot. Two teenagers allegedly opened fire on a group of men, hitting McDaniel on the other end of the parking lot.
Police say McDaniel was an innocent bystander who was not involved in the fight.
Police arrested 18-year-old Kamari Nehemiah Tilmuth on Sunday morning. He is charged with felony murder, four counts of aggravated assault and possession of a firearm during the commission of a crime.
Erron Lamar Dorsey, 17, is wanted in connection with the shooting and remains at large, police say. He faces the same charges as Tilmuth.
Victim was a great-grandfather and Navy veteran
Days after McDaniel’s death, his family is still in shock. The 81-year-old victim was a great-grandfather, Navy veteran and former postal employee.
“My dad was just kind of a fun, loving guy,” said his son, Ted McDaniel. “We always knew he loved us.”
Gloria McDaniel, the victim’s wife of nearly 60 years, is mourning, but even now, she says she has sympathy for the parents of whoever pulled the trigger.
“I just feel like they’ve ruined their lives, too,” she said. “And they did something that was wrong, very, very wrong, and they need to be punished.”
“The consequences of their actions took my father’s life,” Ted McDaniel said. “That’s a really hard pill to swallow. He’ll always be a part of my heart, even though he was taken from us.”
An online fundraiser has been set up to help the family.
