title: MDI High School students volunteer at local nonprofits for Community Service Day
text:
MOUNT DESERT ISLAND — On Oct. 14, the entire freshman class headed out to eight local nonprofits for the biannual Mount Desert Island High School Community Service Day. The nonprofit partners included Loaves and Fishes Food Pantry, Stanwood Wildlife Sanctuary (Birdsacre), the Oceanarium and Education Center, Friends of Acadia in Acadia National Park, the Jesup Library, The Neighborhood House, Camp Beech Cliff, and Maine Coast Heritage Trust's Kittredge Preserve. One of the key goals of the day is to help students gain experience and knowledge of the many ways these nonprofit organizations serve the community through education, stewardship of the outdoors and social connections. In fact, each group explored the history and mission of the partner organization, as well as other ways to volunteer or help in the future, before the actual day of service.
Another goal is to help foster connection within each small Advisory Group, which remains together throughout High School. Advisor leadership and modeling is a key part of the day as well, and each chaperone rose to the challenge. These Advisors included Jen Crandall, Ellen Bailey, Mark Shields, Matt Umphrey, Carrie Joyce, Lyn Gatz, Kate Muzzy, Matthew Mayo, Christien Breau, and Michelle Merica. While most have experience with the format of the day, many opted to visit new locations. The hands-on work kept students engaged, although there was also social time built into the day for snacking, lunch and just chatting.

title: The nightmare every Maine hunter fears
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
This was originally published Oct. 23, 2025.
I had a terrible dream the other night. Not a Stephen King-style horror that haunts you in the dark, but a different kind of nightmare. In it, hunting simply didn’t exist. No rifles, no bows, no shotguns. No hunters wandering the woods. A world without one of America’s oldest traditions.
I thought about how lucky we are to live in a country where, with few exceptions, nearly anyone can hunt. There are safety courses, age requirements and regulations to follow, but for most Americans, the freedom to hunt remains. It is a gift, one that many, including hunters themselves, often take for granted.
But what if we couldn’t? What would happen to wildlife populations and the millions of acres of habitat maintained today in large part because of hunting?
Hunting is not just a pastime. It is a major driver of conservation and economic support. In 1937, Congress passed the Pittman-Robertson Act, which imposed an 11 percent tax on sporting arms and ammunition. Amendments later included pistols, bows, arrows and crossbows. According to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, which administers the funds, more than $22 billion has been collected since the act’s creation. In 2020 alone, over $601 million was allocated to states and U.S. territories.
If not for hunters, much of that money would not exist. In 2020, Alaska would have missed out on about $25 million, California more than $19 million, Texas over $27 million and Pennsylvania nearly $21 million. Maine lost more than $7 million in fiscal year 2021. Those funds support vital wildlife and conservation programs for everyone, not just hunters.
This does not include revenue from hunting licenses. In 2020, more than 15 million licenses were sold in the United States, generating over $1 billion. Combined, these funds are the lifeblood of wildlife agencies, in some states covering more than 80 percent of the revenue used to support programs for game and non-game species alike.
The economic impact extends beyond government coffers. Hunters spend millions annually on clothing, ATVs, game cameras and more. Those dollars fuel jobs for guides, outfitters and sporting goods retailers. According to a report by the National Shooting Sports Foundation, hunting generates 680,000 jobs and adds over $9 million to the U.S. economy every day. Remove hunting, and those jobs and revenues disappear.
Yet few Americans give hunters credit for the bounty of wildlife around them. In the early 1900s, barely half a million whitetail deer existed in the country. Today, that number exceeds 30 million. Elk, pronghorn, turkeys, bears, waterfowl and other game species thrive because hunter dollars have financed research and conservation for more than 80 years. Even songbirds, raptors, amphibians and reptiles have benefited.
It is difficult to imagine what America’s wildlife and habitats would look like today had hunting and its financial contributions vanished. Federal agencies might pick up some of the slack, but considering how things work in Washington, the gap would be significant.
As Theodore Roosevelt said, “In a civilized and cultivated country wild animals only continue to exist when preserved by sportsmen. The excellent people who protest against all hunting and consider sportsmen as enemies of wildlife are ignorant of the fact that in reality the genuine sportsman is by all odds the most important factor in keeping wild creatures from total extinction.”
I don’t know if hunters are born or made, but the passion runs deep. Hunting means different things to different people. For me, it is about putting meat on the table, but it is also much more. The woods and fields are my cathedral, a place where I find peace, rejuvenation and a sense of being whole. Those opposed to hunting might find that elsewhere. I have yet to see it. I feel sorry for those who never understand the need or passion as I do. I hope I never find out.

Ahold Delhaize taking systems offline

title: Husband left unrecognizable after breaking up fight between 2 family dogs
text:
ATLANTA (ANF/Gray News) - A Georgia man’s life changed in a split second when he tried to break up a fight between two family dogs, leaving him severely injured.
Dustin Low suffered severe facial injuries while breaking up a fight between two family dogs. Since then, he’s needed multiple surgeries.
“It was probably a matter of five minutes total action time, and then, the rest was just trying to gather myself, my breath and control the bleeding,” Dustin Low said.
His wife, Chelsea Low, recalls the night she looked at her husband and noticed his facial tissue had been badly damaged.
“He came downstairs and was like, ‘I need help with the pets.’ I’m like, ‘No, you need a hospital,’” Chelsea Low said.
Dustin Low has undergone two major facial reconstructive surgeries since the incident and needs a third to help him return to a sense of normalcy.
“It will get rid of this piece, which is the rest of my forehead flap, and it will sew that back up,” he said.
But medical bills for the surgeries have been stacking up, and the couple are asking for help to get Dustin Low into that third surgery.
“We need $12,310 just to get him on the operating table for the third surgery. They will not do the third surgery until we pay $12,310. That’s for the first two surgeries. The last surgery is $6,500,” Chelsea Low said.
As the Lows pray for a miracle, they say they don’t hold anger toward the dogs and plan to keep them.
“It was a mistake. It was a freak accident. They didn’t want to harm him,” Chelsea Low said.
A GoFundMe has been set up to help the couple.

title: Orono council creates committee on license plate reading cameras
text:
A new committee in Orono will give its council guidance on how to regulate automatic license plate readers.
The committee stemmed from Orono Town Council’s discussion on if the technology should be used in the town. Orono does not currently use automated license plate readers, Town Manager Clint Deschene said in a memo.
Before the committee’s creation, councilors did not agree on what, if any, action regulating the cameras should be taken.
Councils in communities across Maine have discussed how the controversial technology, which captures passing license plate numbers and other identifying information and adds it to a network that can track a person’s movements, should be used because of reported misuses across the country, including wrongly identifying drivers as criminals or using the technology to track people without any legal cause.
Multiple councils have banned the cameras from their towns, but some have continued to use the technology saying that it benefits their police departments.
The council in Orono’s neighboring city, Old Town, held a first reading and public hearing of a proposed ban on automatic license plate readers at its Monday meeting.
Orono Councilors voted unanimously to create the committee and place Councilors John Quinn, Rob Laraway, Deschene and Police Chief Dan Merrill as the members. There was no discussion about the committee before or after the vote. A first meeting date was not set at Monday’s council meeting.
In two previous meetings, council members spoke about three possibilities regarding the cameras — to take no action, to create policy to require council approval of any possible cameras or to pass a ban. Councilors did not agree on what action should be taken at their Oct. 5 meeting, but they did agree that creating a committee to gather more information and input would be helpful.
Councilors Sarah Marx, Quinn and Laraway voiced support for the committee and possible ordinance changes at council’s Oct. 5 meeting. Councilor Jacob Baker said at the Oct. 5 meeting that he was in support of not taking action because the town isn’t using the technology currently and any change would have to be brought in front of the council.
If an ordinance were to be adopted, it could be based on language other Maine municipalities have used, Marx said on Oct. 5. Marx said she favors an ordinance.
“If you want to ensure that there is public discussion about something, the only way to really ensure that is an ordinance. If we make a policy, that doesn’t bind a future council to have to hold a public discussion about it,” she said on Oct. 5.

title: Why I’m voting for Susan Collins
text:
The BDN Opinion section operates independently and does not set news policies or contribute to reporting or editing articles elsewhere in the newspaper or on bangordailynews.com
Bill Green is a retired broadcaster who serves on the boards of the Maine Sports Hall of Fame, Friends of Baxter State Park and the Casco Bay Institute. His sister works for Sen. Susan Collins’ campaign.
Lobster, low-bush wild blueberries, and a particularly distinguished group of U.S. senators.
What state am I talking about?
We make a big deal of the first two products, but we should be more proud of the third. In my lifetime, I believe no state has produced as influential, independent and intelligent a group of senators as we have. I think Margaret Chase Smith, Ed Muskie, George Mitchell, Bill Cohen, and Susan Collins are elite. Add Olympia Snowe, Bill Hathaway and Angus King. That’s not bad.
Other than a paper by former Colby Professor Sandy Maisel, I can’t find an actual ranking of states with the best senators. So, I’ll do one myself: We are the best.
That’s why this year’s Senate race between Susan Collins and Troy Jackson is so discouraging to me. Susan has a long record of Senate accomplishment, set Senate records for her hard work and most importantly brought home the bacon — $1.5 billion in federal financial support over the past five years.
Democrats have jumped on the opportunity to unseat her. When Graham Platner dropped out, Democrats quickly organized a convention and nominated Jackson, a candidate they may be able to control more than Planter. Bernie Sanders and Elizabeth Warren came to Maine to embrace him. Surely, I think someone wrote his script for the first debate.
In that debate Susan would point out something she said he didn’t understand, such as differences between the funding of Medicare and Medicaid. Troy quickly started thumbing through his notes. I was thinking he was going to say, “Just a minute! I’m looking for my answer!”
Later, in response to Susan getting tariffs lifted on road salt, he blurted “We can’t eat road salt,” and was heralded by supporters. I think if he had really driven all those miles that he put in for, he’d be more grateful for road salt.
Susan is a policy expert, but who wants to hear in-depth discussion? Who wants to hear about the nuances of the Ginsburg rule, for example? The answer is other able senators. They want to work with colleagues who think broadly and coherently. I think a new senator who speaks only in slogans is soon consigned to the “Show Horse” section of the Senate: Good on cable, lousy on the job.
Anybody who has watched Susan work the crowds at Maine fairs can see how she connects with Mainers. The affection for her is palpable. But so much of campaigning these days is ads, many of which are lies. The number of times that Susan has been accused of cutting Medicaid (or Medicare, or Social Security) is startling.
The dumbest ad I’ve heard is one of Troy’s. He says: “What this campaign is about is pretty simple.” (I agree.) “If you work hard, you ought to be able to take your kid to the doctor.” (You can.) “You ought to be able to buy groceries.” (We do.) “You ought to be able to retire with Medicare and Social Security that you earned.” (We do.) “It’s time that your hard work paid off.” (It has.) What solutions is he proposing? He sure hasn’t outlined them that I’ve seen.
It’s easy for a candidate to criticize and cast aspersions. It’s harder to write legislation that can get through a sharply divided Senate. Susan Collins has done so many times.
Stephen King took to Threads to say I was wrong to support Susan. There are two big differences between me and Stephen. The first is that he’s really talented. The second is I believe he only votes for Democrats. I have voted for people from both parties many times.
Maine has sent independent, intelligent and influential people to the U.S. Senate. They didn’t all agree with one another, but they understood the job and made their mark for Maine.
I try to pick the better candidate. Except for Bill Hathaway, I believe I voted for everyone on my list above.
To me, Troy Jackson doesn’t belong on that list and Susan Collins most definitely does.

title: More than 1.5 million pounds of hot dogs, bacon and other meats recalled nationwide
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
More than 1.5 million pounds of hot dogs, bacon and other meats recalled nationwide
More than 1.5 million pounds of hot dogs, bacon, deli meat, bratwursts and more have been recalled nationwide.
Kayem Foods Inc. is recalling about 1.58 million pounds of ready-to-eat meat and poultry products because they may have been stored at unsafe temperatures, the U.S. Department of Agriculture said.
Related video above | Recalls explained: How to stay ahead of recalls
The products were made from March 31 to Oct. 7 at the company’s Chelsea, Massachusetts, facility.
They were shipped to retailers and food service locations across the United States and to Hong Kong.
The recalled items carry establishment numbers “EST. M/P 7839,” “EST. P 20935A” or “EST. M 9520” inside the USDA inspection mark.
Product names, package labels and UPC codes can all be found here. Consumers can check those details to see whether they have any of the recalled items.
The company said it began investigating after a customer reported warm products at delivery on Oct. 1.
It found that a warehouse cooler had experienced temperature deviations while storing the products, federal officials said.
No illnesses have been confirmed, but the USDA said some recalled items could still be in consumers’ refrigerators.
Consumers should not eat the products.
They should throw them away or return them to the store where they were purchased. Anyone concerned about an illness should contact a health care provider.

title: Stolen vehicle crashes into pond with 7 juveniles inside, police say
text:
SABATTUS, Maine (WABI) - A vehicle carrying seven juveniles crashed into Sabattus Pond early Sunday morning.
The vehicle was reported stolen out of Auburn, according to the Sabattus Police Department.
Officials said they received multiple calls of a vehicle driving recklessly.
Officers were able to locate the vehicle as they saw the driver run a red light before losing control and driving into the pond.
Two juveniles ran into the woods and were later found by a K9, the other five stayed and cooperated with police, authorities said.
No injuries were reported and officials say charges are pending.

title: Hidden meanings behind emojis raise safety concerns for parents
text:
(Aging Untold) — Emojis such as tears of joy, hearts and thumbs-up are used daily. For Jill Story’s three daughters, emojis represent a different language.
“They have a whole language they use that I’m constantly having to figure out,” Story said.
Moms try to crack the code
A group of mothers sat down to see if they could decode common phrases and symbols used by kids.
When asked about “Code9” or “CD9,” the moms said they didn’t know what it meant.
It means: “parents are around.”
“This is going to be really good to know,” one mom said.
The group was also asked about “GNOC.”
The term: “get naked on camera.”
“Oh, dang. Oh!” the moms responded.
Emojis carry secret meanings
The moms were then shown emojis to decode. One mom was asked about the noodles emoji.
“Nudes, send nudes,” she said, explaining she guessed based on the similarity between “noodles” and “nudes.”
The scissors emoji prompted different guesses among the group. One mom, Kathy, guessed it meant to cut clothes off, while Story guessed it referred to cutting. The scissors emoji refers to self-harm.
Expert advice for parents
Aging Untold expert Amy O’Rourke said the use of coded language among kids reflects a pattern seen across generations.
“So I think about all the generations that have gone before us and how we created our own little world that was separate from the one ahead of us because we wanted to have our own thing. The emojis are the same thing,” O’Rourke said.
O’Rourke said these digital codes often lead to real-world consequences. She said parents should ask questions about what the terms mean.
“Ask a lot of questions, get really curious. What does this mean? What should I know? And make it really fun and interesting, not intrusive to the younger person,” O’Rourke said.
Experts say parents should know who their kids follow on social media and consider following them back to learn the latest slang.
“You think your kids, my kids at home, they’re safe, but there’s a whole world in their hands that is not safe,” one mom said.

title: First National Bank launches $5,000 Dream First Community Grant to strengthen food security
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
DAMARISCOTTA – First National Bank has launched the Dream First Community Grant, a new $5,000 funding opportunity supporting food security-related programming in the Maine communities the Bank serves.
One eligible registered 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization, municipality or school will receive funding to launch a new initiative, expand a promising program, or strengthen an existing service. Applicants must serve residents in Lincoln, Knox, Waldo, Hancock, Penobscot or Washington County.
“Reliable access to nutritious food helps individuals, families, and communities thrive,” President and CEO Tony McKim said. “Through the Dream First Community Grant, we hope to help a local organization turn a thoughtful idea into meaningful action.”
Eligible projects may include mobile food distribution, backpack and weekend meal programs, school and youth nutrition initiatives, senior meal programs, community gardens, fresh produce access, community refrigerators, farm-to-food pantry partnerships, nutrition education, rural food-access programs and innovative pilot projects focused on reducing hunger.
Applicants must demonstrate financial responsibility and submit a completed application and project budget. Grant funds must be used exclusively for food security-related programming and may not be used for general operating expenses.
Applications are through Oct. 31. Applications will be reviewed in November, and the recipient will be announced in December.
For eligibility details and the application, visit www.thefirst.com/dream-first-community-grant.
First National Bank, a subsidiary of The First Bancorp, Inc. (NASDAQ: FNLC), is an independent community bank with 18 offices in Lincoln, Knox, Waldo, Hancock, Washington and Penobscot counties. For more information, please call 1-800-564-3195 or visit www.thefirst.com.

title: What’s the future of Hallowell’s old city hall, fire station?
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
HALLOWELL — Dozens of residents gathered Thursday at the Quarry Tap Room, eager to hear long-awaited news about the development of the historic former fire station and city hall building, which is finally moving forward.
Benjamin Spencer, local developer with commercial real estate firm CORE, presented plans to renovate the building to include three apartments and commercial space while retaining the Hallowell Food Pantry on the lower level.
Spencer, who owns and has done interior renovations for several buildings downtown as well as renovating buildings in downtown Gardiner, said his firm hopes to close the deal in the next month after submitting a bid for the project over a year ago. The city is selling the building for $10,000.
The historic Second Street building was built in 1828 and housed the fire department from 1900 until 2018 when it was relocated to a new building after an anonymous donor pledged $1 million to build a new station in Stevens Commons on Winthrop Street.
In the years following the transition, the future of the building was uncertain. In a nonbinding 2022 referendum, residents indicated they wanted to see it renovated. Now, the project is finally moving forward.
Spencer said the developing team is applying for a $200,000 REvitalizeME Downtown Grant that, with matching funds from CORE, will fund the exterior renovation, estimated to cost $260,000. The interior renovation will cost around $250,000.
Spencer said his team plans to replace the building’s windows, doors and exterior siding first. While the grant requires the facade be maintained in a historical manner for 10 years, the city stipulates the same requirements for the lifetime of the property.
Jesse Gibbon, a partner on the project, owns Hallowell-based G&G Construction, which will complete the exterior renovations. If they receive the grant, Spencer said the team hopes to begin construction as early as possible next year.
When it comes to the interior of the building, there is an agreement to let the food pantry stay in its location on the bottom floor for free for the next 10 years. Spencer hopes to turn the top floor into three market-rate apartments and the ground floor into a retail space, mentioning the possibility of a farmers’ market space.
When asked by an audience member if the apartments would potentially be Airbnbs, Spencer clarified that the apartments would be yearlong leases and not short-term rentals like Airbnbs.
The historic fire department artifacts housed in the old fire station will be moved to the new station, and the weather vane will be returned to the city. Spencer said he also hopes to preserve some amount of public viewing access to the hose tower.
While there are no time stipulations in the agreement, Spencer said they are incentivized to complete the project to get it done but also for the value of his five other downtown properties.
Spencer is excited to undergo the project because the community is so strong in Hallowell, as evidenced by the attendance at the Thursday presentation, he said.
“That’s what excites me about it more than just an older building that needs renovation, you’ve got a strong community behind you as well,” Spencer said.
Julie Howell, manager of the food pantry, said she felt positive leaving Spencer’s presentation and is excited to see the building be taken care of while also allowing the pantry to continue operations.
“For a local developer to want to have an interest in taking on the building and enabling us to stay where we are was just a huge weight off our shoulders,” Howell said. “And so we can just get back to concentrating on what we do.
Howell said she appreciates the experience of the developers and their willingness to work with the pantry.
“We’ll be great neighbors to them, and I think they’re going to be great neighbors to us,” Howell said.

title: KFC switches to Coca-Cola products after nearly four decades serving Pepsi
text:
ATLANTA, Ga. (Atlanta News First/Gray News) — For about 40 years, KFC has exclusively served Pepsi beverages — but next year, that’s set to change.
On Thursday, the fast food giant said its thousands of U.S. locations are switching to a partnership with the Atlanta-based Coca-Cola Company. The change starts in January 2027.
In a statement, the company called the move “another step in the brand’s ongoing effort to refresh its menu and beverage platform and create more reasons for customers to visit.”
Catherine Tan-Gillespie, president of KFC U.S., said both brands have “deep consumer love.”
“This partnership is about more than what’s in the cup,” she said in a statement. “It is another step in our work to evolve KFC, strengthen our restaurants, menu offerings and create a more relevant experience for today’s customers. Coca-Cola shares our ambition for the future of this brand, and I’m excited about what we can create together.”
Dagmar Boggs, The Coca-Cola Company’s North America president of foodservice and on-premise, also shared her excitement.
“By pairing KFC’s iconic food and flavors with the breadth of Coca-Cola’s beverage portfolio and innovation capabilities, we have an incredible opportunity to make every visit more refreshing, create memorable consumer experiences and unlock new growth possibilities together,” she said.
KFC said it’s working to expand its beverage platform, including a new drink lineup featuring iced coffee, boba and shakes at Open House, the brand’s Texas-based innovation restaurant.

title: Organization is trying to help healers amid Oregon nursing shortage
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
PORTLAND, Ore. (Aging Untold)— Oregon faces a nursing crisis that experts say stems not from a lack of licensed nurses, but from workplace conditions that drive healthcare workers away from frontline positions.
The U.S. will see nearly 200,000 job openings for registered nurses each year until 2032, according to the American Association of Colleges of Nursing. Higher nurse-to-patient ratios can increase the likelihood of errors and decrease patient satisfaction, researchers at Ohio University found.
Oregon has more licensed nurses than ever before, but 30% of new nurses leave their first jobs within their first year out of nursing school, according to the Oregon Center for Nursing.
“My belief is that in Oregon, we don’t actually have a nursing shortage. What we have is a vacancy crisis, and that’s because of persistent, unhealthy work environment, increased stress, increased workplace violence,” Christy Simila, director of professional practice at the Oregon Nurses Association, said.
Nurses seek healing after pandemic trauma
Registered nurse Heather Sweeney and therapist Amy Ponteri started “Helping Healthcare Heal” to address what they saw as insufficient resources for healthcare workers in intense settings like emergency rooms.
“We never healed from that — they just give you a pizza party and say, ‘It’s time to move on, COVID’s over, here we go.’ Nobody gave us an opportunity to heal,” Sweeney said.
The organization offers retreats, support groups and continuing education for healthcare workers. Sweeney described the pressure many nurses feel to work extra shifts.
“And then you get all these text messages every day of open shifts, and you feel like you should go pick it up because you don’t want to leave your teammate down. But, then all of a sudden, you’ve worked 60 hours in the week,” Sweeney said.
Nurses find alternative roles
Simila said many nurses are taking jobs adjacent to frontline healthcare settings, such as nurse coaches, consultants or working in call centers doing triage.
Susan Ashenfelter, a nurse who participated in the healing programs, said the retreats helped her process intense experiences.
“I realized I had time to process some really, intense things that I’ve gone through in the last year or two that I had not had time to do,” Ashenfelter said.
Penny Haggerty, another participating nurse, said the experience was transformative.
“It was just like something new happened to me inside myself,” Haggerty said. “Just being with the other women, hearing their stories, learning from the ladies. Just came back empowered.”
New laws address working conditions
A law in Oregon is meant to address nurse-to-patient ratios in hospitals.
“I think hospitals can really start by listening to their nurses and what the nurses need, and really working to create a more healthy work environment, working to create a safer work environment, or where nurses aren’t showing up and potentially being subject to workplace violence as often,” Simila said.

title: Hearts of Pine midfielder Mikey Lopez announces retirement
text:
Hearts of Pine midfielder Mikey Lopez announced on Instagram that Portland’s season finale Saturday will be the final game of his 14-year career.
Lopez, 33, has played 47 games in two seasons with the Hearts of Pine, including 31 last season. He was named the USL League One Comeback Player of the Year in 2025 after Achilles surgery wiped out his 2024 season.
The Hearts of Pine’s captain has played 16 games this season with eight starts.
“I think Saturday will close the circle on my career,” Lopez said in a video posted to Instagram. “Being able to play in front of my family, a sold-out crowd at Fitzpatrick Stadium and playing for (Hearts of Pine coach) Bobby (Murphy) one last time I think is the perfect way to end my career.”
Lopez played for Murphy at a Texas development academy in grades 8-12. He played at the University of North Carolina and was a first-round pick in the 2011 MLS SuperDraft by Sporting Kansas City. He spent three seasons in Kansas City, followed by two with New York City FC. He also played seven seasons in USL Championship, the last six with Birmingham, where he was the franchise’s first captain.
Portland will host Charlotte Independence at 5 p.m. Saturday at Fitzpatrick Stadium. The Hearts of Pine, who reached the USL League One semifinals in their first season, are 7-14-10 and have failed to qualify for the playoffs in their second campaign.

title: Priest dies after being struck by falling cross during livestreamed service
text:
Priest dies after being struck by falling cross during livestreamed Mass in Ecuador
A priest has died after he was hit by a cross that fell during a livestreamed evening Mass in Ecuador.
Related video: Man falls 120 feet into water at Glacier National Park
Roman Catholic priest Patricio Alfredo Sánchez Molinari, of Perpetuo Socorro Church, was seen on video speaking to congregants when a heavy crucifix appeared to detach from the wall, striking the priest on the head.
According to the Associated Press, the cross appeared to fall from behind, with Molinari unable to see it.
The Archdiocese of Guayaquil later issued a statement on Facebook, confirming the priest's death on Saturday, saying he "has left to the House of the Father to enjoy his presence and glory."
People Magazine said cries of panic and distress from congregants could be heard on video shared on social media following the incident.
Multiple outlets said local authorities have not commented on the incident.
Sánchez belonged to the Congregation of the Most Holy Redeemer, a Roman Catholic religious order founded in 1732 with a presence in 80 countries.

Justice Department charges more than 2 dozen in California sweep targeting noncitizen voters
text:
LOS ANGELES (AP) — Federal authorities have arrested more than two dozen foreign nationals Monday in California, who authorities said have illegally registered and voted in U.S. elections.
The statewide sweep is part of a Trump administration effort to root out noncitizen voting ahead of next month’s midterm elections, even though data shows that the problem is incredibly rare, difficult to prove and has not been shown to change the outcome of races.
The arrests also reflect a further escalation in a simmering voter roll fight between the federal government and California that came into focus last week when the Justice Department sued the state and later warned that local election workers who knowingly process or tabulate ballots submitted by noncitizen voters are at risk of investigation and potential prosecution.
The Justice Department said all of those arrested as part of a sweep dubbed Operation Protect the Vote are lawful permanent residents — but not U.S. citizens who are permitted to legally vote. They are charged with crimes including making false statements on a naturalization application and submitting fraudulent voter registrations.
California emerges as a flashpoint for voting dispute
The federal government has made noncitizen voting a priority this year, demanding detailed voter information — including dates of birth, addresses, driver’s license numbers and partial Social Security numbers — from the states.
Before Monday, the Justice Department had charged about 90 people for various types of election misconduct so far this year, including 50 who are alleged to have voted as noncitizens. There were more than 227 million registered voters in the United States during the 2024 presidential election.
A flurry of activity has unfolded in heavily Democratic California, which is not typically regarded as a key battleground state but does have a handful of competitive congressional races that could help determine which party controls the U.S. House for the final two years of President Donald Trump’s term. Over 23 million people are registered statewide.
The administration last week sued California to prevent it from counting mail ballots from people the federal government has identified as “likely” noncitizens until their immigration status can be confirmed.
The complaint was filed after California officials were given, and did not meet, a 48-hour deadline to review a password-protected thumb drive that contained a list of 20,000 names. The federal government says those are likely noncitizens who were sent ballots to participate in the Nov. 3 election, although the secretary of state said the administration has provided no evidence to support that claim. The state mails ballots to all registered voters.
Threatening poll workers
On Friday, the Justice Department followed up with a letter warning that state election officials who knowingly process ballots cast by noncitizen voters are at risk of investigation.
“The legal consequences for either facilitating or ignoring a federal crime are significant. Noncitizen voting in a federal election is a federal crime — and knowingly facilitating such conduct is equally unlawful,” warns the letter from Trent McCotter, the acting deputy attorney general at the Justice Department.
It adds: “If persons knowingly tabulate ballots cast by individuals identified by federal agencies as noncitizens, they risk becoming aiders and abettors to a federal crime.”
The letter is addressed to the Los Angeles County Counsel’s office and also is copied to California Secretary of State Shirley Weber and Los Angeles County Registrar Dean Logan, effectively putting the entire state on notice.
In response to the letter, Logan said his office is focused on conducting a fair and secure election while noting that Election Day is a mere 18 days away.
“The U.S. Department of Justice has chosen to litigate their unverified assertions of voting eligibility. At this point, it is best for this to be addressed in court,” he said.
___
Associated Press writer Eric Tucker contributed to this report from Washington.

title: This dog-like robot adds security layer to businesses nationwide
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WADDELL, Ariz. (InvestigateTV) — A high-tech robot is adding an extra layer of security at businesses across the country, combining AI technology and human expertise to track down security threats.
The robot, covered in sensors and about the size of a dog, conducts automated patrols at locations including a warehouse in Waddell, Arizona. The device checks gates, doors, locks and looks for people in places where they shouldn’t be.
“This robot has patrolled thousands of miles just in this yard,” said Ryan Hodgens of Asylon, the company behind the technology.
Robots patrol facilities nationwide
Hodgens said robots like this patrol distribution centers and manufacturing plants across the country. When on patrol, they provide live video feeds to a monitoring center in Pennsylvania where people are watching.
“We can stop the robot in one place, move the camera over, zoom in 40x to a door to inspect it,” Hodgens said. “We can, if we’re operating at night, switch over to thermal as well, to easily detect heat signatures.”
The technology is also used at large events including the DNC and RNC.
At the Indianapolis 500, the robot operates with a chemical gas detection sensor integrated on board underneath the tunnel system, Hodgens said.
Advanced navigation capabilities
The robot can navigate obstacles from tunnels to stairs thanks to about 20 sensors that are built in. Every single joint moves independently.
“There’s a lot of engineering work that’s gone into the stability piece,” Hodgens said. “In terms of its ability to stay upright, around curves, up and over gravel, uneven terrain here, the stability is truly unmatched.”
The movements sometimes mimic an animal so well that operators almost forget it’s a robot.
“Each one kind of has their own personality,” Hodgens said.
Privacy and operational details
On potential privacy concerns, Hodgens compared DroneDog to other closed circuit cameras.
“This camera happens to have four legs,” Hodgens said. “It’s the same exact kind of architecture on the back-end, in terms of privacy as all these other closed circuit cameras that we’re seeing around.”
The robot has a 90-minute battery life before returning to its charging station to recharge and rest up for the next patrol.
It includes a speaker that can communicate with people in its path using either pre-recorded messages or live communication.

title: The local ballot questions that will drive Maine’s tax bills
text:
Mainers will decide more than who goes to Congress, the Blaine House and the Legislature on Nov. 3, as local ballots across the state carry school mergers, closures and multimillion-dollar fire trucks that will shape tax bills for years.
Many of those questions come from the same pressures shaping bigger elections, including an aging population, shrinking enrollment and inflation pushing property taxes up. In some towns, voters see consolidation as the answer. In others, they are trying to undo it.
Here are some of the nuts-and-bolts questions facing voters around Maine.
Schools
School governance is one of Maine’s hottest issues, even two decades after Gov. John Baldacci’s 2007 consolidation law pushed districts to merge but did not make them stick to it.
In the Mount Desert Island region, voters in eight towns will decide whether to fold their independent school districts into a single regional school unit. Supporters argue a merger would let towns pool resources, adopt one budget and cut duplication.
“I think this is the first time since the consolidation efforts from the Baldacci administration that we have really dug our teeth into it and came up with a plan,” Superintendent Mike Zboray, who leads MDI-area schools, said. “And if it doesn’t pass, we’ll take a look at what we did and how to make changes.”
The proposal has drawn opposition from residents worried about losing local control and about how a combined budget would affect their towns. But the plan would not close any schools. Under the plan, the new school board could not close a school without town approval, according to a presentation from Zboray’s district.
The merger needs majority approval in Bar Harbor, Mount Desert, Southwest Harbor, Tremont and Trenton. Voters in the outer island towns of Cranberry Isles, Frenchboro and Swan’s Island will also weigh in, and each would join the new RSU only if its own voters approve.
Another part of rural Maine is considering withdrawing from its school district. Buckfield, Hartford, and Sumner will vote on whether to secede from the Rumford-based RSU 10 over concerns about losing local control since the district formed in 2009.
Voters in Strong are debating a school district withdrawal as well. Some locals said withdrawing from a Phillips-based district could help protect their local school from being closed.
Other towns are considering closing a school outright. Small class sizes have stretched budgets statewide, and some communities have been willing to give up a local school in exchange for tax relief.
At least two towns, Eddington and Waterford, will decide this November whether to make that trade. Both towns’ ballots will list the estimated annual cost of keeping the school open. That cost is nearly $670,000 for Eddington’s elementary school and about $442,000 for Waterford’s.
Fire
Voters in Caribou and China will decide whether to allow their municipalities to buy pricey new fire trucks. Tariffs, industry consolidation and regulations have driven the cost of new fire trucks up to well over $1 million in some cases, squeezing Maine taxpayers.
Caribou voters will decide whether to allow the city to spend up to $2.9 million to replace its aging aerial ladder truck.
“The city’s current ladder truck has served the city well for many years but has reached the end of its serviceable life,” a statement on the city’s ballot reads.
China voters are considering allowing a smaller expenditure: $750,000 for a new fire apparatus. Residents approved a $200,000 allocation at China’s June town meeting.
Meeting recordings
Two towns, Alfred and Limerick, will vote on whether to begin recording local government meetings. Recordings are common across Maine’s larger towns, but it took a citizens’ petition in Alfred to bring the option to a public vote. The town’s budget committee has estimated that recordings will require nearly $6,000.
If passed, recordings will be made of future annual town meetings, select board, planning board and zoning board meetings. The proposal in Limerick would require the town to stream or broadcast most public meetings.
Daniel O’Connor is a Report for America corps member who covers rural government as part of the partnership between the Bangor Daily News and The Maine Monitor, with additional support from BDN and Monitor readers.

title: Taking time to make time: Four years in retrospect
text:
Some days, as I walk along the familiar paths and take in the well-worn sights of campus, I find myself thinking, “Only two months left.” This thought circulates through my mind relentlessly as I stumble blindly into the midpoint of my final semester. I’ve spent years telling myself that this was what I’d been wanting, that life would really start and everything I’ve been missing would surely fall into place as I finish my time here at the University of Maine.
It’s funny how something like a graduation seems impossibly far away until the moment comes and you find yourself staring down the barrel of the rest of your life. In my first two years here, I spent so little time looking around. All I could think about was the future, the apartment I didn’t have, the classes I couldn’t yet take and the friendships I was waiting to find. When I talk to friends and family who are just beginning their time in college, I sometimes hear that same sense of impatient dissatisfaction in their voices. It is so easy to be cynical when you’re certain there are many great things to come, yet it is so difficult to place stock in the irreplaceable charm of a new beginning.
In the imagination of my adolescence, four years seemed to stretch out as both a lifetime and nothing at all. During my first fall in Orono, despite my best efforts, I could hardly have imagined what my life would look like now. Leaving seemed to be such a distant prospect I was almost certain it would never come. In that sense of perceived permanence, it is easy to let the burden of action fall upon the uncertain future. You let yourself put off joining that club, finding that internship or befriending the interesting strangers you see on campus. When you’re sure there is always more time, taking action feels unnecessary. This may sound like bogus advice from someone who can barely legally drink, yet these are the things I wish I could’ve appreciated a mere three years ago.
I have always found myself itching for a “purpose,” for a new home, a new state, a new job and a new outlook on life, yet it wasn’t until my junior year that something started to click. I remember looking around my apartment and seeing the faces of many people, people I care deeply about. I saw animated conversations, heads tilted back in laughter, music, wild gesticulations and a sense of living jubilation which permeated throughout that room.
Through whatever twists of fate, coincidence and chance, life had occurred such that these people were my people. They were people from all walks of life, all different and strange in their own ways. These were people whose doors I could knock on at any hour and feel welcome. In the throes of a life built around schoolwork, little else seems to matter more than holding close the friendships that we foster in the fictitious pseudoreality of the university setting. Often full of arbitrary stress and seemingly menial work, it was on that night that I truly knew that we subsisted off of the ties we hold to one another. What will really matter a decade down the line was in that room.
So now, as I face an uncertain future, I find myself holding onto these small moments. I find myself wondering if fate will grant me another community like this one, if I will find satisfaction, camaraderie and a purpose that can last a lifetime. I have no answers, yet I know that what I have now is something worth appreciating, and there would be nothing more tragic than realizing that too late.

title: Economic impact study reveals growing list of challenges
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
COURTESY OF THE PROFESSIONAL LOGGING CONTRACTORS (PLC) OF THE NORTHEAST
In late February, the Professional Logging Contractors of the Northeast (PLC) released results of a comprehensive study of the economic impact of Northeast logging and forest trucking, showing the industry contributed an estimated $1.3 billion to the regional economy in 2024.
The study, The Economic Contribution of Logging and Trucking in the Northeast, conducted by Wallace Economic Advisers, LLC, also revealed that in 2024 logging and forest trucking supported approximately 10,543 Northeast jobs either directly or indirectly, generated $393 million in labor income, pumped an estimated $61 million into state and local tax coffers, and remained critical to a range of industries and communities across the region.
At the same time, the study showed the industry is facing an ever-mounting list of challenges that threaten its future, including loss of markets and market uncertainty, rising costs, shrinking profits, worker shortages, and lack of succession planning.
“This is the first truly regional impact study of its kind for the logging and forest trucking industry, and it clearly demonstrates both the immense importance of the industry to the Northeast, and the very real possibility that the industry has reached a breaking point,” Dana Doran, Executive Director of the Professional Logging Contractors of the Northeast, said. “The forest economy of the Northeast is built on a foundation provided by loggers and truckers, and anything that threatens that foundation threatens the entire sector, with dire consequences for the region.”
The study looked at the Northeast region as a whole and also included state by state breakdowns of the data. Maine leads the region in logging output followed by New York, New Hampshire, and Vermont. The impact of the industry in other states in the region is smaller but still significant. Numbers by state for 2024 included:
Maine: 2,744 direct logging and trucking jobs, along with an additional 1,715 indirect jobs, for a total of about 4,460 jobs statewide. Total economic output from logging and trucking reached approximately $534 million, the highest in the region, including $283 million in total labor earnings, and generated an estimated $23 million in state tax revenues. 
New York: 1,911 direct logging and trucking jobs, along with an additional 500 indirect jobs, for a total of about 2,411 jobs statewide. Total economic output from logging and trucking reached approximately $280 million, including $140 million in total labor earnings, and generated an estimated $19 million in state tax revenues. 
New Hampshire: 804 direct logging and trucking jobs, along with an additional 700 indirect jobs, for a total of about 1,504 jobs statewide. Total economic output from logging and trucking reached approximately $243 million, including $94 million in total labor earnings, and generated an estimated $6 million in state tax revenues. 
Vermont: 800 direct logging and trucking jobs, along with an additional 500 indirect jobs across the state. Total economic output ranked fourth in the Northeast at approximately $140 million, including $75 million in labor earnings, and generated an estimated $9 million in state tax revenues. 
Massachusetts: 440 direct logging and trucking jobs, along with an additional 124 indirect jobs, for a total of about 564 jobs statewide. Total economic output from logging and trucking reached approximately $72 million, including $34 million in total labor earnings, and generated an estimated $3.3 million in state tax revenues. 
Connecticut:208 direct logging and trucking jobs, along with an additional 72 indirect jobs, for a total of about 279 jobs statewide. Total economic output from logging and trucking reached approximately $39 million, including $17 million in total labor earnings, and generated an estimated $1.7 million in state tax revenues. 
Rhode Island: 40 direct logging and trucking jobs, along with an additional 24 indirect and induced jobs, for a total of about 64 jobs statewide. Total economic output from logging and trucking reached approximately $8 million, including $2 million in total labor earnings, and generated an estimated $200,000 in state tax revenues. 
The study revealed loggers throughout the region are facing many of the same challenges, but they vary in severity depending on location. Loss of markets — particularly low-grade wood markets — was seen as the top threat to the industry by contractors, and only 14 percent of those surveyed believe there are sufficient markets to sell wood. Other threats included the rapid escalation of operating costs relative to stagnant or declining stumpage and delivered-wood rates, rising equipment prices, and an aging workforce with too few new workers.
The study also highlighted important trends in the industry including a shift toward more cut-to-length logging equipment (47%) versus whole-tree (43%) being utilized by logging contractors. Only 11% of contractors continue to fell trees with chainsaws.
In general, the study revealed the size of logging firms has been declining in recent years. In 2024, respondents reported an average employment total of nine workers, with more than half (52%) working in the woods, three in trucking, and the remaining two working in administrative support or as mechanics. This is less than half the average of 22 workers found in 2014.
The study was conducted in the second half of 2025 and included analysis relying on the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis’ Regional Input–Output Modeling System (RIMS II), a widely used framework for estimating the total effects of economic activity within a defined region. It also included a survey of 140 logging and trucking firms across the Northeast to build a more comprehensive picture of the industry’s status and impact.
Three similar studies have been conducted by the PLC for the state of Maine only, focusing on 2014, 2017, and 2021 data. The new study’s focus on the entire Northeast region is the first attempt to capture what is happening across states including Maine, New York, New Hampshire, Vermont, Massachusetts, Connecticut, and Rhode Island.

title: The Harold Alfond Center for the Advancement of Maine’s Workforce: Short-term training through Maine’s community colleges
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Building Maine’s Talent Pipeline
The Harold Alfond Center for the Advancement of Maine’s Workforce manufactures opportunity. Operating through the Maine Community College System, the Center exists to close the gap between what Maine employers need and who’s available to fill those roles. Its output is measured in industry-recognized credentials, apprenticeships launched, and employer partnerships forged across the state.
The Center functions as the short-term training division of Maine’s community colleges. Employers identify the skills they need, and the colleges build the training that gets people into those jobs — often in a matter of weeks, in fields ranging from medical assisting and EMTs to welding, advanced manufacturing and precision machining, to skilled trades and construction. For many Mainers, that fast, employer-driven credential is just the first step: the colleges’ academic associate degree and certificate programs offer a natural next step, letting workers apply a short-term credential toward a two-year degree and a longer-term career, without starting over at square one.
That mission carries real economic weight. Maine’s labor market is tight, and industries from healthcare to manufacturing report the same challenge: not enough trained workers to fill open positions. The Center was created to mitigate that shortage directly, funding and coordinating programs that move Mainers from unemployed or underemployed into skilled, in-demand careers, and keeping that talent here in Maine. The Center is on track to serve one in seven Mainers in the workforce by 2030.
But the Center isn’t limited to bringing new workers into the pipeline. It’s also focused on keeping current employees growing within it. Through the Maine Workforce Development Compact, employers across the state gain access to training and development resources for their existing workforce. From technical upskilling to leadership development, employers can access up to $1,200 per frontline worker per year to help retain talent, promote from within, and adapt as job requirements shift.
None of this happens in a vacuum. Every pre-hire program, academic pathway, and Compact offering exists because an employer identified a specific skill gap, and that demand-driven design is what makes the model work. It depends heavily on the Center’s education partnerships: Maine’s community colleges serve as delivery partners statewide, connecting workers to pathways like the Alfond Workforce Scholarship, apprenticeships, and industry-recognized certifications. The Center also helped launch Maine’s Workforce Pell program with the Maine Department of Labor, opening federal financial aid to short-term, non-degree training for the first time.
Looking ahead, the next phase is deepening employer and partner collaboration, expanding the list of credentials, serving industry, and making sure every Maine employer, whether hiring or developing the team it already has, has a clear, fast route to the skills it needs.
For a state where workforce shortages touch nearly every industry, the Center’s bet is straightforward: build the pipeline, and Maine’s economy follows.

title: Shooting near Ohio mosque leaves 1 dead but was not connected to the building, police say
text:
COLUMBUS, Ohio (AP) — A shooting in a neighborhood near a mosque in Ohio’s capital city left one person dead Monday but was not connected to the house of worship or those who were inside, police said.
Federal and local authorities descended on the area as the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives said in a post on X that agents were responding to a report of a shooting at the mosque, northeast of downtown Columbus.
Police later said the shooting happened in the parking lot of an apartment complex next to the mosque.
“At the mosque, unfortunately, there was an event going on that had nothing to do with what was going on outside,” said Sgt. James Fuqua. “… But it’s super important that I make it clear that this shooting had nothing to do with an attack on the mosque itself.”
The ATF did not immediately respond to a phone message seeking further information.

title: ‘This can’t keep happening’: Mother calls for more security after son shot twice at same apartment complex
text:
ATLANTA (Atlanta News First/Gray News) — An Atlanta mother is calling for increased security at her apartment complex after her 13-year-old son survived his second shooting there in a year.
“This can’t keep happening,” Shantavia Battle said.
Teen shot while sleeping
Battle said her son was shot four times while sleeping inside their apartment at Capitol Vanira on Hank Aaron Drive on Sunday.
Detectives said the apartment was targeted, with more than 100 shots fired into the unit.
Battle described scrambling to get her family to safety as the gunfire erupted.
“You could hear three different shots, so I told everybody to get on the floor and everybody come into the bathroom,” she said.
Battle’s son has since been released from the hospital and is expected to recover, but she said families at the southeast Atlanta complex need more protection.
“We don’t have security. We don’t have anybody. We don’t have anyone to help us, and it doesn’t make sense,” she said.
Second shooting in a year
The shooting comes about a year after the same boy, then 12, was injured in a drive-by shooting at the complex. Three other boys were also wounded in that shooting.
“I just heard the shots. ‘Dot, dot, dot, dot, dot!’ I hit the ground,” neighbor Robert Jackson said following last year’s shooting.
Atlanta police brought a mobile surveillance unit to the property after that incident. The unit remains in the parking lot, but Battle said it is not enough.
“My baby just went through this a year ago,” she said.
Police response pending
Atlanta News First has contacted Atlanta police to ask whether the department plans to increase patrols at the complex. A response was pending at the time of publication.
Police have not named a suspect or released a motive in Sunday’s shooting.

title: Letter to the Editor: Supporting Trevor Doiron
Meet a man keeping accordion tradition alive through repair and performance
text:
MONTPELIER, Vt. (Aging Untold) — Nathan Longo plays an Italian accordion from the early 1960s, an instrument he said he plays most often.
Longo said performing in front of people gives him stage fright.
Small workshop, growing demand
Longo repairs accordions in a small workshop. He said he is better at fixing the instruments than playing them.
He is one of a handful of people who repair accordions in New England.
“I’m a lot busier than I ever thought I would be,” Longo said.
What began as something to do in retirement has turned into a 30-hour-a-week job.
“There really are more people that are interested in accordion than I ever thought,” Longo said.
Growing up with dyslexia
Longo grew up in Orange County and said he liked to tinker with things.
“It bothers me when something doesn’t work right,” Longo said.
He said he struggled in school as a child and teachers thought he was slow.
“I mean, it took forever for them to teach me how to write my name,” Longo said.
Longo said nobody knew about dyslexia at the time, and he had a poor self-image during that period.
He completed high school and discovered he had a talent for fixing cars. Longo attributed the skill to being dyslexic.
“Dyslexics have a really good three-dimensional visualization,” Longo said.
Longo later made prototypes for high-end machinery in Massachusetts.
From machinery to music
Around age 50, Longo started playing the accordion as a way to keep his brain active.
“Whatever you can, to just stay in the present,” Longo said.

title: ‘Office Space’ actor Richard Riehle dies at 78

(Gray News) — Actor Richard Riehle died Thursday in Los Angeles at age 78.

title: 9 Maine events include ‘Cabaret’ in Auburn and Ogunquitfest
text:
7:30 p.m. Thursday-Saturday, 2 p.m. Sunday. Community Little Theatre, 30 Academy St., Auburn, $25, $22 seniors and students, $17 for 13 and under. laclt.com.
Put down the knitting, the book and the broom and head to Auburn for L/A Community Little Theatre’s production of the Tony Award-winning musical “Cabaret.” Set in a 1920s Berlin nightclub, “Cabaret” delves into the the lives of some locals and expatriates as the Third Reich starts to emerge in Germany. Young American writer Cliff falls for English singer Sally Bowles. At the same time, Fräulein Schneider, owner of Cliff and Sally’s boarding house, sparks up a romance with Herr Schultz, a mild-mannered, Jewish fruit seller. Musical numbers include “Willkommen,” “Don’t Tell Mama” and the always enchanting title song.

During every performance of “La Noce D’Alfonse,” a couple in the audience is spotlighted through a special segment featuring aerial straps, roller skating, juggling, tightwire, swing dancing and other flashy displays. With an homage to Québécois folk traditions, you’ll hear music that merges vintage and contemporary sounds into a live, joyful soundtrack.

Barril drums will provide the rhythmic foundation while dancers spin about the stage. You’ll also learn about the history of Afro-Puerto Rican culture.

Enjoy a rich evening of music and spoken word while supporting the Immigrant Legal Advocacy Project, which provides free statewide immigration legal services to low-income people, along with community education and advocacy. Some of the proceeds will also help presenting artists who have been impacted by recent immigration activity. The show features performances by Pihcintu Multi National Girls Choir, Madeleine Hanna and the Jawahir Arabic Music Ensemble, Somalian oud player and singer Hadithi Abdulle, Franco-American poet Jeri Thériault, poet Richard Blanco (via video) and the Singing Resistance groups of Portland and Brunswick/Topsham. Brunswick comic Mohamed Awale will be hosting. Signed poems donated by Richard Blanco will be available for purchase.

title: Windham teacher receives grant for ‘Drones Not Drugs’ program
text:
Jason Lanoie, a STEM teacher at Windham Middle School, discussed his plans for a STEM-based anti-drug unit after receiving a grant of nearly $2,500 from the town of Windham.
In his application for the town of Windham’s substance abuse prevention grant program, Lanoie said he wanted to show how learning about flying and coding drones was a healthy alternative to using drugs or other addictive substances.
Lanoie said that the growing amount of dispensaries in the Windham area sends a message that drug use is “acceptable” to young people, and he wants to make sure they know there are healthier options.
Currently, the class is set to use four small drones, two donated by the Perloff Family Foundation, one acquired through DonorsChoose, and another purchased with the school budget. Lanoie said that, as part of the anti-drug program, he would like to work with the school resource officer to show off Windham Police Department drones and discuss their use in cracking down on illegal drug operations. Long-term, Lanoie said his goal is to reach a 2:1 ratio of students to drones.
Lanoie spoke extensively about his work with the Perloff Family Foundation for more than a decade, an organization promoting STEM programs throughout Maine. Lanoie has collaborated with them on units focused on air rockets and LEGO robotics, as well as receiving multiple 3D printers from the foundation.
Lanoie will run a Perloff-backed teacher workshop in November, with 15 teachers in southern Maine working with 3D-printed rockets and drones.
Lanoie also has plans for how the drone program will be implemented once Windham Middle School merges with Jordan Small Middle School in Raymond next school year. He hopes to involve fellow STEM teachers Brian Casey and Jen Beaulieu, who currently work at WMS and JSMS respectively, in the project once the new middle school opens, with the hope of establishing a coding and robotics curriculum covering three of the new middle school’s four grades, with drones being studied by seventh graders and up.
Drones Not Drugs was one of two robotics-based grant applications discussed by the Windham Substance Prevention Grant Committee at its Oct. 6 meeting. Drones Not Drugs was approved for its full $2,490 application, with the disbursement made official when the Town Council voted unanimously in favor on Oct. 13.

title: Jean M. Howe
text:
Jean M. Howe, passed away peacefully on Oct. 14, 2026, at the Lincoln Home in Newcastle, Maine, in the company of her loving family and friends just a week shy of her 97th birthday.
Jean was born in Melrose, Massachusetts, on Oct. 23, 1929, to Wirt and Madge (Tuell) McKenney. She graduated from Melrose High School in 1947 and from Boston Business School in 1948.
Jean was a lifelong learner whose boundless curiosity about the world around her shaped her life and passions. A respected ornithologist and botanist, Jean had extraordinary knowledge of the intricate workings of nature. Her expertise and dedication earned her a fellowship in the Josselyn Botanical Society, and she played an instrumental role in the creation of the Coastal Maine Botanical Gardens in Boothbay. There, she enthusiastically shared her knowledge with visitors, fostering a deeper appreciation for the beauty and diversity of the environment. A woman of conviction and action, Jean was a passionate advocate for civil rights, wildlife conservation, and the preservation of the Earth she so dearly loved. Throughout her life, she inspired others not only through her knowledge, but also through her unwavering commitment to protecting the beauty and integrity of the natural world.
A gifted musician, Jean shared her talents generously throughout her life. She studied voice at the New England Conservatory and later sang and played the piano for numerous church congregations, choruses, choirs and jazz ensembles across New England. Her beautiful voice also earned her the extraordinary opportunity to sing with the New York Philharmonic during the 1960s under the direction of the legendary Leonard Bernstein.
On Oct. 3, 1953, Jean married the love of her life, Lemuel Herbert “Bert” Howe. Together, they built a life rooted in family, faith, community, and a shared commitment to serving others. Jean carried this spirit of service throughout her life, generously devoting her time, talents, and boundless energy to the causes and organizations she held dear. She served as director of religious education at the Unitarian Universalist Church in Haverhill, Massachusetts, and as director of the New England Music Festival. An active and dedicated member of every community she called home, Jean willingly lent her leadership and expertise to countless boards of directors, always finding room for one more worthy cause.
Jean was predeceased by her husband, Lemuel “Bert” Howe and grandson, Andrew Goupil.
She leaves behind a loving family who will cherish her memory: her son Benjamin Howe of Portsmouth, New Hampshire; her son James Howe and his wife, Karen, of North Yarmouth, Maine; her son Brian Howe and his wife, Diane, of Boothbay Harbor, Maine; and her daughter Jocelyn Howe of Dresden, Maine. She is also survived by five grandchildren: Jaime Cesar of Framingham, Massachusetts; Joshua Howe of Kennebunk, Maine; Morgan Howe of Clinton, Massachusetts; Christopher Apollonio of Titusville, Florida; Laura Howe of Bozeman, Montana, and three great-grandchildren as well as many beloved nieces, nephews, cousins and friends.
Jean’s life was a testament to the rewards of a curious mind, a generous spirit, a love of music, and a deep appreciation for the natural world. She leaves behind a legacy that will live on in the family she cherished, the communities she served, and the many people whose lives she enriched.
At Jean’s request, she will be laid to rest at Cedar Brook Burial Ground in Limington, Maine.
In lieu of flowers, tribute gifts in Jean’s name may be made to Maine Audubon in support of its work to protect Maine’s wildlife and natural habitats: https://maineaudubon.org/support/give/
Arrangements are entrusted to Hall Funeral Home and Crematory, 975 Wiscasset Road, Boothbay.

title: Brewers-Rays will produce a first-time champion, and maybe the first all-indoor World Series
Kenneth Nelson Spear Sr.
text:
Kenneth Nelson Spear Sr., of Cushing, devoted husband, loving father, and grandfather, went home to be with his lord and savior Jesus Christ on Friday, Oct. 9, 2026.
Ken was born in Damariscotta on Aug. 4, 1946 to parents Kenneth E. and Bernice Spear. Growing up in Midcoast Maine, he grew his love for the sea as he harvested clams and lobsters in the St. George River.
He met the love of his life, Patricia E. Spear, in 1963 as a sophomore at Georges Valley High School. One of her fondest memories is him flicking the bobby pins out of her hair with his pencil while he sat behind her in English class. The high school sweethearts graduated from GVHS in the class of 1965 and celebrated 60 years of marriage on Sept. 11, 2026.
Drafted into the U.S. Army Engineering Corps following graduation, the young couple moved to South Carolina, where they began their family. Ken continued his military service for 36 years in the Maine Army National Guard, reaching the rank of E8 master sergeant.
Though he enjoyed his work as a foreman at Fisher Engineering, he left this position in 1985 to pursue his true passion being a commercial fisherman. He built the F/V Patti E and spent the rest of his career in several fisheries including lobstering and shrimping. He passed down this passion to his sons and grandchildren, who have spent countless hours building lobster boats and hauling traps with him.
In 1988, Ken accepted Christ as his savior at Calvary Baptist Church in Warren. He continued to serve in leadership positions and on building project committees for many years.
Ken lived a full life because he found it hard to sit still much, unless he was offered a game of cribbage, which he most often won. An avid outdoorsman, he enjoyed hunting and fishing with family, especially at their camp on Moxie Pond. Buddy, his beagle, was always at his side. Ken was a man faithful to his God, his family, and his country and we treasure the gift of sharing life with him.
Ken was preceded in death by both parents; son, Kevin E. Spear; brother, Albert J. Spear; grandson, Daniel N. Spear; and many close friends.
He is survived by his beloved wife, Patricia E. Spear, of Cushing; sons and daughters-in-love, Kenneth N. Spear Jr. and Dorie Spear, of Cushing, Dwayne and Dianna Spear, of Brazil, Thomas and Nancy Spear, of Cushing, Daren and Kim Spear, of Cushing; 17 grandchildren and 12 great-grandchildren; sister, Alberta Spear; and many extended family members.
There will be a celebration of Ken’s life at Calvary Baptist Church, at 185 Atlantic Highway in Warren, on Friday, Oct. 23, 2026 at 11 a.m., followed by a committal service with military honors for immediate family members in Cushing.
Arrangements are under the care and direction of Hall Funeral Home of Waldoboro. To extend a condolence or share a story with the Spear family, please visit Ken’s book of memories at hallfuneralhomes.com.

title: Susan Collins’ math doesn’t add up
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Need some straight data on why it’s time to vote Sen. Susan Collins out? The senator takes credit for bringing money to Maine, but the math doesn’t work.
Her one vote allowing the “big, beautiful bill” is estimated to cost Maine a projected $4.125 billion in cuts over 10 years. Compare that to the $3.45 billion she claims to have brought in over 10 years and we get a loss of $675 million. She could have stopped it. She’s playing us, and it’s costing lives. The real costs of that legislation start in January.
Add on the rising costs of the Iran war, heating oil, gasoline, groceries, health insurance, tariffs and devastating hospital closures from her Trump support, and Troy Jackson is the common- sense choice.
Martha White
Rockport

title: 3rd Annual Mid Mall Trunk or Treat returns Friday with family fun, community partnerships, support for Sarah’s House
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
More than 1,000 attendees expected for a free Halloween celebration featuring local businesses, food trucks, entertainment and an opportunity to give back.
BANGOR – The Mid Mall business community is gearing up for one of the area’s anticipated Halloween celebrations! The 3rd Annual Mid Mall Trunk or Treat will take place from 5 to 7 p.m. on Friday, Oct. 23 in the Mid Mall area of Bangor, bringing together dozens of local businesses and organizations for an evening of Halloween fun, community connection and charitable giving.
With more than 1,000 attendees anticipated, the event promises an exciting evening for families, featuring creatively decorated trunks, plenty of candy, food trucks, music, entertainment and activities for children of all ages.
Organized through the efforts of FYZICAL Therapy & Balance Centers and neighboring Mid Mall businesses, the event has continued to grow, attracting participation from businesses and community organizations throughout the Greater Bangor region.
“What started as an opportunity for neighboring businesses to come together and do something fun for local families has really grown into something special,” Benjamin Smith, director of HR & Marketing for FYZICAL Therapy & Balance Centers and event organizer, said. “One of my favorite things about this event is seeing businesses that might otherwise never cross paths come together for a common purpose. Everyone puts their own creative spin on their trunk, the kids have an absolute blast and we get to create a fun, safe and memorable evening for families in our community. We’re expecting our biggest turnout yet, and I couldn’t be more excited!”
This year’s event will also shine a spotlight on Sarah’s House, a local nonprofit organization that provides temporary lodging and a supportive home-away-from-home environment for cancer patients and their caregivers who must travel to the Bangor area for treatment.
Representatives from Sarah’s House will be on-site collecting much-needed items from the organization’s wish list. Attendees are encouraged to bring a donation to help support the important work Sarah’s House does for individuals and families navigating cancer treatment.
In addition, Darling’s Ice Cream Truck for a Cause will be participating, helping raise funds for Sarah’s House while serving up sweet treats during the festivities.
“We wanted this event to be about more than just candy and costumes,” Smith added. “Sarah’s House does incredible work for people during some of the most challenging times in their lives. Being able to introduce more families to their mission, collect needed supplies and help support their work adds a whole other level of meaning to this event. It’s a great example of what can happen when our business community comes together.”
In addition to dozens of decorated trunks and candy stations, attendees can look forward to: Free balloon creations from Rea’s Balloon Creations.
Music and entertainment from an on-site DJ.
Children’s activities with the help of the John Bapst Key Club student volunteers.
Food and refreshments available for purchase from Brick & Embers Pizza, Del’s Lemonade, The Spud Bus, Rizza’s Kitchen, Brush & Batter Bakery and Darling’s Ice Cream Truck.
Creative Halloween displays and festive decorations throughout the event area.
Opportunities to connect with local businesses, nonprofits and community organizations.
Participating businesses and organizations represent a wide variety of industries, from healthcare and professional services to restaurants, real estate and community nonprofits.
The event is free and open to the public, and families are encouraged to come dressed in their favorite Halloween costumes and bring a bag for collecting candy.
Event details
What: 3rd Annual Mid Mall Trunk or Treat
When: Friday, Oct. 23
Time: 5–7 p.m.
Where: Mid Mall area, Bangor, Maine (near FYZICAL Therapy & Balance Centers, 31 Bangor Mall Boulevard) Admission: Free and open to the public
Special community partner: Sarah’s House of Maine
For event updates, participating businesses, and information about Sarah’s House’s wish list, families are encouraged to visit the 3rd Annual Mid Mall Trunk or Treat Facebook event page.

title: This Little-Traveled Maine Road is the Most Haunted in the US
text:
Maine is home to some of the most-chilling ghost stories in the United States.
No, we're not talking about the novels that Maine's Stephen King has penned over the last five decades. Nope. We're talking about real ghost stories.
Some of the most well known Maine ghost stories include the haunted dorms at the University of Southern Maine, the haunting of Skowhegan's Strand Theater, and the haunting of Bucksport's Fort Knox.
👇Scroll down for a list of terrifying Maine ghost stories
Did you know that Maine is home to the most haunted road in the United States?
The Haunting of Maine's Route 2A
According to the Discover Cars website, Route 2A in Maine is the most haunted road in the United States. The winding road, an offshoot of Route 2, runs through an extremely rural section of Aroostook County.
The website explains that this stretch of road is rumored to be haunted by several ghosts. Drivers have reported seeing a woman in white, believed to be a bride killed alongside her husband in a crash on their wedding night. Legend says she wanders the roadside, searching for her lost love.
Two young girls are also said to haunt the area, appearing and disappearing into thin air. Their spirits are believed to belong to two girls who were fatally struck by a truck on the road in 1967. Witnesses describe an overwhelming sense of dread and sadness in the surrounding woodlands.
As a teen I spent a summer as an escort driver for a company moving mobile homes. Because it lacked the low overpasses of the I-95, we occasionally took that road when delivering single-wides or double-wides. While I believe in the ghost stories, I personally never witnessed anything while driving on the road.
Have you ever experienced something strange on this road? Tell us your story.
