title: A ‘purrfect’ ending: Cat missing for 571 days reunites with family
text:
GREENWICH, Conn. (WABC) - A Connecticut family is whole again after reuniting with their beloved cat who had been missing for 571 days.
Kelly Moore’s daughter adopted Turtle, a stray Nebelung cat from Tennessee. He lived with Moore in Greenwich, had been microchipped and had an ear tip indicating he’d been neutered. But one day in March 2025, Turtle disappeared.
“I was rushing out so fast I startled him, and he ran,” Moore said. “I love him so much, and it was just a comedy of errors.”
Moore turned to Rocket Lost Pet Rescue for help after Turtle went missing. Founder Rocco Autero set up cameras near the family’s home to determine whether the cat was still in the area.
“And he was actually. He was showing up. He came by here every night. We caught him on video… but he was afraid of cages,” Autero said.
The sightings of Turtle eventually stopped, leaving Moore fearing the worst.
“I cried so many nights, and I felt responsible because not being aware of the storm door. We were really brokenhearted,” she said.
The big breakthrough came just recently when someone posted on social media about finding a cat in Mamaroneck, New York, about 10 miles from Greenwich, Connecticut. Autero saw the post and had a hunch that cat might be Turtle.
“It’s shocking that he was found, and he traveled a long distance, a lot further than we’ve seen many cats go,” Autero said.
The cat’s microchip ultimately confirmed his identity. It took some cajoling to coax Turtle into a carrier, but he made the trip back home to his family in Greenwich.
“If this can happen, anything can happen. It’s so wonderful, and I’m so happy to have him back,” Moore said.

title: Trump says ‘France is burning.’ What sparked violent protests, 550K marchers and 2,400 arrests
text:
PARIS (AP) — French President Emmanuel Macron on Sunday voiced the public’s “anger” and “shame” over rioting and looting during nationwide protests against rising living costs and poor conditions in schools. At least 2,400 people were arrested.
Macron echoed other government officials in blaming much of the violence on far-left activists, accusing them of attacking police and public buildings to foment chaos.
“Those who looted will have to pay for the damage, and those who sought to bring down the Republic will be held accountable,” Macron said in a televised address to the nation.
He denounced “unrestrained violence” by “insurrectionist elements from radical far-left groups, joined by numerous criminals.”
Macron earlier held an emergency meeting with senior government officials, a day after masked groups set fires and attacked city halls in several cities. He said he had instructed prefects to work with mayors to protect public buildings and businesses in the coming weeks, including by banning protests when necessary.
Flames engulfed the 19th-century City Hall in the city of Limoges, in central France, causing its roof to collapse and nearly destroying the building.
New tensions erupted in Paris on Sunday
In Paris, hundreds of protesters gathered again on Sunday at the Place de la République amid a heavy police presence. Officers used tear gas as tensions flared sporadically in the neighborhood, with small groups of people trying to set bicycles and trash bins on fire.
“The right to protest is a fundamental right. Deliberately and collectively sowing disorder through violence is not,” Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez wrote on X, citing the looting of hundreds of businesses across the country.
Authorities estimated Saturday’s marches had a turnout of about 550,000, while organizers put it at 800,000. Demonstrators answered calls from a labor union, student organizations and activists hoping to revive the “yellow vest” movement, which emerged in 2018 to protest social injustice.
Mass protests in France are often marred by violence on the fringes of otherwise peaceful marches, leading to clashes with police. The arrest tally reported Sunday approached the nearly 2,000 recorded nationwide during a single day of yellow vest protests in December 2018.
Paris police said one person died of a heart attack, without providing details. The Paris prosecutor’s office said it was investigating.
Parisians deplore shattered shops and a damaged square
Dislodged cobblestones, shattered storefronts and broken glass littered the area around Paris’ Place de la République on Sunday. Looting and damage were also reported in other tourist and shopping districts.
Paris police said 855 people were arrested in the capital region. Prosecutors said 557 remained in police custody.
“I am actually stunned by the level of destruction and violence that was expressed,” said government employee Marie Peyreigne, 57, wondering what had led to the mayhem.
Parisians inspecting the damage photographed the partially dismantled base of the square’s central monument, a statue of Marianne, a symbol of France.
Jean Foissy, 74, said he had wanted to join the protest but encountered “a wall of riot police and fires everywhere” and returned home.
“I was very scared,” he said. “I’ve been a Parisian since I was born, so when I got here, it almost made me want to cry because I find it so bad, it hurts me.”
Margaux Eude, 26, said she supported the protest movement but “didn’t think it would escalate like this.”
“It’s the troublemakers who came, and it breaks my heart because it delegitimizes the movement,” she said.
Political leaders trade blame ahead of presidential election
Political leaders traded accusations over Saturday’s violence ahead of next spring’s presidential election.
Far-right leader and presidential hopeful Marine Le Pen criticized Macron’s centrist government as “exhausted, disoriented and seemingly incapable of doing anything other than commenting on its own powerlessness,” in a video posted on social media.
Far-left contender Jean-Luc Mélenchon accused Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu of “playing with fire,” alleging that “by banking on degradation, you have only succeeded in uniting all youths and workers’ unions.”
Mélenchon, who joined the Paris march Saturday, insisted that “my message is clear: those who share our fight have no business in looting or destruction.”
U.S. President Donald Trump posted “France is burning!” on his Truth Social platform, apparently linking the unrest to “the immigration of people from an entirely different world.”
“Close your Borders and take control, before it is too late!” he wrote.
French authorities and police have not linked immigrants to the rioting. Macron, speaking about troublemakers, asked: “How can French people do this to France?”
Hundreds of businesses looted across the country
“The scale of the damage is considerable and unprecedented,” Paris Mayor Emmanuel Grégoire wrote in an open letter. “Paris is a city of freedoms, debate and demonstrations. It must remain so. But it must also be a city where everyone can work and run a business safely.”
The mayors of Paris, Marseille and Lyon, the three largest cities, requested a meeting with the prime minister in the coming days “given the extent of the damage and the seriousness of the situation.”
In Marseille, some protesters briefly forced their way into City Hall’s lobby and a group of people wearing hoods and masks damaged a police station. In Lyon, a fire broke out inside a tourist office.
In Limoges, the City Hall was ravaged by flames after “radical troublemakers” broke in while elected officials, employees, security personnel and members of the public were inside, Haute-Vienne prefect Maurice Barate said. “They deliberately set the building on fire. It is an extremely serious and unspeakable act,” he said.
In eastern France, the Mulhouse prosecutor’s office said an investigation has been opened after a 17-year-old girl was injured during the protests and lost an eye. On Saturday, another investigation was opened after a young protester lost a hand in Saint-Etienne.
The injuries come as police have drawn sharp scrutiny over their use of grenades and other riot-control weapons during recent demonstrations.

title: Maine head football coach Jordan Stevens reacts to 17-14 loss to Bryant on Saturday
text:
ORONO, Maine (WABI) - Maine football suffered its sixth loss in a row when it fell 17-14 to Bryant on Saturday.
Head coach Jordan Stevens spoke about how the defense stood up while the Black Bears’ offense turned the ball over.

But obviously, the turnovers are really the story of the game. I thought defensively, we really responded, which our defense has done all year, just responded in some really adverse situations,” said Stevens, head coach.
Maine’s homecoming game is Saturday at 1 p.m. against Campbell.

title: Stolen car filled with teenagers crashes into Sabattus pond
text:
Stolen car filled with teenagers crashes into Sabattus pond, police say
Police say a vehicle that crashed into Sabattus Pond in Sabattus early on Sunday morning had been stolen from Auburn and was filled with teenagers.
The Sabattus Police Department says several people called to report a vehicle driving recklessly and without lights on early Sunday morning. Officers say they saw the car go through a red light at the intersection of Pleasant Hill Road and Route 126.
A short time later, police say the driver lost control and crashed into the edge of the pond.
Police say there were seven teenagers as young as 13 inside the vehicle at the time. When officers arrived, they say two of the teens had run into the woods. They were found a short time later, with help from a police K9.
Police said no one was hurt but charges were pending in the case.

title: Father leaves 4-month-old baby alone in parked car to argue with baby’s mother at a bar, police say
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WSMV/Gray News) - A 4-month-old baby was left in a car over the weekend while his father went out to the popular bar area, Broadway, in downtown Nashville, according to Metro Nashville Police.
Jordan Hayley, 25, is accused of leaving his infant in the front seat of his running car while he went out to Jason Aldean’s Kitchen + Rooftop Bar.
Police were first alerted to the case Sunday when officers spotted Hayley arguing with a woman outside the bar.
“The female party was screaming at the defendant and he was also exchanging words with her,” police wrote in an affidavit. “Both were in each other’s faces.”
Officers broke up the dispute. When speaking with the woman, she told police she was upset because Hayley was supposed to be caring for their 4-month-old daughter, and she didn’t know where the child was.
“In short, she was worried about her child’s welfare,” the affidavit says.
Hayley told Metro Nashville Police the baby should be with her maternal grandmother, but the woman “denied that being possible,” according to arrest papers.
Police detained Hayley and took his car keys. They found his vehicle parked and running near the honky tonk bars on Broadway, an area “known to be heavily trafficked with disorderly and intoxicated individuals.”
In the front seat, the 4-month-old girl was found alone. The affidavit says she was in a baby seat facing the wrong direction.
The 25-year-old man was arrested, and the infant was reunited with her mother. Hayley is charged with leaving an unattended child in a motor vehicle and child neglect, per Davidson County court records.
His bond was set at $5,000 for the neglect charge and $1,500 for leaving the child in the car. Records show a judge is scheduled to review his case in court Friday morning.

title: ‘This can’t keep happening’: Mother calls for more security after son shot twice at same apartment complex
text:
ATLANTA (Atlanta News First/Gray News) — An Atlanta mother is calling for increased security at her apartment complex after her 13-year-old son survived his second shooting there in a year.
“This can’t keep happening,” Shantavia Battle said.
Teen shot while sleeping
Battle said her son was shot four times while sleeping inside their apartment at Capitol Vanira on Hank Aaron Drive on Sunday.
Detectives said the apartment was targeted, with more than 100 shots fired into the unit.
Battle described scrambling to get her family to safety as the gunfire erupted.
“You could hear three different shots, so I told everybody to get on the floor and everybody come into the bathroom,” she said.
Battle’s son has since been released from the hospital and is expected to recover, but she said families at the southeast Atlanta complex need more protection.
“We don’t have security. We don’t have anybody. We don’t have anyone to help us, and it doesn’t make sense,” she said.
Second shooting in a year
The shooting comes about a year after the same boy, then 12, was injured in a drive-by shooting at the complex. Three other boys were also wounded in that shooting.
“I just heard the shots. ‘Dot, dot, dot, dot, dot!’ I hit the ground,” neighbor Robert Jackson said following last year’s shooting.
Atlanta police brought a mobile surveillance unit to the property after that incident. The unit remains in the parking lot, but Battle said it is not enough.
“My baby just went through this a year ago,” she said.
Police response pending
Atlanta News First has contacted Atlanta police to ask whether the department plans to increase patrols at the complex. A response was pending at the time of publication.
Police have not named a suspect or released a motive in Sunday’s shooting.

title: Monday Five and Five: Tournament Time Is Almost Here
text:
Monday Five and Five: Big Performances and Tournament Time
We’ve reached that point of the fall season where everything starts moving pretty quickly.
There are only a few regular-season soccer games left, the tournament picture is almost set, and our cross country teams are getting ready for regional championship weekend.
Before we get there, though, there were plenty of performances from the past week worth another look.
Here are my five from last week, followed by five things I’ll be keeping an eye on this week.
Five From Last Week
5. Drew Lamoreau Scores Four for Easton
Drew Lamoreau had himself an afternoon Saturday.
Lamoreau scored four times as Easton picked up a 7-1 win over Southern Aroostook. Mason Pelletier added two goals, Aaden Tibbetts scored once and Josiah Ellis finished with two assists.
Four goals in one game is more than enough to earn a spot in this week’s Five and Five.
4. Fort Kent Gets It Done in Overtime
Fort Kent and Madawaska needed a little extra time Thursday before the Warriors came away with a 2-1 overtime win.
Madawaska has been one of the strongest teams in Class D North throughout the fall, making this a particularly good late-season win for Fort Kent.
With tournament soccer right around the corner, it was also the kind of game both teams should benefit from having played.
3. Two Hat Tricks and an Overtime Winner
If you like offense and close soccer games, Van Buren and Ashland gave us a good one.
Emily Lapierre scored three times for Van Buren, including the game-winner just 2:35 into overtime, as the Lady Crusaders pulled out a 4-3 victory.
Ashland’s Sadie Trams matched her with a hat trick of her own.
Seven goals, two hat tricks and overtime. That one pretty much had everything.
2. Ava Ezell Passes 150 Career Goals
Another week, another major milestone for Houlton’s Ava Ezell.
Ezell scored five goals and added three assists in Houlton’s 9-1 win over Schenck/Stearns, pushing her past 150 career goals.
Five goals and three assists would have been a huge afternoon by itself. Adding another career milestone makes it an easy choice for this week’s countdown.
1. Conor Schmidt Keeps Scoring
At this point, Conor Schmidt has become a regular part of the conversation.
The Katahdin standout scored five goals in a 6-1 win over Southern Aroostook, then scored both goals in a 2-0 victory over Wisdom.
Gage Phillips deserves some attention from that Wisdom game as well, finishing with 18 saves in the shutout.
For Schmidt, that’s seven more goals in two games after the huge numbers he put up the week before.
That earns him the No. 1 spot this week.
Five to Watch This Week
5. The Last Few Regular-Season Soccer Games
We’ve finally reached the end of the regular season.
There are still some important County matchups on the schedule Monday through Wednesday, and at this point every goal and every result can have an effect on where teams land when tournament play begins.
Fort Fairfield and Madawaska, Southern Aroostook and Central Aroostook, Van Buren and Easton, Ashland and Schenck/Stearns, and Presque Isle and Fort Kent are among the matchups worth following as teams put the finishing touches on their regular seasons.
4. Van Buren and Katahdin Meet Again
Here’s another game that could be interesting heading into tournament time.
Van Buren and Katahdin meet Monday on the boys side, with both teams looking to finish strong.
Van Buren has spent the season hanging around the middle of the North 8-Person tournament picture, while Katahdin has put together an 11-win season despite sitting lower in the standings than that record might suggest.
And with Schmidt scoring the way he has lately, Katahdin certainly isn’t a team anyone will want to overlook.
3. Fort Fairfield and Madawaska Close Things Out
Fort Fairfield and Madawaska meet Monday in what should be another good Class D doubleheader.
Both programs have been part of the tournament conversation throughout the season, and this gives them one more good test before everything becomes win-or-go-home.
At this point in October, that makes games like this worth paying attention to.
2. The Soccer Brackets Are Almost Here
This might be what I’m looking forward to most once the final whistles blow Wednesday.
We’ve spent the entire fall watching teams move up and down the standings, and now we’re about to find out where everyone actually lands.
Seeds, prelim matchups and possible tournament paths should all become much clearer this week.
That also means we’re getting very close to the part of the season where one goal, one save or one overtime winner can keep a season alive.
1. County Runners Head to the North Regionals
Soccer might be winding down, but cross country is moving right into championship season.
County runners head to Belfast Saturday for the North Regional Championships after another big showing at the PVC Championships.
Caribou’s boys, Presque Isle’s girls and Houlton/GHCA’s boys all head into the weekend after winning PVC team championships.
Pierce Gorneault and Emma Graves also arrive after earning individual PVC titles for Caribou.
Saturday is the next big test, with spots at the state championships on the line.
Here We Go
This is one of my favorite parts of the fall season.
The regular season is almost behind us, the brackets are coming, and championship meets are here.
We’ll have plenty to follow over the next several days as teams and athletes from across The County start chasing postseason hardware.

title: A history lesson on healthcare in Maine
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
In 2009, Democratic Gov. John Baldacci promised a $45 million payment on Maine’s $373 million debt to Maine hospitals. That payment did not happen until three years later in 2006.
When Baldacci left the Blaine House, he left a $484 million debt, which Republican Gov. Paul LePage paid off. Prior to this payment, the Maine hospitals were on the verge of financial failure. When Gov. LePage left office in 2019, the state had a financial surplus.
Jump ahead to Democratic Gov. Janet Mills. Almost half of birthing centers are closed and a number of hospitals as well. If Mainers think for a moment that the Democratic candidate Hannah Pingree is going to save our healthcare system, they need to look at history.
If people really think that socialized medicine is the answer, they should move to Canada.
Leo Mazerall Jr.
Stockton Springs

title: Students build device to help Gulf War veteran return to archery
text:
ANGOLA, Ind. (InvestigateTV) - A group of Trine University engineering students spent months designing a device to help a Navy veteran regain the ability to shoot a bow, after injuries left him without the use of his left arm.
Chester Evitt, a Navy veteran who served in the Gulf War, was shot in the arm during his service. A second injury three years ago worsened his condition.
“Because I’ve lost most of the use of my left arm, I can’t hold anything in it. I can’t shoot my bow,” Evitt said.
Evitt told his doctor at the VA about his problem with the bow. That conversation started a chain of events that eventually connected him with the Trine University engineering team through a program called Project S.E.R.V.E.
According to the organization’s website, Project S.E.R.V.E. aims to “improve the lives of veterans and emergency responders living with injuries or disabling conditions through student-led engineering projects.”
The Trine team’s work
Students Ava Dobbins, Cooper Clark, Andrea Mendoza and Jake Welker collaborated with Evitt virtually for months — Evitt from his home in Montana, the team from Trine University in Angola — before meeting in person for the first time this week at Thunder Lakes Guns Ammo and Archery in Angola.
The team worked through multiple designs before settling on a 3D-printed device that attaches to Evitt’s back to support the bow.
“It really needs to just hold it up for him and kind of be that skeleton that he can’t,” Welker said.
Welker said the project carried personal significance.
“The military runs very deep in my family, like most people from the Midwest, and it means a lot to me,” he said.
Testing the device
Evitt tested the device with the students present.
“Oh, my goodness,” Evitt said after the test. “Life-changing. They’re giving me back something that was took from me.”
Evitt also reflected on the bond he made with the students themselves.
“As a father that’s raised four kids, I’d be proud to call any one of them my own,” he said. “With all the negativity going on in the world, here’s a prime example of our future.”
The team has eight weeks to complete final adjustments before a formal presentation at Trine University.
Evitt said he plans to fly back from Montana once they’re finished and take the finished device home. He can’t wait to reclaim his passion for archery, something he says he first fell in love with at the age of eight.

title: Israeli police arrest 10 following weekend attacks on a journalist and diplomats
text:
Israeli police arrest 10 following weekend attacks on a journalist and diplomats
Israeli police said they arrested 10 people on Monday in connection with a wave of settler violence that included attacks on a foreign journalist and European diplomats in the occupied West Bank over the weekend.
Israel had come under heavy international criticism for the attacks. Israeli police did not identify the suspects or specify their roles in the attacks, which came during a spike in settler violence during the annual Palestinian olive harvest season.
On Friday, Washington Post photographer Heidi Levine was beaten by a crowd of young male settlers, leaving her with several broken ribs and vertebrae in the village of Abu Falah. She also underwent surgery on a finger that was nearly severed and is recovering from what appeared to be stab wounds to her lower body, which required stitches.
A day later, masked settlers attacked a group of European diplomats and others visiting the Christian village of Taybeh.
Settler violence has surged in recent years, and rights groups say that attackers are rarely arrested or punished for attacks on Palestinians.
From her hospital bed Sunday, Levine said she was “shocked and insulted” that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had cast doubt on the attack, which was witnessed by a crowd of people, by calling it “alleged.”
U.S. Ambassador Mike Huckabee condemned the attack as a “despicable act of terror carried out by masked cowards” and said they should spend years in prison. Israel's president and several opposition politicians also spoke out against the attack.
The attack on diplomats targeted Belgium's consul general, French and Polish diplomats and Catholic representatives.
“Impunity for violent settlers must end,” Belgian Foreign Minister Maxime Prevot said afterward.
Israeli police said they have been collecting evidence and witness statements since the weekend attacks. The suspects were transferred for questioning. Officials said the Shin Bet internal security agency, the paramilitary border police force and the Israeli military had all participated in the investigation.
Police said Monday’s operation also targeted people suspected of violating military orders declaring a closed military zone and offenses involving illegal construction. Officials said they seized several vehicles and items linking suspects to alleged offenses.

title: Professional Logging Contractors (PLC) of the Northeast Holds 31st Annual Meeting

text:
COURTESY OF THE PROFESSIONAL LOGGING CONTRACTORS (PLC) OF THE NORTHEAST
The Professional Logging Contractors (PLC) of the Northeast held its 31st Annual Meeting May 7-8, raising $134,610 for Log A Load For Kids and presenting awards to businesses and individuals from across Maine, Vermont, and New York for their contributions to the logging industry.
The meeting was held at the Samoset Resort in Rockport, with more than 200 people attending the main events on Friday. This was the third annual meeting of the PLC since its expansion in 2023 from a Maine organization to a regional one serving loggers and forest truckers across the Northeast.
The annual meeting is the PLC’s largest event and highlighted by the Log A Load for Kids Auction raising money for Children’s Miracle Network (CMN) which goes to hospitals in Maine, Vermont and New York. Families served by the hospitals were in attendance for the event, which also marked a major milestone — the PLC’s Log A Load efforts have now raised more than $3 million since 1995.
“This special group of people always steps up when it comes to supporting the kids and their families, and I am proud they came through once again in spite of the
difficult year the industry has had to help us reach the $3 million mark on total funds raised since this effort began more than three decades ago,” Dana Doran, Executive Director of the PLC, said. “No matter how tough things get, our members, supporters, and friends reach deep every year at our Log A Load for Kids Auction to support the children and families served by Children’s Miracle Network. I am so grateful for the generosity shown here, and I know the families and the hospitals are grateful as well.”
The Annual Meeting spanned two days, beginning Thursday with a tour of Vinalhaven island including stops at a wind farm, lighthouse, historic granite quarry, and a local brewery, and an evening social gathering at the Samoset Resort.
The second day began with a panel featuring candidates for Maine governor followed by a business meeting for all PLC Member contractors, with board and officer elections, and then a special presentation by Matt O’Malia of Timber HP that was also attended by Maine Governor Janet Mills.
The evening events included the traditional Log A Load for Kids Auction, dinner, and the PLC awards ceremony. PLC’s special guest for the evening, Maine native and two-time Olympic gold medalist Seth Wescott, took part in the auction and donated items for it.
Awards were presented to the following individuals and organizations during the evening portion of the event:
PLC Logger of the Year Awards: These awards recognize PLC Logging Contractors for their commitment to the sustainability of the industry and logging as a profession. This year for the third time the award went to two companies, one from Maine and one from Vermont. The winners are: Southwind Forestry of Pawlet, Vermont; and T. Condon Timber Harvesting of Ashland, Maine.
PLC Community Service Award: This award is given annually to a PLC member, Supporting Member or affiliated organization that has demonstrated a significant commitment to giving back to their community. The winner this year is: TNT Road Company Inc. of Fort Kent, Maine.
PLC Supporting Member Award: The PLC Supporting Member of the Year Award is presented annually to a PLC Supporting Member that has demonstrated an unprecedented commitment to logging contractors in Maine. The winner this year is: Pro Pac Industries of Saint-Côme–Linière, Quebec.
PLC President’s Award: The President’s Award is presented to individuals or organizations within the PLC which have a significant and positive impact on the PLC and the logging industry in Maine. The winner this year is: Peter Collins, Sales Manager for Milton CAT.
PLC Impact Award: Each year, the PLC recognizes persons or organizations from the public sector who have demonstrated a commitment to the logging industry and made a significant impact for its improvement. This year the award goes to: The Vermont Department of Forests, Parks and Recreation.
Master Logger Supporter’s Awards: The Master Logger Supporter’s Awards were created to recognize individuals and organizations that have been outstanding supporters of the Master Logger Certification Program® and the standard it represents. The winner this year is: The New York Watershed Agricultural Council.
PLC Supporting Member Acadia Insurance presented its annual Acadia Safety Award to Scott Madden of Madden Timberlands Inc. of Glenburn, Maine.

title: ChappyWrap
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Company Story
ChappyWrap was founded in 2006 by my mom, Beth, inspired by a blanket from my childhood that our family affectionately called “Lamby.” It went everywhere with us – on the couch, in the car, to the beach – and became synonymous with home and comfort.
My mom set out to create a better version of that beloved family blanket: incredibly soft and comfortable, but also beautiful, durable and easy to care for. She named the company ChappyWrap after Chappaquiddick island.
I joined my mom in the business in 2018, and together we relaunched ChappyWrap with a renewed vision for what the brand could become. What started as a small mother-daughter business has grown into something beyond our wildest dreams: a nationally recognized consumer brand with a team of 20 people, headquartered here in Maine.
My mom passed away in March 2025, so carrying forward the company we built together has taken on an even deeper meaning for me. At its core, ChappyWrap is still about exactly what it was when she started it: creating something that brings comfort, connection and a feeling of home. Today, I run the business alongside my husband, Drake, and we work to continue to grow the business while never losing sight of what initially inspired it.
Made in Maine
Our blankets aren’t manufactured in Maine, but ChappyWrap is very much a Maine-based business. Our headquarters, team and so much of the creative and strategic work, heart, and hustle behind the brand are based here. I’m really proud that we’re building a business based in and inspired by Maine. There can sometimes be an assumption that to build a significant consumer brand, you need to be in New York, Los Angeles or another major market. Our experience has been very different. We’ve built an incredibly talented team here, created sophisticated roles across marketing, creative, merchandising, product and operations, and reached customers all over the country while remaining firmly rooted in Maine as our home and as such an important part of our story. As ChappyWrap grows nationally, I love that Maine will always be home for our brand.
Products and Innovation
We’re best known for our signature ChappyWrap blankets, which sit at the intersection of function, design, comfort and emotional connection. They’re beautiful enough to live in your home but durable and washable enough to actually live your life with them. What really differentiates us is the relationship people develop with their Chappies. We hear from customers who have one on every bed, bring them on every family trip, give them as wedding or baby gifts, or have children who won’t sleep without theirs. We want to create the blanket you reach for every single day, the one that becomes a part of your home, family and everyday life.
Looking Ahead
What excites me most is how much opportunity we still see ahead of us. We’ve built a strong foundation and deeply loyal customer community, but in many ways it feels like we’re still only at the beginning of what ChappyWrap can become. Success for us isn’t simply about becoming as big as possible. It’s about building an enduring brand – one our customers continue to feel deeply connected to, where talented people want to build their careers, and something that my mom would be proud of. If we can continue growing, creating meaningful careers here in Maine and protecting the heart of what we created together, that would feel like success to me.

title: Japan launches spacecraft to mysterious moons of Mars in a bold mission to bring home soil samples
text:
A Japanese spacecraft rocketed toward Mars on Tuesday on an unprecedented quest to explore its mysterious moons and bring back samples.
Five of the world’s space agencies joined forces for the five-year mission that will attempt to land a robotic prospector plus a rover on Phobos, the larger and closer of Mars’ two pint-sized moons.
The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency, which is leading the bold sampling effort, launched the spacecraft before dawn from the country’s main spaceport on Tanegashima Island.
While NASA has successfully landed nine spacecraft on Mars over the past 50 years and China scored a 2021 touchdown, no one has ever ventured onto Phobos or its sidekick Deimos. And no one has managed to fetch samples from Mars, let alone its moons.
If successful, bits of dust, soil and rocks from Phobos will arrive on Earth in 2031.
“There’s a lot of adrenaline and a lot of excitement and a lot of wow,” said NASA astrophysicist Tom Statler, who’s involved with the project.
Japan has an edge going in, with two asteroid sample returns already under its cosmic belt.
Phobos is a lumpy, potato-shaped rock just 14 miles (22 kilometers) or so across. Examining pieces of it can explain how Mars’ moons — and possibly moons elsewhere — came to be.
Dubbed MMX for Martian Moons Exploration, the $578 million mission features a hefty 5-ton spacecraft that should reach Mars by late next summer. It will sync up with Phobos’ tight orbit around the red planet, before ejecting the French-German rover that’s named Idefix after the white terrier in the Asterix comics.
No bigger than a microwave oven, Idefix will plop onto Phobos by itself, bouncing for several minutes before coming to a halt in the moon’s extraordinarily low gravity.
The four-wheeled rover is designed to right itself if it lands upside down. All bets are off, though, if it sinks into soft soil or gets wedged between rocks, said the French Space Agency’s Julien Baroukh. Once the rover’s solar panels are deployed, the vehicle can no longer right itself, he added, which is why it will move at a glacial 1 millimeter per second (0.04 inches per second).
Idefix will serve as a “scout for safety,” according to Baroukh, as it prowls around Phobos for 100 days. Japanese flight controllers want to avoid powdery soil and rough terrain when the mothership — a four-legged stationary lander — descends to the surface to gather samples in late 2028 or 2029.
The lander will spend just two hours on Phobos, drilling and vacuuming up at least one-third of an ounce (10 grams) of material, before launching back into space. It will study Deimos during a series of flybys before leaving the Martian neighborhood in 2030 and hustling back to Earth for a 2031 sample delivery in the Australian desert.
It’s a treacherous undertaking, with wreckage littering the path.
The moons’ names aren’t exactly comforting: Phobos is Greek for fear and Deimos means dread. They’re the twin sons of the god of war Ares — Mars in Roman mythology.
Russia stumbled in all three of its Phobos attempts as well as many other Mars endeavors. In its only other Mars mission, Japan failed to get a spacecraft into orbit around the red planet. Even NASA has had its share of flops in a bid to answer the burning question: Did life ever exist on Mars?
By studying Mars’ moons, scientists hope to learn whether Phobos and Deimos formed in the aftermath of an ancient collision between Mars and a battering space rock. It’s also possible that the moons might be stray asteroids that became ensnared in Mars’ gravity.
Either way, scientists anticipate finding traces of Mars on Phobos, making the samples an irresistible two-for-one that should help demystify planetary and moon formation, and perhaps even the recipe for life. The findings will help shape future Mars missions, including those by astronauts, said NASA’s acting planetary science director Lindsay Hays.
“It is a once-in-a-lifetime chance. We are part of the first sample return mission from the Martian system,” said the Germany Space Agency’s rover chief Markus Grebenstein.
Japan isn’t the only one looking to claim the scientific riches packed into the Martian system’s rocks and dirt. China plans to launch a sample return mission to Mars in 2028, while NASA is still debating how to retrieve the more than 30 sample tubes collected by the Perseverance Mars rover, the new champion for off-Earth driving.
Japan and China could be neck-and-neck in getting samples back from the Martian system. Both are targeting 2031.
Japan is investing $350 million in this mission. NASA is contributing $87 million, the French Space Agency about $68 million, the German Space Agency about $56 million and the European Space Agency some $17 million.

title: Concerned about litter
text:
Dear Editor:
Do you, of a certain age, remember the anti-littering campaign of the 1960s and 1970s? There were the billboards along highways (Keep Maine Green, Don't be a litterbug!). There were warning signs announcing fines. There were school programs to educate children. I don't advocate that we bring back billboards but I do think it's time to re-educate the public and to reinstate signage for fines.
Littering is still against the law, though walking along our roads one wouldn't think so. Over the past few years I have noticed an increase in the trash littering our lovely towns. Take a stroll now along West Street down Western Avenue. The roadsides are covered in cans and bottles, paper cups and plastic bags. Walk the loop around Southport and there are full trash bags and all manner of garbage in the ditches.
What is causing this lack of civic concern and what can we do about it? Certainly we could have volunteer clean-up days. We could put up signage stating that litterers will be fined. Something should be done. We live in a most beautiful location. Let's try to keep it that way.
Michele Valliere
Boothbay Harbor

title: 🎃 HALLOWEEN WARNING! Don’t Visit Stephen King’s Bangor House on October 31! 👻
text:
Stephen King’s Bangor, Maine House Is Off-Limits On Halloween
Halloween is almost here! Come to Bangor, but don't stop on West Broadway!
You really can't drive down West Broadway in Bangor without spotting someone gawking at Stephen King's famous house. Trust me, I know...I live right in the neighborhood!
Just about every day, when I drive past the street, there's at least one car parked along the side of the road, with people snapping pictures, trying to get a better look at the property, or simply soaking in the excitement of being there.
It's all pretty normal to me, but Stephen King's house draws fans from all over the world who want to see where the master of horror lives.
With the spookiest night of the year arriving soon, plenty of people are making the trip to Bangor to catch a glimpse of the iconic home belonging to the city's most famous resident.
Read More: CP Holiday Train Returns To Hermon & Greenville, Maine Next Month
Here's a helpful hint: If you're thinking about stopping by Stephen King's West Broadway home to trick-or-treat, you'll be out of luck.
In fact, the master of horror himself has made it clear: Don't come to my house on Halloween.
It's a lot of people to accommodate, and the Halloween tradition at the house is no longer happening. Besides, Stephen and his wife, Tabitha, spend much of their time at their second home in Florida.
But don't worry, there are other ways to celebrate Halloween Stephen King-style!
As any hardcore Stephen King fan knows, Bangor helped inspire the fictional town of Derry, Maine, which has appeared in several of his novels and short stories.
No Stephen King sightseeing trip is complete without a few classic stops, including Mount Hope Cemetery, the Paul Bunyan statue, the corner of Jackson and Union streets, the Thomas Hill Standpipe, and, of course, the famous West Broadway house.
Just remember to be respectful of the neighborhood and the people who live there. You can admire the property from a distance without trespassing or disturbing the residents.
If you're planning a visit, Sk-Tours offers a unique experience for Stephen King fans right here in Bangor.
The people behind the tour — Penney, Jamie, and Stu — are perfect guides for the job. They spent two decades owning and operating a bookstore specializing in King's books and memorabilia. You can learn more about their story here.
So, if you're heading to Bangor for a little Halloween horror, there's plenty to explore. Just remember: enjoy the Stephen King sights, but leave the trick-or-treating at his house off your itinerary!
Happy Halloween!

title: Facebook Marketplace deal turns into robbery. Tips to protect yourself
text:
MARTINEZ, Ga. (WRDW/WAGT/Gray News) — Three Augusta residents are facing robbery charges after deputies said they stole a PlayStation 5 during a Facebook Marketplace meetup.
Columbia County Sheriff’s Office deputies were called Friday afternoon to Fierce Fitness for a reported “robbery by sudden snatch.”
Investigators said a 23-year-old man arranged online to sell a PlayStation 5 for $500 and agreed to meet three buyers in the parking lot.
When they arrived, the victim walked to the vehicle with the console and power cord so the buyers could plug it in and test it.
After he handed the game console through a door, the man in the backseat slammed the door, and the driver sped away without paying.
As deputies headed to the scene, license plate readers picked up the Ford Escape traveling into Richmond County.
Deputies stopped the SUV a short time later and detained all three occupants.
The stolen PlayStation was recovered in the vehicle, and deputies said they also seized marijuana and a firearm.
The three occupants − a 22-year-old man, a 20-year-old man and a 24-year-old woman − were arrested, charged with robbery and booked into the Columbia County jail.
Don’t let it happen to you
Here are some tips to help keep you safe:
- Choose a safe meeting spot. Whenever possible, meet at a law enforcement “exchange zone,” such as a police station lobby or a camera-monitored parking lot, instead of a random parking lot.
- Don’t meet at anyone’s home. Avoid inviting strangers to your house, and don’t agree to meet at their residence or in a secluded area.
- Stick to daylight hours. Schedule exchanges during the day in a busy, well-lit public place.
- Bring another adult. Take a friend or family member with you so you’re not alone during the transaction.
- Stay aware of your surroundings. Keep your eyes up instead of on your phone, and park in a spot where you can leave quickly if something doesn’t feel right.
- Keep communication on the platform. Use Facebook Messenger for all messages and avoid sharing your personal phone number, home address or email when possible.
- Be cautious with cash and payments. Don’t carry large amounts of cash. If you’re using digital payments, make sure you fully inspect the item before sending money.
- Check who you’re dealing with. Look at the buyer or seller’s profile for friends, photos and previous Marketplace activity. Be extra careful with brand-new or nearly empty accounts.
- Don’t ignore red flags. If the other person repeatedly tries to change the time or location at the last minute, or if the deal seems too good to be true, cancel the meetup and walk away.

title: Former Maine writer John Gould’s Lisbon home destroyed by fire Sunday
text:
A fire early Sunday morning in Lisbon destroyed well-known author John Gould’s hand-built house, which was soon to be a renovated into a recovery home.
According to the Maine Department of Public Safety, a fire broke out at 51 Gould Road around 3 a.m. Firefighters found the residence fully engulfed and beginning to collapse when they arrived. The home was unoccupied and no one was inside, according to authorities.
The property had been recently sold to Lewiston-based An Angel’s Wing Inc., which posted on Facebook Sunday morning the property was planned as a recovery house for those struggling with alcohol and substance abuse disorder.
“This property represented so much hope, hard work, and planning for the future, and seeing it damaged this way is heartbreaking,” the group posted. “We are still processing the loss and determining what comes next.”
The home was built by Maine author and columnist John Gould in 1940. In his book “The House That Jacob Built,” Gould mentions that his great-grandfather, Jacob Gould, built the original house on the lot in the 1780s before it burned down. John rebuilt the house himself.
Gould died in 2003 at the age of 94. He was the author of numerous books and columns on Maine life, including writing a weekly column for The Christian Science Monitor for more than 60 years.
Debra York, executive director of An Angel’s Wing Inc., said that last Friday members of her team brought over three carloads of furnishings to the house such as bedding and cookware, donated by community members, and left it in the home’s livingroom area.
York said she’s waiting to see what their insurance company tells them before making any decisions about the property.
York said the organization was still in the planning process for the home. Leaders were considering using it as a recovery home for eight veterans providing 24/7 care, but nothing was finalized.
An investigation into the fire is ongoing.

title: 13 Maine Halloween happenings for scares and screams
text:
There is no escape from Maine’s scariest season.
No, we’re not talking about tourist season. Halloween is approaching and there are haunted houses, graveyard tours, old horror movies and other scary stuff in cities and towns across the state. Whether you’re in southern York County, on the Midcoast or in Central Maine, it’s easy to find some spooky fun this month.
Here are some suggestions for ways to get your scare on.
Friday-Saturday, and Oct. 30-31. Maine Maritime Museum, 243 Washington St., Bath. mainemaritimemuseum.org
The museums hosts a spooky tour of its Kennebec River campus called “Dead Reckoning: Shipyard Death & Disturbances.” There’ll be a seance in the Donnell House, where unexplained encounters have been reported over the years, and an escape room. There’s also a self-guided walking tour with stories about some of the gruesome working conditions at the historic shipyard that was on the site. Tickets are $25.
‘DRACULA‘
Friday-Saturday. Westbrook Performing Arts Center, 471 Stroudwater St., Westbrook. porttix.com
The Portland Ballet’s professional company presents “Dracula,” based on the 1897 Gothic novel by Bram Stoker, with a score by Rachmaninoff. Because of its mature themes, “Dracula” is recommended for ages 11 and up. Tickets are $35-$45.
Thursday-Sunday, through Oct. 31. TM Wentworth Road, Lebanon. hauntedgrandviewmanor.com
This haunted attraction is a mix of scary trails and creepy buildings, including the Grandview Funeral home, cemeteries, hillbilly shacks and slaughterhouses. Beware the Pig Man, who is always waiting for you. Tickets are $25. There are also “no scare” nights on Thursdays, for $10.
Friday-Sunday, and Oct. 29-31. The Leavitt Theatre, 259 Main St., Ogunquit. leavittheatre.com
This is a haunted tour of the 101-year-old Leavitt Theatre, featuring terrifying clown dens, twisted apothecaries and the infamous Leavitt Chainsaw Massacre. Tickets are $25.
Oct. 30-Nov. 1. Mayo Street Arts, 10 Mayo St., Portland. mayostreetarts.org
Mayo Street hosts a walk-through haunted house full of handmade creatures, sets, sounds and characters. Free, but donations are welcomed.
Oct. 31. Strand Theatre, 345 Main St., Rockland. rocklandstrand.com
This classic horror film from 1933 stars Claude Rains, who mostly appears covered in bandages. It’s a prime example of the power of suspense and how sometimes it’s scarier NOT to see something. Based on the novel by H.G. Wells. Tickets are $12, $9 for seniors and students.
Thursday-Saturday, through Oct. 31. Wallingford’s Orchard, 1240 Perkins Ridge Road, Auburn. wallingfordsorchard.com
Wallingford’s is a peaceful, scenic place to pick fruit – when the sun shines. But at night this time of year, it becomes a nightmare full of creepy creatures and scary structures. It’s a haunted walk “through some of your darkest nightmares.” Tickets are $30.
Saturday. Waterville Opera House, 1 Common St., Waterville. watervillecreates.org
This showing of the classic and campy 1975 film features an opportunity to meet and take photos with actress Patricia Quinn, who played Magenta. She’ll also take questions from the audience. There’ll be a costume contest and a shadow cast performance by the group Rocky for Equality. Tickets are $60-$170.
The film will also be shown, with the same shadow cast, at the Waldo Theatre in Waldoboro on Oct. 30. Tickets are $20-$50.
Friday-Saturday. Johnson Hall Opera House, 280 Water St., Gardiner. johnsonhall.org
This event features ghost stories, unexpected scares and characters from the past taking over the historic opera house. More than 50 community performers, ages 6 to 83, will perform short scenes. Audience members will also travel through Johnson Hall in small groups, moving from one scary scene to another. Tickets are $14.64.
Oct. 22. Old York Museum Center, 3 Lindsay Road, York. oldyork.org
The Old York Historical Society puts on several events each year for its “Spooky Season.” On Thursday people can take a lamp-lit tour of York’s Burial Ground titled “Gone But Not Forgotten: Revolutionary York.” The life stories of 18th century townsfolk will be told by costumed guides. Tickets are $20. There are also a couple of free events for families at the Old York Museum Center, including pumpkin carving on Oct. 29 and trick-or-treating with a pumpkin lighting on Oct. 30.
Friday-Saturday through Oct. 31, plus Oct. 29. Aquaboggan Water Park, 980 Portland Road, Saco. trailofterrormaine.com
This annual haunted walk has been completely revamped and expanded, with new scenes and a 30-minute walk through the woods — unless something makes you run. The terror is still spearheaded by a creature called the Banshee, who has taken over the woods. Scenes are filled with lights, sounds, and creeps lurking everywhere. Tickets are $25, $10 for children 10 and under.
Sunday and Oct. 31. Waldo Theatre, 916 Main St., Waldoboro. thewaldotheatre.org
Before Vincent Price did the scary narration on Michael Jackson’s hit song “Thriller,” he was a longtime star of horror films. The Waldo Theatre is hosting a festival in his honor, including a screening of the 1963 film “The Raven,” an irreverent take on Edgar Allan Poe’s classic poem, directed by Roger Corman. Tickets are $12, $9 for seniors and students.
On Oct. 31, Everyman Repertory Theatre presents a staged reading of a new play called “I Know It’s Gruesome, But is It Art? The Vincent Price Murder Case.” It’s set in the 1960s in the London art scene, during the filming of a Price film called “Witchfinder General.” Tickets are $20.
WALK AMONG THE SHADOWS
Thursday-Sunday. Eastern Cemetery, 224 Congress St., Portland. Spiritsalive.org
This is a nightly tour of Portland’s oldest cemetery, established in 1668. Costumed actors will bring long-dead folks to life and tell some of the city’s dramatic stories, including the destruction of Fort Loyall in 1690 by French and Inidgenous forces, an 1893 reservoir break on North Street, Benjamin Tukey’s ill-fated celebration of the American victory at Saratoga and the 1647 Mary Martin infanticide case. Adult tickets are $10 cash or $12.51 on Eventbrite.

title: FIRST ALERT WEATHER: Sunshine Expected All Week Long, with Cooler Temperatures Arriving Late Week
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - Good evening everyone and happy Monday. A quiet stretch of fall weather continues across Northern Maine this week, with plenty of sunshine expected through Wednesday. Temperatures will turn a little cooler Tuesday and Wednesday before another warmup arrives the second half of the weekend.
Mostly clear skies are expected overnight, with temperatures dropping into the lower to mid 30s across much of Aroostook County. Caribou is expected to fall to around 35 degrees, with Presque Isle near 33 and Houlton around 33. Some patchy fog may develop after midnight, particularly in sheltered river valleys where winds become light. A weak cold front will cross Northern Maine late tonight into early Tuesday, but moisture will be limited enough that no precipitation is expected.
Tuesday will feature plenty of sunshine across the region. Temperatures in Caribou will start in the mid 30s Tuesday morning before climbing through the 40s and reaching around 50 degrees during the afternoon. Rain chances remain at zero through the day. Winds will shift to the north behind tonight’s cold front, with gusts up to around 25 mph possible across northeastern Aroostook County.
Another mostly sunny day is expected Wednesday. High temperatures will reach around 50 degrees in Caribou and Presque Isle, with lower 50s toward Houlton. Areas farther north and west will generally remain in the upper 40s to around 50. Wednesday night turns chilly again, with widespread upper 20s expected across Northern Maine.
Cloud cover begins to increase somewhat Thursday and Friday, although the forecast remains largely dry. A storm system developing well offshore of the Mid-Atlantic and New England coast will be responsible for some of that cloud cover. Most forecast guidance keeps the system far enough offshore that significant impacts are not expected across Northern Maine.
Temperatures stay fairly seasonable through much of the week. Caribou is forecast to reach around 53 Tuesday, 50 Wednesday and 50 Thursday before cooler air knocks Friday’s high back into the mid 40s. Temperatures then begin climbing again over the weekend, reaching around 50 Saturday and potentially approaching 60 degrees Sunday. High pressure is expected to remain the dominant weather feature through late this week, keeping Northern Maine generally dry despite several weak frontal passages.
The next several days remain straightforward: plenty of sunshine Tuesday, more sunshine Wednesday and partly sunny skies Thursday. For the latest forecast details, check out the First Alert Video Forecast attached to this article. Have a great evening!

title: Timber harvest visits help Maine forest rangers keep a presence
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
COURTESY OF THE MAINE FOREST SERVICE
Did you know that Maine’s Forest Rangers have made more than 5,000 site visits to timber harvests over the last 4 years? Wildfire-related duties are not the only reason Rangers venture into the forest. From Eliot to Fort Kent, T5 R20 WELS to T11 R3 NBPP, and everywhere in between, Rangers keep a presence in the woods throughout their patrol areas. Staying aware of harvest activities and conducting inspections are ways that Rangers fulfill an important objective: to enhance the safe, sound, and responsible management of the forest for this and future generations.
Rangers routinely inspect commercial timber harvesting operations to ensure that landowners and loggers are complying with various aspects of Maine’s Forest Practices Act. Specifically, Rangers check on Forestry Operations Notifications, proper marking of property lines, and compliance with Maine’s clearcutting regulations. During these inspections, Rangers also look at truck haul road and skid trail water crossings, as well as any harvesting activity within the shoreland zones. These areas are reviewed to ensure operations meet state and local water quality standards and are not causing erosion or sedimentation problems. Rangers regularly collaborate with Maine Forest Service District Foresters and other field staff on this important work.
Rangers bring their wildfire prevention expertise to these inspections and may also check timber harvesting equipment to ensure their exhaust systems are properly equipped with spark arrestor control devices. Harvesting slash accumulation in statutorily protected areas such as near utility lines, property lines, railways, dwellings, and roadways is another inspection element Rangers examine and address when needed. Compliance with the State’s spark arrestor and slash laws prevent the start of wildfires and limit their spread when they do occur.
Ranger visits on nights and weekends are a way to keep an eye on loggers’ equipment when they are not there. “Timber Asset Security” checks are meant to protect these valuable investments from theft and vandalism. Additionally, Rangers may provide courtesy checks on other property such as gates and communicate any issues to the landowner if found. The best-case scenario is that everything looks good, and the only sign of the Ranger’s visit is a courtesy card left to let you know they were there.
While most site visits are Ranger-initiated, complaints from forest landowners regarding the unlawful cutting of trees, timber theft and trespass, and failure of the logger to pay for trees that have been cut and sold also prompt investigation. Forest Rangers are the lead authority when it comes to presenting timber theft and trespass cases for prosecution at the District Court level and work with the District Attorney’s Office to hold violators accountable and obtain the appropriate restitution for the landowner.
Maine’s Forest Rangers are proud of the role we serve in protecting Maine’s valuable forest resources and ensuring the sound and responsible management of the forest for this and future generations. If you are a logger, forester, land manager or landowner and have questions or would like assistance, please contact your local Forest Ranger.

title: How Miley Cyrus paid tribute to her 'eternal' bond with Dolly Parton during a performance
text:
How Miley Cyrus paid tribute to her 'eternal' bond with Dolly Parton during a performance
Miley Cyrus is holding on to her memories of Dolly Parton. During her concert at the Hollywood Bowl in Los Angeles on Friday, Oct. 16, the singer paid tribute to her late godmother in an emotional six-minute speech that included a rendition of one of her most notable songs.
"I only got to see Dolly Parton live in concert one time in my entire life, and it was here," she told the audience about the significance of the space she opted to host her two-night limited performances of Bass Persuades. It was Cyrus’s first time performing at the iconic venue.
The singer then recalled asking Parton if she could attend that show without performing alongside her, hoping to experience the concert as a regular audience member. Parton agreed, but she had other plans. She opened that show with "The Best of Both Worlds," the theme song from Cyrus’s Disney Channel series Hannah Montana, before announcing to the crowd that her goddaughter was in the audience.
Cyrus joked that the moment defeated her plan to watch the show quietly. Looking back, however, she said it was worth it. "This memory is gold to me," she said.
The singer grew more emotional as she reflected on how she continues to feel Parton’s presence following her death in August.
"Me and Dolly, we are eternal," she continued. "Nothing in this life could ever tear us apart."
Cyrus then tearfully expressed how much she misses her godmother, telling the audience, "I’m gonna see her again, and I can’t fucking wait ’cause I miss her."
Before launching into "Jolene," Cyrus also celebrated Parton’s lasting musical legacy. “Some of the greatest music that we have today was written, produced, and performed by my aunt Dolly, and this is one of those songs.”
"She’s right here beside me every day," Cyrus noted. "All the time, more than she could be when she was here. I feel her, more now than ever."

title: Meet the researchers leaving the US because of Trump's funding cuts and politicization of science
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Halley Froehlich was sure she’d spend her scientific career in the United States. Her family has been in America since the 1700s.
But over the past two years, delayed federal grants and fears about the future motivated her to pack her life into boxes. She moved to Finland with her husband and daughter and is continuing her research — studying how fish, shellfish and seaweed that humans eat are responding to climate change — at the University of Helsinki.
When the Trump administration began upending U.S. scientific research last year, dismantling the federal grant-giving process and attempting to exert more political influence over what projects get funded, foreign universities saw an opportunity. They adopted programs to lure U.S. researchers abroad, promising more stable streams of funding and academic freedom.
Since then, many have taken the bait. While there is no way to quantify the overall change across the nation, scientists, researchers and professional groups say the shift is clear, unprecedented and concerning.
“You can almost talk to any vice president for research at a university and they will tell you of one or two top faculty that they’ve lost,” said Tobin Smith, senior vice president of government relations and public policy for the Association of American Universities.
White House spokesperson Liz Huston said Trump is “ending waste” and is “committed to keeping America the world leader in scientific innovation, and that means funding real science.”
But more than half of American states have lost scientists to recruitment programs in other countries, according to an April report from the Business for Federal Research Funding Coalition. Last March, early-career biomedical scientists were about 20 percentage points less likely to say they would “now” stay in the U.S., compared to their recollection of how they felt six months earlier. And physics Ph.D. graduates in 2025 left the U.S. at the highest rate in 30 years, according to the American Institute of Physics.
Countries including Canada, France, Belgium and Finland are touting their recruits from U.S. institutions, a disturbing and surprising development, scientists say, for a country that far and away leads the world in Nobel prizes for medicine, physics and chemistry.
“It used to be the shining city on the hill where we all want to go,” said Christine Stawitz, now at the University of Birmingham in England. “That reputational loss, I think, is hard to quantify, but also really damaging.”
Some American scientists are moving abroad. Here’s why
Stawitz left her job at the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration last year to become a research software engineer in the United Kingdom. She said NOAA no longer aligned with her values, especially after she was asked to strip websites of references to climate change and diversity, equity and inclusion topics.
She says the upheaval in U.S. science is a common subject at scientific meetings. “People talk about the U.S. at conferences in the U.K. now like, I don’t know what’s going on there. It’s not good,” she said.
Froehlich’s decision to leave was a slow burn. She was already concerned about school safety and gun violence in the U.S. when the nation’s research landscape was overturned. Then, at the University of California, Santa Barbara, her colleagues’ grants kept getting postponed or canceled. Student researchers burst into her office in tears, unsure how to navigate their futures. She worried about future federal funding for her own research, which involves climate change.
“The cumulative effect of those things ultimately ended up making us really serious about, I don’t think here is our home anymore,” said Froehlich. She was recruited through an initiative by the Research Council of Finland and now has five years of guaranteed funding totaling about $3 million. She moved into a flat by the Baltic Sea in Helsinki and is taking Finnish lessons offered by the university.
And international scientists are leaving the US
International researchers who were drawn to the U.S. for its reputation as a global leader in science are also seeking different places to do their work.
Married biologists James Letts and Maria Maldonado were recruited to Australia’s Monash University and left behind their posts at the University of California, Davis. Letts is from Canada, and Maldonado from Argentina. Both got their doctoral degrees in New York and spent over a decade doing science in the U.S.
Grant-related uncertainty — including having to lay off a staff scientist while waiting for stalled funding — made them take the leap.
“All I want to do is do great science and make discoveries, but I want my work to mean something as well. And the opportunity to do that seemed very difficult in the U.S.,” Letts said.
Forty percent of the U.S. science Nobel Prizes were won by immigrants. Omar Yaghi, a 2025 Nobel Prize winner for chemistry, left his post at the University of California, Berkeley this year to direct an artificial intelligence lab at China’s Tsinghua University.
The consequences of losing scientific talent
The U.S. is still a science powerhouse, full of institutions around the country with robust research communities and well-resourced institutions that attract foreign scientists. Even if every European country threw open its doors, there still wouldn’t be enough capacity to accommodate every American scientist.
And not everyone is leaving. Many scientists are choosing to stay, searching for new sources of research funding or pivoting to jobs in industry.
But the erosion of reputation and the talent drain may not be over. The Trump administration has cut or frozen up to $174 billion in federal grants since the president’s second term began, according to a tracking tool released by the States United Democracy Center and the organization Grant Witness. And a proposed rule from the Office of Management and Budget could give political appointees more control over what future projects are funded. A resolution approved by Congress has delayed a final decision on the rule until December.
Scientists who have moved away and those still in the U.S. are worried about what’s left behind. They say the next generation of scientists may struggle with fewer graduate programs, money and mentorship — and it could take a decade or longer for the U.S. scientific enterprise to truly feel those effects.
Major research institutions accepted 15% fewer applicants for fall 2026 doctoral programs compared to last year, according to admissions data collected by the Association of American Universities. One of the students impacted was a mentee of Smith’s.
“What is one of my pieces of advice to that young man? Next year, look in Canada,” he said.

title: Please, no recalls in Bar Harbor!
text:
Charles Sidman is proposing not one but three petitions for which he plans to gather signatures at the Nov. 3 election. At the very least, I urge you not to sign the petition that would create a recall provision for elected municipal officers and officials.
For petition-filing requirements, the bar is low. It takes just five registered voters to initiate the petition process by presenting an affidavit to the town clerk that authorizes circulation of the petition to local voters. Supporters then have 60 days to gather signatures amounting to 10% of the voters in the last gubernatorial election to put the petition before the voters.

title: Jean M. Howe
text:
Jean M. Howe, passed away peacefully on Oct. 14, 2026, at the Lincoln Home in Newcastle, Maine, in the company of her loving family and friends just a week shy of her 97th birthday.
Jean was born in Melrose, Massachusetts, on Oct. 23, 1929, to Wirt and Madge (Tuell) McKenney. She graduated from Melrose High School in 1947 and from Boston Business School in 1948.
Jean was a lifelong learner whose boundless curiosity about the world around her shaped her life and passions. A respected ornithologist and botanist, Jean had extraordinary knowledge of the intricate workings of nature. Her expertise and dedication earned her a fellowship in the Josselyn Botanical Society, and she played an instrumental role in the creation of the Coastal Maine Botanical Gardens in Boothbay. There, she enthusiastically shared her knowledge with visitors, fostering a deeper appreciation for the beauty and diversity of the environment. A woman of conviction and action, Jean was a passionate advocate for civil rights, wildlife conservation, and the preservation of the Earth she so dearly loved. Throughout her life, she inspired others not only through her knowledge, but also through her unwavering commitment to protecting the beauty and integrity of the natural world.
A gifted musician, Jean shared her talents generously throughout her life. She studied voice at the New England Conservatory and later sang and played the piano for numerous church congregations, choruses, choirs and jazz ensembles across New England. Her beautiful voice also earned her the extraordinary opportunity to sing with the New York Philharmonic during the 1960s under the direction of the legendary Leonard Bernstein.
On Oct. 3, 1953, Jean married the love of her life, Lemuel Herbert “Bert” Howe. Together, they built a life rooted in family, faith, community, and a shared commitment to serving others. Jean carried this spirit of service throughout her life, generously devoting her time, talents, and boundless energy to the causes and organizations she held dear. She served as director of religious education at the Unitarian Universalist Church in Haverhill, Massachusetts, and as director of the New England Music Festival. An active and dedicated member of every community she called home, Jean willingly lent her leadership and expertise to countless boards of directors, always finding room for one more worthy cause.
Jean was predeceased by her husband, Lemuel “Bert” Howe and grandson, Andrew Goupil.
She leaves behind a loving family who will cherish her memory: her son Benjamin Howe of Portsmouth, New Hampshire; her son James Howe and his wife, Karen, of North Yarmouth, Maine; her son Brian Howe and his wife, Diane, of Boothbay Harbor, Maine; and her daughter Jocelyn Howe of Dresden, Maine. She is also survived by five grandchildren: Jaime Cesar of Framingham, Massachusetts; Joshua Howe of Kennebunk, Maine; Morgan Howe of Clinton, Massachusetts; Christopher Apollonio of Titusville, Florida; Laura Howe of Bozeman, Montana, and three great-grandchildren as well as many beloved nieces, nephews, cousins and friends.
Jean’s life was a testament to the rewards of a curious mind, a generous spirit, a love of music, and a deep appreciation for the natural world. She leaves behind a legacy that will live on in the family she cherished, the communities she served, and the many people whose lives she enriched.
At Jean’s request, she will be laid to rest at Cedar Brook Burial Ground in Limington, Maine.
In lieu of flowers, tribute gifts in Jean’s name may be made to Maine Audubon in support of its work to protect Maine’s wildlife and natural habitats: https://maineaudubon.org/support/give/
Arrangements are entrusted to Hall Funeral Home and Crematory, 975 Wiscasset Road, Boothbay.

title: Eagles QB Jalen Hurts expected to miss the rest of the season with blood clots, AP source says
text:
PHILADELPHIA (AP) — Philadelphia Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts is expected to miss the rest of the season because of blood clots in his lungs, a person familiar with the situation told The Associated Press on Monday.
The person spoke to the AP on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of a health matter.
Hurts was placed on injured reserve Saturday, two days after the Eagles revealed he has a blood clot in his calf. He missed the first of at least four games in Philadelphia’s loss to the Carolina Panthers on Sunday.
The Eagles and Hurts’ agent, Nicole Lynn, released more information on his condition Monday. They said Hurts has deep vein thrombosis and a bilateral pulmonary emboli, meaning a blood clot has traveled from the legs to the lungs.
His treatment involves blood thinners, and he won’t be allowed to participate in any football activities until he is off them.
The Eagles and Lynn said Hurts was expected to make a full recovery. “He is clinically stable and has no significant functional limitations,” their statement said.
Eagles coach Nick Sirianni was the only member of the organization made available to the media on Monday — not general manager Howie Roseman or any member of the team’s medical staff — and largely deflected questions about Hurts’ health or how the team handled the situation.
“I’m not a medical expert,” Sirianni said. “I lean on our guys in all those situations. I’m a football coach. I lean on our medical experts in every situation. I have full trust and full faith in them. It’s not just me that has major care for our players. It’s them, as well.”
The Eagles previously said Hurts was injured when he took a cleat to his calf area on Oct. 4 in a game against the Los Angeles Rams.
Hurts informed the medical staff of the injury after practice on Oct. 8. The Super Bowl 59 MVP was back at practice the next day before the team left for London to play Jacksonville. Hurts was initially diagnosed by specialists in London with a left calf superficial vein thrombosis.
Sirianni declined to say Monday why the Eagles allowed Hurts to fly home with a blood clot. He referred to statements the Eagles and Hurts’ agent released over the last week that addressed the timeline of his injury and treatment.
He had no answers on specific questions about Hurts and his blood clots.
“I understand you want this information on this,” Sirianni said. “I fully trust the people that are involved in helping us all make these decisions. We have great people here.”
Hurts hadn’t missed more than two games in a season since becoming the full-time starter in 2021. He has led the Eagles to five straight playoff appearances, three NFC East titles and two Super Bowl appearances, beating the Chiefs 40-22 two years ago.
Tanner McKee started for Hurts against the Panthers. McKee finished 26 of 45 for 215 yards and a touchdown in the 25-14 loss. The Eagles (2-4) have lost four consecutive games for the first time since 2020.
Sirianni added that beleaguered offensive coordinator Sean Mannion was still the play-caller.
Hurts has eight touchdown passes and three interceptions with 933 yards passing this season. He is in the middle of a five-year, $255 million extension, including $179.3 million guaranteed, that takes him through the 2028 season.
The Eagles stunned fans when they drafted Hurts out of Oklahoma in the second round in 2020. They seemingly had Carson Wentz entrenched at QB and had more pressing needs. But Hurts supplanted Wentz and became one of the top quarterbacks in the NFL.
“I haven’t been without Jalen for an extended period of time,” Sirianni said. “I have the utmost confidence in Tanner. But I miss him. I know that will be the case. Jalen and I have been together, head coach and quarterback, for six years.”
___
AP Pro Football Writer Rob Maaddi in Tampa, Florida, contributed to this report.

title: A very fall-like calm weather week ahead

title: Aging Untold: Here’s what you should know if you’re raising grandkids full-time
text:
(Aging Untold) — On this episode of Aging Untold, we look into the emotional and financial realities grandparents face when stepping in to raise their grandchildren full-time.
We also examine the root causes of nurse burnout, hear how two frontline caregivers launched a program to help colleagues heal and discuss what needs to change to keep experienced nurses at the bedside.
Finally, we meet a Vermont retiree whose passion for playing and repairing accordions turned into a thriving second act.
If your role has shifted from being a grandparent to full-time, day-in, day-out parenting of your grandchildren, the transition can bring deep love and purpose — but also real stress on time, money and energy.
The Aging Untold experts are breaking down what you need to know and the resources available.
“You’ve got to give yourself grace to get through this,” gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said.
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke said one of the first practical steps grandparents should take is establishing legal guardianship.
Oregon is facing a nursing crisis. Experts say it is not from a lack of licensed nurses, but from workplace conditions that drive healthcare workers away from frontline positions.
Registered nurse Heather Sweeney and therapist Amy Ponteri started “Helping Healthcare Heal” to address what they saw as insufficient resources for health care workers in intense settings like emergency rooms.
More than one factor contributes to nursing burnout. Workload, staffing shortages, safety concerns, documentation demands and the loss of meaningful connection with patients are all pushing experienced nurses away from the bedside, according to the Aging Untold experts.
We talked about what nurses are facing — and what hospitals and health care systems could do to help them stay in a field they entered to care for people.
Nathan Longo plays an Italian accordion from the early 1960s, and he also repairs accordions in a small workshop.
He said he is better at fixing the instruments than playing them.
What began as something to do in retirement has turned into a 30-hour-a-week job.
