title: Hancock Lumber
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
At Hancock Lumber, “Made-in-Maine” isn’t simply a statement about where we manufacture, it’s part of who we are.
Our roots go back to 1848, when our company began in Casco, Maine, harvesting timber and milling logs into lumber. Seven generations later, we’re still growing trees and milling them into Eastern White Pine products, manufacturing trusses and wall panels, investing in Maine communities, and helping professional builders create the homes and spaces where people live, work, and gather.
Today, Hancock Lumber is a seventh-generation, family-owned integrated forest products company with 750 employees and a network of lumberyards, Eastern White Pine mills, component manufacturing facilities, and thousands of acres of timberland.
Our manufacturing story starts in the forest, where we partner with landowners and logging contractors to responsibly manage timberlands and selectively harvest Eastern White Pine, a renewable resource that takes 80 to 100 years to mature. From there, Eastern White Pine moves through our sawmills in Bethel, Casco, and Pittsfield, where Team Hancock transforms logs into world-class pine boards used for siding, trim, millwork, and furniture. The manufacturing process also produces by-products like shavings, sawdust, and bark mulch with 100% of the log fiber utilized and zero material wasted.
Our Made-in-Maine story continues to evolve.
In addition to pine, we manufacture roof and floor trusses and wall panels that help professional builders build faster, safer, and more efficiently. In early 2027, we’ll take another generational step forward with the opening of a new 44,000-square-foot component manufacturing facility in Oxford.
Featuring advanced automation and manufacturing technology, Oxford will significantly increase our wall-panel capacity and introduce precut and labeled framing packages. Combined with our existing truss capabilities, Hancock Lumber will provide builders with integrated framing solutions through a single point of contact—helping reduce jobsite labor, improve precision and efficiency, get structures weather-tight faster, and enable our customers to do more with the people they have.
For us, innovation has never meant leaving our roots behind. It means building on them.
That philosophy extends to our people and our commitment to building a people-first, values-driven culture. Hancock Lumber’s shared-leadership philosophy recognizes that the people closest to the work have valuable knowledge, ideas, and experience that can move the business forward and strengthen the customer experience. We strive to create workplaces where people feel trusted, respected, valued, and heard—and where everyone has opportunities to learn, grow, lead, and build a meaningful career.
Investing in people is also an investment in Maine. Careers across manufacturing, forestry, design, logistics, technology, sales, and the building trades help strengthen Maine’s workforce, communities, and economy while creating opportunities for the next generation.
Being in business since 1848 says more about our commitment to the future than it does about our past. We’re proud to keep investing in Maine—in our people, our mills, our manufacturing capabilities, our communities, and the professional builders who shape them. From growing pine to making boards, trusses, wall panels, and framing packages, there’s a common thread running through 178 years of Hancock Lumber history:
Rooted in Maine since 1848. Building for generations to come.

title: Politicians have a rich history of telling each other to zip it
text:
According to a 1922 edition of an internal company newspaper of JC Penney (The Dynamo), a husband or wife has “good grounds for divorce” if one tells the other to shut up. Political rivalry, though, is nothing like a marriage.
Given how ugly campaigning has become, I’m not at all perturbed that Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Troy Jackson told Sen. Susan Collins to “shut up” during last week’s Senate debate. It came after a student in the audience yelled out.
Collins could be heard saying over the shouts, “This must be a Troy Jackson supporter.”
Jackson told CNN that Collins “accused me of setting that up. I had no idea who it was. I mean, I was surprised whenever he jumped up out of there. … I just think that was another situation where she was talking down to me.”
Collins told Fox News that Jackson’s response “seemed like such an automatic quick reply” that it struck her as a “very telling” example of his mistreatment of women.
Oh, come on. Sen. Collins has put up with President Donald Trump’s incessant insults toward women with barely a peep. Furthermore, she didn’t seem to register Jackson’s rejoinder as an insult to women on the night it happened.
A glance at history shows this shouldn’t be an issue. In 1969 at the University of Edinburgh, Queen Elizabeth’s patrician husband Prince Philip presided over a meeting that a 22-year-old student disrupted with unwanted questions. The prince wasn’t having it.
“Shut up and grow up,” Philip shouted. Cheers and laughter followed, according to the Associated Press.
Back in 1982, a Republican congressional candidate from California, Gary Arnold, kept interrupting President Ronald Reagan. Fed up, the normally avuncular president pointed at him and told Arnold, “Shut up!”
The GOP audience applauded.
A couple of years later, when Walter Mondale gave a speech during his bid to oust Reagan that a group of GOP backers disrupted. Mondale turned to them and said, “Shut up, will ya!” The place erupted in cheers.
When angry relatives of American military personnel listed as missing in action confronted President George H.W. Bush in 1992, Bush had a quick response to them: “Shut up!”
“I didn’t blow my cool. I just made an emphatic point,” the president later said.
Even as august a figure as Winston Churchill once got so fed up with the heckling of a communist member of Parliament, William Gallagher, that he turned to the Scotsman with a lion’s glare in 1947 and told Gallagher, “Shut up, Moscow!”
Almost nobody criticized Reagan, Mondale, Bush or Churchill for their words.
Honestly, is there anyone who hasn’t wanted to tell a politician: oh, shut up? I’ve certainly had that desire on many occasions. I wouldn’t be surprised to find out I did it a time or two.
My best advice to Jackson? Stop talking about this, stop taking questions about it — and start telling Mainers who you are and what you stand for.

title: College student dies after falling in creek during hiking trip
text:
TUCKER COUNTY, W.Va . (WXIX/Gray News) - A missing University of Cincinnati student hiking in West Virginia was found dead Monday.
Thomas Donnelly, 21, who was part of an eight-member group from the UC Mountaineering Club, went hiking in the Red Creek Trail and Fisher Springs Trail area of Tucker County on Oct. 9, according to West Virginia State Police.
The group was trying to cross a creek when they hit elevated water levels and swift currents, state police explained.
Donnelly lost his footing and was swept downstream by the swift-moving water, state police said.
A 911 call was made around 11:30 a.m. Oct. 11 to report Donnelly was missing.
Search-and-rescue efforts began but were suspended that evening because of approaching inclement weather and diminishing daylight, state police said.
The search resumed Monday. Donnelly’s body was found around 2 p.m. that day.
“This loss is incredibly heartbreaking and has had a significant impact for many members in the Bearcat community. Our thoughts are with Thomas’ family, friends, and classmates that have been impacted by this tragic news. Please keep Thomas’s family in your thoughts during this difficult time,” UC Dean of Students Shaka Sydnor said in a statement.

title: 2 stabbed during altercation inside popular California corn maze
text:
2 stabbed during altercation inside popular California corn maze
A Sacramento man was arrested after two people were stabbed Friday night inside a corn maze at Cool Patch Pumpkins in Dixon, Calif., according to the Solano County Sheriff’s Office.
Deputies responded to the popular fall attraction around 9:15 p.m. after an altercation was reported in the maze, the Sheriff’s Office said.
A 19-year-old woman from Dixon, California, and a 20-year-old man from Vallejo, California, were taken to a hospital. Authorities have not released information about their conditions.
Deputies arrested a 28-year-old Sacramento man and recovered a weapon at the scene, according to the Sheriff’s Office. Officials have not released the suspect’s name or said what may have led to the violence.
“There was an altercation between some people yesterday in the corn maze,” said Seth Cooley, whose family runs Cool Patch Pumpkins. “Police were called. They responded really fast.”
The pumpkin patch reopened Saturday, with families returning to the grounds and entering the corn maze. Cooley described the stabbing as an isolated incident and said the farm prioritizes visitors’ safety.
“We’re a family-oriented pumpkin patch,” Cooley said. “Always have been.”
Security cameras are visible around the property, and a liability notice is posted at the entrance.
Cooley confirmed that security personnel are on-site but declined to provide details about the farm’s security measures.
“I’m not going to go into detail on that right now,” Cooley said. “I don’t think it’s relevant to what happened.”
Natalie Murphy and Emily Gove traveled from San Francisco for a fall outing and said they had not heard about the stabbing before arriving. Both said they felt safe during their visit.
“Joking aside, we felt completely safe, and nothing stood out,” Gove said.
“It really does seem like a family-type of place,” Murphy said.
The women said the violence was difficult to imagine at a family attraction and expressed concern for the victims.
“I hope that everyone is doing OK and that maybe some safety measures are taken and people feel comfortable coming here,” Gove said.
Cooley said the pumpkin patch would continue welcoming visitors.
“This was an isolated incident,” he said. “It’s a beautiful day. We hope to see you guys out here. We’re not going to let one incident with one individual ruin a great day for thousands of people.”
The investigation remains active, according to the Sheriff’s Office. Cool Patch Pumpkins remains open.
The corn maze is widely known for being one of the largest in the world.

title: Officer’s use of force was justified in shooting death of 1-year-old Kohen Wiley at a Walmart, AG says
text:
SENATOBIA, Miss. (WMC/Gray News) — A police officer’s use of force that resulted in the death of a 1-year-old child was justified, the Mississippi Office of the Attorney General announced Monday.
The announcement marks the conclusion of the state’s investigation into the death of 1-year-old Kohen Wiley, who was shot and killed June 14 in the parking lot of a Walmart in Senatobia.
On that day, Senatobia police responded to the Walmart for a call about someone trying to steal diapers.
Officials said the call involved Wiley’s mother and great aunt.
Wiley was inside a car with his mother, who was holding him, and his great-aunt, who was driving, when an officer fired toward the vehicle. Wiley and his great-aunt were shot. Wiley died from his injuries.
The officer who fired his gun was placed on administrative leave, which city leaders said was standard practice after deadly police shootings.
The Mississippi Bureau of Investigation assigned five agents to the case to gather statements and reviewed witness accounts, body-camera and dashcam video and Walmart surveillance video.
In an initial account of the shooting, state investigators said: “Officers attempted to stop the vehicle, but the driver drove in the direction of the officers, almost striking one. An officer then discharged their weapon and the vehicle fled the scene.”
The killing has drawn comparisons to other instances where Black people lost their lives over accusations of petty criminal offenses, such as the murder of George Floyd.
Attorney Ben Crump, who rose to prominence representing the families of Floyd and other Black people killed by police, emphasized that the officers’ own report says they saw two women and a child get into the car. He questioned why the officer would shoot, knowing there was a kid inside.
“They want us to believe that it was a life-or-death situation,” Crump said at the time of the shooting. “They told us that, but they have not showed us that.”

The band is recognized worldwide as living legends of gospel music. Celebrated by The National Endowment for the Arts and The Recording Academy/Grammys with Lifetime Achievement Awards, inducted into the Gospel Music Hall of Fame, and winners of six Grammy Awards, they have attained the highest levels of achievement in a career that spans over 70 years.
The Blind Boys are known for crossing multiple musical boundaries with their remarkable interpretations of everything from traditional gospel favorites to contemporary spiritual material by songwriters such as Eric Clapton, Prince, and Tom Waits. They have appeared on recordings with many artists, including Lou Reed, Peter Gabriel, Bonnie Raitt, Willie Nelson, Aaron Neville, Susan Tedeschi, Ben Harper, Patty Griffin, and Taj Mahal.
Tickets cost $45-$55; operahouse.org.
CASTLEBAY
Check out Castlebay at 7:30 p.m. Wednesday, Oct. 28, at Camden Opera House, 29 Elm St., Camden.
The duo has been musically weaving together the heritage of New England and the Celtic lands since 1987. Julia Lane and Fred Gosbee have loved and researched traditional music for most of their lives and blend history, legend and experience into their personable performance style.
Their concerts feature poignant ballads sung in Lane’s ethereal soprano and Gosbee’s rich baritone interspersed with joyous dance tunes played on Celtic harp, guitar, fiddle and tin whistle. Castlebay treats the audience to a musical journey through time and across the Atlantic. The duo also presents special theme concerts on various aspects of Celtic lore, nautical life or Colonial America.
For more information about the free concert visit camdenoperahouse.com.

Mark it down: the Black Violin “Be Free” Tour is set to begin at 7:30 p.m. Thursday, Nov. 5, at Johnson Hall Opera House, 280 Water St. in Gardiner.
The tour is a high-energy, genre-defying experience that merges the duo’s classical training with the pulse of hip-hop.
Grammy-nominated duo Wil Baptiste and Kev Marcus invite audiences into a night of boundary-breaking music, where soaring strings, bold beats, and messages of authenticity and self-expression take center stage.
Tickets cost $69.24; johnsonhall.org.

title: No time for banged-up Patriots to recover
text:
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. — The Patriots are testing the boundaries of the “next man up” mentality that is preached across a league in which injuries are guaranteed every week.
New England has just three days to recover coming off a 26-19 win over the New York Jets, during which it lost three offensive linemen to injuries.
Right tackle Morgan Moses (ankle) and left guard Alijah Vera-Tucker (hamstring) were Week 1 starters, while Ben Brown (knee) was starting at right guard for the second straight week. Brown was in the lineup after Mike Onwenu (ankle) was placed on injured reserve after two games and Greg Van Roten, his original replacement, went on IR the following week.
“As bad as it is and as unfortunate as it is, that’s just the way this game goes,” left tackle Will Campbell said. “I feel like some guys stepped up big for us.”
The Patriots, who play at Chicago on Thursday night, are banged up at other spots. Wide receiver Romeo Doubs exited in the first quarter with a shoulder issue following his touchdown catch and was placed on injured reserve Monday. Coach Mike Vrabel acknowledged the injuries will require everyone to remain fluid this week.
“We’ll just have to figure out who we have available and find 48 to put out there,” Vrabel said.
Rookie Caleb Lomu, a week after coming in for Campbell, jumped in at right tackle for Moses, with Walter Rouse subbing in at right tackle and Matt Pryor at left guard.
Lomu, Rouse and Pryor helped open lanes that allowed the Patriots to eventually run out the clock in the fourth quarter.
“Everybody prepares as a starter. I can’t wait to watch those guys that prepare all week without knowing whether they’re going to get an opportunity to play,” Vrabel said. “And then when they do, take advantage of it, and that’s a testament to those players.”
What’s working
Despite the offensive line injuries, the group kept Drake Maye off the turf. The quarterback wasn’t sacked Sunday, the first time that’s happened this season. He has been sacked only twice over the past three games after being taken down nine times in the first three.
What needs help
Ball security. The Patriots are second in the NFL this season with 13 turnovers (six lost fumbles, seven interceptions), behind the Los Angeles Chargers with 15 (seven fumbles, eight INTs).
Fixing that is a top priority.
“We’ll rep it more. We’ll put more time into it, I guess. I don’t know how you can put any more time into the amount of ball security drills we do,” Vrabel said. “I’m certainly cognizant. You can put it on me. That’s probably the easiest thing.”
Stock up
Lomu and Pryor. They allowed zero pressures on Maye during their combined 106 snaps.
Stock down
WR DeMario Douglas. He caught a 9-yard touchdown in the second quarter, but also had a 39-yard catch that ended with him getting the ball ball punched out from behind by Jamien Sherwood. The fumble led to a Jets field goal.
Injuries
The Patriots have moved quickly to replenish the backup depth on the offensive line, adding Andrew Rupcich and Jacob Rizy to the practice squad.
Key number
2 — The number of consecutive games Maye has gone without a turnover.
Next steps
The Patriots have a short turnaround before heading to Chicago for Thursday’s primetime matchup.

title: Politicians have a rich history of telling each other to zip it
text:
According to a 1922 edition of an internal company newspaper of JC Penney (The Dynamo), a husband or wife has “good grounds for divorce” if one tells the other to shut up. Political rivalry, though, is nothing like a marriage.
Given how ugly campaigning has become, I’m not at all perturbed that Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Troy Jackson told Sen. Susan Collins to “shut up” during last week’s Senate debate. It came after a student in the audience yelled out.
Collins could be heard saying over the shouts, “This must be a Troy Jackson supporter.”
Jackson told CNN that Collins “accused me of setting that up. I had no idea who it was. I mean, I was surprised whenever he jumped up out of there. … I just think that was another situation where she was talking down to me.”
Collins told Fox News that Jackson’s response “seemed like such an automatic quick reply” that it struck her as a “very telling” example of his mistreatment of women.
Oh, come on. Sen. Collins has put up with President Donald Trump’s incessant insults toward women with barely a peep. Furthermore, she didn’t seem to register Jackson’s rejoinder as an insult to women on the night it happened.
A glance at history shows this shouldn’t be an issue. In 1969 at the University of Edinburgh, Queen Elizabeth’s patrician husband Prince Philip presided over a meeting that a 22-year-old student disrupted with unwanted questions. The prince wasn’t having it.
“Shut up and grow up,” Philip shouted. Cheers and laughter followed, according to the Associated Press.
Back in 1982, a Republican congressional candidate from California, Gary Arnold, kept interrupting President Ronald Reagan. Fed up, the normally avuncular president pointed at him and told Arnold, “Shut up!”
The GOP audience applauded.
A couple of years later, when Walter Mondale gave a speech during his bid to oust Reagan that a group of GOP backers disrupted. Mondale turned to them and said, “Shut up, will ya!” The place erupted in cheers.
When angry relatives of American military personnel listed as missing in action confronted President George H.W. Bush in 1992, Bush had a quick response to them: “Shut up!”
“I didn’t blow my cool. I just made an emphatic point,” the president later said.
Even as august a figure as Winston Churchill once got so fed up with the heckling of a communist member of Parliament, William Gallagher, that he turned to the Scotsman with a lion’s glare in 1947 and told Gallagher, “Shut up, Moscow!”
Almost nobody criticized Reagan, Mondale, Bush or Churchill for their words.
Honestly, is there anyone who hasn’t wanted to tell a politician: oh, shut up? I’ve certainly had that desire on many occasions. I wouldn’t be surprised to find out I did it a time or two.
My best advice to Jackson? Stop talking about this, stop taking questions about it — and start telling Mainers who you are and what you stand for.

title: Week Seven Is Loaded: 14 County Athletes Battle for Your Vote
text:
Week Seven Is Stacked: 14 County Athletes Battle for Your Vote
Another week of fall sports is in the books, and the latest Athlete of the Week ballots feature some of the biggest performances we have seen as the regular season winds down.
Seven boys and seven girls from across Aroostook County have earned spots on the Fall Week Seven ballots after big scoring games, championship cross country performances and nominations submitted by the people who watched them compete.
Voting is open now. You can vote once per hour in both the boys and girls polls through Thursday at 3 p.m.
The Week Seven winners will be announced Friday morning.
Boys Athlete of the Week Nominees
Conor Schmidt, Katahdin
Schmidt continued his huge offensive season with 7 goals across two reported games. He scored five times in one contest before accounting for both goals in Katahdin’s 2-0 victory over Wisdom.
Aiden Gagnon, Madawaska
Gagnon put together a productive stretch for the Owls with 4 goals and 2 assists across two reported games, including a 3-goal, 2-assist performance.
Drew Lamoreau, Easton
Lamoreau exploded for 4 goals in Easton’s 7-1 victory over Southern Aroostook. His nomination also noted that he has spent much of his high school career playing on the defensive side of the field.
Cooper Willard, Houlton
Willard found the back of the net three times, recording a hat trick in Houlton’s 5-0 win over Schenck/Stearns.
Easton Daigle, Fort Kent
Daigle was nominated after scoring 3 goals over his last three games, becoming an important part of the Fort Kent attack down the stretch.
Preston Lavoie, Wisdom
Lavoie was nominated for his team-first attitude, sportsmanship and support of his teammates. His nomination highlighted the way he celebrates the success of others, including his reaction after a teammate scored, along with his positive attitude and willingness to encourage those around him.
Paxton Darrell, Presque Isle
Darrell turned in a strong postseason cross country performance, finishing third at the PVC Large School Championship in 17:36.09 and leading the Wildcats in a tightly contested team race.
Girls Athlete of the Week Nominees
Emily Lapierre, Van Buren
Lapierre had a huge week for the Crusaders, scoring 6 goals across two games.
She recorded a hat trick against Ashland, including the overtime game-winner, then followed it with another hat trick against Easton.
Ava Ezell, Houlton
Ezell put together another massive offensive performance with 5 goals and 3 assists in one game while also surpassing 150 career goals.
Ellie Cyr, Wisdom
Cyr continued her high-scoring fall with 5 goals across three reported games, including both goals in Wisdom’s 2-1 victory over Katahdin.
Brooklynn Thibodeau, Washburn
Thibodeau earned her place on the ballot after a huge performance against MSSM, finishing the game with 3 goals and 2 assists.
Emily Hallett, Presque Isle
Hallett normally makes her impact as a defensive sweeper for the Wildcats, but she provided one of the more unusual scoring moments of the week when she scored against John Bapst from beyond midfield.
Taylor Lausier, Van Buren
Lausier found the net against MSSM and continued contributing to the Van Buren attack later in the week, earning her a public nomination and a place on the Week Seven ballot.
Emma Stubbs, Southern Aroostook
Stubbs was nominated for the effort and commitment she consistently brings to her team, with her nomination highlighting how she continues to go above and beyond and give maximum effort.
Time to Vote
Week Seven brings together some very different reasons for recognition.
There are multi-goal performances, championship cross country results, defensive standouts and athletes whose teammates and supporters wanted to make sure their contributions did not go unnoticed.
Now it is up to County sports fans.
Vote once per hour in both the boys and girls polls through Thursday at 3 p.m.
The Fall Week Seven Athletes of the Week will be announced Friday morning.

title: Interest in trapping grows in Maine
text:
AUGUSTA — The class gathered in a small clearing, under orange and yellow leaves, and trained their attention on Ronald Fournier. He held a metal cable with a loop on the end, used to trap the paw of a black bear.
“You’re always checking live restraining devices how often?” Fournier asked the group.
“Every day,” nine people said in unison.
“When?” Fournier asked.
“In the morning,” they answered together.
Fournier, recreational safety supervisor for the state Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife, gave a satisfied nod. This class is mandatory for anyone who wants to get a trapping license in Maine. In recent years, the state has seen a surge of interest.
In 2020, Maine had 4,381 licensed trappers, according to department data. By 2025, that number had increased to 5,345.
Fournier surveyed participants to understand the shift and learned that new trappers were less interested in selling fur for profit than they were in decades past. In general, he said, they wanted a trapping license in order to be more self-sufficient, whether they planned to harvest meat for their family or manage pests and predators on their properties.
“The No. 1 choice was to expand on their hunting and outdoor activities and broaden their outdoor skills,” he said. “Right behind that was trapping for personal use to make craft items and garments. People wanted to trap a couple of furbearers to make a pair of beaver mittens or a hat for the family.”
Brian Bernosky, president of the Maine Trappers Association, said trappers used to be more reluctant to share their knowledge because they wanted to guard the tricks that helped supplement their income or they were afraid to encounter people opposed to the practice. Today, he sees a broader culture of mentorship.
“If we don’t share it with everybody and share all the great things we know, we are going to go by the wayside,” said Bernosky, 43, of Bradford.
State rules say that a trapping license is valid from July 1 to June 30 of the following year. Anyone applying for an adult license in Maine needs to prove that they have taken the state course at least once.
Fournier said Maine requires more education than most states in order to get a trapping license. Generally, people need to complete homework in advance and attend a full-day course that includes an exam. The curriculum includes practical and legal information, as well as tips on how to represent trappers well to private landowners and to the general public.
On an overcast Friday in October, Joshua Dostie knelt on the floor of the classroom at the Sportsman’s Alliance of Maine Outdoor Center in Augusta to demonstrate the proper setting of beaver traps. The participants listened as he talked about making ethical choices in the field — how to confirm the presence of beavers in an area, when to move on from a location, how to avoid catching species that aren’t the target and how to make sure the trap will kill the animal immediately so it does not suffer additional stress.
“If we as trappers want to keep our seasons as manageable as they are, we have to make good decisions,” said Dostie, a recreational safety coordinator for the Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife.
Maggie Morgan, 34, of Bowdoinham, joined Dostie and Fournier at the recent course as a volunteer instructor. She used to be a more active hunter, but now prefers trapping in part because it is more flexible around her family’s schedule. She said she is seeing more women and kids in these courses, and her own two children enjoy helping her prepare equipment at home and accompanying her to check traplines.
“If I spend three hours out in the woods deer hunting, I may or may not get a deer,” Morgan said. “Whereas if I spend three hours over the course of a few days tending a trapline, and I get a few beaver, that feeds the family and makes a few hats. I feel like it’s more productive.”
Brooke Blood, of Avon, signed up for the trapper education course because she is interested in becoming a game warden and wanted to build her skills in the outdoors. She was looking forward to learning about species that are less familiar to her, such as beaver or otter.
“I’ve been hunting, but trapping, I don’t have any experience with,” said Blood, 30.
Adam Austin, of Belgrade, got a trapping license more than a decade ago in order to help with animal control at his job, but he hadn’t renewed it or kept up with the practice. One way he plans to use his license is to target the predators that have been killing his chickens for years, but the 51-year-old also wants to spend more time outside after a recent cancer diagnosis and treatment.
“It’s not about the pelts, the money or anything like that,” Austin said. “It’s learning about the animals.”

title: Democrats gain ground with AAPI adults as trust in Republicans fades, AP-NORC/AAPI Data poll finds
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Asian Americans, Native Hawaiians and Pacific Islander adults have become more disillusioned with President Donald Trump and Republicans as the Nov. 3 midterm elections approach, according to a new AP-NORC/AAPI Data poll, giving Democrats a substantial edge on major issues like the economy and health care.
The survey, which was conducted from Sept. 8-15 by AAPI Data and The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research, reveals that Trump’s standing on the economy has fallen among AAPI adults over the course of his second term.
About one-quarter of AAPI adults approve of the way Trump is handling his job as president overall. Only about 2 in 10 approve of his performance on the economy, which the vast majority of AAPI adults see as one of the most important issues for the upcoming election.
But although AAPI adults trust Democrats more than Republicans on a wide range of issues, views of the Democratic Party itself are still split.
Rebecca Larocco, a 45-year-old Korean American in Corning, Iowa, voted for Trump in 2016 and is leaning Republican in the midterm elections. She approves of his immigration policies but is unsure about Trump’s handling of the economy as the Iran war continues to compound gas prices.
“Where I’m at, it’s went up almost $1.50 (a gallon),” she said. “I didn’t expect to go into war at all, that has been definitely unexpected and I’m not sure… I’m just hoping they’ll do what they’re saying and get our economy back on track, get immigration and crime lowered.”
The economy is a top issue for AAPI adults
The economy remains top of mind for an overwhelming majority of the AAPI adult population when they consider the midterms. With the ongoing Iran war affecting gas prices and other costs staying elevated, Americans overall are deeply pessimistic about the state of the economy and see it as a high priority for the midterms. That includes AAPI adults — according to the poll, about 9 in 10 rank the economy as one of the most important issues for the upcoming election, and about 8 in 10 say this about the cost of living.
The economy, the cost of living and healthcare dwarf other issues for AAPI adults. About 7 in 10 AAPI adults say healthcare is one of the most important issues for the election, while only about half say this about foreign policy, crime, immigration, election fairness or climate change.
At the same time, Trump’s economic approval among AAPI adults has dropped about 10 percentage points over the course of the year, and there are other signs his popularity has waned with this group. In late 2024, just after the election, about 4 in 10 AAPI adults had a “somewhat” or “very” favorable view of Trump. That’s fallen to about 3 in 10 now.
“What the data show is that any gains that he made not only during the 2024 election — there was a bit of a honeymoon period that Trump enjoyed after the election before Inauguration Day — that has now largely disappeared,” said Karthick Ramakrishnan, founder and executive director of AAPI Data.
Len Takahashi, 57, of Universal City, Texas, describes himself as conservative but voted for Democrats in the last three presidential elections and for Republicans in midterm elections. For this midterm election, he is simply open to candidates who prioritize the economy.
“I would like policies that look in the best interest of the American public,” said Takahashi, who is Japanese American. “That could be bringing down spending, a balanced budget of U.S. spending, bringing down inflation, working towards a more stable economy and, lastly, just a better atmosphere between the far left and far right.”
AAPIs trust Democrats more on most issues but are not entirely sold on the party
Democrats have gained at Republicans’ expense since Trump returned to the White House when it comes to AAPI adults’ trust in handling many key issues.
In a March 2025 poll, AAPI adults were evenly divided over which political party would better handle the economy and immigration. Now, Democrats have a roughly 20-percentage-point advantage on both issues.
Meanwhile, around two-thirds of AAPI adults have a “somewhat” or “very” unfavorable view of the GOP. Only about one-quarter have a “somewhat” or “very” favorable view.
But while trust in the Democrats on specific issues has increased, AAPI adults are ambivalent about the party as a whole. About half, 48%, of AAPI adults have a “somewhat” or “very” unfavorable impression of the Democratic Party, while 44% have a “somewhat” or “very” favorable impression.
A separate AP-NORC survey of registered voters in September found, similarly, that while voters in general are deeply dissatisfied with Trump and the GOP, few think either party is capable of solving important problems.
Louise Rider, 40, is a Democrat living in Chicago. She believes Democrats are better than Republicans across all issues but says she’s unhappy with how the party has governed.
“I don’t think the Democrats are doing great, I think they need a lot of change as a party,” she said. “It’s kind of a helpless feeling, that nothing will get done with both parties unless there’s major changes.”
Some Republicans still stand behind Trump. James Finley, 74, of Lenox, Massachusetts, said Trump deserves some understanding because he cannot bring down high prices overnight. When it comes to Republicans in general, Finley is a little more critical.
“They’ve had the majority for a couple of years,” said Finley, whose ancestry includes Japanese heritage. “I think they could have done a little bit more or maybe a lot more in terms of passing certain things that I wanted to pass.”
Still, he sticks to the party line and because “all I ever hear from Democrats is to get Trump,” Finley said.
AAPIs concerned about fair midterm elections
As the election approaches, many AAPI adults are worried about problems with misinformation, legal challenges to the results, and voter suppression. About half of AAPI adults say it’s a “major problem” in U.S. elections that people who are eligible are not allowed to vote, while about two-thirds see foreign government attempts to influence results as a “major” problem.
Looking ahead to the November election, about half of AAPI adults are “extremely” or “very” concerned about fake or false information about the candidates, and about half also feel this way about legal challenges to the election results.
Finley is unsure if the voting process can be tightly monitored to prevent undocumented or unregistered people from attempting to vote.
But Takahashi, the conservative from Texas, is worried that Trump will try to manipulate the election.
He’s concerned, he said, that Trump would amplify claims of “fraud in the election system” should the midterms not go in his favor. “(He’ll) make that a point to distract the American public,” he said.
___
Tang reported from Phoenix and Jiang from New York.
___
The poll of 1,023 U.S. adults who are Asian American, Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander was conducted Sept. 8-15, using a sample drawn from NORC’s probability-based Amplify AAPI Panel, designed to be representative of the Asian American, Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander population. The margin of sampling error for all respondents is ±4.7 percentage points. This poll is part of an ongoing project exploring the views of Asian Americans, Native Hawaiians and Pacific Islanders, which are usually not highlighted in other surveys because of small sample sizes and lack of linguistic representation.

text:
Bend school shooting victim's parents hire attorneys to probe school plans and gun purchase
The parents of one of three children killed in last week's shooting at an elementary school in Oregon have hired attorneys to investigate the school's protocols and how the teenage gunman got his weapon.
Rhoam Summer, 5, was one of three children killed along with a teacher in the attack Thursday at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, a mountain-ringed city of about 100,000 in central Oregon. The other two children killed were ages 8 and 11, and a fourth student and another teacher were wounded, police have said.
Related video above: Experts offer advice on additional measures schools could take to prevent or delay a shooter from gaining entry
The attorneys announced the investigation Saturday, saying it will probe various issues, such as whether the school had an active shooter protocol in place and how the gunman, 16-year-old Griffin J. John II, acquired the 12-gauge pump-action shotgun police say he used and where it was originally purchased.
Bend-La Pine Schools Superintendent Steven Cook said Friday that the school district has “invested heavily” in security cameras, door locks, fencing and other security measures.
“We practice lockdowns with students and staff twice a year at every school,” Cook said. “Rest assured, we will take a hard look at everything that we have done, and what more needs to be done to ensure that our students, our staff and our families are safe in our schools.”
Rhoam's parents, Kelik and Lillian Summer, initially hired attorneys Friday to handle media interview requests, Tim Williams, a personal injury attorney in Bend and co-lead counsel for the parents, said in a phone interview. The boy's parents released their own statement remembering their son as strong and kind with a love for rainbows and unicorns along with sharks and dinosaurs.
“He was 5 years old,” the statement said. “He wanted to go to the pumpkin patch, learn to ride horses, learn to play an instrument, and be a bunny for Halloween.”
Of interest is how the shooter, a minor, accessed his weapon, Williams said.
A law enforcement official briefed on the shooting last week told The Associated Press the shooter’s gun was bought by his mother. The official spoke to The Associated Press on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to publicly discuss the investigation.
“We don’t know if the shooter’s mother qualified to own a firearm. We don’t know whether or not the dealer was aware that the firearm was being bought for a minor,” Williams said, adding that there are “various issues there we’re trying to suss out.”
Under Oregon law, a minor may possess a shotgun if provided by a parent or by someone else with the parent’s consent.
The attacker’s mother, Shauntai Nickerson, has not responded to messages from The Associated Press. Nickerson on Friday told some reporters outside her apartment near the school that if she could have done something to prevent the shooting, she would have.
Police said John got into the school by shooting through locked doors. Authorities said he was not currently enrolled in the Bend-La Pine district but had once been a special needs student at the school.
Williams said they are trying to determine "whether the school district is liable or not, and if it is, work with the school district to come to some sort of conclusion, you know, and resolution, ideally safeguarding this from happening again in the future.”
Classes and activities were suspended Monday and Tuesday across the district. No reopening plan has been announced for Silver Rail.

title: UMaine field hockey secures a win on the road
text:
SMITHFIELD, R.I. — On Friday, Oct. 16, the UMaine field hockey team traveled to Rhode Island to take on its conference rival, Bryant University.
Entering the game, the Black Bears stood at a .500 record at 6-6 and 1-1 in conference play. This game would be crucial in staying near the top of the leaderboard for America East, giving the team better positioning as the season moves forward.
The game began at a fast pace, as Maine made it a point to get the offense rolling early, and it executed. Within the first five minutes of game time, the Black Bears scored the opening goal from the stick of fourth-year forward Saylor Kuefler, who scored her fourth goal of the season. The goal was assisted by third-year forward Emily Chisholm.
It was not just the offense that stood out this game; the defensive hero was the first-year goalie from the Netherlands, Annabel Halkes. In the first 15 minutes, Halkes tallied five saves to completely shut down the Bulldogs’ offense in the first period.
The second period was filled with defense from both teams and ultimately led to a slower game in terms of the offense. Bryant only put one shot on goal this period, and it was saved by Halkes once again.
Finally, about 10 minutes into the period, the Black Bears got a goal. Maine scored its second goal shortly before halftime to push the lead to 2-0. The goal came from second-year forward Martha Barrat, for her sixth goal of the season. The goal was once again assisted by Chisholm, for her second of the game.
Maine entered halftime with a 2-0 lead and a masterclass of defense left on the field. The second-half game plan would be to continue the shutout and walk away with the conference win.
When that second half started, both teams struggled, and only one shot on goal was recorded, which was saved by Halkes. The period saw a combined 16 fouls.
The nature of the game spilled into the fourth period, as both teams continued their foul troubles for a majority of the quarter.
With about four minutes left, things heated up for the Bryant attack. The Bulldogs had multiple chances to score and took every opportunity they had with repeated shots on goal. Their gameplay would have given trouble to most goalies, but once again, Halkes stood strong.
The first-year player played masterfully. She made five saves in the span of two and a half minutes, completely stonewalling the Bryant attack and putting the game to bed for a Maine win.
The Black Bears moved to 7-6 with this win and 2-1 in the conference, which is good for a four-way tie for first place in the conference. If the Maine defense persists throughout conference play, the team has a real chance of winning America East this season.
Maine continues its season with a visit to Northeastern and another away conference game against the University of Massachusetts Lowell this week.

title: Strangers came to the rescue when this Maine moose wouldn’t budge
text:
The annual Maine moose hunt is often a family affair, not just for the fellowship and fall fun. These animals are big critters, and once one is down, whether on the edge of a bog or in the middle of a clear-cut, getting it out of the woods and onto a trailer or truck bed “ain’t no easy thing.” A lot of hands and backs can make the job possible, if not easy.
There are almost as many theories about how to get a moose out of the woods as there are moose hunters. It pays to have a plan.
Our friends Becky Unobskey and Scott Hosmer, from Great Pond, invited Mark Cain and me to join their September moose hunt a few weeks ago. Both Mark and I had been on several moose hunts and were familiar with effective extraction methods, or so we thought. My chainsaw-powered winch was supposed to be the ace in the hole.
Although we found plenty of moose sign in Zone 5, saw several cows and calves early in the week and had a couple of bulls hang up just out of range or disappear into thick cover, we just couldn’t close the deal.
Then, on the next-to-last day of the hunt, amid a cold, overcast sky and light drizzle, we got a break. At first light, a medium-sized bull appeared in a clear-cut. Scott Hosmer, Becky’s subpermittee, dropped the animal about 100 yards from the logging road with three shots from his .30-06. The bull weighed 578 pounds field-dressed and had six points. Ideal table fare.
After some celebratory hugs and photos, we began the extraction. For the first 20 yards or so, my chainsaw-powered winch did its job, slowly but surely moving the moose toward the road. No sweat. Then the winch’s carburetor balked. Under the load, the dang thing just wouldn’t take the gas. The moose was still about 50 yards from the road. We considered quartering the animal, which wasn’t a bad option under the circumstances, but Becky really wanted to weigh her first moose at the tagging station and take photos.
While we scratched our heads, a truckload of bird hunters showed up. There’s more than one way to skin a cat — or get a moose out of the woods. Putting our heads together, we attached a heavy rope to the moose, ran it to my truck’s trailer ball and then connected it to the bird hunters’ trailer hitch. It was a makeshift pulley system. Simple geometry, right?
And it worked. The bird hunter slowly drove his truck forward, using the trailer ball on my truck as a fulcrum. Inch by inch, the rope pulled the moose to the road. Slick as a smelt.
As luck would have it, the bird hunters had a Starlink dish atop their truck. It gave us a connection we otherwise wouldn’t have had, allowing us to contact a friend back in town. He agreed to find us using our coordinates and bring a trailer to transport the moose to a meat processor in Crystal.
During the two-hour wait for our friend to arrive, the bird hunters decided to stick around and help us muscle the moose into the trailer. Conversation flowed, mostly about hunting. Before long, a worrisome extraction had turned into a festive gathering on a logging road. One of the bird hunters remarked that it was more fun than driving around looking for birds that didn’t seem to be around.
It was a good day in so many ways. It also reminded me of the old saying that “it takes a village.”
Maine sportsmen tend to be good folks, always willing to lend a hand when others are in need. Our moose hunt was made memorable not only by the bull in the clear-cut, but also by the people who came to our aid: St. Albans residents Michelle and Brian Crocker and Stephen Bubar, and Patten residents Bob Bates and Paul Levesque.

title: Pres. Trump defends decision to pause sanctions
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - With a little over two weeks until Election Day, a number of high-profile Republicans are breaking with President Trump on his approach to Russia and President Vladimir Putin. In many cases, these are Republican senators in unexpectedly tight re-election races.
Before they left town, Congress passed the Lindsey Graham Sanctioning Russia Act of 2026. The provisions were supposed to go into effect late last week. However, before they could, the President signed an executive order waiving the sweeping new sanctions and tariffs against Russia before they were scheduled to take effect.
President Trump wrote on Truth Social over the weekend, “My decision on Russia is a very simple one. I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine, and don’t want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table. Great progress - he said - is being made.”
Before he departed for his latest rally in Wichita, Kansas, President Trump reiterated the message in that Truth Social, telling reporters, “I’m in the midst of negotiating a deal. When you’re negotiating a deal, you don’t do that to the people you negotiate. And the deals to Ukraine deal. Also, I’m negotiating with them on Iran because they’ve been very well behaved on Iran. Also, I’m negotiating with them on hostages. And I’m also negotiating on diesel. So when you when you, that’s my business. When you’re negotiating, you don’t do that.”
But since that decision, Mike Rogers, running to be the next Republican Senator from Michigan, has said he opposes buying Russian diesel fuel. And Senator Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska) as well as Rep. Ashley Hinson (R-Iowa) now running for the Senate- said they too are opposed to buying diesel fuel from Russia
Meanwhile, The Wall Street journal reported over the weekend that Russian President Vladimir Putin has proposed a summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping and President Donald Trump to end the Ukraine war. Ukraine president Volodymyr Zelenskyy is not a part of those plans.
Despite the President’s approach to Russia, diesel prices have remained high. And that has impacted the trucking and farming industries -creating more headwinds for Republicans trying to maintain control of both the House and the Senate.

title: Japan’s new space mission will land on one of Mars' moons, which have long baffled scientists
text:
Mars’ two tiny moons shouldn’t exist. A new mission has launched to reveal their secrets
Mars’ largely unexplored moons are getting their moment in the spotlight now that a first-of-its-kind mission has taken flight.
The red planet has many unsolved riddles, but the Japanese-led Martian Moons eXploration project will focus solely on two of the biggest curiosities orbiting nearby. Phobos and Deimos have long baffled scientists, who have been eyeing the small, lumpy moons for clues about the early days of Mars.
“This is kind of like one of the major outstanding mysteries of solar system formation, the origin of Phobos and Deimos, so we really do need a mission like MMX to figure this out,” said Dr. Daniel Glavin, senior scientist at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, and participating scientist on the MMX mission.
Related video above: New space mission set to explore Mars' moons
Previous Mars missions have observed the peculiar pair whenever convenient. Orbiters circling the red planet have snapped images of the rocky bodies over the years, while rovers including Curiosity and Perseverance have captured some fantastic “googly eye” eclipses when Phobos moved between Mars and the sun. But even after decades of observations, scientists still don’t know how Phobos and Deimos came to be.
“What are these little space potatoes? We can’t explain Phobos or Deimos right now. They shouldn’t exist, but they do,” said Dr. Abigail Fraeman, research scientist at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena, California. “They’re super weird, they’re super small and they’re super puzzling.”
MMX lifted off aboard an H3 rocket from the Yoshinobu Launch Complex at the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency’s Tanegashima Space Center in southwestern Japan’s Kagoshima Prefecture at 3:41 p.m. ET Monday (4:41 a.m. JST Tuesday).
The risky robotic mission is an international collaboration — including scientific instruments from NASA, the European Space Agency, France’s National Center for Space Studies and the German Aerospace Center — that aims to collect more than 0.4 ounces (10 grams) of material from Phobos and return to Earth in 2031.
The detailed observations and samples captured by MMX might reveal the missing pieces to Phobos and Deimos’ origin story — and could even unveil secrets about the red planet itself. If the samples contain pieces of Mars, MMX could potentially be the first mission to successfully bring back Martian material to scientists on Earth in a race alongside China.
Landing on an enigmatic moon
American astronomer Asaph Hall discovered the red planet’s unusual moons in 1877. He named them after the two mythological sons of the Roman god Mars: Phobos, meaning fear, and Deimos, signifying dread.
Phobos is a doomed moon, drawing 6 feet closer to Mars every 100 years. Scientists expect the lumpy rock to crash into the planet in roughly 50 million years or break up into a rocky ring that stays in orbit. The object’s defining feature is Stickney crater — a gaping cavity, about 6 miles wide, that takes up approximately half of the tiny moon’s surface. Thousands of meteorite impacts have also scarred Phobos over time.
Meanwhile, more distant and diminutive Deimos is slowly spiraling away from Mars. The moon has a smoother surface than Phobos but is still heavily pockmarked and covered in a perplexing amount of dust.
Scientists are weighing two leading hypotheses about how these oddballs came to orbit around Mars. One concept suggests that a large object slammed into Mars, launching rocky material that coalesced into Phobos and Deimos, Glavin said. The other hypothesis purports that the two moons are asteroids that came too close to Mars and were drawn in by its gravity.
“None of our data fit either hypothesis correctly,” said Fraeman, who is also a participating scientist on MMX. Japan’s expedition to the enigmatic moons could find new data that supports one of the existing hypotheses or illuminate an entirely different formation backstory, Fraeman added.
The mission will primarily focus on scouting and visiting Phobos, the larger and closer of the two moons to Mars, but along the way it will also take images of Deimos to help scientists better understand similarities and differences between the fraternal moons.
Carrying a small rover named Idefix, the MMX spacecraft — a stack of three modules for propulsion, exploration and returning to Earth — will spend about a year traveling to Mars and then orbit Phobos for about three years.
A suite of instruments aboard the spacecraft’s lander, called the exploration module, will enable scientists to gather a variety of data, including measurements on terrain, minerals, chemical elements and space radiation. Two Super Hi-Vision cameras will take the highest-definition images of Mars and its moons in 4K and 8K.
The spacecraft will first deploy the Idefix rover, developed by the German Aerospace Center and France’s National Center for Space Studies, in early 2029. The robotic explorer will make initial observations that will help mission scientists and engineers determine sites for MMX’s four-legged lander to collect samples directly on Phobos.
The rover will drop from about 131 to 328 feet down to the surface of Phobos; the tiny moon’s weak gravity should cushion its fall and enable the rover to bounce before sticking its landing.
After autonomously releasing its wheels and solar panels and maneuvering into an upright position, Idefix will embark on a 100-day mission. The gravity on Phobos is so weak that Idefix, which weighs roughly 55 pounds, will only weigh about 0.5 ounces during its surface operations.
The drink crate-size rover will scout out areas of scientific interest and potential safe landing spots. The mission team will then select two separate sites for the MMX lander to touch down.
Images taken by current orbiters show that Phobos appears to have one lighter side and one darker side — almost as if it has two different types of surfaces, Glavin said. That’s why the plan is to collect a sample from each of these two regions — on the side of Phobos that faces Mars and the opposite side facing away from the planet, said Dr. Tomohiro Usui, a scientist at the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency, or JAXA, who has worked on the mission for 10 years.
“We’re going to choose a first landing site and then do some landing operations, and after that we’re going to lift off and get back to orbit,” Usui, professor in the department of solar system sciences at Japan’s Institute of Space and Astronautical Science, told CNN. “It takes another several months for the search of the next landing site. Landing operations are very risky.”
The MMX lander has two different ways to collect rocks and dust from Phobos. A coring sampler will drill down 0.8 inches and store the subsurface material in a tube aboard the spacecraft’s sample return capsule. A separate pneumatic sampler will use pressurized gas to kick up surface material and collect it in a tube.
After the samples have been stored aboard the MMX lander, it will lift off, make observations of Deimos and begin the journey back to Earth in 2030.
Insights gained from MMX’s tour of the Martian moons could even aid with the planning of crewed missions to Mars in the future, Usui said.
Revealing Martian secrets
The MMX lander is like a Swiss army knife of many different components, providing scientists various ways to try to decode the mysterious origins of Phobos and Deimos.
Ahead of the samples returning to Earth, researchers will be able to get a sneak peek at initial remote-sensing data beamed back in real time from MMX instruments such as the Mars-moon Exploration with gamma-rays and neutrons spectrometer, or MEGANE.
MEGANE data could reveal signs of volatile elements, or chemical elements with low boiling and melting points, such as hydrogen, sodium and chlorine on Phobos and Deimos, for example. These elemental composition measurements could provide key clues that lend credibility to one origin hypothesis over another, said David Lawrence, planetary scientist at the Johns Hopkins University’s Applied Physics Laboratory and science lead for MEGANE.
“If you had a giant impact, what happens is the materials get very hot, and you will cook off these volatile elements,” Lawrence said. “In contrast, a lot of asteroids that we see have higher abundances of these volatile elements.”
Fraeman, who focused part of her doctoral thesis on Phobos’ composition, will do a combined analysis of MEGANE data and observations captured by the MMX InfraRed Spectrometer, or MIRS. The spectrometer will use near-infrared light to measure minerals, organic matter and water-related substances on Phobos.
Even though the Martian moons are mission priorities, scientists anticipate that MMX’s data will also reveal previously unknown aspects of Mars’ past.
“If Phobos is made from bits of Mars that were thrown up and then recoalesced, that could give us some important new clues about the composition of the planet and what it was like when it was much younger,” Fraeman said.
Even if the rocky neighbor doesn’t contain remnants of Mars, Phobos would be equally intriguing if it’s a captured asteroid or comet — which could have transported water and other volatile elements from the edge of the solar system to Mars’ vicinity, Fraeman said.
If Phobos and Deimos were enriched with water and organics, “that could have been a seed for life on Mars,” Glavin said.
“That’s what I’m particularly interested in: the origin of life. Are we alone? Did it happen on Mars?” he added. “Studying the samples from Phobos and analyzing Deimos as well is part of that whole story.”
Glavin has worked on previous sample collection missions, like OSIRIS-REx, which returned an unexpected wealth of organic material from the near-Earth asteroid Bennu. For MMX, his team will look for amino acids, the molecules that form proteins, and other chemical building blocks of life in the Phobos samples as well.
“Amino acids seem to be literally everywhere we look in the solar system,” Glavin said. “What we’re going to be looking at is differences in the number and complexity of amino acids, but also their relative abundances, which can tell us about their origin.”
Phobos and Deimos likely have existed for billions of years, which means the moons might be witnesses of Mars’ evolution. Given its proximity, Phobos has served as a little dustpan, collecting material that has swept away from the planet’s thin atmosphere.
“There could be pieces of Mars that have landed on the surface of Phobos, much like pieces of Mars have landed on Earth,” Fraeman said. “When we bring samples back from Phobos, there could be little bits of Mars mixed in there.”
MMX is not the only craft racing toward the red planet. China’s Tianwen-3 mission, which aims to launch in 2028 and return samples directly from Mars back to Earth, is also expected to return in 2031.
“The early 2030s could really be banner years of explanation for Mars,” Glavin said.

title: Volunteer quilters make memorial quilts for grieving families visiting Maine
text:
Volunteer quilters make memorial quilts for grieving families visiting Maine
Camp Sunshine sends each family home with a homemade memorial quilt at the end of its bereavement session. Those quilts are made by a talented group of volunteers.
Volunteer quilters make memorial quilts for grieving families visiting Maine
Camp Sunshine sends each family home with a homemade memorial quilt at the end of its bereavement session. Those quilts are made by a talented group of volunteers.
At Camp Sunshine's child bereavement sessions, each family is sent home with a memorial quilt made by a talented group of volunteers. The facility in Casco offers overnight experiences for children experiencing life-threatening illnesses and their families. Families are invited to return for bereavement upon the death of that child.
Betsy Moseley is a longtime volunteer with the camp and the leader of the quilting group. "I do a bunch of sessions, but this is the one I refuse to miss," she said about the bereavement weekend.
“It’s just really amazing," she said. "You look at these pictures, and you just want to cry all day about these poor kids. We turn that into, at least we try to turn that into, a joy.” The volunteers pack into a room on the second floor where they work side by side behind their sewing machines.
On the first day of the session, families fill out a questionnaire about their child's interests and pick the fabric. Golderina Venson picked yellow, pink and teal fabrics she thought her daughter Mahogany Sky would have liked.
“She’s very musical, so we’re looking for things that have music in it," Venson said. "She self-taught herself the piano, so piano things. She was diagnosed at 10, so Mickey Mouse, Minnie Mouse — those types of things she was into as well.”
The volunteers then have two to three days to put it all together before revealing the finished project to the families. Moseley said, "They just cannot give you enough love to let you know how much they appreciate what you’ve done for them and how beautiful their quilts are.”
In the moments between quilting, the volunteers spend their time sewing other items that will be sold in the camp store. Camp Sunshine's director of family engagement said, “They’re just a very big part of everything that we do here at camp, and we couldn’t do it without them.”
Interested volunteers can apply to help with an upcoming session on the camp's website.
