title: Supreme Court denies petition to hear challenge to Maine's gun waiting period
text:
Supreme Court denies petition to hear challenge to Maine's 72-hour gun waiting period
The U.S. Supreme Court will not take up a case that challenges Maine's 72-hour waiting period to purchase a firearm.
The nation's highest court denied a petition filed by gun rights groups, who asked the Supreme Court to review the Boston-based First Circuit U.S. Court of Appeals' prior ruling that said the Maine law is likely constitutional.
The Maine law requires gun sellers to wait 72 hours before giving a firearm to a buyer. It was passed in response to the Lewiston mass shootings that killed 18 people on Oct. 25, 2023. Gun rights advocates have argued the law violates their Second Amendment rights.
The three-day waiting period went into effect in August 2024, but a U.S. District Court judge put the law on hold in February 2025 as he ruled in favor of gun rights groups who filed a federal lawsuit.
In April 2026, the First Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that the law can take effect while the case continues, as it determined that the waiting period does not block people from owning guns and only slows down the process.
"In our view, this likely renders the act a burden on, but not an infringement of, the Second Amendment right to keep and bear arms," the federal appeals court said in its decision.
First Circuit Court of Appeals judges also pointed to evidence lawmakers relied on showing waiting periods can reduce suicides and violence.

title: 13 Maine Halloween happenings for scares and screams
text:
There is no escape from Maine’s scariest season.
No, we’re not talking about tourist season. Halloween is approaching and there are haunted houses, graveyard tours, old horror movies and other scary stuff in cities and towns across the state. Whether you’re in southern York County, on the Midcoast or in Central Maine, it’s easy to find some spooky fun this month.
Here are some suggestions for ways to get your scare on.
Friday-Saturday, and Oct. 30-31. Maine Maritime Museum, 243 Washington St., Bath. mainemaritimemuseum.org
The museums hosts a spooky tour of its Kennebec River campus called “Dead Reckoning: Shipyard Death & Disturbances.” There’ll be a seance in the Donnell House, where unexplained encounters have been reported over the years, and an escape room. There’s also a self-guided walking tour with stories about some of the gruesome working conditions at the historic shipyard that was on the site. Tickets are $25.
‘DRACULA‘
Friday-Saturday. Westbrook Performing Arts Center, 471 Stroudwater St., Westbrook. porttix.com
The Portland Ballet’s professional company presents “Dracula,” based on the 1897 Gothic novel by Bram Stoker, with a score by Rachmaninoff. Because of its mature themes, “Dracula” is recommended for ages 11 and up. Tickets are $35-$45.
Thursday-Sunday, through Oct. 31. TM Wentworth Road, Lebanon. hauntedgrandviewmanor.com
This haunted attraction is a mix of scary trails and creepy buildings, including the Grandview Funeral home, cemeteries, hillbilly shacks and slaughterhouses. Beware the Pig Man, who is always waiting for you. Tickets are $25. There are also “no scare” nights on Thursdays, for $10.
Friday-Sunday, and Oct. 29-31. The Leavitt Theatre, 259 Main St., Ogunquit. leavittheatre.com
This is a haunted tour of the 101-year-old Leavitt Theatre, featuring terrifying clown dens, twisted apothecaries and the infamous Leavitt Chainsaw Massacre. Tickets are $25.
Oct. 30-Nov. 1. Mayo Street Arts, 10 Mayo St., Portland. mayostreetarts.org
Mayo Street hosts a walk-through haunted house full of handmade creatures, sets, sounds and characters. Free, but donations are welcomed.
Oct. 31. Strand Theatre, 345 Main St., Rockland. rocklandstrand.com
This classic horror film from 1933 stars Claude Rains, who mostly appears covered in bandages. It’s a prime example of the power of suspense and how sometimes it’s scarier NOT to see something. Based on the novel by H.G. Wells. Tickets are $12, $9 for seniors and students.
Thursday-Saturday, through Oct. 31. Wallingford’s Orchard, 1240 Perkins Ridge Road, Auburn. wallingfordsorchard.com
Wallingford’s is a peaceful, scenic place to pick fruit – when the sun shines. But at night this time of year, it becomes a nightmare full of creepy creatures and scary structures. It’s a haunted walk “through some of your darkest nightmares.” Tickets are $30.
Saturday. Waterville Opera House, 1 Common St., Waterville. watervillecreates.org
This showing of the classic and campy 1975 film features an opportunity to meet and take photos with actress Patricia Quinn, who played Magenta. She’ll also take questions from the audience. There’ll be a costume contest and a shadow cast performance by the group Rocky for Equality. Tickets are $60-$170.
The film will also be shown, with the same shadow cast, at the Waldo Theatre in Waldoboro on Oct. 30. Tickets are $20-$50.
Friday-Saturday. Johnson Hall Opera House, 280 Water St., Gardiner. johnsonhall.org
This event features ghost stories, unexpected scares and characters from the past taking over the historic opera house. More than 50 community performers, ages 6 to 83, will perform short scenes. Audience members will also travel through Johnson Hall in small groups, moving from one scary scene to another. Tickets are $14.64.
Oct. 22. Old York Museum Center, 3 Lindsay Road, York. oldyork.org
The Old York Historical Society puts on several events each year for its “Spooky Season.” On Thursday people can take a lamp-lit tour of York’s Burial Ground titled “Gone But Not Forgotten: Revolutionary York.” The life stories of 18th century townsfolk will be told by costumed guides. Tickets are $20. There are also a couple of free events for families at the Old York Museum Center, including pumpkin carving on Oct. 29 and trick-or-treating with a pumpkin lighting on Oct. 30.
Friday-Saturday through Oct. 31, plus Oct. 29. Aquaboggan Water Park, 980 Portland Road, Saco. trailofterrormaine.com
This annual haunted walk has been completely revamped and expanded, with new scenes and a 30-minute walk through the woods — unless something makes you run. The terror is still spearheaded by a creature called the Banshee, who has taken over the woods. Scenes are filled with lights, sounds, and creeps lurking everywhere. Tickets are $25, $10 for children 10 and under.
Sunday and Oct. 31. Waldo Theatre, 916 Main St., Waldoboro. thewaldotheatre.org
Before Vincent Price did the scary narration on Michael Jackson’s hit song “Thriller,” he was a longtime star of horror films. The Waldo Theatre is hosting a festival in his honor, including a screening of the 1963 film “The Raven,” an irreverent take on Edgar Allan Poe’s classic poem, directed by Roger Corman. Tickets are $12, $9 for seniors and students.
On Oct. 31, Everyman Repertory Theatre presents a staged reading of a new play called “I Know It’s Gruesome, But is It Art? The Vincent Price Murder Case.” It’s set in the 1960s in the London art scene, during the filming of a Price film called “Witchfinder General.” Tickets are $20.
WALK AMONG THE SHADOWS
Thursday-Sunday. Eastern Cemetery, 224 Congress St., Portland. Spiritsalive.org
This is a nightly tour of Portland’s oldest cemetery, established in 1668. Costumed actors will bring long-dead folks to life and tell some of the city’s dramatic stories, including the destruction of Fort Loyall in 1690 by French and Inidgenous forces, an 1893 reservoir break on North Street, Benjamin Tukey’s ill-fated celebration of the American victory at Saratoga and the 1647 Mary Martin infanticide case. Adult tickets are $10 cash or $12.51 on Eventbrite.

title: Cuddledown
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Our Roots
Founded in Yarmouth, Maine, during the 1973 energy crisis, Cuddledown began by manufacturing European-style down comforters to help New Englanders combat rising heating costs. What started as a local operation quickly scaled into a national brand through catalogs and e-commerce, as well as partnerships with luxury hotels and resorts.
Commitment to Quality & Sustainability
Today, our purpose remains the same as it was in 1973: a commitment to exceptional quality manufacturing and a passion for creating better sleep. We source the finest materials from around the world and combine them with thoughtful, hands-on craftsmanship in our Maine factory. Our luxury down bedding, including exceptional high-end fills such as eiderdown, sets Cuddledown apart with a level of quality and expertise rarely found in the industry. Our OEKO-TEX® and RDS certifications further reflect our commitment to responsible sourcing and manufacturing. From down and synthetic comforters in a range of warmth levels and sizes to more than 30 styles of pillows and our featherbeds, our broad product offering is designed to meet the needs of discerning hospitality partners, retailers, and customers.
Driving Maine’s Economy
We’re proud to call Maine home while supporting nearly 60 employees at our Yarmouth factory and business offices, as well as our Freeport Outlet store. Many of our team members have been with us for decades, a reflection of the strong relationships and shared commitment at the heart of our business. We’re proud to make premium-quality bedding here in Maine and to work alongside other Maine businesses through Cuddledown Wholesale, partnering with hundreds of local inns, resorts, hotels, retailers, and interior designers. Together, we help support the communities and economy we’re fortunate to call home. We’re also proud to supply comfortable bedding in support of the Maine-based Travis Mills Foundation and its inspiring work helping veterans and their families.
Looking Ahead
As we look to the future, we’re excited to continue growing Cuddledown and the partnerships that have helped make our business what it is today. We see tremendous opportunity to grow alongside our Maine business partners while expanding our relationships across the country. And as that growth continues, so will our commitment to manufacturing in Maine. Over the next three years, we plan to expand our manufacturing capabilities with new machinery, creating additional opportunities for Maine jobs while allowing us to continue making the quality bedding our customers and partners have come to expect.

title: ‘This is a business decision’: Kansas farmer says Trump policies cost Republicans his vote
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
‘This is a business decision’: Kansas farmer says Trump policies cost Republicans his vote
Economic challenges, including high diesel prices and tariffs, are causing frustration among farmers, with some reconsidering their support for Republicans as President Trump visits Kansas to rally voters.
‘This is a business decision’: Kansas farmer says Trump policies cost Republicans his vote
Economic challenges, including high diesel prices and tariffs, are causing frustration among farmers, with some reconsidering their support for Republicans as President Trump visits Kansas to rally voters.
President Donald Trump traveled to Kansas on Monday to rally Republican voters ahead of the midterm elections, as rising operating costs and shrinking profits fuel frustration among some farmers, a traditionally reliable Republican constituency.
The economic pressures are raising concerns about voter turnout in a state Trump won by 16 percentage points in 2024, where Republican Sen. Roger Marshall faces a challenge from Democrat Adam Hamilton.
For Kansas seed farmer Vance Ehmke, the financial impact has been substantial.
"God only knows what we've lost in terms of tariffs. But with the diesel fuel costs right now, that's $50,000 in counting," Ehmke said in an interview with Hearst Television.
Ehmke said he's a registered Republican who never voted for Trump, but he blames the administration's trade and foreign policies for contributing to his financial challenges. He says his frustration is now affecting how he plans to vote in November.
"Stand by Trump, and you have lost my vote," Ehmke said, directing his message at Sen. Roger Marshall and other Republicans who support the president. "This is a business decision. I'm a Republican, but I'm also a farmer. And we're looking at the consequences of those policies to our business and just very, very, very bad news."
The financial challenges extend beyond one farm. The U.S. Department of Agriculture projects nationwide net farm income will fall 5.5% this year after adjusting for inflation, while production expenses are expected to rise 4.5% before inflation. Fuel and oil expenses alone are projected to increase nearly 30%.
Despite the expected decline, inflation-adjusted net farm income is forecast to remain above its 20-year average.
The Kansas Farm Bureau's political action committee has endorsed Marshall for reelection, but the organization's president, Glenn Brunkow, told the Associated Press that economic frustration could discourage some farmers from voting, even if they have no plans to support Democrats.
Ryan Flickner, the Kansas Farm Bureau's senior director of advocacy, said some farmers have already decided how they'll vote while others are still weighing the economic challenges.
"Other cases, they really are experiencing some pain at the pump or some pain in purchasing those input goods, and they're ultimately going to have to wrestle with that decision on who to vote for here in the last three weeks," Flickner said.
As Trump prepared to leave the White House for Kansas, Hearst Television asked Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins what she would say to farmers reconsidering their Republican support because of rising costs.
"Well, I think what's really important, there's never been a more pro-farmer, pro-rancher president than this one," Rollins said.
Rollins defended the administration's agricultural policies, arguing Trump inherited a farm economy struggling with higher production costs and a growing agricultural trade deficit.
"We have now cut that in half. Input prices are coming down," Rollins said, referring to the trade deficit.
The administration has also taken steps to provide financial assistance.
In December, it announced a $12 billion aid package for farmers. Earlier this month, Trump signed an executive order easing restrictions on the tax-free use of red-dyed diesel in agriculture.
Federal payments to farmers are projected to increase nearly 70% this year, reaching $47.4 billion, according to the USDA. Even with that assistance, inflation-adjusted farm profits are expected to decline.
Rollins acknowledged that farmers continue to face financial pressures, particularly during harvest season.
"So yes, diesel prices especially, are certainly high right now. The farmers are at harvest," Rollins said.
She also indicated that additional short-term assistance could be announced Monday night.
"Tonight, we'll have a quick announcement," Rollins said, referring to a possible short-term solution for farmers.
When pressed for details about what that relief might include, Rollins did not elaborate.
The potential announcement comes as Republicans work to maintain support among rural voters ahead of the Nov. 3 elections, with the economic challenges facing farmers adding another issue to the debate in Kansas and other agricultural states.

title: Houlton Band of Maliseet Indians endorses Troy Jackson in U.S. Senate race
text:
HOULTON, Maine (WABI) - The Houlton Band of Maliseet Indians has endorsed Democrat Troy Jackson for U.S. Senate.
Tribal Chief Clarissa Sabattis announced the endorsement in a statement Monday, praising Jackson’s record on tribal sovereignty as Maine Senate President.
“From championing clean drinking water initiatives to his role in creating the commission to reexamine the 1980 Maine Indian Claims Settlement Act, Troy has consistently proven that he listens to indigenous voices and stands with the Wabanaki people. The council of Houlton Band of Maliseet Indians and myself are proud to endorse a leader who respects our inherent sovereignty and will carry that fight directly to Washington,” Sabattis said.
In a statement, Jackson said, “When the Wabanaki Nations have a vibrant economy, health care, infrastructure and educational opportunities, all of rural Maine benefits.”
The endorsement comes after the Pleasant Point Passamaquoddy Tribe announced its support for incumbent Republican Sen. Susan Collins.

title: Aging Untold: Here’s what you should know if you’re raising grandkids full-time
text:
(Aging Untold) — On this episode of Aging Untold, we look into the emotional and financial realities grandparents face when stepping in to raise their grandchildren full-time.
We also examine the root causes of nurse burnout, hear how two frontline caregivers launched a program to help colleagues heal and discuss what needs to change to keep experienced nurses at the bedside.
Finally, we meet a Vermont retiree whose passion for playing and repairing accordions turned into a thriving second act.
If your role has shifted from being a grandparent to full-time, day-in, day-out parenting of your grandchildren, the transition can bring deep love and purpose — but also real stress on time, money and energy.
The Aging Untold experts are breaking down what you need to know and the resources available.
“You’ve got to give yourself grace to get through this,” gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said.
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke said one of the first practical steps grandparents should take is establishing legal guardianship.
Oregon is facing a nursing crisis. Experts say it is not from a lack of licensed nurses, but from workplace conditions that drive healthcare workers away from frontline positions.
Registered nurse Heather Sweeney and therapist Amy Ponteri started “Helping Healthcare Heal” to address what they saw as insufficient resources for health care workers in intense settings like emergency rooms.
More than one factor contributes to nursing burnout. Workload, staffing shortages, safety concerns, documentation demands and the loss of meaningful connection with patients are all pushing experienced nurses away from the bedside, according to the Aging Untold experts.
We talked about what nurses are facing — and what hospitals and health care systems could do to help them stay in a field they entered to care for people.
Nathan Longo plays an Italian accordion from the early 1960s, and he also repairs accordions in a small workshop.
He said he is better at fixing the instruments than playing them.
What began as something to do in retirement has turned into a 30-hour-a-week job.

title: The New? Interpol Tests New Sound with Its Latest Album
text:
Avid music listeners may have noticed a trend of late: this past summer has been one filled with new albums coming from bands who got their start in the early 2000s. The Strokes, Arctic Monkeys and now Interpol have each added to their discography this summer, amongst many others.
Interpol’s new album, This Mirror Weighs a Ton, stands as the New York-based post-punk band’s contribution to this year’s new sounds.
Released Aug. 28, 2026, This Mirror Weighs a Ton has reinvigorated interest in the band, helped to kick off their ongoing tour, and largely earned the appreciation of critics, which is certainly no small feat.
Slow drumming that sounds as if it was played through water opens the eponymous lead track of the album before frontman Paul Banks joins in with his characteristic vocals.
“See Out Loud” follows “This Mirror Weighs a Ton” as Banks adopts his classic, slightly distraught singing over spacey guitar work. Mixed with the boxy bass and drums, this second track represents a resurgence of a sound more typical of Interpol.
“Iron City” follows “See Out Loud” and brings back the more produced sound of the first track while “Wounded Soldier” slows the album down again and strips it back to a sound more like “See Out Loud.”
The remaining songs all continue to present a refreshing play between the more experimental, electronic sound championed by the lead-off song on this new album and a more bare-bones sound that recalls Interpol’s rise to prominence in 2002 with their debut album, Turn on the Bright Lights. After this gold-selling album, Interpol went on to release another six albums before This Mirror Weighs a Ton, with the most recent coming out in 2022.
Across these six intervening albums, Interpol largely kept to the sound which had brought them to fame in 2002. The characteristic straining guitar paired with bulky basslines (pioneered by the legendary Carlos D, who left the band after their third album) and Banks’ desolate voice and lyrics have become beloved by many over the past 24 years.
In contrast, This Mirror Weighs a Ton represents a new direction and a new sound. While This Mirror Weighs a Ton is certainly an enjoyable album which anyone should be happy to listen to, when listening to this most recent release and then playing Turn on the Bright Lights, it becomes clear which I’d rather listen to.
While This Mirror Weighs a Ton has kept much of the introspective, thought-provoking style and is certainly a good album, its electronic and more chaotic sound falls short of the more existentialist, stripped-down style for which Interpol has earned a spot as one of the most influential post-punk and 21st century rock bands.
Put simply, This Mirror Weighs a Ton is an altogether enjoyable experience but Turn on the Bright Lights is a majestic experience.

title: Check Your Fridge: Kayem Products From March Through October Under USDA Recall
text:
What Mainers Need to Know About a Massive Recall of Kayem Meats
A variety of Kayem ready-to-eat meats have been recalled after reports that they may have been stored at the wrong temperature.
Kayem Meats Issues a Huge Recall of Ready-to-Eat Meats
After working in a deli for several years, I'm very particular about the meat I serve. If it's the least bit questionable, I'll throw it out rather than risk making people sick.
So I was very interested when I read about this massive recall of Kayem meats that the USDA says may not be safe.
READ MORE: Maine Harvest Festival Returns to Bangor
The products are RTE, or ready-to-eat meats, like hot dogs, bologna, bacon, kielbasa, chicken sausage, and more.
Kayem Meats Recalled After Being Stored at Inappropriate Temperatures
According to the USDA recall, these Kayem products distributed from Chelsea, Massachusetts, were stored in a refrigerator that experienced temperature deviations.
The Kayem products in question were produced between approximately March 31, 2026, and October 7, 2026.
That means if you bought any Kayem products over the summer, it's probably part of this recall.
USDA Has Lists of UPCs and Product Pictures for International Kayem Meats Recall
People are urged to check their refrigerators and freezers for Kayem meats with a UPC that appears on this long list of recalled products.
You can find pictures of the affected meats on the USDA website.
I looked through the pictures and realized the 'Old Tyme Red' hot dogs in my refrigerator may be part of this recall.
Anyone with Kayem products listed in the worldwide recall should throw the meat away or return it to the store for a full refund.
So far, the USDA says no one has reported getting sick from the affected products.

title: The Maine Forest Service: 135 years of stewardship
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
COURTESY OF THE MAINE FOREST SERVICE
With almost 90% of the state forested, it may be hard to believe that Maine woodlands have been harvested for over 300 years. However, over 17 million acres of Maine forests stand as a testament to the benefits of responsible stewardship. Long before the state’s founding, they have been integral to a web of natural resources that shape the culture, economy, and identity of the people who live here. For 135 years, the Maine Forest Service (MFS) has worked alongside these forest stewards to protect that legacy.
“Maine is the most forested state in the nation. Everybody here depends on our forests,” said MFS Director Patty Cormier. “They’re part of all our lives, whether we realize it or not.”
In the earliest days of what would become MFS, Forest Commissioners’ Reports provided an overview of wildfires and fire prevention, reflecting the agency’s core mission. Foreshadowing evolving needs, these reports also discussed forest health and conditions and provided stewardship advice for landowners.
Today, the MFS Forest Policy and Management Division (FPM) is dedicated to helping landowners and others steward Maine’s forests. Providing accessible, reliable, and objective guidance is core to its mission.
“Our cornerstone is providing information on everything related to trees and forests,” FPM Division Director Morten Moesswilde said. “We assist folks in the field every day: a logger who wants input on their operation, private consulting foresters who need another set of eyes, and especially woodland owners of every background. We offer technical guidance to anyone.”
From Fort Kent to Kittery, the Division’s ground efforts are led by District Foresters. These 12 professionals work in every Maine community, meeting with landowners, loggers, foresters, nonprofit organizations, students, and community members to inform and inspire science-based stewardship. The heart of the work is a “walk-and-talk,” an in-person meeting that helps define and reach landowner goals.
“Some people want woodlands to provide income, and others just want a quiet place to take a walk,” said District Forester Julie Davenport, who serves across Franklin and Kennebec counties. “My job is to help them understand their property, determine what could work, and connect them with the people and information they need to make that happen. Ultimately, I hope to make connections between people and forests that last.”
The forests being managed today took root generations ago. Tending them requires a long-term perspective. MFS also anticipates changes and promotes policies that support landowners and businesses far into the future. Through research, monitoring, and targeted program management, MFS informs decision-makers and the public about forest conditions and their impact on forest products, recreation, water quality, and wildlife.
Today, Maine’s forests face new challenges as the state’s population and people’s connections to the woods change. Climate change and shifts in global forest products markets are also shaping how forests are managed and how they support local jobs and communities.
“Maine is facing issues that require thoughtful approaches that draw from deep perspectives,” Cormier said. “Fortunately, we have a 135-year-long history of rising to the challenge of protecting our forests, forest economy, and the people that depend on them.”

title: Trade dispute bars liquor delivery through Maine to Canadian island
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Harvey Newman, his wife Brenda and their company, Island Trucking, are a lifeline for the residents of Campobello Island.
Newman, 73, has been transporting all manner of goods from the New Brunswick mainland via Maine since he was 17. Their bonded truck is essentially the only way to get goods from the rest of Canada to Campobello when the limited seasonal ferry from Deer Island isn’t running, and it runs only four or five months each summer. Additionally, their bond makes it possible for other companies to deliver building materials, groceries, dairy products, plumbing and electrician services and more to the island.
Normally, their operation works like a well‑oiled machine. The Newmans report having great relationships with the U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) officers in Calais and Lubec, and their cargoes routinely transit from Calais to Lubec and back into Canada at Campobello without incident.
That was not the case, though, on Tuesday, September 29, when Newman stopped at the U.S. border in Calais. Just as he does every day, he reported at the CBP office and presented his bill of lading to the officer, expecting his truck to be sealed for transit through Maine. But that Tuesday was different. At midnight, the Trump administration’s latest salvo in the trade war with Canada took effect, and Newman was caught in the crossfire. On board his truck he had four pallets of Canadian alcoholic beverages destined for the grocery store on the island. Imports of Canadian alcohol into the U.S. were blocked by the new regulations, and the CBP officers interpreted the law as saying that the alcohol could not go through, even though it wasn’t being imported.
After lengthy but cordial discussions and appeals to higher authorities and still no resolution, Newman made the decision to turn his truck around, reenter Canada and return via Deer Island. Brenda Newman completed various U.S. customs forms, and he set out, finally reaching Campobello at 3 p.m., much later than usual. The booze made it to Campobello, but that wasn’t Newman’s biggest concern that day.
He could have unloaded the alcohol in Canada and returned through Calais with the rest of the load. But that would have taken too long. Along with the alcohol, the truck was carrying Canada Post mail as well as a large delivery of prescription medicines and vaccines that had to get dispensed without delay at both the health center and Campobello Lodge, the local nursing home. So Newman went via Deer Island to ensure delivery that day.
As Brenda Newman worked through the documentation, she left a message for Harvey Matthews, mayor of Campobello, informing him of the incident and of their work around.
John Williamson, the member of Parliament for Charlotte Southwest, upon hearing from the mayor, reached out to Global Affairs Canada and to U.S. Ambassador Pete Houkstra. Susan Holt, premier of New Brunswick, and various other officials have also been involved in discussions, negotiations and press statements to address the issue.
By 4 p.m. on Thursday, October 1, the situation appeared to be resolved and Newman was told that alcohol can once more transit via Maine to Campobello on his truck. However, there has yet to be any formal announcement or press release.
Williamson, pointing out that he is the only MP in Canada who must travel through a foreign country to reach some of his constituents, comments that Campobello is “a piece of territory in this country that isn’t being provided services that are available everywhere else in Canada.” The incident renewed calls by politicians and the public for a year‑round ferry to Campobello from the New Brunswick mainland.
This isn’t the first time that CBP has interfered with Island Transport’s truck. In 2019 Canada Post packages, sent via the bonded truck, were being opened and searched by CBP officers.
At that time, a public affairs officer for CBP stated that CBP officers “possess broad search authority to ensure the safety and admissibility of all goods entering the United States. This includes the ability to inspect and search all persons, baggage and merchandise arriving in – or transiting through – the United States.”
The current situation drew international attention. Newspapers, TV channels and the internet spread the story far and wide. Rumors, false and inaccurate information abounded. Millions of viewers, readers and listeners heard the news, and commentary circulated widely. But Brenda Newman was surprised that “not one politician nor any press took the time to contact us to learn what really happened.”
Campobello Value Foods, reacting to the uncertainty generated by all the news coverage, elected to have another supplier make its delivery via ferry the next day, at additional expense to avoid any stock outages.
Canada’s Privy Council Office was asked for comment on the steps being taking by the Canadian government in response to this situation. As of this writing, there has been no response apart from “we received your request and are working on it.” However, in an earlier email to another news source they stated, “The Government of Canada is assessing the implications of the new U.S. import restrictions for this supply route and is working with partners, including relevant U.S. authorities and the Government of New Brunswick, to determine next steps to support reliable access to essential goods, services and mail for the residents of Campobello Island.”
Regardless, Island Trucking has been making its scheduled run each day since the incident without any issues.

title: Maine voters must choose between listener and lecturer
text:
Brenda Power is a retired educator who lives in Ellsworth. She received the UMaine Distinguished Professor award in 1999.
I attended a town hall meeting of Troy Jackson’s in Ellsworth and witnessed a remarkable exchange.
A young woman stood up and said to Troy, “I want to support you. But I am an immigrant. I watch your campaign ads. You talk about the logging blockade in the 1990s, and how you worked so hard to keep foreigners from taking Maine jobs. How do I know you will support and help people like me, and not see me as a foreigner taking a Maine job?”
Her voice was shaky and lightly accented. Everyone could see how much courage it took for her to stand up and ask her question.
Troy paused. You could tell he was as moved as the audience by the question. He responded, “Thank you for speaking up. I’m sorry.”
He then explained how it was never his intention to castigate the Canadian workers. He saw the problem at that time as the same one we face today throughout Maine and the U.S. — large, wealthy corporations in Canada were using their workers as pawns.
He said he would have supported those Canadian workers immigrating to Maine for a better life, and was dedicated to finding pathways for immigrants in Maine, because we desperately need and want immigrants here. He vowed to look at the ad and improve his message, and thanked her for identifying a problem he needed to address.
After the session ended and most everyone left to partake in the pizza provided, Troy made a beeline to that woman for a private conversation. I noticed Troy mostly listened. At the end, he pulled out a contact card and wrote down a personal cellphone number, urging the woman to call if she wanted to continue the dialogue.
I couldn’t help but contrast that exchange with another I read about recently.
The last conversation Sen. Susan Collins had with Maine Planned Parenthood representatives was reportedly almost eight years ago, just weeks before the Kavanaugh vote. Nicole Clegg, the head of the Maine Planned Parenthood Action Fund, flew down with a small group of Maine women to D.C. in early August 2018, all of whom either worked with Planned Parenthood, or had received abortion care.
When they sat down to talk with Collins, they were stunned when she gave them little time to share their stories. As Clegg explained, “Before we could even have these women share their experiences, Senator Collins wanted to share her displeasure at the fact that during Colby [College’s] graduation ceremony, where she was the speaker, many Colby students wore ‘I Stand with Planned Parenthood’ stickers. That set the tone for the meeting. I left deeply regretful that I had asked these women to come down and do this. Because it was clear to me it did not have an impact. I actually communicated to their office to say ‘I can’t bring constituents into this space if I don’t think they are going to be respected.’”
Planned Parenthood of Maine has not had a conversation with Collins since.
These Maine women all showed great courage. One is an immigrant who worries any step outside her Maine home might bring her face to face with ICE. Yet she comes to a town hall to confront a candidate because she wants to understand his views and share her experience. The others flew to D.C. to share deeply personal trauma with a powerful legislator who was supposed to be their voice in Congress. One person listened. The other lectured.
It’s no wonder Troy Jackson has evolved in his views over the past 15 years, leading the Maine Legislature to pass one of the most thoughtful abortion rights laws in the country. And it’s also no wonder Susan Collins has “evolved” to support militant anti-abortion judges.
I hope Maine voters will also show some courage in the coming weeks. We have a choice to vote for someone who shows up and welcomes those who challenge him so that he can become a better representative. Or we can vote for the senator who hasn’t held a town hall in 25 years, preferring to lecture those who challenge her in private. The choice couldn’t be more clear.

title: Why experienced nurses are leaving — and what could bring them back
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(Aging Untold) — The emotional weight of nursing can be immense, but burnout is not caused by one factor alone. Workload, staffing shortages, safety concerns, documentation demands and the loss of meaningful connection with patients are all pushing experienced nurses away from the bedside.
The Aging Untold experts are exploring what nurses are facing — and what hospitals and health care systems could do to help them stay in a field they entered to care for people.
Nursing has become more demanding — and less personal
For many nurses, the pressure begins with the number of patients they are expected to care for. When staffing does not keep pace with demand, nurses can feel overwhelmed before they have a chance to provide the personal care that drew them to the profession, the Aging Untold experts say.
“There’s no way you can have adequate care when you have this short staff and you’re not replenishing that. It’s so easy to get burnout,” Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said.
Rogers recalled a time when nurses offered guidance and encouragement to physicians in training, creating a more personal, supportive environment. She said that sense of connection can be difficult to maintain when the system focuses primarily on numbers and patient volume.
Safety concerns add to the strain
Nurses also may face unsafe situations on the job, including violence from patients and the risks that can come with treating people in emergency settings.
Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, said she did not have a difficult time recruiting nurses because they wanted to get out of the hospital.
One nurse told O’Rourke that a patient grabbed her by the throat and shook her during the COVID-19 pandemic.
“She was scared to death and the hospital didn’t seem to take enough action. Well, who could blame her for leaving?” O’Rourke said.
“Sam” Cradduck, a gerontologist, said safety issues can be especially complicated in hospital emergency rooms, where nurses may encounter patients with serious injuries as well as people connected to violent incidents.
Delirium and hyperconfusion among older patients can sometimes lead to combative or violent behavior, which can create another layer of stress for nurses who are already working under pressure, Cradduck added.
When care becomes a transaction
“Care is about a relationship, not a transaction,” Cradduck said. “And unfortunately, the system has created transactional relationship instead of the relationship.”
Nurses often enter the field because they want a meaningful career centered on helping others. But administrative demands and a growing focus on documentation can make the work feel increasingly transactional, the experts say.
Documentation can pull nurses away from patients
O’Rourke described a familiar conflict: A patient needs help getting out of bed or going to the bathroom, but the nurse also has charting requirements to complete. Electronic medical record systems can change, adding new training and documentation demands to an already full workload.
The result can be a difficult choice between being present with a patient and keeping up with the records, forms and insurance-related requirements that surround care.
Nurses need meaningful support after trauma
The COVID-19 pandemic exposed many weaknesses in the health care system, but the underlying problems existed before the pandemic, Cradduck said.
Cradduck said nurses witnessed deaths and worked through sustained pressure — yet the response was not always equal to the trauma they experienced.

title: Rooted in the game: How Maine trees power America's pastime
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WRITTEN BY DYLAN SAVAGEAU
Maine hardwood finds its way into countless products, from flooring and furniture to more distinctive items — like baseball bats. During the two seasons I worked at Dovetail Bat Company, I had a firsthand look at nearly every stage of the process. Tree-length logs arrived at the yard and passed through a series of transformations, being cut into 40-inch sections, shaped into billets, and eventually turned into the finished bats swung by major leaguers and little leaguers alike on fields all over the world.
There were only 10 people working at the company when I was there, including then-owners Paul and Theresa Lancisi. My job titles covered about as much ground as the shop itself: bat turner and lathe operator, wood cutter, billet maker, kiln operator, finisher, and tractor operator. In a small shop, you do whatever needs doing.
Dovetail Bat Company works primarily with three Maine hardwoods: rock maple, yellow birch, and white ash. Each has its own characteristics, but all three have to meet the same basic requirements. The grain needs to be straight, and the wood has to be free of defects that could compromise the durability of the finished bat.
But the process actually begins long before a log reaches the Dovetail yard.
“Foresters are the start of our extremely important supply chain,” explained Ben Chase, CEO of Dovetail Bat Company. “They decide which trees get harvested and how they’re handled. By the time a log reaches us in Shirley, its quality is largely fixed.”
Where the tree grew, how it was cut, and how it was handled afterward can all affect the yield and grade of the billets.
A bat log is a different product than a veneer log, saw log, or pulpwood, so getting the right material depends on the people making those decisions in the woods.
The logs are split before being sawn with a laser-guided system that follows the grain. The target is a grain slope of between zero and three degrees.
That number might not mean much to somebody walking through the shop. But it means plenty to the players using the bats.
A defect in the wrong place could send a piece of wood down a very different path. When I was there, the worst material was bundled and sold as firewood. Pieces that were sound enough for a bat but didn’t meet Major League or Minor League specifications would become tournament or batting-practice bats, sold at a lower price.
Chase put it this way: “A tree can be perfectly good lumber with a slight spiral or slope in the grain, but that same tree can produce a bat that breaks.”
Once the wood is cut and split, the next job is getting it through the kiln.
The wood is stacked between heavy metal plates and dried for 14 days. I remember those plates being heavy, hot, a pain to move, and loading and unloading them was some of the more physically demanding work in the shop’s process.
After drying, the wood is turned into cylindrical billets, then graded, weighed, and stored in a climate-controlled room. At that point, a piece of Maine hardwood has become the raw material for a baseball bat.
Once a billet is ready, a high-tech CNC machine cuts the initial outline of the bat. From there, we would take over at the lathe, measuring the entire profile and sanding the bat down to the exact specifications for a particular model or player. Every bat has its own dimensions, and getting those measurements right was critical to producing a bat that met the required specifications.
The final steps included sanding and a traditional bone-rubbed process. Rubbing the barrel with a bone compresses the wood’s pores, helping to harden the surface before the bat moves on to the finishing stages.
All of the bats we made were built to professional-quality standards, but Major League Baseball had additional requirements. Grain straightness, barrel size, and paint specifications were more exacting at the Major League level.
That extra scrutiny makes sense. A baseball bat has a pretty demanding job. It has to take repeated, hard contact from some of the faster throws and strongest swings in the game without failing.
By the time I was working there, Dovetail bats were already being used by Major League players. The company made its MLB debut in 2014 with the pennant-winning Kansas City Royals, and Pete Alonso used Dovetail bats during his record-setting 2019 rookie season with the New York Mets.
That season gave me one of the strangest experiences of working at Dovetail Bat Company. I watched Alonso use one of our bats in the 2019 Home Run Derby and more in the All-Star Game, and watched Jeff McNeil swing a Dovetail in the All-Star Game as well. Alonso went on to win the Derby and was named National League Rookie of the Year while also leading the MLB in home runs with 53 that season, breaking the all-time rookie home run record.
I had watched those bats being made in a shop in Shirley, Maine. And then they were on national television.
I started watching a lot more baseball while I worked at Dovetail because I wanted to see how many of our bats I could spot. Teams I never thought I’d give my time to started becoming a blast to watch. Growing up a Red Sox fan, I started paying attention to the whole league. It also made the connection between baseball and Maine’s working forest pretty hard to miss.
Maine is a forest state, with trees covering nearly 90 percent of its land. A 2024 analysis estimated that the forest products industry contributes $8.3 billion to the state’s economy and supports more than 29,000 jobs.
Most people probably think of Maine forest products as lumber, paper, pulp, or firewood. A baseball bat is a much more specialized product, but the basic idea is the same: take a resource grown in the working forest and add value to it through skilled labor and manufacturing.
Maple, birch, and ash each have their own characteristics. The differences aren’t necessarily obvious to somebody walking through the shop. After enough time around the wood, though, you learn what you’re looking at.
You learn to notice grain. You learn to spot defects. You learn that a piece of wood can look perfectly good and still not be the right piece of wood for a baseball bat. Eventually, you start looking at trees a little differently.
A section of Maine hardwood can become a billet, then a piece of sporting equipment used by a player in front of millions of people around the world. That’s a long way to travel for a tree.
I still think about the logs coming into the yard, the heat coming off the kiln plates, the noise of the lathe even through my headphones, and the rows of finished bats waiting to leave Shirley.
Most of the work was physical, repetitive, and truthfully, pretty damn hard. But there was also something satisfying about knowing exactly where the raw material came from and what it was going to become.
We were taking some of Maine’s most familiar raw material and turning it into a highly specialized product that could compete at the highest level of the sport.
Not bad for a little shop in Shirley, Maine.

title: Winter is inevitable: An inaccessible campus shouldn’t be
text:
OPINION: It feels like winter is approaching Orono fast this year. Snow and ice will soon become part of daily life at the University of Maine, and winter accessibility can be treated as a matter of groundskeeping rather than part of ensuring students can access their university.
Snow removal is necessary to keep campus functioning, and it should be about more than clearing parking lots and making roads passable. We can have accessible buildings, designated parking spaces and accommodations available to students, but those resources mean little if the routes connecting them become difficult or unsafe to navigate. Accommodations only work when students can reach them. Providing an accessible classroom does not solve the problem if the sidewalk leading to it is impassable. A designated accessible parking space is less useful when the surrounding snow prevents someone from safely reaching the building.
For students with disabilities, winter weather can introduce barriers that others may not have to consider. An icy sidewalk can make independent travel difficult for someone with a mobility impairment. A poorly cleared entrance can make getting into a building an obstacle before class even starts. What we may see as simple seasonal inconveniences can actually interfere with students’ ability to attend class, access campus resources and participate in university life.
This issue doesn’t affect just students with disabilities. Nearly everyone who has spent a Maine winter walking across campus knows the experience of slipping on an icy sidewalk or struggling to navigate a snow-covered entrance. The difference is that not everyone faces the same consequences. For people like me, an icy walkway means an embarrassing fall and a bruised leg. For another student, it could mean a serious injury or the inability to access their classes independently.
Winter maintenance deserves to be approached with a broader perspective. When snow removal is viewed primarily as groundskeeping, the focus can easily fall on keeping roads and parking areas clear. Those are important responsibilities, but pedestrian access deserves deliberate attention too. Sidewalks, crosswalks, curb cuts, ramps and dorm entrances are not secondary features of campus infrastructure. They are essential connections between the places students need to go. A proactive winter accessibility plan could help make those connections safer and more reliable.
Of course, Maine weather is unpredictable, and it may not always be possible to clear every walkway immediately during or after a storm. The expectation shouldn’t be a perfectly cleared campus. It should be preparation and communication. When a pedestrian route can’t be cleared promptly, students should have access to information about conditions and safer alternatives. Clear communication allows students to plan ahead rather than discover that their usual route is unusable while already on their commute.
The conditions of our campus shape how students experience their education, and those conditions do not affect everyone equally. UMaine can’t control the weather, but it can take a more intentional approach to preparing for it. Winter accessibility should be treated as an essential part of campus planning rather than an item on a groundskeeping checklist.

title: Mechanized logging operations an forest trucking program in its 10th year
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
COURTESY OF THE PROFESSIONAL LOGGING CONTRACTORS (PLC) OF THE NORTHEAST
The Mechanized Logging Operations and Forest Trucking (MLOFT) Program, a unique hands-on training course that prepares students for careers in the logging industry, is in its tenth year of classes at an active harvest site in central Maine.
The certificate program for operators of mechanized logging and forest trucking equipment will run for 20 weeks. Classes began June 22 on the Kennebec Valley Community College (KVCC) Alfond Campus on U.S. Route 201 in Hinckley and will run through Nov. 5, when students will graduate.
“The demand for qualified logging operators and forest truckers in our region remains high, and this program continues to address that need in the most efficient and affordable way for the industry,” Dana Doran, Executive Director of the Professional Logging Contractors of the Northeast (PLC), said. “This is our 10th year of operation and that is a testament to the enduring value of the program. There is no better opportunity for anyone interested in starting a career in the logging industry, and thanks to continued support and generosity from industry sponsors and supporters and the State of Maine, students can access this training at little to no cost.”
Students in this year’s class include: Odin Tanguay, Yarmouth, ME; Jackson Newton, Anson ME; Hunter Newton, Buckfield, ME; Emily Pierce, Albion, ME; Samuel Armstrong, Richmond, ME; Lochlan Campbell, Starks, ME; Nicholas Clewly, Pittsfield, ME; Bowen Leighton, Starks, ME; Chandler, McMichael, Vassalboro, ME.; Josh Perry, Waldoboro, ME; Hunter Lafoe, Harrington, ME; Caleb McKusick, Abbott, ME; Peyton Plourde, Solon, ME; Isaac Jordan, Londonderry, VT; and Evan Ford, East Dorset, VT.
The program is administered by KVCC in partnership with the PLC and includes a strong emphasis on safety as well as giving students an understanding of the variables of timber growth, tree species, and markets. Students pay no tuition or fees. The program provides all personal protective equipment (PPE) and scholarships from Skowhegan Savings Bank to assist with living expenses. Local housing is available at reduced cost to students who live beyond a reasonable commuting distance from the program.
The opportunity to earn a CDL-A permit and receive preparation for the state driving exam was a significant addition to the program in 2023 and has expanded opportunities for graduates while increasing benefits to logging employers who need more mechanized logging operators and truck drivers.
Students in the program harvest timber and operate trucks using sophisticated state-of-the-art machines like those they will encounter in the logging industry. The hands-on experience students gain operating equipment is an opportunity unavailable anywhere else in the region.
The program was created in 2017 by the Maine Community College System, the PLC, and industry partners. Dozens of graduates are working in the Northeast’s logging industry today, and the demand for additional equipment operators and truck drivers remains high due to the rapidly aging workforce in the logging industry.
Most logging in the region now relies on mechanized equipment. The industry also relies almost exclusively on heavy trucks to move wood. With the majority of logging operators and forest truckers at or nearing retirement age, the demand for new workers in the logging industry is high and most students in the certificate program have had job offers before graduating.
Logging is a vital part of the Northeast’s forest products sector, contributing an estimated $1.3 billion to the region’s economy in 2024.

title: Does MaineCare cover chiropractic visits?
text:
Yes.
MaineCare, Maine’s Medicaid program, covers certain chiropractic services, including spinal manipulation, examinations to diagnose spinal conditions and certain X-rays.
For adults 21 and older, coverage generally includes 12 visits per calendar year. Additional visits require prior authorization, documentation of medical necessity and a referral from a medical provider. Members younger than 21 need a referral beyond 12 visits, but not prior authorization.
MaineCare does not cover all forms of medical treatment. For example, acupuncture and massage therapy are excluded.
The federal government recently approved a plan that will allow eligible tribal health organizations to bill MaineCare for traditional Wabanaki healing services. Coverage is not yet available; Maine officials tentatively anticipate launching the benefit on Oct. 1, 2027. The state and Wabanaki Nations are still determining which healing practices will qualify, who can provide them and how the benefit will work.
This fact brief is responsive to conversations such as this one.

title: Police say man strangled woman during domestic assault in Rockland
text:
ROCKLAND, Maine — A Thomaston man was arrested Sunday accused of strangling a woman during a domestic assault.
Samuel N. Atwood, 58, of Thomaston, was arrested by Rockland police and charged with felony domestic violence aggravated assault, and a misdemeanor charge of domestic violence criminal threatening.
He was taken to the Knox County holding facility in Rockland and then had an initial appearance Oct. 19 via Zoom with the state court in Knox County where Judge Sarah Gilbert set bail at $750 cash. Assistant District Attorney Mari Wells had requested that amount while defense attorney of the day James Gioia had asked for personal recognizance bail.
An affidavit filed with the court by Rockland police states that the department responded to a reported domestic dispute on Chestnut Street. The woman said Atwood pushed her down on a bed, put one of his hands around her neck and the other over her mouth and nose. She struck her head on the bottom of the window sill when she was forced down, according to the affidavit.
The woman said while she was struggling to breathe, he told her he was going to kill her.
A witness reported hearing their arguments but this time it was more intense and the witness heard the woman saying “Sam no, Sam don’t, and Sam stop.” The witness said he also heard a loud thud shortly before police were called to the scene.
Atwood denied the dispute was ever physical.
This story appears through a media partnership with Midcoast Villager.

title: Former Somerset County Jail official faces new sexual assault charges
text:
A former top-ranking supervisor at the Somerset County Jail, fired in 2024 amid domestic violence allegations and an internal affairs investigation, now faces several sexual assault charges.
Cameron Arcidi, 29, of Etna, is charged in Somerset County with four Class A felony counts of gross sexual assault, as well as Class D misdemeanor counts of domestic violence assault, domestic violence stalking and domestic violence terrorizing, court records show.
In Knox County, Arcidi is charged with one Class A count and one Class C count of gross sexual assault.
The Knox County grand jury returned its indictment Oct. 7; the Somerset County grand jury on Thursday.
Arcidi, who was the assistant jail administrator and held the rank of captain, was arrested and booked Friday afternoon at the Penobscot County Jail in Bangor, according to records available online. He was released on $5,000 cash bail, an intake staffer said Monday morning.
Paul Cavanaugh, Maine’s interpersonal violence prosecutor, said in a telephone call Monday that authorities informed Arcidi of the requested bail amount before his arrest on the new charges and he planned to turn himself in.
Arcidi had previously been charged with misdemeanor domestic violence assault and domestic violence stalking. In May, prosecutors dismissed those charges without prejudice — meaning they could file them again. In his brief explanation of the dismissal, Cavanaugh noted he planned to present the case to the grand jury, and Arcidi should not have been on bail while that happened.
Arcidi, who pleaded not guilty to the previous charges, also denies the new allegations, his defense attorney Walter McKee said via email Monday.
Arcidi’s arraignment date was not listed in court records as of Monday. Cavanaugh said he did not yet know when it is set.
He said he expects the two new cases to eventually be transferred to the same county. The previous charges had been moved from Somerset County to Kennebec County.
The new charges stem from further investigation into allegations made from a woman that led to the initial charges in 2024, said Cavanaugh.
Cavanaugh is an assistant district attorney with statewide jurisdiction specializing in cases involving law enforcement officials and potential conflicts of interest with local district attorneys’ offices.
A Maine State Police detective is now listed in court records as the primary investigator. A Somerset County Sheriff’s Office detective assigned to the Somerset County District Attorney’s Office had conducted the initial investigation.
The alleged victim has a protection from abuse order against him, which a judge earlier this year extended to run through 2036, filings in Skowhegan District Court show. Arcidi agreed to the protection order in 2024 and its recent extension, records show.
The Morning Sentinel does not identify alleged victims of sexual assault without their permission.
The offenses in Somerset County are alleged to have occurred at a residence, and the offenses in Knox County are alleged to have occurred at the Samoset Resort in Rockport, Cavanaugh said.
The Somerset indictment alleges Arcidi sexually assaulted the woman by compulsion on Nov. 18, 2022; March 26, 2023; Feb. 17, 2024; and March 9, 2024, all in Pittsfield. It alleges the domestic violence assault occurred May 13, 2024, and the domestic violence terrorizing and stalking between Nov. 17, 2022, and May 13, 2024, also all in Pittsfield.
The Knox indictment alleges Arcidi sexually assaulted the woman March 20, 2024. Cavanaugh said the two separate counts on that indictment stem from the same incident, but one alleges sexual assault by compulsion and the other by lack of consent.
The dates on the indictments closely follow allegations from the woman described in a police affidavit supporting the misdemeanor charges initially filed in 2024, as well as in an affidavit she filed in 2024 in support of the protection order.
The criminal investigation began in July 2024, a few weeks after she obtained the protection order, according to an affidavit from Ronnie Blodgett, at the time a Somerset County sheriff’s detective assigned to the district attorney’s office.
Meanwhile, a sheriff’s office internal affairs investigation into Arcidi was also underway, Blodgett wrote. The woman also worked at the county jail as a corrections officer.
The woman wrote in her affidavit and told Blodgett of multiple instances in which Arcidi forced her to have sex despite her objections. She also provided Blodgett with several audio and video recordings and photos, documenting some of those alleged incidents and others involving physical abuse.
The woman also told Blodgett that Arcidi also threatened to revoke her keycard access at the jail and took screenshots of him monitoring her on jail security cameras, the affidavit states.
The woman said Arcidi “controlled many aspects of her life like her working, telling her she should be subservient to him, that she needed to submit to him, that he would force her to engage in intercourse even after she had said no on multiple occasions,” Blodgett wrote in the conclusion of the affidavit. “(The woman) said she would fear what Arcidi would do next and things got progressively worse as the relationship went on.”
Blodgett obtained a warrant for Arcidi’s arrest on the domestic violence charges about a week after he was assigned the case, records show.
Arcidi was placed on administrative leave the same day he was arrested, Somerset County Sheriff Dale Lancaster said previously.
Two months later, the Somerset County Board of Commissioners voted unanimously to terminate Arcidi at Lancaster’s recommendation, following a brief, closed-doors executive session.
It remains unclear what exactly led to Arcidi’s firing. Lancaster said at the time that the criminal investigation and the internal investigation were running parallel to each other, but he would not comment on the nature of the internal investigation.
At the time, the county’s lawyer, in response to a public records request, declined to release Lancaster’s recommendation, saying it could interfere with the criminal proceedings. The Morning Sentinel on Monday requested the record again.
Arcidi started working at the jail as a corrections officer in 2017. He held positions of case manager, disciplinary hearings officer and special projects lieutenant before becoming captain and assistant administrator in 2024, the sheriff’s office said in Facebook post announcing his promotion.
Before his termination, Arcidi’s disciplinary record consisted of a written warning from a supervisor in 2018 regarding his use of a jail computer to access “MSN sites.” The supervisor told him to stop violating the county’s policy and to ask for more tasks to perform when bored at work.
HOW TO GET HELP
IF YOU or someone you know has experienced sexual violence, you can call the statewide Sexual Assault Crisis and Support Line at 1-800-871-7741 for free and confidential help 24 hours a day.
TO LEARN more about sexual violence prevention and response in Maine, visit the Maine Coalition Against Sexual Assault website at mecasa.org.
FOR MORE information about mental health services in Maine, visit the website for the state’s chapter of the National Alliance on Mental Illness.

title: This Little-Traveled Maine Road is the Most Haunted in the US
text:
Maine is home to some of the most-chilling ghost stories in the United States.
No, we're not talking about the novels that Maine's Stephen King has penned over the last five decades. Nope. We're talking about real ghost stories.
Some of the most well known Maine ghost stories include the haunted dorms at the University of Southern Maine, the haunting of Skowhegan's Strand Theater, and the haunting of Bucksport's Fort Knox.
👇Scroll down for a list of terrifying Maine ghost stories
Did you know that Maine is home to the most haunted road in the United States?
The Haunting of Maine's Route 2A
According to the Discover Cars website, Route 2A in Maine is the most haunted road in the United States. The winding road, an offshoot of Route 2, runs through an extremely rural section of Aroostook County.
The website explains that this stretch of road is rumored to be haunted by several ghosts. Drivers have reported seeing a woman in white, believed to be a bride killed alongside her husband in a crash on their wedding night. Legend says she wanders the roadside, searching for her lost love.
Two young girls are also said to haunt the area, appearing and disappearing into thin air. Their spirits are believed to belong to two girls who were fatally struck by a truck on the road in 1967. Witnesses describe an overwhelming sense of dread and sadness in the surrounding woodlands.
As a teen I spent a summer as an escort driver for a company moving mobile homes. Because it lacked the low overpasses of the I-95, we occasionally took that road when delivering single-wides or double-wides. While I believe in the ghost stories, I personally never witnessed anything while driving on the road.
Have you ever experienced something strange on this road? Tell us your story.

title: Phyllis Graber Jensen Shares Love of Documentary Photography at Bates Art Museum Artist Talk
text:
Anyone who has scrolled through Bates College’s Instagram has likely seen the same credit beneath photo after photo of students on the field, at internships and on stage: “Phyllis Graber Jensen/Bates College.”
For 31 years, Graber Jensen photographed campus life, from candid shots of students crossing the Quad to seniors’ champagne celebrations after finishing their capstones. For many prospective students browsing the college’s social media, her images were a first look at Bates.
Graber Jensen retired this year. At a Sept. 19 Artist Talk at the Olin Arts Center, she reflected on her career and her belief that photography serves as a historical record.
She has photographed what she calls a close-knit community, along with students’ efforts to improve the campus and the world beyond it.
Graber Jensen’s retirement this year marked the end of her 31 years as a photographer and media producer at Bates.
During her Artist Talk, Graber Jensen shared her lifelong passion for photography and how her earlier experiences in activism, sociology and anthropology transcribed into her photographic values of historical preservation.
Graber Jensen believed that “one of the important and unique roles that [college photographers] play is to document the history of the institution.”
During her Artist Talk, she expressed her love for sports as a child despite it being a male-dominated field at the time; “I loved them all,” she recounted.
Her gender, however, impacted others’ reception of her. She said,“What I did not like to be called was a tomboy. What I did not like to hear was, ‘You’re so good for a girl.’”
When Graber Jensen learned she couldn’t play varsity tennis at Jamaica High School because she was a girl (the school had no girls’ team, and city rules barred girls from boys’ teams), she filed a complaint with the New York City Commission on Human Rights. Her case drew widespread attention, and the New York City Board of Education voted to let girls compete on boys’ teams in non-contact sports.
This showed her journalism’s ability to shape a story’s trajectory.
At her exhibition, Graber Jensen said she wanted to help viewers differentiate between images created purely for commercial purposes and those for historical preservation.
She walked through her photographic journey in roughly chronological order, pausing selectively at contact sheets and photo essays from her years as a photojournalist.
Among other career moments, Graber Jensen included her work at the Boston Herald.
As a photographer for Bates Communications and Marketing, she aimed to present the college in a positive light, but she also saw it as her job to preserve the institution’s history, both the good and the bad.
Stopping in front of a 2016 photo of students protesting police brutality, she explained that she photographed campus demonstrations, knowing that the images would never be published, because they were “part of institutional history.”
When asked how her time documenting institutional history shaped her work at Bates, Graber Jensen said, “I’m always looking for ways to challenge authority.”
“I’m always looking to present the college and its members in a positive light,” she said. “But I’m always looking to give a voice to people who have different points of view.”
Someone else’s name will appear under the photos on Bates’ Instagram now. But Graber Jensen’s work isn’t going anywhere.
“One hundred years from now,” she said, “These images will be part of the record.”

title: Interest in trapping grows in Maine
text:
AUGUSTA — The class gathered in a small clearing, under orange and yellow leaves, and trained their attention on Ronald Fournier. He held a metal cable with a loop on the end, used to trap the paw of a black bear.
“You’re always checking live restraining devices how often?” Fournier asked the group.
“Every day,” nine people said in unison.
“When?” Fournier asked.
“In the morning,” they answered together.
Fournier, recreational safety supervisor for the state Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife, gave a satisfied nod. This class is mandatory for anyone who wants to get a trapping license in Maine. In recent years, the state has seen a surge of interest.
In 2020, Maine had 4,381 licensed trappers, according to department data. By 2025, that number had increased to 5,345.
Fournier surveyed participants to understand the shift and learned that new trappers were less interested in selling fur for profit than they were in decades past. In general, he said, they wanted a trapping license in order to be more self-sufficient, whether they planned to harvest meat for their family or manage pests and predators on their properties.
“The No. 1 choice was to expand on their hunting and outdoor activities and broaden their outdoor skills,” he said. “Right behind that was trapping for personal use to make craft items and garments. People wanted to trap a couple of furbearers to make a pair of beaver mittens or a hat for the family.”
Brian Bernosky, president of the Maine Trappers Association, said trappers used to be more reluctant to share their knowledge because they wanted to guard the tricks that helped supplement their income or they were afraid to encounter people opposed to the practice. Today, he sees a broader culture of mentorship.
“If we don’t share it with everybody and share all the great things we know, we are going to go by the wayside,” said Bernosky, 43, of Bradford.
State rules say that a trapping license is valid from July 1 to June 30 of the following year. Anyone applying for an adult license in Maine needs to prove that they have taken the state course at least once.
Fournier said Maine requires more education than most states in order to get a trapping license. Generally, people need to complete homework in advance and attend a full-day course that includes an exam. The curriculum includes practical and legal information, as well as tips on how to represent trappers well to private landowners and to the general public.
On an overcast Friday in October, Joshua Dostie knelt on the floor of the classroom at the Sportsman’s Alliance of Maine Outdoor Center in Augusta to demonstrate the proper setting of beaver traps. The participants listened as he talked about making ethical choices in the field — how to confirm the presence of beavers in an area, when to move on from a location, how to avoid catching species that aren’t the target and how to make sure the trap will kill the animal immediately so it does not suffer additional stress.
“If we as trappers want to keep our seasons as manageable as they are, we have to make good decisions,” said Dostie, a recreational safety coordinator for the Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife.
Maggie Morgan, 34, of Bowdoinham, joined Dostie and Fournier at the recent course as a volunteer instructor. She used to be a more active hunter, but now prefers trapping in part because it is more flexible around her family’s schedule. She said she is seeing more women and kids in these courses, and her own two children enjoy helping her prepare equipment at home and accompanying her to check traplines.
“If I spend three hours out in the woods deer hunting, I may or may not get a deer,” Morgan said. “Whereas if I spend three hours over the course of a few days tending a trapline, and I get a few beaver, that feeds the family and makes a few hats. I feel like it’s more productive.”
Brooke Blood, of Avon, signed up for the trapper education course because she is interested in becoming a game warden and wanted to build her skills in the outdoors. She was looking forward to learning about species that are less familiar to her, such as beaver or otter.
“I’ve been hunting, but trapping, I don’t have any experience with,” said Blood, 30.
Adam Austin, of Belgrade, got a trapping license more than a decade ago in order to help with animal control at his job, but he hadn’t renewed it or kept up with the practice. One way he plans to use his license is to target the predators that have been killing his chickens for years, but the 51-year-old also wants to spend more time outside after a recent cancer diagnosis and treatment.
“It’s not about the pelts, the money or anything like that,” Austin said. “It’s learning about the animals.”

title: Longtime CNN anchor Christiane Amanpour leaving network after a storied career of 43 years
text:
Longtime CNN anchor Christiane Amanpour will be leaving CNN after 43 years at the network.
The network’s chief international anchor will scale back her daily show, “Amanpour,” on CNN International to once a week at the beginning of 2027, and end the show at the end of May, leaving the network the following month. She said in a statement that she looks forward to “interesting new projects down the line.”
Amanpour, 68, also will end her PBS show, “Amanpour and Company,” at the end of the year, she said in her statement, shared by CNN. She will continue her podcast, “The Ex Files,” with her ex-husband, Jamie Rubin, a former U.S. diplomat.
“After many months of thought and a few sleepless nights, I have decided to separate from CNN, my partner of 43 fantastic years!” Amanpour said in the statement.
Amanpour also said she would “always be rooting for CNN and maintaining its history of independent journalism. Remember: always be truthful, not neutral.”
Amanpour’s exit coincides with a new era at CNN as it comes under a new owner, Skydance. After a yearlong process, Skydance-owned Paramount closed its $81 billion buyout of Warner Bros. Discovery on Oct. 6. The merger unites under one roof two giants in TV news — CBS and CNN.
On a personal front. Amanpour has spoken openly about her 2021 diagnosis of ovarian cancer and its later recurrence, calling it “the invisible killer.” She has urged others to “get all the scans that you can.”

title: A look inside the Maine State Museum ahead of Oct. 24 reopening
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine — The Maine State Museum reopens Oct. 24 after six years closed to the public, with a mother-and-calf pair of whale skeletons among the first things visitors will see.
“What I love about this exhibit is watching people come in and interact with Vector [the mother whale]. The sense of awe, the sense of relationship that you can create in a space like this,” said Paula Work, Curator of Natural Sciences.
New additions and renovations
The reopening includes new technology, interactive displays and the museum’s first purpose-built education space.
The building first closed during the pandemic. After reopening, staff found mechanical and structural problems that also needed to be addressed.
The state renovated the building while the museum raised more than three million dollars for exhibits through grants, businesses, foundations, individual donors and state support.
“It is magical to see the place coming back to life,” said Teresa Murphy, Objects Conservator.
New exhibits highlight Maine history
The museum’s offerings include a new interpretation of the St. Mary, a ship built in Phippsburg in 1890 and wrecked on its first voyage.
Cornelia “Fly Rod” Crosby, whose materials were already in the museum’s collection, now has an exhibit of her own, bringing new attention to a woman who helped shape Maine’s outdoor history.
Director Bernard Fishman has led the museum through the closure and its transformation.
“It’s a great source of pride for me. Certainly it’s all a legacy that we want to leave, for a generation or two, and then things will change again,” Fishman said.
The first two floors reopen Oct. 24. The upper floors remain under renovation.

title: LSU student, fiancé killed when they were hit by a car while walking back from friend’s birthday
text:
BATON ROUGE, La. (WAFB/Gray News) — A 21-year-old Louisiana State University student and her fiancé were killed when they were hit by a car.
The Baton Rouge Police Department said Mia Camille Dawson, 20, was driving a 2016 Nissan Rogue around 2:40 a.m. Sunday when she veered off the road and hit two pedestrians on the right shoulder.
Leah Victoria Fonte, 21, died at the scene, police said. Her fiancé, Shane David Hirstius, 21, was taken to a local hospital, where he later died from his injuries.
Police said officers found Dawson shortly after the crash. She was booked into the East Baton Rouge Parish Prison on charges of operating while impaired, reckless operation of a vehicle, hit-and-run driving, vehicular homicide and vehicular negligent injuring.
The Third District Volunteer Fire Department said Hirstius was one of its operators/firefighters and remembered him as a dedicated first responder.
In a social media post, the department said the couple had been celebrating a friend’s birthday before they were hit by the vehicle.
The circumstances of the crash are under investigation.
Fonte was a senior at LSU studying biological sciences on a pre-dental track, according to the department.
