title: Wilton schools aim for gains in reading, math proficiency
text:
Academy Hill and G.D. Cushing schools, both in Wilton, are targeting improvements in mathematics and reading proficiency this school year.
Regional School Unit 9 administrators say a 2% growth goal reflects recent academic performance and the time needed for instructional changes to take hold.
Principal Amy Watson outlined the priorities during the school board’s Oct. 13 meeting. G.D. Cushing School will focus on reading proficiency, while Academy Hill School will concentrate on mathematics, with progress measured through Northwest Evaluation Association Growth assessments.
The Oregon-based organization is a research-based, nonprofit that supports students and educators worldwide by creating assessment solutions that precisely measure growth and proficiency, and provide insights to help tailor instruction, according to its Linked in page.
Watson, who is in her first year leading both Wilton schools, said she is reviewing student performance data to identify areas needing additional instructional support. She indicated that G.D. Cushing had not fully met its reading goal last year.
A board member questioned whether the district’s 2% improvement target was too conservative.
Assistant Superintendent Monique Poulin said the target was established during summer planning for the district’s federal Title I grant. She clarified in a follow-up email that it represents a two-percentage-point increase in achievement growth from fall to spring compared with other students at the same grade level. The district met its overall growth goal last year, although results varied among schools, Poulin told the board.
“I think that we are shooting in the right direction,” Poulin said.
She said the district has generally experienced about 2% annual growth over the past three years and is working toward a broader goal of having 80% of students meet expectations through regular classroom instruction.
Poulin also emphasized that changes in curriculum and teaching practices take time to produce results, citing research suggesting implementation can take five to seven years.
“It is not something that happens quickly,” she said.
Both Wilton schools are participating in a districtwide evaluation of Eureka Math², commonly called Eureka Squared, and Illustrative Math, two mathematics curricula designed to develop students’ understanding of mathematical concepts.
Eureka Math² emphasizes a sequence of connected mathematical concepts that build on one another across grade levels, combining reasoning, problem-solving and practice. Illustrative Math uses a problem-based approach in which students explore mathematical questions, discuss strategies and explain their reasoning.
Five teachers at the two Wilton schools are participating in the pilots. Megan Lewia is testing Eureka Squared in kindergarten, while Jamie Leo and Catherine McShane are using it in fourth and fifth grades, respectively. Kayla Greenleaf is piloting Illustrative Math in first grade, and Haley Teacutter is testing it in second grade.
Poulin said the evaluation will consider student performance, teacher feedback and the time required to prepare and deliver lessons. The district expects to select one of the two programs before the end of the school year.
Watson also reported that both schools are continuing Building Assets, Reducing Risks, known as BARR, a school improvement model designed to strengthen relationships among students, teachers and families. The schools are participating in Thrive, an additional year of coaching that includes monthly meetings and training for new staff.
As part of the program, staff members send postcards home to promote positive communication with families.
Watson is expected to present updated student achievement figures during her next school board report, according to Poulin.

title: Penobscot County man accused of burning his own camper and car
text:
A Medway man has been arrested for allegedly starting fires in two Penobscot County towns that destroyed his own camper and car.
The camper fire was reported shortly before 11 p.m, Sept. 30, on Turnpike Road in Medway. The fire destroyed the camper and damaged a nearby mobile home and storage shelter, according to the Maine fire marshal’s office, whose investigators were called in to determine the cause.
The fire marshal’s office was called the next day to a car fire in a Woodville gravel pit. Investigators determined that both the camper and the car were owned by Paul York, 41, of Medway.
On Monday, East Millinocket police arrested York on a warrant obtained by the fire marshal’s office.
He was taken to Penobscot County Jail and is charged with two counts of arson, aggravated criminal mischief and violating conditions of release.

title: Money is ruining our politics, and our country
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The BDN Opinion section operates independently and does not set news policies or contribute to reporting or editing articles elsewhere in the newspaper or on bangordailynews.com
Chris Wright is a retired carpenter and licensed social worker from Belfast.
The noise is the constant emails, texts, and TV and social media ads created to sway our votes. We all have good reasons to be angry: a lot is broken and it’s not getting fixed. That can leave us feeling furious and powerless at the same time. But, if we step back from the noise and the emotional roller coasters, if we gather our wits and courage and use our good brains, we can tackle what many Americans believe is the biggest problem with our government: Money.
To start with, our governmental system isn’t the problem. Our founding ideas of equality, religious freedom, and the consent of the governed, were seen by the rest of the world as quite radical, and are a great foundation from which to work. The problem I see is the corruption by those addicted to great wealth and power. In 1938, President Franklin D. Roosevelt said, “the liberty of a democracy is not safe if the people tolerate the growth of private power to a point where it becomes stronger than their democratic state itself.” The Bible says that the love of money is a root of all evil. Not that money is evil, it’s greed and lust for money that corrupt.
I believe today’s largest corrupters are the tech companies. Seemingly overnight — without our consent — the tech giants have gobbled up our personal information and now, with fantastic riches at stake, they’re rushing headlong into a threat much greater than the atomic bomb: AI ( artificial intelligence).
While Americans agonize between spending for food, housing, heating fuel, and healthcare, lobbyists fight against policies that provide a livable wage, and programs that support families, like childcare and parental leave. We watch from the sidelines as the inequity between the fantastically rich and the rest of us grows, while most wealth distributes upwards towards those looking for yet one more vacation home.
The Supreme Court’s ruling in the Citizens United case allows corporations to pour millions of dollars into campaigns through Super PACs. In 2024, it could cost $50 million to $75 million to mount a statewide campaign: much of this from super PACs. There are approximately 25 lobbyists for every member of Congress.
Politicians keep using the word “extreme.” I find it extreme that in the world’s richest country, half of us struggle to meet our bills. I find it extreme that other well-to-do countries pay for healthcare with citizen’s tax dollars, while Americans go bankrupt with medical debt.
If we Americans are not going to shoulder our responsibility to drive money out of politics, I think we might as well just give up and say, OK, run right over us.
Our main tool is our vote. We must pay attention to which candidates in Maine and across our nation are actually addressing the reality that much of our government is controlled by corporations and the super wealthy, and not the people.
I believe we must dismantle the two-party system. Many other nations don’t have the election circuses we do. Presently, the two parties mainly control who gets to run. Do we really have so few people out of 350 million who might lead us?
I believe we must overturn Citizens United, which effectively gives big money much of what it needs to buy our elections using super PACs, which aren’t obligated to tell us where their money comes from. Why in the world would we, as Americans, not be able to tell who is buying our elections? Because it’s been designed and written that way intentionally. All that super PAC money is in addition to the millions that the billionaires are currently spending on their favored candidates.

title: Parent spotlight: PIE Chair Heather McArdle
text:
Heather McArdle and her husband Scott have been together for over 17 years. They have three kids: Caleb, who just started his freshman year at Wentworth Institute of Technology, Jace, a seventh grader at Wiscasset Middle High School, and Emberly, a fourth grader at Wiscasset Elementary School. The family has been part of the Wiscasset school community since Jace started kindergarten in 2019.
Heather has always supported classrooms by buying snacks and cleaning supplies when they were needed, and she joins as many field trips as she can. She started volunteering with PIE when Jace was in fourth grade, helping with a few events. Later she learned that the PIE board members at the time were leaving and needed new people. “I decided to give it a shot,” she said. This is her second year on the board, and she is the chair.
Partners in Education is made up of parents, family and community members who work together to support Wiscasset schools in ways that go beyond what the school budget can provide. At meetings, the group goes over upcoming events and gets organized. Any community member is welcome to join. “It’s always nice to have different opinions and perspectives,” Heather said. “I’ve loved working with this group. We complement each other very well, and all keep the same focus at the forefront: the kids.”
One of her favorite PIE events is the Fall Festival, the group’s yearly give-back to the community. Many of the volunteers are school staff, and seeing the kids have a blast is very rewarding for her. Her favorite PIE moment came last year at the first ever Big Wolverines/Little Wolves event. PIE provided supplies for WMHS students to put together holiday gifts for WES students. Members of the WMHS Student Council then took the gifts to WES and delivered them to classrooms. They got to walk their old halls, visit their previous teachers, and had a great time, all while brightening the day for the kids at WES.
Heather helps wherever she can, whether it’s field trips or events. She also filled in at the Snack Shack for the Boosters once and hopes to do it again. As a stay at home mom, she feels lucky to be able to be involved. “Once I started helping and joining on trips, I found I really loved supporting and interacting with all students, not just my own,” she said. For her, the most rewarding part is seeing the kids’ faces and the impact PIE has had in all the ways it has supported them. She also said the gratefulness of the staff whenever PIE provides food or treats makes her day.
As a parent, Heather said her kids have made lifelong friends in Wiscasset and so many great memories. School performances stand out for her as a chance to watch her kids shine and grow. Both of her kids in the Wiscasset schools have had amazing teachers, and she can tell they really care. Communication is huge for her as a parent, and she said the Class Dojo app at WES makes it easy to stay informed.
She felt welcomed in the school community even before she got involved with PIE, with smiles and conversation, invites to events, and updates on what’s coming up. What she values most is that “we all know each other, and it feels kind of like a family.”
If you’ve been thinking about volunteering, Heather knows getting started can seem daunting. Her advice is to reach out and start the conversation. “We are happy to help find the right fit for your schedule,” she said. You can also pop into a PIE meeting and introduce yourself. There are many ways to help, from donating to volunteering your time to spreading the word, and any support is appreciated.
For families thinking about enrolling their child in our schools, Heather said to take advantage of all the opportunities to connect with other families, both at school events and outside of them. “The more support from all of us, the better for our students and staff.”
The Wiscasset School Department thanks Heather and everyone at PIE for their hard work and support. We appreciate all that you do for our students and staff.
FMI: Heather can be reached at wiscassetpiechair@gmail.com

title: Portland officials urged to advocate for residents affected by CMP transmission project
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
PORTLAND — Mayor Mark Dion will prepare and submit testimony to the Maine Public Utilities Commission in response to growing public concern over a Central Maine Power proposal to upgrade its electric grid in North Deering.
Public outcry over the project has snowballed over the last few weeks as residents have learned about the project, many from the appearance of lawn signs or from a neighbor knocking on their door.
CMP’s project to upgrade and rebuild transmission lines between Yarmouth and Portland, with a separate section in Westbrook, is designed to strengthen the energy grid in Greater Portland, the company said. The first phase of the project in the section north of Portland will cost an estimated $547 million.
The City Council on Monday unanimously approved a resolution authorizing Dion to prepare testimony after more than a dozen residents criticized the lack of public information and outlined concerns about expanding infrastructure that runs along property lines and recreational trails.
Following the council vote, Dion told the audience, “You’ve been heard, we’re going to do our best to stand … between (CMP) and you to get some good answers.”
Some told the council Monday that neighbors are still finding out about the project just days before a deadline to submit public testimony. A group organized as the Alliance for Responsible Infrastructure has notified and rallied neighbors in opposition, and urged Portland officials to independently verify the need for such upgrades.
Last week, the town of Falmouth passed a resolution opposing the project, asking regulators to consider alternatives.
In reviewing the proposal, the PUC is tasked with determining if the project would serve a public need. The review process, which typically takes a year, started in July. Residents pointed out that a Nov. 10 public meeting on the project in Portland takes place after the Oct. 30 deadline for testimony — a deadline that was originally a week earlier.
Dion said he’s spoken with CMP officials to relay the local concerns, and that as an intervener in the PUC process, Portland “will have a presence throughout.”
In Portland, the CMP line runs past residential areas between Ocean Avenue, past the former city landfill and dog park, crossing Ledgewood Drive and Allen Avenue Extension. Perhaps the most impacted neighborhood would be the area off Alice Street, Curtis Road and Hope Avenue, where the lines cross over backyards and sheds.
Ben Haber, who lives on Hope Avenue, told the council Monday that the project would “destroy the neighborhood,” and he asked officials to advocate on behalf of residents.
Charise Corsino, who lives on Curtis Road, said new poles could be up to 110 feet tall, and that residents who simply want to know more about the plans have been stonewalled.
“The information has been deeply inadequate,” she told Portland councilors, arguing that Portland’s power needs “don’t require us to accept a massive buildout through existing neighborhoods.”
A CMP spokesperson previously told the Portland Press Herald that with over 200,000 customers in Greater Portland, as well as critical facilities such as hospitals, schools and residences, the upgrades are needed to provide better protection from power outages.
The council was slated to discuss its legal rights later Monday in an executive session with an attorney who specializes in public utility processes.
The sustainability and transportation committee will hold a panel discussion Wednesday with Central Maine Power, citizen advocates and Maine Public Advocate Heather Sanborn.
DATA CENTERS
Also on Monday, the council voted unanimously to support a resolution that asks planning staff to draft new regulations on large data centers in the city.
Once drafted, the language would be considered by the planning board and then the City Council in response to concerns from officials and residents over the potential for data center development proposals coming forward without adequate guidelines.
Councilor Pious Ali, who forwarded the proposal, said “we have seen how it’s going in other parts of the country,” and that the planning board should review and “advise us accordingly.”

title: A history lesson on healthcare in Maine
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
In 2009, Democratic Gov. John Baldacci promised a $45 million payment on Maine’s $373 million debt to Maine hospitals. That payment did not happen until three years later in 2006.
When Baldacci left the Blaine House, he left a $484 million debt, which Republican Gov. Paul LePage paid off. Prior to this payment, the Maine hospitals were on the verge of financial failure. When Gov. LePage left office in 2019, the state had a financial surplus.
Jump ahead to Democratic Gov. Janet Mills. Almost half of birthing centers are closed and a number of hospitals as well. If Mainers think for a moment that the Democratic candidate Hannah Pingree is going to save our healthcare system, they need to look at history.
If people really think that socialized medicine is the answer, they should move to Canada.
Leo Mazerall Jr.
Stockton Springs

title: Students build device to help Gulf War veteran return to archery
text:
ANGOLA, Ind. (InvestigateTV) - A group of Trine University engineering students spent months designing a device to help a Navy veteran regain the ability to shoot a bow, after injuries left him without the use of his left arm.
Chester Evitt, a Navy veteran who served in the Gulf War, was shot in the arm during his service. A second injury three years ago worsened his condition.
“Because I’ve lost most of the use of my left arm, I can’t hold anything in it. I can’t shoot my bow,” Evitt said.
Evitt told his doctor at the VA about his problem with the bow. That conversation started a chain of events that eventually connected him with the Trine University engineering team through a program called Project S.E.R.V.E.
According to the organization’s website, Project S.E.R.V.E. aims to “improve the lives of veterans and emergency responders living with injuries or disabling conditions through student-led engineering projects.”
The Trine team’s work
Students Ava Dobbins, Cooper Clark, Andrea Mendoza and Jake Welker collaborated with Evitt virtually for months — Evitt from his home in Montana, the team from Trine University in Angola — before meeting in person for the first time this week at Thunder Lakes Guns Ammo and Archery in Angola.
The team worked through multiple designs before settling on a 3D-printed device that attaches to Evitt’s back to support the bow.
“It really needs to just hold it up for him and kind of be that skeleton that he can’t,” Welker said.
Welker said the project carried personal significance.
“The military runs very deep in my family, like most people from the Midwest, and it means a lot to me,” he said.
Testing the device
Evitt tested the device with the students present.
“Oh, my goodness,” Evitt said after the test. “Life-changing. They’re giving me back something that was took from me.”
Evitt also reflected on the bond he made with the students themselves.
“As a father that’s raised four kids, I’d be proud to call any one of them my own,” he said. “With all the negativity going on in the world, here’s a prime example of our future.”
The team has eight weeks to complete final adjustments before a formal presentation at Trine University.
Evitt said he plans to fly back from Montana once they’re finished and take the finished device home. He can’t wait to reclaim his passion for archery, something he says he first fell in love with at the age of eight.

title: Letter: Vote for candidates who will oppose Trump administration cuts to science
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Letters submitted by BDN readers are verified by BDN Opinion Page staff. Send your letters to letters@bangordailynews.com
The Trump administration is not making America healthy again. The mission statement of the National Institutes of Health includes: “NIH’s mission is to … enhance health, lengthen life, and reduce illness and disability.”
As noted by the Brennan Center, a non-partisan law and policy organization, the Trump Administration froze or cut $2.3 billion in previously approved NIH grants in 2025. These cuts not only disrupted research progress but also had serious consequences for patients, as trials of potential new medical treatments were delayed or halted.
The effects of these cuts will be felt for decades — advances in biomedical research rely on consistent funding over the years, and interruptions to funding now will result in fewer new drugs in the future. These disruptions also threaten to shrink the scientific workforce across the country, including Maine.
I edited biomedical research grants at The Jackson Laboratory and the MDI Biological Laboratory, both in Bar Harbor, for a total of 28 years. Scientists at these institutions dedicate their lives to bettering human health. The uncertain prospects for research funding makes it difficult for them to plan their research projects and their career paths. The turbulent research landscape can also discourage motivated young students from pursuing careers in science.
If we want to steer biomedical research back on course, and create and protect jobs in Maine, I believe we need to vote for candidates who will oppose the Trump administration’s reckless approach to scientific research.
Stephen Sampson 
Southwest Harbor

title: Florida brings more charges against former Cuba president Raul Castro
text:
MIAMI (AP) — Former Cuban President Raúl Castro is facing more charges in Florida related to the 1996 downing of civilian planes flown by Miami-based exiles after the U.S. government indicted the former leader earlier this year.
Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier on Monday accused Castro, 95, of directing spies to infiltrate that the exile group Brothers to the Rescue and ordering the attack on their planes. The state charge of conspiracy to commit first-degree murder is based largely on a federal indictment announced in May that included charges of murder and destruction of an airplane.
It remains unclear whether Castro will ever step foot in a U.S. courtroom. Uthmeier said the arrest warrant will restrict Castro’s ability leave the island nation and prevent him from traveling to any place with an extradition agreement with the U.S.
“I’m not ignorant of the fact that Raúl Castro is an older man who’s probably not looking to march himself into Miami,” Uthmeier said. “I think others would get him before the court of law would, but at the end of the day, we stand ready to prosecute the case.”
According to the state complaint, Castro was the Minister of the Revolutionary Armed Forces and First Vice President of Cuba when he gave the final authorization to shoot down the planes. Cuban Directorate of Intelligence agents operating as part of the Wasp Network in the Miami area and the Florida Keys infiltrated Brothers to the Rescue and reported flight plans, investigator said.
On Feb. 24, 1996, three unarmed Cessna aircraft departed Opa-Locka Airport in Miami-Dade County. Well outside Cuba’s territorial waters, Cuban MiGs destroyed two of the civilian planes with air-to-air missiles, killing the four occupants, the complaint said. Both aircraft were traveling away from Cuba and received no warning despite contact with Havana air traffic control, U.S. officials said.
Cuban President Miguel Díaz-Canel called the federal indictment earlier this year a political stunt that sought only to “justify the folly of a military aggression against Cuba.” He accused the U.S. of lying and manipulating events surrounding the shootdown.
“Our historic federal indictment laid the groundwork, and James and his team have now taken the important step of bringing charges under Florida law,” U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of Florida Jason Reding Quiñones said at a news conference.
Castro took over as president from his ailing older brother Fidel Castro in 2006 before handing power to a trusted loyalist, Díaz-Canel, in 2018.
While he retired in 2021 as head of the Cuban Communist Party, he is widely believed to wield power behind the scenes, underscored by the prominence of his grandson, Raúl Guillermo Rodríguez Castro.
Meanwhile, U.S. President Donald Trump has been threatening military action in Cuba ever since U.S. forces captured former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, the Cuban government’s longtime patron.
After ousting the Venezuelan leader earlier this year, the White House ordered a blockade that choked off fuel shipments to Cuba, leading to severe blackouts, food shortages and an economic collapse across the island.

title: InvestigateTV+: A rise in Lyme disease cases
text:
(InvestigateTV) — InvestigateTV+ heads to a state where Lyme disease cases have more than quadrupled to examine a rise in cases nationwide and the effort to prevent future infections.
Plus, a drop in test results during and after the COVID-19 pandemic underscores its impact on education. We uncover the age groups experts say are missing more milestones and strategies to reverse the trend.
How Lyme disease cases are rising in the Midwest
Michigan health leaders say everyone needs to think about Lyme disease now.
“Our state’s Lyme disease rates have been increasing over the past 10 years pretty dramatically. And we are actually now a high incidence state based on CDC’s definition of Lyme disease incidence,” said Rachel Burkholder, with the Michigan Department of Health and Human Services.
Burkholder said the state has seen a more than 350% increase in Lyme disease cases in five years, from 471 cases in 2020 to more than 2,000 in 2025.
What we’ve learned about pandemic learning loss
Schools are seeing the first wave of children born during the COVID-19 pandemic. Many teachers are reporting seeing speech and vocabulary delays in their classrooms.
Researchers examining how the pandemic affected child development found that children born in 2020 are not the age group facing the biggest challenges, according to a Johns Hopkins Medicine study.
Dog-like robot acting as security
A high-tech robot is adding an extra layer of security at businesses across the country, combining AI technology and human expertise to track down security threats.
The robot, covered in sensors and about the size of a dog, conducts automated patrols at locations. The device checks gates, doors, locks and looks for people in places where they shouldn’t be.
A possible return to archery
A group of Trine University engineering students spent months designing a device to help a Navy veteran regain the ability to shoot a bow, after injuries left him without the use of his left arm.
Chester Evitt, a Navy veteran who served in the Gulf War, was shot in the arm during his service. A second injury three years ago worsened his condition.
“Because I’ve lost most of the use of my left arm, I can’t hold anything in it. I can’t shoot my bow,” Evitt said.

title: Why Troy Jackson says he doesn’t regret telling Susan Collins to ‘shut up’ during Maine Senate debate
text:
WASHINGTON — Maine Democrat Troy Jackson says he does not regret telling Sen. Susan Collins that she should “shut up” after the Republican suggested a protester who interrupted their recent debate was one of his campaign’s backers.
“She said that it was a Troy supporter. She accused me of setting that up. I had no idea who it was,” said Jackson, a former president of the state Senate who is trying to deny Collins, the longest-serving Republican woman in Senate history, a sixth-term. He spoke in an interview with CNN’s “State of the Union” that aired Sunday.
During their final debate Thursday night in the closely contested race as the Nov. 3 election nears, a protester opposing data centers began yelling as Collins spoke. While moderators asked for that person to be removed, the senator said the demonstrator was “obviously one of Troy’s supporters.”
Jackson responded: “Oh, shut up. I don’t even know that kid.”
The Sunrise Movement group posted on its Instagram page that the outburst came from one of its members. In a caption of an Instagram post, the group’s page said: “We’re proud of this Sunrise volunteer who took action yesterday.”
The New York Times said the protester, Henry Elgie, a 19-year-old student at Bowdoin College in Brunswick, told the newspaper in an interview Saturday that he had “zero coordination” with Jackson’s campaign. “I do not know Troy Jackson personally or at all,” he was quoted as saying.
The Sunrise Movement is a left-wing political advocacy organization that champions the Green New Deal, aimed at transitioning the U.S. economy to 100% renewable energy. The group, which has local arms around the country, regularly organizes protests, sit-ins and climate strikes.
Jackson told CNN that he shook hands with Collins after each of their debates.
“But what I’m not going to be is talked down to by Sen. Collins,” he said. He added: “I’m fighting for Mainers and I just think that was another situation where she was talking down to me and I’m not going to apologize for that.”
Collins told Fox News’ Sean Hannity on Friday that she was “struck by how reflective the response, ‘Oh, shut up,’ was.” Collins said “the fact that it seemed like such an automatic, quick reply was very telling.”
She cited what she said was “the reputation” that Jackson had in the Maine Legislature “particularly when he’s dealing with women with whom he disagrees. So in some ways it didn’t surprise me.”
Some state lawmakers who worked with Jackson have criticized him as having a temper, including once throwing a plastic water bottle on the ground in frustration while disagreeing with a female lawmaker. Asked by reporters during the campaign about the confrontations, Jackson said, “I wear my heart on my sleeve.” He took responsibility for his outburst and apologized to those he had confrontations with at the time.
Jackson was asked on CNN about some Republicans who are saying there were stories that he was aggressive in his tone to women from his time in the Legislature and that his remark Thursday night was another example of that.
Jackson said some Republicans have been spending millions “attacking me and my family, making untrue claims. … So it doesn’t surprise me.”

title: Father leaves 4-month-old baby alone in parked car to argue with baby’s mother at a bar, police say
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WSMV/Gray News) - A 4-month-old baby was left in a car over the weekend while his father went out to the popular bar area, Broadway, in downtown Nashville, according to Metro Nashville Police.
Jordan Hayley, 25, is accused of leaving his infant in the front seat of his running car while he went out to Jason Aldean’s Kitchen + Rooftop Bar.
Police were first alerted to the case Sunday when officers spotted Hayley arguing with a woman outside the bar.
“The female party was screaming at the defendant and he was also exchanging words with her,” police wrote in an affidavit. “Both were in each other’s faces.”
Officers broke up the dispute. When speaking with the woman, she told police she was upset because Hayley was supposed to be caring for their 4-month-old daughter, and she didn’t know where the child was.
“In short, she was worried about her child’s welfare,” the affidavit says.
Hayley told Metro Nashville Police the baby should be with her maternal grandmother, but the woman “denied that being possible,” according to arrest papers.
Police detained Hayley and took his car keys. They found his vehicle parked and running near the honky tonk bars on Broadway, an area “known to be heavily trafficked with disorderly and intoxicated individuals.”
In the front seat, the 4-month-old girl was found alone. The affidavit says she was in a baby seat facing the wrong direction.
The 25-year-old man was arrested, and the infant was reunited with her mother. Hayley is charged with leaving an unattended child in a motor vehicle and child neglect, per Davidson County court records.
His bond was set at $5,000 for the neglect charge and $1,500 for leaving the child in the car. Records show a judge is scheduled to review his case in court Friday morning.

title: Shooting near Ohio mosque leaves 1 dead but was not connected to the building, police say
text:
COLUMBUS, Ohio (AP) — A shooting in a neighborhood near a mosque in Ohio’s capital city left one person dead Monday but was not connected to the house of worship or those who were inside, police said.
Federal and local authorities descended on the area as the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives said in a post on X that agents were responding to a report of a shooting at the mosque, northeast of downtown Columbus.
Police later said the shooting happened in the parking lot of an apartment complex next to the mosque.
“At the mosque, unfortunately, there was an event going on that had nothing to do with what was going on outside,” said Sgt. James Fuqua. “... But it’s super important that I make it clear that this shooting had nothing to do with an attack on the mosque itself.”
The ATF did not immediately respond to a phone message seeking further information.

title: Police shooting that killed a 1-year-old Mississippi boy was justified, officials say
text:
Police shooting that killed a 1-year-old Mississippi boy was justified, state attorney general's office says
Mississippi’s attorney general says a Senatobia police officer was justified in the use of force in the June shooting death of a 1-year-old boy while responding to a shoplifting call.
Community members and civil rights leaders have been calling for "justice for baby Kohen Wiley" ever since he was shot and killed.
The shooting occurred in mid-June as Senatobia officers responded to a shoplifting call at a local Walmart, where they saw Vellesiya Wiley, Kohen’s mother, carrying her son as she and a friend left the store, got into a car and began driving away. Wiley and her friend are both Black. Police reports indicate diapers and baby clothes were allegedly stolen.
According to a statement released shortly after the shooting by the Mississippi Bureau of Investigation, officers attempted to stop the vehicle, but the car drove toward law enforcement, prompting an officer to fire into the car, striking Kohen and his mother’s friend.
In a video released days after the shooting, Vellesiya Wiley denied that she or her friend stole anything and disputed that her friend, who was driving, headed toward the officers. Ben Crump, a nationally renowned civil rights attorney who is representing Kohen’s family, has said results of a preliminary independent autopsy indicate Kohen was shot from the side of the car, not the front, contradicting officers’ claims that the car was heading toward them.
"They were called over a box of diapers, and a family now has to bury their baby. You cannot put those two things next to each other and call it reasonable policing. Shoplifting a box of diapers ends up with you shooting into a moving vehicle. This 1-year-old baby couldn't put his hands up. A 1-year-old baby is not a threat to officers with a gun," said attorney Ben Crump during a press conference on June 22.
Sister station WAPT reached out to Crump, who is representing Wiley, for comment following the news from the attorney general's office. Below is the entire release from Fitch's office:
"Today, the Office of the Attorney General announced it has completed the review of a June 14, 2026 incident in Senatobia involving one officer with the Senatobia Police Department. In this incident, the Attorney General’s Office found the use of force was justified. Pursuant to Section 45-1-6 of the Mississippi Code, the review followed an investigation by the Mississippi Bureau of Investigation."
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: ‘We’re going to die’: Couple recount terrifying emergency landing during American flight
text:
ST. LOUIS (KMOV/Gray News) - A couple on board an American Airlines flight that had to make an emergency landing about 15 minutes after takeoff feared they wouldn’t make it home to their kids.
Tessa and Mark Springer, a couple from Waterloo, Illinois, were flying from St. Louis to Pennsylvania for work. Their flight took off Saturday morning from St. Louis Lambert International Airport, but trouble started before the plane even left the ground.
“We heard just this really horrible noise coming from the back of the plane. It was like... real loud buzzing, kind of grinding sound,” Mark Springer said.
Before takeoff, the pilot came over the intercom.
“The pilot comes back on and says, ‘Uh, there’s a problem with the engine on the airplane,’” Mark Springer said. “‘We can’t get it started.’”
The Springers say the plane took off roughly two hours later.
‘We’re going to die’
About 15 minutes into the flight, Mark Springer says conditions suddenly changed.
“All of a sudden, the plane just felt like it hit... like in a car, when you slam on your brakes... and everybody kind of lunges forward. Then, maybe a minute later, the plane just kind of goes boom and drops. All of the oxygen masks fall, and we just kind of looked at each other like, ‘Is this serious? Is this real?’” Mark Springer said.
He says the cabin filled with haze, and the flight attendant started shouting emergency orders.
Tessa Springer says she texted her children, “Problem on our plane, we love you guys.”
“I was like, ‘We’re going to die,’” she said.
However, the plane turned back to Lambert and was able to land safely.
Evacuation on the runway
The Springers say they evacuated the plane by jumping from the wing, with strangers catching each other on the way down. Tessa Springer took photos while they waited next to the runway for transportation back to the terminal.
The couple are now home – grateful but shaken up.
“I just kept closing my eyes and seeing my kids and thinking about them losing both of us at the same time,” Tessa Springer said. “I don’t think I’ll ever be able to get on another airplane ever again.”
American Airlines said in a statement that the flight returned to Lambert after an odor was reported on board. The plane was pulled from service for inspection.

title: Canadian man who took a bird from Las Vegas' Flamingo casino could face prison if convicted
text:
LAS VEGAS (AP) — A visitor from Canada maliciously harmed a flamingo at an iconic Las Vegas hotel by removing the bird from its enclosure and taking it to his room earlier this year, prosecutors said Monday at the man’s trial.
His attorney said it was a drunken act and no harm was intended.
Mitchell Fairbarn of Ontario is charged with two counts of felony animal cruelty in Nevada district court. Authorities allege that on March 3, he entered the flamingo habitat at the Flamingo Las Vegas Hotel and Casino and took a bird named Peachy.
Video played at the trial showed Fairbarn holding the flamingo in an elevator and carrying it down a hotel hallway.
Fairbarn faces up to five years in prison on each count if convicted of felony animal cruelty. If jurors should find him guilty on the lesser charge of misdemeanor animal cruelty, he faces up to six months in jail on each count.
Prosecutors said Fairbarn willfully caused the bird physical pain, noting feathers were found on the hotel floor and video showed the bird squawking while Fairbarn handled it.
But defense attorney Josh Tomsheck said his client regrets his actions while intoxicated and never meant to harm the bird, a key element in the felony charge.
Jurors were expected to begin deliberations after both sides presented closing arguments Monday morning.
Fairbarn has been unable to leave the U.S. since the incident.

title: Retired pilot helps historical society buy Neil Armstrong's boyhood home for tours
text:
TOLEDO, Ohio (AP) — Ken Schreiber was 9 when Neil Armstrong took his first steps on the moon in 1969 — a moment he would never forget. Like Armstrong, he too became a military fighter pilot.
So when Schreiber read a story in August that Armstrong’s boyhood home in Ohio was for sale and later learned no one had come forward to preserve it, he surprised even himself by making an offer.
“I just thought somebody has got to step up to the plate,” Schreiber said, remembering his father’s advice to “make a mark in life.”
The sale is scheduled to be finalized Monday. The local historical society will take ownership thanks to Schreiber’s $400,000 donation. He spent 20 years in the U.S. Air Force and retired as a pilot with American Airlines.
The Auglaize County Historical Society plans to restore the well-preserved home to its appearance during Armstrong’s boyhood, when he built model planes in the dining room and tested them in a basement wind tunnel he created.
Armstrong’s boyhood home could open for tours by 2030
The goal is to have the home ready for its first public tours by 2030 to mark the 100th anniversary of Armstrong’s birth, said Gerald Siesel, the historical society’s president.
The two-story home in Wapakoneta has long been a stop for visitors to the Armstrong Air and Space Museum curious about the astronaut’s early life, but it has never been open to the public.
The historical society has already started researching what the house would’ve looked like in the 1940s and talking with community leaders about raising money to renovate and maintain the home, Siesel said.
“Even now when this opportunity came our way, we realized we can’t do it ourselves,” he said.
House played a big role in Armstrong’s first steps to the moon
Armstrong’s family moved often during his childhood before settling in western Ohio when he was a teenager.
The house at 601 W. Benton St. played a big role in his life. He conducted experiments while living there and made his first solo flight and earned his pilot’s license at age 16.
Armstrong’s old bedroom is now decorated with photos and paintings of the moon landing and autographed photos of astronauts who’ve visited.
Little has changed on the outside, and the layout inside is similar too, though it has been updated.
The home went up for sale in August for the first time in nearly 40 years.
Karen Mikesell, a retired history teacher, bought the place in 1988 and is just one of a handful of people who’ve owned the home since Armstrong’s parents moved in the mid-1960s.
Over the years, she hosted nine astronauts, including Buzz Aldrin, who flew to the moon with Armstrong and Michael Collins in 1969.
Aldrin stepped inside the bedroom upstairs a few years after Armstrong died in 2012, Mikesell recalled, “and the tears just streamed down his cheeks.”
She said she felt a responsibility to preserve its past and to “keep it like the Armstrongs had” as much as possible. Mikesell, who’s 82, hoped someone would buy the house to help preserve it and inspire future generations.
That’s where Schreiber came in. He first asked friends to chip in but then donated the $400,000 on his own to help the historical society acquire the house.
New life for the Armstrong house
Schreiber, who grew up in Dayton, about 60 miles (96 kilometers) south of Armstrong’s hometown, always admired him for his achievements, modesty and character.
Despite growing up so close, Schreiber had never visited the Armstrong Air and Space Museum until this summer. He also toured the house.
“It was almost like the ghost of Neil Armstrong was there,” he said. “I could imagine him running up and down the stairs.”

title: Elon Musk to give SpaceX shares to ‘every kid in America’
text:
(CNN) - Elon Musk says he plans to give kids a stake in SpaceX.
Musk made the announcement on X, writing that he will give one SpaceX share to “every kid in America” next year.
SpaceX is a $2 trillion aerospace and artificial intelligence company. Based on the number of children in the United States, the potential giveaway could be worth billions of dollars.
Musk did not explain how the shares would be distributed.

title: Typhoon Champi strengthens to Category 5 but moves away from land; Trudy weakens
text:
Typhoon Champi strengthens to Category 5 but moves away from land; Trudy weakens
Typhoon Champi has moved from the western Pacific into the Philippine Sea and has become a Category 5 super typhoon, according to the U.S. National Weather Service.
Related video: Couple weds waist-deep in floodwaters after heavy rains flood church
It had maximum sustained winds of 160 mph (258 kph) by late Monday Asia time, and was not near land.
Champi earlier passed close to Guam, and the governors of Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands requested emergency disaster declarations Friday.
U.S. President Donald Trump approved the emergency declaration for Guam. The Federal Emergency Management Agency said federal assistance was available for the territory to supplement local response efforts.
Airports, harbors and some health facilities in the territories were closed. Relief supplies were unlikely to reach the islands for three to five days, FEMA said Saturday.
Meanwhile, former hurricane Trudy weakened to a tropical storm early Monday after it lashed parts of Mexico’s Pacific coast with rain and winds.
The storm had maximum sustained winds of 60 mph (100 kph) and was moving west at 6 mph (9 kph), according to the U.S. National Hurricane Center in Miami.
Trudy was moving away from the coast and its center was forecast to pass south of the Baja California Peninsula on Monday and Tuesday.
Some further rainfall was possible in the region where the ground has been saturated by successive storms.

title: Mississippi AG says officer's force was justified during shoplifting call in which boy was killed
text:
Mississippi’s attorney general says a Senatobia police officer was justified in the use of force during a June shoplifting call that ended in the fatal shooting of a 1-year-old boy.
The conclusion of the state’s investigation into the shooting death of Kohen Wiley follows months of mourning and calls for justice, both nationally and in the small town about 40 miles (65 kilometers) south of Memphis, Tennessee, where the shooting took place.
The shooting occurred in mid-June as Senatobia officers responded to a shoplifting call at a local Walmart, where they saw Vellesiya Wiley, Kohen’s mother, carrying her son as she and a friend left the store, got into a car and began driving away. Wiley and her friend are both Black. Police reports indicate diapers and baby clothes were allegedly stolen.
According to a statement released shortly after the shooting by the Mississippi Bureau of Investigation, officers attempted to stop the vehicle, but the car drove toward law enforcement, prompting an officer to fire into the car, striking Kohen and his mother’s friend.
In a video released days after the shooting, Vellesiya Wiley denied that she or her friend stole anything and disputed that her friend, who was driving, headed toward the officers. Ben Crump, a nationally renowned civil rights attorney who is representing Kohen’s family, has said results of a preliminary independent autopsy indicate Kohen was shot from the side of the car, not the front, contradicting officers’ claims that the car was heading toward them.
The shooting is the latest in a string of incidents that has eroded trust between the Senatobia police department and the city’s Black citizens.
Last year, a Senatobia officer threatened a Black woman with a Taser, pulling her from her car and onto the ground and arresting her during a confrontation over an accessible parking space in the same Walmart lot where Kohen was shot. Two years earlier, a Senatobia police officer was fired for arresting a Black 10-year-old for urinating in public.
More recently, former Senatobia Police Chief Harold Vanderford was fired by the city’s board of aldermen, after reporting by The New York Times, Mississippi Today and Verite News alleged he used racist slurs in private text messages.

title: Maine theaters are the place to get your fill of horror movies this week
text:
If you’re like me, this is the time of year where cinematic scares are your go-to choice of moviegoing entertainment. Still, some Halloween seasons feel a little too realistically unnerving for a mere fictional boogeyman to rattle your cage like it used to (Hi — America is teetering on the brink of economic collapse! Sleep tight!).
Anyway, this year’s Halloween season movie picks are a mixed-treat bag of traditional theatrical scares and a few that perhaps hit a little too close to home to be popcorn-munching fun. So whether you trust your local movie house to be your escape or your window into horrible real things you didn’t even know you should be afraid of, we’ve got you covered.
Damnationland
Friday at the State Theatre, 609 Congress St., Portland
No Maine Halloween season is complete without Damnationland, the all Maine-made horror and dark fiction short film anthology festival that’s been keeping Mainers happy/terrified for an amazing 16 years. Each Damnationland attracts Maine’s best and brightest filmmakers, actors, and crews, all dedicated to creating one impossible-to-define night of scares and suspense — all with that indefinably alluring Maine flavor. This year’s Damnationland features works from Maine filmmakers Joseph Aaskov, Alexa Allen, Trixie B and Victoria Gabor, Jin Defillipis, Mason Hawkes and Luis Valmadrid and Robert Moore. Check out damnationland.com/ for tickets and showtimes, and to see which theater near you the Damnationland terror tour pulls into next.
‘NAZA’
Starting Sunday at PMA Films, 7 Congress Square, Portland
And here’s the real horror. This documentary from the equally controversial and necessary Oscar winner “No Other Land” delves once more deep into the dark heart of the Israel-Gaza conflict. Interviewing Israeli soldiers on the darkened rooftops of Tel Aviv, the film shows how, after the Oct. 7 attack by terrorist group Hamas, IDF military were told, “No one is innocent in Gaza.” What’s resulted is an unthinkable, still ongoing campaign of indiscriminate civilian deaths of Palestinians, some 60,000 of them dead or wounded children. Or, as the film’s title., translated from its Israeli military acronym, calls them, “collateral damage.” There are those actively trying to suppress this film. See it for yourself.
‘Ghost in the Cell’
Sunday at the Colonial Theatre, 163 High St., Belfast.
No Halloween movie rundown would be complete without a full-on gorefest, and this Indonesian/South Korean flick from Joko Anwar (“Impetigore”) sees an already brutal prison beset by an invisible force that starts killing prisoners and guards indiscriminately — and in truly creative and disgusting ways. This supernatural horror has received good reviews from some of your heartier critics.
‘Begotten’
Wednesday, Oct. 28 at SPACE, 538 Congress St., Portland
Leave it to multimedia space SPACE to interpret “Halloween movie” less as “slasher in hockey mask” than “destabilizing mind-screw that leaves you bewildered and deeply disturbed.” That’s the only description I’ve ever come up with for E. Elias Merhige’s 1996 black-and-white, virtually wordless artistic assault on the brain and the senses. It has something to do with Mother Earth and the truly horrible things her creations and creator subject her to, and plays out like one of David Lynch’s less coherent fever dreams. Enjoy!
‘Ozzy & Black Sabbath: Back to the Beginning’
Wednesday, Oct. 28 and Thursday, Oct. 29 at Nickelodeon Cinemas, 1 Temple St., Portland
There was a time when British heavy metal band and its dynamic, diminutive lead singer Ozzy Osbourne were every parent’s worst nightmare. Their ominous lyrics, crunching riffs, and Osbourne’s infamous (possibly apocryphal) bat-biting antics struck fear into suburban types everywhere. This concert, filmed just 17 days before Osbourne’s 2025 death might be more of an old-timers’ reunion than a satanic rock coven, but the filmed concert does feature the original Sabbath lineup playing together for the first time in ages. And if the ailing Osbourne had to perform sitting down, you know he did it from a bat-winged throne.
‘Christmas at the Kringles’
Opening everywhere Friday, Oct. 30.
Horror and comedy are a damnably tough blend — when it works, you get “Shaun of the Dead.” When it doesn’t, you want to swear off both comedies and horror movies for a solid month. Luckily for us, this poisoned candy cane stars some surefire comic talents like Thomas Lennon, Rob Riggle, Donald Faison, Arden Myrin, Ron Livingston and Rachel Bilson in a tale of bloodily mandatory holiday cheer.
New arrivals are at first charmed by their Christmas-obsessed neighbors the Kringles and their year-round wonderland of twinkling lights. Unfortunately, not getting into the Christmas spirit is grounds for execution with an array of holiday-themed implements by Lennon and Myrin’s outwardly cheery married duo. The perfect Halloween treat for those of us horrified that stores are putting their Christmas displays up already.
Dennis Perkins is a freelance writer who lives in Auburn with his wife and his cat.

title: Portland landlord, tenants union agree to $3.6M settlement over years of complaints
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
PORTLAND — Members of the city’s tenant unions raised their fists in unison Monday in front of the 102-unit Trelawny Building on Congress Street after announcing a $3.6 million settlement with landlord Geoffrey Rice.
The settlement, detailed at a midday news conference, comes after years of rent control violations and legal action between the Trelawny Tenants Union, the city and Rice, who owns 19 residential properties in Portland.
Members of the Trelawny union and the Portland Tenants Union called the settlement monumental for Portland renters, as it ensures that affected tenants will be reimbursed and resolves complaints filed against the embattled landlord.
According to the agreement, Rice will roll back rents across his residential properties to the legally allowable rent charged on Dec. 1, 2022, and a $3.6 million escrow account will be used to pay back tenants all amounts charged above that 2022 rent. It will also be used to pay a $250,000 fine to the city of Portland.
In return, the union has agreed to halt complaints against Rice for past violations. The agreement also signals that Rice, who is in his late 80s, may be preparing to sell some of his properties.
Ethan Strimling, the former Portland mayor and a spokesperson for the Trelawny Tenants Union, said he believes Rice came to the negotiating table because, in order to sell his properties, he needed to clear past violations.
Strimling said the agreement covers all of Rice’s residential properties, which include some 300 units and more than a thousand current and past tenants.
“This has been a long road for all of us, but I am hopeful we are finally seeing the light at the end of the tunnel,” he said.
The agreement lays out that as Rice sells properties, funds will be added to the settlement account. The Trelawny Tenants Union will also hold mortgages on 10 of Rice’s properties to give the union leverage.
According to a news release, negotiations on the settlement occurred over the past four months, and were capped by a 20-hour session over two days between the tenants unions, Rice, the city and a mediator.
Jeremy Dean, an attorney for Rice, said Monday that the agreement “provides a process and mechanism that will bring every one of (Rice’s) properties into full compliance” with the city’s rent control ordinance.
“No stone will be left unturned, and Mr. Rice’s tenants are the primary beneficiaries of the process that was agreed upon,” he said. “I’m honored to have been part of this process, and I’m looking forward to seeing it through.”
Ian Jacob, a union member and longtime tenant of Rice’s, thanked Rice for “doing the right thing” for all of his tenants.
Because the city is a party to the agreement, the City Council unanimously supported a resolution affirming the terms Monday night.
Mayor Mark Dion called the settlement a “significant win for tenants of the city.” He said that, while not required, the council resolution acknowledges the settlement as affirming what rent control is supposed to do in the city, as well as recognizing the work done by legal staff in getting the parties through mediation.
Giselle Taylor, a member of the tenants union’s mediation team, said the group will audit all properties to determine the amounts owed to each tenant “to ensure they are paid back as fast as possible,” and that reimbursements will come with 10% interest.
The group said it expects almost every tenant across Rice’s properties to get back “hundreds, if not thousands, of dollars.”
“When we come together as tenants we will always have so much more power than we have when we’re just alone,” Taylor said. “I’m proud we live in a city that has rent control so the people who work here can afford to live here.”
The Portland Tenants Union has launched a form on its website where current and previous tenants are asked to provide updated information to ensure refunds are properly issued.
Strimling said rents have already been rolled back at the Trelawny Building and 59 State St., a 42-unit building, but the remaining properties will be subject to the coming audit.
The $3.4 million figure was calculated based on the rebates issued from the first two buildings. Strimling said there is a contingency in case it’s not enough, or to reimburse Rice if it’s too much.
City Councilor Wes Pelletier, a former member of the Trelawny Tenants Union, said the settlement establishes a “clear precedent” for these types of violations moving forward after years of trying to hold Rice — and the city — accountable for enforcing the rules, which have been affirmed by voters several times.
“We can’t rely on the city alone, we have to rely on each other to make this stuff happen,” he said.
The news conference occurred Monday in front of the building at 655 Congress St. where facade work is nearly complete following a multiyear process that also led to a lawsuit between Rice and the city.
A lengthy back and forth regarding proposed changes to Portland’s rent control ordinance garnered a tremendous amount of feedback in September when the council passed a resolution calling for several operational changes, including verifying base rents established in 2020 and creating an online rental registration system that flags incorrect or missing rental information.
The Housing and Economic Development Committee is slated to discuss potential ordinance changes Tuesday.
Editor’s note: This story was updated on Oct. 20 to reflect the City Council’s unanimous passage Monday night of a resolution affirming the terms of the settlement.

title: Here's what we know about the service member who fell to his death at a college football game
Jalen Hurts out for season after doctors find multiple blood clots in his lungs
text:
Jalen Hurts out for season after doctors find multiple blood clots in his lungs
Philadelphia Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts is expected to miss the rest of the season because of blood clots in his lungs, a person familiar with the situation told The Associated Press on Monday.
The person spoke to The Associated Press on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of a health matter.
Hurts was placed on injured reserve Saturday, two days after the Eagles revealed he has a blood clot in his calf. He missed the first of at least four games in Philadelphia's loss to the Carolina Panthers on Sunday.
The Eagles and Hurts' agent, Nicole Lynn, released more information on his condition Monday. They said Hurts has deep vein thrombosis and a bilateral pulmonary emboli, meaning a blood clot has traveled from the legs to the lungs.
His treatment involves blood thinners, and he won't be allowed to participate in any football activities until he is off them.
Related video above | Eagles offensive lineman Lane Johnson retires after 14 seasons
The Eagles and Lynn said Hurts was expected to make a full recovery. “He is clinically stable and has no significant functional limitations,” their statement said.
Eagles coach Nick Sirianni was the only member of the organization made available to the media on Monday — not general manager Howie Roseman or any member of the team's medical staff — and largely deflected questions about Hurts' health or how the team handled the situation.
“I'm not a medical expert," Sirianni said. “I lean on our guys in all those situations. I'm a football coach. I lean on our medical experts in every situation. I have full trust and full faith in them. It's not just me that has major care for our players. It's them, as well.”
The Eagles previously said Hurts was injured when he took a cleat to his calf area on Oct. 4 in a game against the Los Angeles Rams.
Hurts informed the medical staff of the injury after practice on Oct. 8. The Super Bowl 59 MVP was back at practice the next day before the team left for London to play Jacksonville. Hurts was initially diagnosed by specialists in London with a left calf superficial vein thrombosis.
Sirianni declined to say Monday why the Eagles allowed Hurts to fly home with a blood clot. He referred to statements the Eagles and Hurts' agent released over the last week that addressed the timeline of his injury and treatment.
He had no answers on specific questions about Hurts and his blood clots.
"I understand you want this information on this," Sirianni said. “I fully trust the people that are involved in helping us all make these decisions. We have great people here.”
Hurts hadn’t missed more than two games in a season since becoming the full-time starter in 2021. He has led the Eagles to five straight playoff appearances, three NFC East titles and two Super Bowl appearances, beating the Chiefs 40-22 two years ago.
Tanner McKee started for Hurts against the Panthers. McKee finished 26 of 45 for 215 yards and a touchdown in the 25-14 loss. The Eagles (2-4) have lost four consecutive games for the first time since 2020.
Sirianni added that beleaguered offensive coordinator Sean Mannion was still the play-caller.
Hurts has eight touchdown passes and three interceptions with 933 yards passing this season. He is in the middle of a five-year, $255 million extension, including $179.3 million guaranteed, that takes him through the 2028 season.
The Eagles stunned fans when they drafted Hurts out of Oklahoma in the second round in 2020. They seemingly had Carson Wentz entrenched at QB and had more pressing needs. But Hurts supplanted Wentz and became one of the top quarterbacks in the NFL.
“I haven't been without Jalen for an extended period of time,” Sirianni said. “I have the utmost confidence in Tanner. But I miss him. I know that will be the case. Jalen and I have been together, head coach and quarterback, for six years.”

title: New Orrington boat launch dedicated to former weekly newspaper owner
text:
Orrington residents will soon have access to launch their boats in the Penobscot River at a boat landing named after a longtime resident.
Alan Baker, 97, has been part of a multiyear effort to increase river access in Orrington. Now, a boat landing bearing Baker’s name on the Penobscot River is projected to open in June 2027.
Baker, who was formerly the owner and publisher of the Ellsworth American, and members of Orrington’s boat landing committee attended a ceremonial gathering at the site Monday morning. The landing is being built in South Orrington on McGinn Road. Work had already begun at the site on Oct. 16.
U.S. Sen. Susan Collins attended the groundbreaking in support of Baker. The senator was not involved with funding the project, but has long been friendly with Baker and has submitted multiple tributes to him into Senate records.
C-SPAN and the Wall Street Journal attended the event but Collins, who is involved in a contentious reelection campaign against Democratic nominee Troy Jackson, did not take any questions from reporters after the ceremony.
When it opens next year, the landing will give more access to the Penobscot River from the east river bank, which is limited between Milford and Castine. When asked about his thoughts on the landing being dedicated to him, Baker said: “It’s a little bit daunting. I’m not used to that.”
Planning for the plot of land used for the landing began six years ago, boat landing committee member Keith Bowden said Monday. The landing will have a boat ramp for put-in, a playground and picnic area, Bowden said.
“This is going to be enjoyed by a lot of people as well as the boaters,” Bowden said.
The idea for more amenities than just a boat ramp in Orrington came from Baker’s comments about how the Ellsworth marina and boat launch attracts residents to the space to eat lunch or enjoy the sights, Bowden said.
The project, which started with initial walks of the plot of land during the COVID-19 pandemic, is funded by state grants, town funds and the Greenfield Environmental Trust, a private environmental trust. More than $2 million in funding was secured for the project, Craig Morin, an engineer on the project, said.
During the years the project was taking shape, the process involved “kissing a lot of frogs” before everything came together, Orrington Town Manager Chris Backman said. Working with funders, residents and Sen. David Hagan, R-Hampden, made the process easier, Backman said.
By living in Hampden before many environmental cleanups of the Penobscot River took place, Hagan said he remembers when bald eagles and sturgeon weren’t seen along the river. Now, Hagan said he’s been able to see much wildlife in the area, and the boat landing will allow more area residents to access it.
“The fact that Orrington is participating in this massive mercury cleanup and putting this beautiful thing in to be able to park my boat somewhere on this side of the river will be a great thing,” Hagan said.
