title: President Trump says he will close historic DC golf course for 15 months of renovations
text:
President Trump says he will close historic DC golf course for 15 months of renovations
President Donald Trump on Sunday announced plans to close a historic public golf course in the nation's capital for 15 months and redevelop it despite a court challenge to his long-sought renovation.
Trump posted on social media about his intent to shutter the East Potomac Golf Course, not far from the White House, starting Nov. 15 to make it “one of the Best and Most Spectacular Golf Courses anywhere in the World.”
Related previous coverage in the video player above: Judge bans Trump from removing trees on public DC golf course
A judge last week, however, ordered a halt to his redevelopment plans until at least Oct. 26 after scolding the government for starting a large-scale tree removal at the course over a holiday weekend while providing little notice to the court or the plaintiffs trying to stop the makeover.
Trump did not acknowledge the legal fight in his post, which included an artist's rendering for the course redesign.
“When completed, it will be open to the Public while, at the same time, designed to the Highest Level of Golf and able to hold World Class Tournaments such as the U.S. Open, the PGA Championship, the Ryder Cup, and the Presidents Cup,” Trump wrote.
Democracy Forward, which is representing the plaintiffs challenging his renovation plans, responded by saying that the course is part of a national park and recreation facility that is meant for everyone to enjoy.
“Our litigation is intended to protect this community jewel for the people and communities it serves and we will continue to work with our plaintiffs to defend it from unlawful and harmful intrusion,” Skye Perryman, the president and CEO of the group, said in a statement.
The judge in the case took notice of Trump's online message and ordered the government to notify her by 8 p.m. EDT Sunday whether its position had changed from a court filing Friday that said “at most” Trump has given “preliminary thought” to the rebuilding plan and “there is no final agency action.”
The government responded by repeating that “there is no final agency action” because the National Park Service has not completed its review and the plan is not final. The filing, signed by Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward, also said the government, in stating this position, had not been representing “the actual position or mental impressions” of Trump but instead had relied on his public statements.
Capital makeover extends well beyond the fairways
Trump, a golf aficionado who plays often, had already announced plans to makeover the links as part of his broader push to renovate and refurbish places around Washington, including the White House and the Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts. Many of his projects, including plans for a huge ballroom at the White House, the installation of his own name on the Kennedy Center and construction of a massive arch, have been challenged in courts.
The 106-year-old park and course has been the subject of many emergency hearings as the president has sought to renovate it. While it has been open to Washingtonians of all income levels, opponents of Trump's plans to turn it into a high-end course have argued it will alter the character of the space and make it less affordable to people.
Trump in his post echoed arguments he has made to justify his plans to remake the Kennedy Center, arguing it is in such dangerous condition that it needs to close.
“The current Course is old, broken, dilapidated, and of no further use or effect. It is in very poor condition, with falling, dangerous, and disease infested trees and, importantly, a collapsing and hazardous seawall,” Trump wrote.
Debris from the demolition of the White House East Wing to make way for his ballroom project has also been dumped on the grounds. The National Park Service has said the debris tested positive for lead, chromium and other toxic metals.
Trump also sought to justify the National Park Service's removal of hundreds of trees that the judge paused, writing in his announcement that when the golf course was originally built, “it was famous for no trees, with views of Washington, D.C., for all to see, but now, it is completely overgrown, dysfunctional, and unsafe.”
Legal case returns to court and the administration seeks to remove the judge
Trump’s post outlining a clear plan for construction complicates a federal court hearing scheduled for Monday in a lawsuit filed by the DC Preservation League and two golfers opposing the construction.
U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes has ordered key members of the Republican administration to testify on the recent tree-cutting and whether those actions are tied to the president’s plans for the historical public links.
The administration on Friday asked for Reyes to be replaced on the case, questioning her impartiality and citing what it called “egregious” behavior from the bench in response to an emergency hearing Oct. 12. Her frustration boiled over in a three-hour hearing when she lambasted the government’s attorney for the lack of notification she and the plaintiffs received before the trees were chopped down.
At the upcoming hearing, the judge is expected to address the request that she step aside. Meanwhile, over the weekend, the plaintiffs asked that she grant them a more long-standing preliminary injunction in the case and/or a stay.
___
Associated Press writer Gary Fields in Washington contributed to this report.

title: For equal rights for LGBT citizens, Collins has been in the room where it happens
text:
Ken Mehlman is a businessman and former chairman of the Republican National Committee (2005-2007). Michael S.C. Soto is the co-leader of the Equality and Fairness for All Americans Coalition.
One of the most memorable songs in “Hamilton” is “The Room Where It Happens.”
It tells the story of a 1790 dinner where Alexander Hamilton, Thomas Jefferson and James Madison struck a deal. Hamilton won federal assumption of the states’ war debts. Jefferson and Madison won a capital on the Potomac. Aaron Burr, who sings the song, is left outside wondering how it all came together.
Washington still works much the same way. Debates happen in public, and public opinion shapes what is possible. But the details are usually settled in smaller rooms, among members of Congress, with the White House and with the advocates and stakeholders who will live with the results.
We have spent our careers in and around those rooms. One of us has worked in Republican politics, the other in progressive politics. We don’t agree on everything. But we have both worked to advance freedom and equal opportunity for gay and transgender Americans, and we have learned that who is in the room matters.
When it comes to gay rights, Sen. Susan Collins has been in that room for a long time.
In 2010, she and Sen. Joe Lieberman led the effort to repeal “Don’t Ask, Don’t Tell,” allowing gay and lesbian Americans to serve openly in the military. She supported federal hate crimes protections and workplace protections. She opposed amendments to ban same-sex marriage, publicly supported marriage equality and signed the Republican brief urging the Supreme Court to recognize same-sex marriages nationwide. In 2019, she joined Democratic Sens. Jeff Merkley, Tammy Baldwin and Cory Booker in introducing the Equality Act.
Some of the most important rooms in Washington are the ones where budgets get written. As chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, Collins secured more than $2.5 billion for the Ryan White HIV/AIDS Program this year, including $525 million that had been slated for cuts. Last year she stopped a proposed $400 million cut to PEPFAR, the global AIDS program that has saved an estimated 26 million lives. That work earned her the 2025 Champion Award from U.S. Business Action to End HIV.
Over time, she has become the Republican that Democratic senators call first when they want to move equality legislation forward. The Respect for Marriage Act shows why.
In 2022, many married same-sex couples worried their marriages were not fully secure under federal law. Congress had a chance to act, but only if a bill could reach 60 votes in the Senate. That meant bringing Republicans along without losing Democrats.
Collins and Baldwin led that effort, working with Sens. Rob Portman, Thom Tillis and Kyrsten Sinema. Much of the work happened quietly. They met with colleagues one at a time, listened to concerns about religious liberty and wrote language that addressed those concerns while keeping the heart of the bill intact. The final law repealed the Defense of Marriage Act and required federal and state recognition of same-sex and interracial marriages.
It passed the Senate 61-36 with support from Democrats, Republicans, equality advocates and religious organizations. President Biden signed it into law.
Some people hear the word “compromise” and worry it means supporters of equal rights must settle for less. That is not what happened here. The religious liberty language did not weaken the protections for married couples. It ensured everyone had a seat at the table and answered honest concerns so the bill could win the votes it needed and stand up in court. Sen. Collins knew the difference. She knew what could change and what could not, and people on both sides trusted her to keep her word.
That kind of legislating rarely makes headlines. It is slow, and it often happens out of view. But it is how lasting protections get written into law.
Washington is more divided today than at any point in our careers. That makes lawmakers who can work across party lines to solve our country’s biggest challenges more valuable and harder to find.
The room where it happens is less glamorous than Broadway makes it look. But for more than two decades, whenever the rights and lives of gay and transgender Americans have been on the table, Susan Collins has been in that room. And the laws that came out of it are stronger because she was there.

title: Woodstove fire heavily damages Aroostook home
text:
A fire started by a woodstove heavily damaged a Castle Hill home on Saturday.
The Mapleton, Castle Hill and Chapman Fire Department received word of the structure fire shortly after 1 p.m., Maine Department of Public Safety spokeswoman Shannon Moss said Monday.
It was the second heating-related blaze in three days, the fire department said on social media.
Crews arrived to find the mobile home engulfed in flames but were able to put out the fire.
A 60-year-old man, the home’s only occupant, had tried to put it out himself and injured his hand, Moss said.
The department did not release the man’s name.
Investigators from the state fire marshal’s office determined the fire was accidental and had originated near a working woodstove. As the heat ignited the wall behind the stove, the fire spread throughout the home.
The fire marshal’s office reminds anyone using heating appliances to make sure they are safely installed, maintained and placed within required distances from any combustible materials, including walls and furniture, Moss said.

title: U.S. Supreme Court declines to hear appeal of Maine’s gun sale waiting period
text:
The U.S. Supreme Court has declined to hear a challenge to Maine’s 72-hour waiting period for firearm purchases.
Justices on Monday denied a petition for a writ of certiorari in the case, one of dozens they declined to take up. The court, as is its standard practice, did not explain its reasoning for declining to hear the appeal.
The 1st U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled in April that the law is likely constitutional.
The law requires a 72-hour waiting period for a gun buyer to take possession of a firearm after purchasing it.
The law, as well as one expanding background check requirements, was enacted in 2024, six months after a gunman killed 18 people in the Lewiston mass shooting. Lawmakers designed the “cooling off” period to reduce suicides and homicides sparked by impulsive firearm purchases. It took effect without the signature of Gov. Janet Mills, who faced pressure from both gun owners and safety advocates.
The lawsuit was brought by a gun buyer, a firearms training business and three firearms dealers who argued that the law interfered with the rights of victims of domestic violence to immediately protect themselves and that it caused significant business losses for firearms dealers.
In February 2025, a federal judge granted a preliminary injunction, blocking enforcement of the law. That spring, a federal appeals court upheld the pause pending the state’s appeal.
The 1st Circuit concluded in April that the plaintiffs were unlikely to succeed in their constitutional challenge to the law and vacated the injunction. The Supreme Court’s decision leaves that ruling in place, allowing the law to be enforced while the lawsuit continues in federal court.
“We know from reporting from the Department of Public Safety that Maine’s 72-hour waiting period has already worked to save lives from preventable gun deaths in our state,” Nacole Palmer, executive director of the Maine Gun Safety Coalition, said in a written statement Monday. “Despite the gun lobby’s best efforts, our waiting period law will continue to save lives and we expect and hope that it will continue to be upheld.”
The Office of the Maine Attorney General declined to comment on Monday. Attorney General Aaron Frey is the defendant in the lawsuit, which was filed by Andrea Beckwith, who runs self-defense classes for victims of domestic violence, state Rep. James White, who owns J. White Gunsmithing, and other Maine gun stores and gun owners.
Joshua Raines, president of Gun Owners of Maine, said that while the Second Amendment group disagrees with the justices’ decision not to hear the appeal, “it wasn’t a surprise that they declined to take this on as it is only an injunction.”
“The lawyers will now take the main case back to the Maine court system, and we 100% expect the courts to overturn and nullify the Maine law based on previous federal case law,” Raines said in an emailed statement Monday.

title: US airman who died after rappel fall at a college football game in Texas is identified
text:
The U.S. airman who died after a rapid fall while rappelling from the rafters of a stadium before a college football game in Texas was a 15-year service member from Georgia, according to the Air Force.
U.S. Air Force Tech. Sgt. Ian Patterson died after being taken to a hospital following Saturday’s fall at the Alamodome in San Antonio, Nellis Air Force Base said in a statement. He had been rappelling toward the ground when spectators watched him plunge to the field prior to Navy’s game against University of Texas at San Antonio.
The military says an investigation is underway. The demonstration was part of a pregame program for the crowd during the annual “Salute to Armed Forces and Veterans” game in San Antonio.
“This tragedy is felt deeply across the 57th Wing,” U.S. Air Force Brig. Gen. Scott C. Mills, 57th Wing commander, said in a statement.
Patterson was a Tactical Air Control Party instructor assigned to the 6th Combat Training Squadron, Detachment 2, and served for 15 years, according to the military. He was from Fort Stewart, Georgia, and had numerous decorations and commendations.
A video of the fall that was posted on social media showed Patterson in combat fatigues quickly descending to the ground feet first. The fall occurred with fans in the stands and a band and cheerleaders assembled nearby on the field. He was treated on the field for several minutes and taken away.
The sister of Patterson’s wife declined to comment.
Game was delayed after emergency response
Officials delayed the start of the game for about 10 minutes following the fall.
UTSA head coach Jeff Traylor said his team could see the effect that it had on the crowd of over 23,000 people as soon as players arrived on the field for the game, which his team won 38-34. Traylor said he had only been told there had been an “incident” that would delay kickoff.
“You could tell the energy was just gone,” he said. “It just really puts things in perspective. It really does.”
Air Force says demonstration included a team of specialists
Patterson was one of four military service members who were scheduled to participate in the pregame rappelling demonstration.
According to an Air Force website, the service members who were participating in the rappelling demonstration were part of a team that embeds with Army and Marine units and helps to direct air and artillery strikes from forward ground locations.
Part of their training includes learning to rapidly drop by rope, sometimes from helicopters that are 100 feet (about 30 meters) or more above the ground.

title: Maine needs a change in Senate leadership
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
This year’s U.S. Senate race is a crucial one. On the right side of the aisle, Republicans are fighting tooth and nail to maintain their control of both the House and Senate. On the other hand, Democrats are doing everything they can to break the Republican Party’s congressional majority and bring balance back to Washington. In the middle of all this controversy stands the state of Maine, which is expected to experience one of the most closely contested elections in the United States.
Maine’s tightly contested election has come down to two candidates. Troy Jackson, a fifth-generation logger from Allagash, Maine, will be the Democratic candidate. His opponent will be Republican Sen. Susan Collins, running for her sixth consecutive term in the U.S. Senate. The only question on everyone’s mind is which of them is better for Maine’s citizens and students.
To know the answer to this question, we first must understand who the candidates are and what they are seeking to achieve.
Jackson, the Democratic nominee, has built a very strong grassroots movement centered around the working-class people. With support from organizations such as the Maine AFL-CIO and People Power Maine, Jackson’s campaign is heavily focused on making Maine more affordable by cutting taxes for working families and lowering the cost of necessary prescription medications for Maine residents.
Jackson has built his campaign on holding those in power accountable, and it is something he has done for a while now. “It seems like the government only works for those at the top,” stated Jackson during a press conference in 2025. “Career politicians cater to people with money, power and influence, ignoring the voices of everyday working people.”
Alternatively, Collins’ campaign has been built on her previous work as a Maine senator. Collins often cites her work as one of the most bipartisan servants in Washington as a point of leverage, showing she is not afraid to cross party lines to protect Mainers.
“A major difference between Troy and me [is that] I vote independently. Of all the hundred senators, the studies show that I am the most bipartisan member of the Senate,” said Collins during the most recent Maine Senate debate. “We don’t need more people who will vote in a straight party line. We need people who will ask the question, ‘What is best for Maine?’”
While both nominees certainly build a good case on the surface level, when looking into Collins’ most recent term as Maine senator, we begin to see different narratives arise.
According to the most recent CQ Roll Call, Collins sides with President Donald Trump on 92% of her votes. While this may not inherently be bad, some of these votes, such as her vote to advance Trump’s “big beautiful bill,” have had an adverse effect on Maine people.
As is well known, Trump’s “big beautiful bill” would go on to cut Medicaid funding nationwide, making healthcare less affordable for many low-income families. A reported 9,100 Mainers have already lost their healthcare, including 2,850 children, as a result of this bill that Senator Collins voted to pass.
Furthermore, Collins was a deciding vote in a bill that sent $70 million in federal funding to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). ICE has been a heavily scrutinized government agency during the second Trump administration, due to multiple civilian deaths (including one in Biddeford, Maine) and their use of excessive enforcement.
On the contrary, Jackson has been very outspoken in his view that ICE should be disbanded, which is something I certainly believe many Americans and Mainers can get behind. ICE has been a stain on this great nation’s legacy. Hiding behind masks, hurting members of the general public and their lack of restrictions, particularly regarding not releasing the footage of their body cams, is simply sickening. Jackson suggests we “put that money into Customs and Border Patrol. They have training, they’re law enforcement, people respect them, [and] we don’t respect ICE.”

'God covered us': Actor, singer recounts intense moments after plane skids off runway
text:
'God covered us': Actor Donnie Wahlberg recounts intense moments after plane skids off runway
Actor and singer Donnie Wahlberg shared a video on social media over the weekend, saying he was on board a plane that skidded off the runway at Las Vegas' main airport.
Video: 'God covered us': Actor Donnie Wahlberg shares scary plane incident
In an Instagram video posted hours after the incident, the "Boston Blue" star said he was aboard an aircraft at Harry Reid International Airport when it overshot the runway as the plane attempted to take off.
"We were taking off and didn’t get up in the air and ran out of runway. I'm just going to tell you these pilots saved our lives. And God covered us," Wahlberg, 57, said.
He said the aircraft went off the runway and into a fence. The actor said the plane was able to avoid "heavy" airport equipment and vehicles.
"Thankful to God, of course, and to our incredible pilots who did an amazing job of keeping us safe and avoiding a serious disaster," he said in the post's caption. "The airplane did take some lumps — but we did not. Thank you to all the emergency personnel on the ground in Las Vegas! You all were absolutely wonderful. All glory to God! By His grace, we are all ok."
People Magazine, in reference to the Federal Aviation Administration, said Wahlberg was on a Dassault Falcon 50 bound for Toronto Pearson Airport in Canada. Eight people were aboard the plane when the pilot aborted the takeoff and the plane went off the runway.
Harry Reid International Airport said no known injuries were reported and that some travelers may have experienced delays.
A ground stop was put in place at the airport at 12:50 p.m., but it was lifted by 2:30 p.m.

title: Student hospitalized with life-threatening injuries after being hit on the way to a bus stop
text:
LEXINGTON, Ky. (WKYT/Gray News) - A student was taken to a hospital with life-threatening injuries after being hit by a vehicle on the way to a bus stop Tuesday, authorities said.
Lexington police were called to Briar Hill Road on the city’s east side around 7:25 a.m. on Oct. 13 for a crash involving a student.
Fayette County Public School spokesperson Miranda Scully confirmed a student was hit on their way to a bus stop.
The student was taken to a hospital with life-threatening injuries.
Police said the investigation is ongoing and they do not expect to file criminal charges at this time. Police later confirmed the bus did not have its stop arm extended when the student was hit.
This is the second time this school year a student was hit at a bus stop in central Kentucky.
A new state law, House Bill 7, co-sponsored by Rep. Chad Aull, D-Lexington, took effect in July. It raises the fines for failing to stop when a school bus stop arm is out to $300 for a first offense and $500 for subsequent offenses. The law also allows school districts to install cameras to help identify violators.
“The fact that another kid, another family has to go through a situation like this, it’s just tragic, it’s so easily avoidable,” Aull said.
Aull said he believes stronger penalties and increased awareness will help prevent future incidents.
“I think it’s a tool that every school district in the state of the Commonwealth ought to deploy because I do think it will help reduce traffic incidents around buses if all school districts implement it,” Aull said.

title: Justice Department charges more than 2 dozen in California sweep targeting noncitizen voters
text:
Justice Department charges more than 2 dozen in California sweep targeting noncitizen voters
Federal authorities charged more than two dozen foreign nationals Monday in California as part of a statewide sweep targeting people who officials say have illegally registered or voted in U.S. elections.
Video above: Early voting push ramps up amid ballot counting battle
The arrests are part of a Trump administration effort to root out noncitizen voting ahead of next month's midterm elections, even though data shows that the problem is incredibly rare, difficult to prove and has not been shown to change the outcome of races.
Federal officials on Monday blamed California officials for the alleged crimes, accusing them of facilitating noncitizen voting through inadequate voter roll maintenance and hiding it from the public. The charges escalated a simmering voter roll fight that came into focus last week when the Justice Department sued California and warned that local election workers who knowingly process or tabulate ballots submitted by noncitizen voters are at risk of investigation and potential prosecution.
The Justice Department said the 28 people who were charged as part of a sweep dubbed Operation Protect the Vote are lawful permanent residents — but not U.S. citizens who are permitted to legally vote. They are charged with crimes including making false statements on a naturalization application and submitting fraudulent voter registrations.
“This causes real damage to real elections and real damage to American citizens," Trent McCotter, the acting deputy attorney general at the Justice Department, said during a news conference in Los Angeles.
Rob Bonta, California's Democratic attorney general, said Monday that there is no widespread voter fraud in California and that while “one-off” examples of voter fraud are possible, those instances are “a drop in the bucket” considering the state has 23 million registered voters.
Bonta said he expects his state to prevail in the federal government's lawsuit, saying the Republican administration “has provided us with no facts of any ineligible voters, just a conclusory statement with no evidence to back it.”
California emerges as a flashpoint for voting dispute
The federal government has made noncitizen voting a priority this year, demanding detailed voter information — including dates of birth, addresses, driver’s license numbers and partial Social Security numbers — from the states. While some states voluntarily handed over the information, the department sued 30 states and the District of Columbia to obtain it — lawsuits that so far have been unsuccessful.
The Justice Department said Monday it has charged 113 people in 20 states with illegal voting and illegal registration offenses over the last several weeks, It earlier said it had charged about 90 people for various types of election misconduct so far this year, including 50 who are alleged to have voted as noncitizens. There were more than 227 million registered voters in the United States during the 2024 presidential election.
The operation Monday involved the four U.S. attorneys' offices across California in what the Justice Department intended as a statewide show of force.
Among the dozens of people arrested was a 72-year-old Belize-born man who is accused of voting illegally in four elections.
Dozens of federal agents descended on Omar Alexander Muñoz's residential cul-de-sac in Commerce, a small city in Los Angeles County, to make the arrest. Muñoz was put in handcuffs in his pajamas and taken into federal custody downtown.
Esmeralda Muñoz, 70, said her family was furious that agents showed up to their home in full tactical gear with guns drawn to arrest her husband before dawn.
“It’s a show for them,” she said, calling it a “shame” that government officials arrived with camera crews and news helicopters.
She and her three children and 10 grandchildren are all U.S. citizens, she said; Omar Muñoz is a legal permanent resident, she said, and they didn’t realize that he was registered to vote. When they do talk about politics, Esmeralda said Omar has been a vociferous supporter of Trump.
The arrests were the latest in a flurry of activity that has unfolded in heavily Democratic California, which is not typically regarded as a key battleground state but does have a handful of competitive congressional races that could help determine which party controls the U.S. House for the final two years of President Donald Trump’s term.
The administration last week sued California to prevent it from counting mail ballots from people the federal government has identified as “likely” noncitizens until their immigration status can be confirmed.
The complaint was filed after California officials were given, and did not meet, a 48-hour deadline to review a password-protected thumb drive that contained a list of 20,000 names. The federal government says those are likely noncitizens who were sent ballots to participate in the Nov. 3 election, although the secretary of state said the administration has provided no evidence to support that claim. The state mails ballots to all registered voters.
McCotter said the 20,000 number was likely to rise.
“That’s just the floor,” he said.
DOJ accuses California of ‘state-facilitated voter fraud’
McCotter said the lawsuit against California was necessary because “state-facilitated voter fraud is unacceptable,” and accused state officials of creating the last-minute emergency before Election Day by not working with the Justice Department sooner to check alleged noncitizen voters.
Explaining why it was important to address voting by noncitizens even thought it's rare, he noted that some races in California have been decided by just hundreds of votes.
Bill Essayli, the top federal prosecutor in Los Angeles, criticized the state's election officials for not cooperating with the department's demands.
“Why is California refusing to show their voter rolls?” he asked. “What are they afraid of? What are they hiding?”
As part of its lawsuit, the Justice Department filed paperwork Monday seeking a court order that would force California to set aside ballots from suspected noncitizens and to independently, or in conjunction with the federal government, verify their citizenship status before tabulating their mail-in ballot. The Justice Department asked for the order to be entered in time for the Nov. 3 election.
Absent that order, the government said, “there is a significant risk that American votes will be diluted.”
Requests for comment sent Monday to the secretary of state and governor's office were not immediately returned. Newsom on Monday published a series of X posts seeking to undermine the Justice Department's announcement.
“WOW. First Assistant Bill just admitted in front of the press that not all of those arrested today may have voted,” he wrote in one post, referencing Essayli.
A warning for poll workers
On Friday, the Justice Department followed up with a warning that state election officials who knowingly process ballots cast by noncitizen voters are at risk of investigation.
A letter from McCotter reads: “If persons knowingly tabulate ballots cast by individuals identified by federal agencies as noncitizens, they risk becoming aiders and abettors to a federal crime.”
The letter is addressed to the Los Angeles County Counsel’s office and also is copied to California Secretary of State Shirley Weber and Los Angeles County Registrar Dean Logan, effectively putting the entire state on notice.
In response, Logan said his office is focused on conducting a fair and secure election while noting that Election Day is a mere 18 days away.
“The U.S. Department of Justice has chosen to litigate their unverified assertions of voting eligibility. At this point, it is best for this to be addressed in court,” he said.
Associated Press writer Eric Tucker contributed to this report from Washington.

title: President Trump signs executive order aimed at improving women's health. How could it impact you?
text:
President Trump signs executive order aimed at improving women's health. How could it impact you?
President Trump signed an executive order creating a women's health task force and a division at the National Institutes of Health to advance research, diagnostics, and treatments for women's health issues.
President Trump signs executive order aimed at improving women's health. How could it impact you?
President Trump signed an executive order creating a women's health task force and a division at the National Institutes of Health to advance research, diagnostics, and treatments for women's health issues.
President Donald Trump signed an executive order Monday aimed at improving women's health outcomes, establishing a women's health division at the National Institutes of Health and a White House women's health task force.
"Today's order also establishes the White House women's health task force, which will mobilize the entire federal government to coordinate action focused on improving women's health," Trump said.
The initiative, led by First Lady Melania Trump, aims to promote new research, advance diagnostic technology, and improve treatments for women's health issues, including cardiovascular disease and maternal health.
"Previous generations fought for women's rights. Our generation will fight to discover the cures that will ensure a woman can live her life in health and to the fullest," Melania Trump said.
The issue of women's health has recently gained bipartisan support. Last month, the Senate held its first hearing on menopause, addressing gaps in research, training, and care.
Dr. Rachel Rubin, a urologist and sexual medicine specialist, highlighted the challenges and opportunities presented by the executive order.
"It's going to require heavy funding. It's going to require businesses to be interested and manufacturers to be interested. It's going to require research support, and it's going to require a lot of advocacy, and I think there's bipartisan support for this, and so it's a real opportunity for everybody to lead in this space and really make some big changes," Rubin said.
The women's health task force was expected to hold its first meeting today at the White House.

title: How to avoid getting stuck with two mortgages during a move
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — Buying a new home before selling a current one can leave homeowners juggling two mortgages, or without a place to move into right away. A current home could sell quickly, while finding and closing on the next one may take longer in a competitive market.
Kate Wood, with NerdWallet, said lining up a sale and purchase perfectly is difficult in an imbalanced market, but there are ways to manage the overlap.
One option is a sale contingency, which ties the purchase of a new home to the successful sale of the current one.
“A sale contingency basically states some aspect of the purchase is contingent on, relies on you having successfully sold your home,” Wood said. “So when you are approaching a seller with this, saying, ‘Hey, in order for me to buy your home, I need to have sold my home,’ it’s a good idea to be working with a real estate agent that’s going to help you craft a really compelling offer.”
Wood noted that a sale contingency can make it harder to compete against cash buyers or those who are already pre-approved.
Another option is a bridge loan, which provides short-term financing to cover the gap between buying and selling.
“A bridge loan basically gives you a loan for 12 months or so that allows you to have the cash to make that next home purchase,” Wood said. “So you’re buying your next home, and then when you sell your previous home, you use proceeds from that sale to pay off the bridge loan.”
A home equity line of credit, or HELOC, is another option, though Wood said it needs to be set up before a home is listed for sale. A HELOC allows a homeowner to borrow against the equity in their current home to fund the purchase of a new one, then repay the loan using proceeds from the sale.

title: Medicare Advantage selection system is a disaster
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The Medicare Advantage system is broken. With open enrollment approaching, increasing costs and decreasing benefits are in the news. But a less discussed issue is that the array of charges and benefits is now so complex that a reasonable consumer cannot make an informed decision.
In Kennebec County alone, the 32 Advantage plans that include drug coverage differ in at least 11 respects. Without even considering medications, an informed consumer would have to consider 352 data points in various combinations in order to choose her best plan.
Excluding the plans marketed exclusively to those with special needs, there are still 17 plans requiring the consideration of 187 data points. Dental coverage is particularly vexing, with its disorienting set of copayments, co-insurances, covered and uncovered services, in- and out-of-network coverage and premiums. The result is a mind-boggling array of choices that stultify rather than clarify consumer choices.
In 1990, the federal government simplified the Medigap marketplace by requiring insurers to offer set menus of benefits from which beneficiaries can choose. Insurance companies then compete based on price and service. Applying this framework to the muddle that is Medicare Advantage would turn it into a workable system that allows consumers to make informed decisions.
Eileen Ringel
Oakland

title: Hannaford still offline a week after cyberattack on French supermarkets
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Hannaford supermarkets were still offline Monday, a week after Dutch owner Ahold Delhaize shut down its websites and apps following a “cybersecurity incident.”
The outage began the same day that cyberattacks disrupted supermarket refrigeration systems across France. A spokesperson for Hannaford, which operates 68 stores in Maine, said the company does not believe the issues are related. But some Hannaford locations have recently experienced refrigeration problems.
“The issue impacting some of our stores is specific to the refrigeration equipment itself, not other factors,” spokesperson Caitlin Cortelyou said in an email Monday.
About 700 French supermarkets experienced widespread food loss and some fires on Oct. 12, when hackers forced refrigeration units into continuous defrost cycles and set temperatures as high as 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit), according to The Associated Press.
Ahold Delhaize announced the same day that it had taken “some systems offline to help protect them” as “precautionary measures following (a) cybersecurity incident,” according to the company’s website.
The company said its stores — including Albert Heijn in the Netherlands, Delhaize in Belgium and Hannaford, Stop & Shop, Food Lion and Giant in the United States — would stay open while its websites and apps were offline.
On Monday, Ahold Delhaize announced that its European stores were back online and that e-commerce services at its U.S. stores “are expected to come back in the coming days.”
The company said it had no evidence that suggests any sensitive customer, associate or partner data was taken. It also didn’t note a connection to the cyberattacks on supermarkets in France.
“As the investigation is ongoing, we are not sharing further details that could compromise security measures or interfere with our response efforts,” the company said.
Based in Scarborough, Hannaford operates 188 stores across the Northeast and is Maine’s second-largest employer, with about 9,500 workers in stores from York to Fort Kent.
Hannaford confirmed Monday that it continued to experience a network issue affecting some services, including its website, mobile app, and Hannaford To Go pickup and delivery.
“This is related to a security issue within the network of our parent company, Ahold Delhaize,” Cortelyou said. “While we can’t comment on another company’s issue, we do not have any reason to believe the Ahold Delhaize matter is related to the issue impacting some French retailers.”
She noted that Hannaford stores remain open and continue to welcome customers, and that customers can continue to shop with the store online through Instacart, DoorDash and Uber Eats.
French Finance Minister Roland Lescure told Parliament last week that while the cyberattacks on refrigeration systems posed no risk to France’s food supplies, the attack “touches the heart of our food security,” AP reported.

title: Service member who died in rappelling accident at college football game identified
text:
(Gray News) - The United States Air Force identified the service member who died in a rappelling accident at a college football game on Saturday.
Tech. Sgt. Ian Patterson was attempting to rappel from the rafters as part of a demonstration before the football game between the University of Texas at San Antonio and the U.S. Naval Academy when he fell. The game was the university’s annual Salute to Armed Forces and Veterans event.
He was taken to the hospital, where he later died.
GRAPHIC WARNING: The video may be disturbing to some viewers.
Patterson was a Tactical Air Control Party instructor assigned to the 6th Combat Training Squadron, Detachment 2, Joint Base San Antonio, Texas, according to Nellis Air Force Base.
He was from Fort Stewart, Georgia, and served for 15 years. His decorations included the Air and Space Commendation Medal with three oak leaf clusters; the Army Commendation Medal, Air and Space Achievement Medal and Army Achievement Medal, each with one oak leaf cluster. In 2022, Patterson was named the Air Force Special Warfare Enlisted Instructor of the Year at the Headquarters Air Force level, according to the Air Force.
“This tragedy is felt deeply across the 57th Wing,” said U.S. Air Force Brig. Gen. Scott C. Mills, 57th Wing commander. “Tech. Sgt. Patterson and his service mattered immensely to our wing, and to the family, friends, and teammates who had the privilege of knowing and serving alongside him. Our team is now focused on standing beside Ian’s family, loved ones, and fellow Airmen as we navigate this profound loss together.”
The rappelling accident is under investigation.

title: A ‘purrfect’ ending: Cat missing for 571 days reunites with family
text:
GREENWICH, Conn. (WABC) - A Connecticut family is whole again after reuniting with their beloved cat who had been missing for 571 days.
Kelly Moore’s daughter adopted Turtle, a stray Nebelung cat from Tennessee. He lived with Moore in Greenwich, had been microchipped and had an ear tip indicating he’d been neutered. But one day in March 2025, Turtle disappeared.
“I was rushing out so fast I startled him, and he ran,” Moore said. “I love him so much, and it was just a comedy of errors.”
Moore turned to Rocket Lost Pet Rescue for help after Turtle went missing. Founder Rocco Autero set up cameras near the family’s home to determine whether the cat was still in the area.
“And he was actually. He was showing up. He came by here every night. We caught him on video… but he was afraid of cages,” Autero said.
The sightings of Turtle eventually stopped, leaving Moore fearing the worst.
“I cried so many nights, and I felt responsible because not being aware of the storm door. We were really brokenhearted,” she said.
The big breakthrough came just recently when someone posted on social media about finding a cat in Mamaroneck, New York, about 10 miles from Greenwich, Connecticut. Autero saw the post and had a hunch that cat might be Turtle.
“It’s shocking that he was found, and he traveled a long distance, a lot further than we’ve seen many cats go,” Autero said.
The cat’s microchip ultimately confirmed his identity. It took some cajoling to coax Turtle into a carrier, but he made the trip back home to his family in Greenwich.
“If this can happen, anything can happen. It’s so wonderful, and I’m so happy to have him back,” Moore said.

title: Husband, wife charged in interstate shooting death of 17-year-old: ‘Senseless act’
text:
ST. LOUIS COUNTY, Mo. (KMOV/Gray News) — A husband and wife from Texas are facing charges in connection with the death of a 17-year-old who was shot on Interstate 170 in Missouri.
Willie Herndon, 42, and his wife, Taiya Herndon, 45, were charged in connection with the shooting death of Alyssa Wilson, 17, last Wednesday.
Charges filed against couple
St. Louis County Prosecutor Melissa Price-Smith said Willie Herndon faces charges of first-degree murder and armed criminal action. Taiya Herndon faces a charge of hindering prosecution for driving Willie Herndon to Illinois after the shooting.
Willie Herndon is being held on a $1 million cash-only bond. Taiya Herndon is being held on a $500,000 cash-only bond.
Surveillance video shows shooting
The Major Case Squad of Greater St. Louis said at a news conference Monday that surveillance video showed a white SUV pulling over to the shoulder on southbound I-170 just south of St. Charles Rock Road.
Investigators said Willie Herndon exited the vehicle and stood outside briefly. A gunshot was then fired and he got back into the vehicle before driving away. Investigators said Taiya Herndon was also inside the vehicle.
The car was registered to Taiya Herndon, according to police.
Officers were then called to the southbound lanes of the interstate near Midland Boulevard in Overland for a crash around 7:20 p.m. When they arrived, officers said they found Wilson shot inside the crashed car. She was taken to a hospital, where she later died.
Victim was a high school senior
Wilson was a senior at McCluer North High School. She was a student-athlete and office aide and planned to attend college next year, the school said.
Arrest made in Illinois
Officials said investigators used license plate readers to identify the suspected vehicle and tracked it to a hotel in Caseyville, Illinois.
Law enforcement then arrested the couple from Arlington, Texas.
Investigators found evidence in the hotel room after executing a search warrant, including the gun. Willie Herndon gave details about his involvement in the shooting, as well as information “pertaining to possible ongoing investigations in other areas,” officials said.
Father speaks at news conference
During Monday’s news conference, Wilson’s father, Robert Hickman, thanked law enforcement for working to secure justice. He said Wilson was 60 days from turning 18, and the family planned a vacation to a Disney theme park.
“This was a senseless act, and we ask that everyone take a look at yourselves inside and make sure that next time something happens like this, you think before something happens,” Hickman said.

title: No time for banged-up Patriots to recover
text:
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. — The Patriots are testing the boundaries of the “next man up” mentality that is preached across a league in which injuries are guaranteed every week.
New England has just three days to recover coming off a 26-19 win over the New York Jets, during which it lost three offensive linemen to injuries.
Right tackle Morgan Moses (ankle) and left guard Alijah Vera-Tucker (hamstring) were Week 1 starters, while Ben Brown (knee) was starting at right guard for the second straight week. Brown was in the lineup after Mike Onwenu (ankle) was placed on injured reserve after two games and Greg Van Roten, his original replacement, went on IR the following week.
“As bad as it is and as unfortunate as it is, that’s just the way this game goes,” left tackle Will Campbell said. “I feel like some guys stepped up big for us.”
The Patriots, who play at Chicago on Thursday night, are banged up at other spots. Wide receiver Romeo Doubs exited in the first quarter with a shoulder issue following his touchdown catch and was placed on injured reserve Monday. Coach Mike Vrabel acknowledged the injuries will require everyone to remain fluid this week.
“We’ll just have to figure out who we have available and find 48 to put out there,” Vrabel said.
Rookie Caleb Lomu, a week after coming in for Campbell, jumped in at right tackle for Moses, with Walter Rouse subbing in at right tackle and Matt Pryor at left guard.
Lomu, Rouse and Pryor helped open lanes that allowed the Patriots to eventually run out the clock in the fourth quarter.
“Everybody prepares as a starter. I can’t wait to watch those guys that prepare all week without knowing whether they’re going to get an opportunity to play,” Vrabel said. “And then when they do, take advantage of it, and that’s a testament to those players.”
What’s working
Despite the offensive line injuries, the group kept Drake Maye off the turf. The quarterback wasn’t sacked Sunday, the first time that’s happened this season. He has been sacked only twice over the past three games after being taken down nine times in the first three.
What needs help
Ball security. The Patriots are second in the NFL this season with 13 turnovers (six lost fumbles, seven interceptions), behind the Los Angeles Chargers with 15 (seven fumbles, eight INTs).
Fixing that is a top priority.
“We’ll rep it more. We’ll put more time into it, I guess. I don’t know how you can put any more time into the amount of ball security drills we do,” Vrabel said. “I’m certainly cognizant. You can put it on me. That’s probably the easiest thing.”
Stock up
Lomu and Pryor. They allowed zero pressures on Maye during their combined 106 snaps.
Stock down
WR DeMario Douglas. He caught a 9-yard touchdown in the second quarter, but also had a 39-yard catch that ended with him getting the ball ball punched out from behind by Jamien Sherwood. The fumble led to a Jets field goal.
Injuries
The Patriots have moved quickly to replenish the backup depth on the offensive line, adding Andrew Rupcich and Jacob Rizy to the practice squad.
Key number
2 — The number of consecutive games Maye has gone without a turnover.
Next steps
The Patriots have a short turnaround before heading to Chicago for Thursday’s primetime matchup.

title: Vitamin C if you’re feeling sick: Evidence-based life hack? Or dated superstition?
text:
Vitamin C if you’re feeling sick: Evidence-based life hack? Or dated superstition?
It happens every common cold season. The moment a headache, scratchy throat or the sniffles set in, you search for something to stop its progress: Perhaps a mega-dose of vitamin C will do the trick.
Fall and winter are citrus season, anyway — cue the oranges and the grapefruits. Gulp a large glass of OJ. Or maybe grab one of those immune system supplements.
This story was originally published on PolitiFact.com.
Airborne advertises its “zesty orange” flavored “immune support supplement” with 1,000 milligrams of vitamin C. The brand Emergen-C offers daily drink powders in “Super Orange” to “fight back” and “support” your immune system.
The products’ packaging and websites caution not to take their ads as science: “These statements have not been evaluated by the Food and Drug Administration,” they read. “These products are not intended to diagnose, treat, cure or prevent any disease.”
Most of the research on using vitamin C as an illness treatment has centered on the common cold, which can be caused by over 200 viruses and has no cure. And it shows that, after symptoms start, vitamin C is not an effective cold remedy.
Vitamin C acts as an antioxidant and helps the body absorb iron. It is needed to make wound-healing proteins and is important for the immune system — but human bodies can’t make it. It’s important to get it from dietary sources or supplements.
Across trials spanning more than 50 years, providing vitamin C as a treatment immediately after cold symptoms began did not shorten a cold’s duration or lessen its severity, according to a 2013 study published in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews.
Vitamin C studies published in 2016 and 2023 reiterated that data on the vitamin’s effectiveness as a cold treatment lacked consistency and warranted further study.
In 2016, Creighton University School of Pharmacy and Health Professions researchers said because vitamin C supplements are inexpensive and relatively safe, people experiencing cold symptoms could reasonably “see for themselves if therapeutic vitamin C is beneficial, but they should know that the data behind its use are largely inconsistent.”
Vitamin C can’t stop a cold in its tracks, but regular consumption may benefit some people
It turns out that regular vitamin C consumption — not taking it as an acute-care treatment — can have benefits for helping a person’s immunity against colds.
“Getting enough vitamin C is important, and regular supplementation before symptoms begin may modestly shorten colds,” said Jerry Lio, an Ohio State University microbial infection and immunity professor. “But we cannot assume the same benefit from starting a supplement or eating an extra orange only when we begin to feel sick.”
Adult women need about 75 milligrams of vitamin C each day, and men need about 90 milligrams. A person’s daily vitamin intake shouldn’t exceed 2,000 milligrams.
That said, vitamin C does not consistently reduce everyone’s risk of getting a cold.
People might benefit if they engage in intense physical activity or are exposed to cold temperatures, or both. Using regular vitamin C might reduce their risk of developing a cold, studies find. Some older trials found that marathon runners, skiers and soldiers who were exposed to cold environments halved their common cold risk by regularly taking vitamin C.
Those findings can’t readily be expanded for the general public, however.
Regularly administered vitamin C does not affect how often people in the general population develop common colds, said the 2013 Cochrane review.
“The key is to get enough vitamin C regularly to support normal immune function,” Lio said. “Taking more than you need does not necessarily improve your immune response or provide greater protection against infection.”
It can potentially reduce a cold’s severity and length — but researchers cautioned against deciding to add a regular vitamin C supplement just from that finding alone.
A vitamin C supplement greater than or equal to 0.2 grams per day reduced a cold’s duration by about 8% in adults and 14% in children, while a supplement of 1 to 2 grams per day reduced a cold’s duration by 18% in children, the Cochrane review found.
“If you were going to have a common cold that lasts about seven days, it may cut it down about 13 hours,” Dr. Jesse Bracamonte, a Mayo Clinic family physician, told the Mayo Clinic Care Network.
That invites the question of whether it is worthwhile or practical to incorporate a regular vitamin C supplement, particularly when people tend to get at least some of their vitamin C from their normal, balanced diet.
“In our opinion,” the Cochrane review researchers wrote, “this level of benefit does not justify long‐term supplementation in its own right.”
Students or workers who have to budget their vacation or sick time may differ.
PolitiFact Staff Researcher Caryn Baird contributed to this report.

title: The Best New Shows on TV and Streaming This Week
text:
The Best New TV Shows You Can Watch This Week
Every week, ScreenCrush gives you what you need to know about the week’s best new streaming TV shows. If you’re in the market for a new series to stream, or you need a last-minute binge, or you are just trying to keep tabs on the latest seasons of old favorites, we have got you covered.
We love movies, but sometimes you don’t want a 90-minute, one-and done entertainment. Sometimes you want that deep dive that’s going to take days or weeks to finish. Sometimes you want long-term storytelling and rich characters. Sometimes you need a good TV show.
Regardless of what kind of show you’re looking for — new or returning, drama or comedy, high or lowbrow — we have you covered. Here’s this week’s batch of new TV shows and series.
READ MORE: Iconic Movie Lines That Weren’t in the Original Script
New TV Shows, New Seasons & New Streaming Series Out This Week
This week you can watch returning favorites Lupin and Nobody Wants This, plus there’s an intriguing new comic mystery series on Hulu. Also, if you’ve ever wondered what the Stanford prison experiment would look like as a reality series, wait no longer! Netflix made exactly that.
Get your watchlist and queues ready — and if you want even more recent streaming TV recs, be sure to go here.
The New Stanford Prison Experiment
The Stanford Prison Experiment is one of the most notorious cases in the history of psychology. What was meant to be a two-week study of a prison environment and the way subjects respond to their roles within it wound up getting so badly out of hand that it got shut down within days. So ... why not do it again, but this time as a reality show! What could go wrong??
Where to watch The New Stanford Prison Experiment: Premieres on October 21 on Netflix.
Lupin
In the fourth batch of episodes of this popular thriller based on a classic gentleman thief of French literature, Omar Sy’s master crook is back, freshly released from prison. But, per Netflix, “the emergence of a mysterious copycat forces Lupin to return to his most brilliant schemes.” Heck yeah, love a brilliant scheme.
Where to watch Lupin: Part 4 premieres on October 23 on Netflix.
Phony
This one looks intriguing. Sam Nivola plays a teen who enjoys a close relationship with his mom (Connie Britton). But then he’s in a car accident and when he wakes up in the hospital ... his mother has been replaced by another woman. But no one believes him when he insists that this new lady is not his real mom. What’s going on here? I suspect an AI deepfake.
Where to watch Phony: Premieres on October 22 on Hulu.
Nobody Wants This
Netflix’s hit romantic comedy series about the opposites-attract relationship between a rabbi and an agnostic woman is back for a third season starring Kristen Bell and Adam Brody. The season’s guest stars include Sarah Silverman and Andrew Rannells.
Where to watch Nobody Wants This: Season 3 premieres on October 22 on Netflix.
The Flores Massacre
HBO Max’s latest true crime docuseries follows “Matías Bagnato, the sole survivor of the Flores Massacre, one of the most shocking criminal cases in Argentine history.”
Where to watch The Flores Massacre: Premieres on October 22 on HBO Max.

title: The Lincoln County News
text:
Ronald H. Hall, 87, of Nobleboro, passed away peacefully on Sept, 27, 2026 at Maine Medical Center in Portland with his loving family by his side.
Ronald was born on April 16, 1939 in Brooks to Galen Hall and Thelma (Gibbs) Hall. Throughout his life, Ronald was known for his dedication to his work and the simple pleasures that brought him happiness.
Ronald spent over 40 years working at H.E. Seargent’s, where his commitment and outstanding performance were recognized when he received the People’s Choice Award for Outstanding Performance in both 1995 and 1997. His many years of service reflected his strong work ethic and dedication.
Outside of work, Ronald enjoyed watching NASCAR, spending time fishing, and dancing. He also had a special love for lemon meringue pie, a favorite treat that brought a little extra sweetness to life. These simple joys, along with the time he shared with family and friends, made up many of the memories that will be cherished by those who knew and loved him.
Ronald was predeceased by his parents, Galen and Thelma Hall, and his son, Ronald Hall Jr.
He is survived by his wife, Diane Hall, of Nobleboro; daughters, Gloria, of Madison, and Sandra Holt, of Bangor; stepdaughters, Pam Sicard, of Saco, Lori Carrier, of St. Lucy, Fla., and Paula Corbin, of Nobleboro; and stepson, Jimmy Martin, of Rockwall, Texas, along with several grandchildren, great-grandchildren, nieces, and nephews.
Per Ronald’s request, his family will honor his life privately.
Arrangements are under the care and direction of Hall Funeral Home, at 949 Main St. in Waldoboro. To extend a condolence or share a story with the Hall family, please visit Ronald’s Book of Memories at hallfuneralhomes.com.

title: Letter: Bangor’s future should be decided by the people of Bangor
text:
Letters submitted by BDN readers are verified by BDN Opinion Page staff. Send your letters to letters@bangordailynews.com
Neighbors, is Bangor’s democracy for sale? An influx of large campaign donations from outside our community threatens the very foundation of our municipal elections: the ability of ordinary residents to run for office and represent our neighbors.
Local government should be where public service begins, not where financial barriers and outside money push our neighbors out of the process. When campaigns become increasingly expensive, we risk losing good people who bring professional experience, community knowledge, independent thinking, a genuine commitment to public service, and a deep love of Bangor.
Do we want wealthy people from Cape Elizabeth determining Bangor’s future? I believe the appearance that people who don’t live here can exert outsized influence over our elections undermines public trust. When outside donors can inject substantial sums into local races, whose interests are being served?
Municipal government should be accountable to the people who live with its decisions, not shaped by whoever can spend the most money to influence an election.
I think this is a five-alarm fire for the future of municipal elections in Bangor. If we allow outside money to become the price of political participation, we risk creating a system in which the people willing and able to serve are increasingly limited to those who can attract major financial backing.
Bangor’s democracy belongs to Bangor’s people. We need an urgent, serious conversation about campaign finance transparency, outside spending, and preserving fair access to local office. We cannot wait until good people stop stepping forward to ask how we got here.
Cara Pelletier
Bangor

title: ‘God is going to grow something out of this’: Fire rips through church building
text:
CLEVELAND COUNTY, N.C. (WBTV/Gray News) - A fire tore through a North Carolina church Sunday morning, collapsing the roof and forcing cancellation of services.
The fire broke out shortly after 7 a.m. on Oct. 18 at Dover Baptist Church on Polkville Road in Shelby.
“No services today. Pray for our church. Our building is currently on fire,” wrote church officials in a social post.
Cleveland County Fire said crews responded to the massive fire as flames tore through the roof and the front sanctuary of the church.
Photos taken by WBTV showed the aftermath of the fire, with a large portion of the roof collapsed into the one-story building as multiple fire trucks responded.
Authorities said no one was injured and the church was reportedly unoccupied when the fire started.
The pastor, Jerry Reed, said the loss is difficult, but he remains hopeful.
“It seems like a setback. It’s heartbreaking to share this with our church members,” Reed said. “But we’ve had an outpouring of support from other churches and the community, and we just feel that God is going to grow something out of this. That this is not the end of our story.”
The cause remains under investigation, but officials said no foul play was suspected.
“Thank you to everyone who has prayed for us. Our building is gone, but the church is not!” wrote the church.

title: Man accused of dressing up as security guard to sneak into Tennessee-Alabama game
text:
KNOXVILLE, Tenn. (WVLT/Gray News) — A 20-year-old man has been charged after he allegedly dressed up as a security guard to sneak into the University of Tennessee’s football game against Alabama on Saturday.
According to court records, officers saw a man, later identified as Blake Bible of Morristown, drinking a White Claw while wearing a uniform from Axis, the security company paid to work events at the University of Tennessee, near the G10 ramp on Phillip Fulmer Way just before 3:30 p.m.
Officers said the Axis supervisor confirmed that Bible did not work for Axis and that he stole a polo shirt and hat to enter the game.
Bible was taken into custody and charged with theft of property.
He is scheduled to be arraigned in court on Oct. 30.
Tennessee won their third-straight at home against Alabama, leading to thousands of fans storming the field after and a $500,000 fine from the SEC.

title: 13 Maine Halloween happenings for scares and screams
text:
There is no escape from Maine’s scariest season.
No, we’re not talking about tourist season. Halloween is approaching and there are haunted houses, graveyard tours, old horror movies and other scary stuff in cities and towns across the state. Whether you’re in southern York County, on the Midcoast or in Central Maine, it’s easy to find some spooky fun this month.
Here are some suggestions for ways to get your scare on.
Friday-Saturday, and Oct. 30-31. Maine Maritime Museum, 243 Washington St., Bath. mainemaritimemuseum.org
The museums hosts a spooky tour of its Kennebec River campus called “Dead Reckoning: Shipyard Death & Disturbances.” There’ll be a seance in the Donnell House, where unexplained encounters have been reported over the years, and an escape room. There’s also a self-guided walking tour with stories about some of the gruesome working conditions at the historic shipyard that was on the site. Tickets are $25.
‘DRACULA‘
Friday-Saturday. Westbrook Performing Arts Center, 471 Stroudwater St., Westbrook. porttix.com
The Portland Ballet’s professional company presents “Dracula,” based on the 1897 Gothic novel by Bram Stoker, with a score by Rachmaninoff. Because of its mature themes, “Dracula” is recommended for ages 11 and up. Tickets are $35-$45.
Thursday-Sunday, through Oct. 31. TM Wentworth Road, Lebanon. hauntedgrandviewmanor.com
This haunted attraction is a mix of scary trails and creepy buildings, including the Grandview Funeral home, cemeteries, hillbilly shacks and slaughterhouses. Beware the Pig Man, who is always waiting for you. Tickets are $25. There are also “no scare” nights on Thursdays, for $10.
Friday-Sunday, and Oct. 29-31. The Leavitt Theatre, 259 Main St., Ogunquit. leavittheatre.com
This is a haunted tour of the 101-year-old Leavitt Theatre, featuring terrifying clown dens, twisted apothecaries and the infamous Leavitt Chainsaw Massacre. Tickets are $25.
Oct. 30-Nov. 1. Mayo Street Arts, 10 Mayo St., Portland. mayostreetarts.org
Mayo Street hosts a walk-through haunted house full of handmade creatures, sets, sounds and characters. Free, but donations are welcomed.
Oct. 31. Strand Theatre, 345 Main St., Rockland. rocklandstrand.com
This classic horror film from 1933 stars Claude Rains, who mostly appears covered in bandages. It’s a prime example of the power of suspense and how sometimes it’s scarier NOT to see something. Based on the novel by H.G. Wells. Tickets are $12, $9 for seniors and students.
Thursday-Saturday, through Oct. 31. Wallingford’s Orchard, 1240 Perkins Ridge Road, Auburn. wallingfordsorchard.com
Wallingford’s is a peaceful, scenic place to pick fruit – when the sun shines. But at night this time of year, it becomes a nightmare full of creepy creatures and scary structures. It’s a haunted walk “through some of your darkest nightmares.” Tickets are $30.
Saturday. Waterville Opera House, 1 Common St., Waterville. watervillecreates.org
This showing of the classic and campy 1975 film features an opportunity to meet and take photos with actress Patricia Quinn, who played Magenta. She’ll also take questions from the audience. There’ll be a costume contest and a shadow cast performance by the group Rocky for Equality. Tickets are $60-$170.
The film will also be shown, with the same shadow cast, at the Waldo Theatre in Waldoboro on Oct. 30. Tickets are $20-$50.
Friday-Saturday. Johnson Hall Opera House, 280 Water St., Gardiner. johnsonhall.org
This event features ghost stories, unexpected scares and characters from the past taking over the historic opera house. More than 50 community performers, ages 6 to 83, will perform short scenes. Audience members will also travel through Johnson Hall in small groups, moving from one scary scene to another. Tickets are $14.64.
Oct. 22. Old York Museum Center, 3 Lindsay Road, York. oldyork.org
The Old York Historical Society puts on several events each year for its “Spooky Season.” On Thursday people can take a lamp-lit tour of York’s Burial Ground titled “Gone But Not Forgotten: Revolutionary York.” The life stories of 18th century townsfolk will be told by costumed guides. Tickets are $20. There are also a couple of free events for families at the Old York Museum Center, including pumpkin carving on Oct. 29 and trick-or-treating with a pumpkin lighting on Oct. 30.
Friday-Saturday through Oct. 31, plus Oct. 29. Aquaboggan Water Park, 980 Portland Road, Saco. trailofterrormaine.com
This annual haunted walk has been completely revamped and expanded, with new scenes and a 30-minute walk through the woods — unless something makes you run. The terror is still spearheaded by a creature called the Banshee, who has taken over the woods. Scenes are filled with lights, sounds, and creeps lurking everywhere. Tickets are $25, $10 for children 10 and under.
Sunday and Oct. 31. Waldo Theatre, 916 Main St., Waldoboro. thewaldotheatre.org
Before Vincent Price did the scary narration on Michael Jackson’s hit song “Thriller,” he was a longtime star of horror films. The Waldo Theatre is hosting a festival in his honor, including a screening of the 1963 film “The Raven,” an irreverent take on Edgar Allan Poe’s classic poem, directed by Roger Corman. Tickets are $12, $9 for seniors and students.
On Oct. 31, Everyman Repertory Theatre presents a staged reading of a new play called “I Know It’s Gruesome, But is It Art? The Vincent Price Murder Case.” It’s set in the 1960s in the London art scene, during the filming of a Price film called “Witchfinder General.” Tickets are $20.
WALK AMONG THE SHADOWS
Thursday-Sunday. Eastern Cemetery, 224 Congress St., Portland. Spiritsalive.org
This is a nightly tour of Portland’s oldest cemetery, established in 1668. Costumed actors will bring long-dead folks to life and tell some of the city’s dramatic stories, including the destruction of Fort Loyall in 1690 by French and Inidgenous forces, an 1893 reservoir break on North Street, Benjamin Tukey’s ill-fated celebration of the American victory at Saratoga and the 1647 Mary Martin infanticide case. Adult tickets are $10 cash or $12.51 on Eventbrite.

title: Supreme Court to hear case on race in middle school admissions
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Supreme Court agreed Monday to hear a case about the role race plays in middle school admissions, three years after a majority on the high court struck down affirmative action in college admissions.
The case involves admissions to four selective middle schools in Montgomery County, Maryland, a diverse suburb of Washington, D.C. A group of parents said in a lawsuit that the district’s admissions policy to four magnet schools is designed to boost the admission of Black and Latino students while disadvantaging Asian American kids.
The high court said Monday it will weigh if the parent group has enough evidence of discrimination for the case to move forward.
The case was originally dismissed because Asian American students were not underrepresented compared with their share of the applicant pool. Justices will now consider whether a group claiming to be targeted by a race-neutral policy must show it was disproportionately harmed in order to prove intentional discrimination.
If the court rules for the parent group, the Association for Education Fairness, it could revive the lawsuit.
The lawsuit originates from a change in admissions policy that began a decade ago, when a consulting group was hired to evaluate how the school system chose students for its middle school magnet programs. The district then changed its admissions policies, factoring the poverty levels of the schools the students attended into the process. The share of Asian American students, who were clustered in more affluent, high-performing schools, subsequently fell.
The parent group sued in 2020. Not long after, the school system, which educates more than 150,000 students, changed its admissions practices to eliminate an extra in-person exam. Now, students qualify for a lottery according to their performance on standardized tests. But students in more affluent schools, where Asian American students are concentrated, must perform better on the standardized exam to enter the lottery.
The Fourth Circuit Court of Appeals affirmed a lower court’s decision to dismiss the case. In its ruling, the court said the parent group had failed to show that Asian Americans students were harmed, because they were still being admitted at higher rates than the applicant pool. The Fourth Circuit was relying on a recent ruling in a different school admissions case, where parents challenged admissions practices at a highly selective magnet high school in Virginia. Those parents lost in part because Asian American students were still overrepresented relative to the applicant pool.
The attorneys for the Montgomery County parents argued it’s not enough to compare whether a targeted racial group is represented fairly compared with the group of students who apply. Other evidence of discrimination should also be considered, they wrote.
“Under the applicant pool benchmark, the government can set specific racial targets, hit them, and avoid even an inquiry into discriminatory intent,” so long as it hasn’t explicitly called out race in its process, they wrote in their appeal to the Supreme Court.
The school system has consistently argued the new admissions policy, called the Pandemic Plan due to the timing of its release, is race-neutral.
“The Pandemic Plan is a colorblind lottery,” attorneys wrote in a brief asking the Supreme Court not to take up the case. “Nothing about the Pandemic Plan, its history, or its purpose is offensive to the Constitution.”
The court is expected to hear arguments in the coming months.

title: Eagles QB Jalen Hurts expected to miss the rest of the season with blood clots, AP source says
text:
PHILADELPHIA (AP) — Philadelphia Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts is expected to miss the rest of the season because of blood clots in his lungs, a person familiar with the situation told The Associated Press on Monday.
The person spoke to the AP on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of a health matter.
Hurts was placed on injured reserve Saturday, two days after the Eagles revealed he has a blood clot in his calf. He missed the first of at least four games in Philadelphia’s loss to the Carolina Panthers on Sunday.
The Eagles and Hurts’ agent, Nicole Lynn, released more information on his condition Monday. They said Hurts has deep vein thrombosis and a bilateral pulmonary emboli, meaning a blood clot has traveled from the legs to the lungs.
His treatment involves blood thinners, and he won’t be allowed to participate in any football activities until he is off them.
The Eagles and Lynn said Hurts was expected to make a full recovery. “He is clinically stable and has no significant functional limitations,” their statement said.
Eagles coach Nick Sirianni was the only member of the organization made available to the media on Monday — not general manager Howie Roseman or any member of the team’s medical staff — and largely deflected questions about Hurts’ health or how the team handled the situation.
“I’m not a medical expert,” Sirianni said. “I lean on our guys in all those situations. I’m a football coach. I lean on our medical experts in every situation. I have full trust and full faith in them. It’s not just me that has major care for our players. It’s them, as well.”
The Eagles previously said Hurts was injured when he took a cleat to his calf area on Oct. 4 in a game against the Los Angeles Rams.
Hurts informed the medical staff of the injury after practice on Oct. 8. The Super Bowl 59 MVP was back at practice the next day before the team left for London to play Jacksonville. Hurts was initially diagnosed by specialists in London with a left calf superficial vein thrombosis.
Sirianni declined to say Monday why the Eagles allowed Hurts to fly home with a blood clot. He referred to statements the Eagles and Hurts’ agent released over the last week that addressed the timeline of his injury and treatment.
He had no answers on specific questions about Hurts and his blood clots.
“I understand you want this information on this,” Sirianni said. “I fully trust the people that are involved in helping us all make these decisions. We have great people here.”
Hurts hadn’t missed more than two games in a season since becoming the full-time starter in 2021. He has led the Eagles to five straight playoff appearances, three NFC East titles and two Super Bowl appearances, beating the Chiefs 40-22 two years ago.
Tanner McKee started for Hurts against the Panthers. McKee finished 26 of 45 for 215 yards and a touchdown in the 25-14 loss. The Eagles (2-4) have lost four consecutive games for the first time since 2020.
Sirianni added that beleaguered offensive coordinator Sean Mannion was still the play-caller.
Hurts has eight touchdown passes and three interceptions with 933 yards passing this season. He is in the middle of a five-year, $255 million extension, including $179.3 million guaranteed, that takes him through the 2028 season.
The Eagles stunned fans when they drafted Hurts out of Oklahoma in the second round in 2020. They seemingly had Carson Wentz entrenched at QB and had more pressing needs. But Hurts supplanted Wentz and became one of the top quarterbacks in the NFL.
“I haven’t been without Jalen for an extended period of time,” Sirianni said. “I have the utmost confidence in Tanner. But I miss him. I know that will be the case. Jalen and I have been together, head coach and quarterback, for six years.”
___
AP Pro Football Writer Rob Maaddi in Tampa, Florida, contributed to this report.
