title: Tenants' union reaches $3.6 million settlement with Portland landlord
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Trelawny Tenants Union reaches $3.6 million settlement with Portland landlord
The Trelawny Tenants Union has agreed to a $3.6 million settlement with Geoffrey Rice, the Portland landlord who was accused of illegally raising rent.
The union said the settlement was reached Sunday following four months of negotiations that culminated in a 20-hour session that stretched over two days.
As part of the agreement, Rice has agreed to roll back all rents to the Dec. 1, 2022 compliant rent at all 19 of his residential properties in Portland, which covers more than 300 units.
Rice will also deposit $3.6 million into an escrow account, of which $2.86 million will be used to reimburse more than a thousand current and previous tenants, including interest; $230,000 will be paid to the union to cover past and future costs, including a $50,000 donation; $250,000 will be paid to the city of Portland in the form of a fine; and $260,000 will be in contingency to cover possible overages in fines.
The union said that in return, it agrees to file no more complaints against Rice for past violations. In addition, the union said it will assist Rice's office in bringing rents into compliance in anticipation of Rice selling his properties.
"After years of hard work, we have finally come to terms with Mr. Rice. Those terms ensure that all past and present tenants are fully reimbursed for charges above and beyond what is allowable by rent control," Trelawny Tenants Union treasurer Ethan Strimling, a member of the union's mediation team, said in a statement. "This has been a long road for all of us, but I am hopeful we are finally seeing the light at the end of the tunnel."
Until the escrow account is fully funded, the union will hold a mortgage on 10 of Rice's properties. The union said reimbursements to tenants will be determined through an audit that must be signed off on by the union.
Since the city of Portland is part of the agreement, the City Council must affirm the terms of the settlement at the next possible council meeting.

title: What to know as Kingfield, Strong vote on leaving school district
text:
On Nov. 3, the communities of Kingfield and Strong will decide whether or not to leave Maine School Administrative District 58.
Both towns’ votes are independent of each other. Strong could vote to leave the district while Kingfield decides to stay.
Here’s what either option on the ballot means for you before you head to the polls.
A “yes” vote would count in favor of leaving the district. If passed, the town would form its own independent school administrative unit. Ownership of Kingfield Elementary School or Day Mountain Regional Middle School in Strong would transfer to the new district. High school students would be guaranteed acceptance into Mount Abram High School in Salem Township.
Voting “no” would oppose leaving MSAD 58. If rejected in either town, the withdrawal process would end and that community would be unable to pursue withdrawal for another two years.

title: France's prime minister calls for localized curfews in cities to curb rioting and looting
text:
France's prime minister calls for localized curfews in cities to curb rioting and looting
French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu says he has instructed prefects to impose “very limited” and “localized” curfews in cities to prevent more rioting and looting, following this weekend's violence that notably targeted city halls, other public buildings and hundreds of businesses across the country.
CNN video: Students block Louvre access in Paris protest
Speaking after an emergency meeting with top government officials, Lecornu said “on Saturday, despite scenes of severe violence and extensive property damage, no one was killed, and that is a miracle” as he defended the work of police officers faced with violent groups of people.
Lecornu said details of the areas to be placed under curfew will be provided later Monday.
The instructions come as Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez offered his resignation on Sunday but President Emmanuel Macron asked him to stay to respond to police needs in an emergency situation.
Macron refused Laurent Nuñez's resignation “given the need for continued command of law enforcement in the current context,” Macron's office said in a statement Monday.
He instructed Nuñez “to take all necessary steps to ensure full transparency about the failures in planning and intelligence-gathering that led to the violence,” the statement said.
Macron also asked for the introduction of “new policing tactics on the ground as quickly as possible” to put an end to violent events.
On Sunday evening, groups of people set fires to trash bins, bicycles and other objects in the streets and looted businesses in Paris, Lyon, Marseille and other cities, a day after major violence erupted Saturday during nationwide protests against rising living costs and poor conditions in schools. At least 2,400 people were arrested across the country.
“I submitted my resignation because I am responsible for everything that is happening,” Nuñez said, speaking on France Inter radio.
“Now, the real issue is ensuring that this doesn’t happen again. … We obviously need to be better at anticipating the kind of mobilization that is unfolding,” he said.
Nuñez blamed violence on “hordes of troublemakers and looters” and “far-left activists” and acknowledged that police strategy needs to be adapted “in the face of extremely mobile groups.” Authorities said groups of hundreds of people sought confrontations with police and targeted public buildings, including city halls and other public offices.
Nuñez acknowledged that authorities had “lost control” in some major cities on Saturday, with hundreds of businesses looted.
“You can’t look shopkeepers in the eye when hundreds of businesses have been looted and say we haven’t lost control in some of these major cities. Obviously,” Nuñez said.
Flames engulfed the 19th-century City Hall in Limoges, in central France, causing its roof to collapse and nearly destroying the building.
In Marseille, the prefect banned any protest or other gathering from noon to 8 p.m. Monday.

title: George D. Richardson Jr.
text:
The gale force wind that was George Dewey Richardson Jr. fell calm on Oct. 12, 2026, when George took his last breath at his beloved home overlooking Jewett Cove with his wife and family by his side. George was first and foremost a gruff, stoic fisherman who claimed that he had been given more than nine lives after surviving several near-death experiences at sea, and a cancer diagnosis. He never imagined he would remain an active part of the Westport community until age 90.
George was a person of dedication and determination who responded to issues, and to life, in meaningful ways. His deep love of Westport Island and its community along with his caring for residents in need of assistance serves as an example of how a community should function. He will be remembered as a confident man who valued positive relationships, stood up for fairness and followed through with action in the completion of any task he took on. He will be missed by many.
George was born in Bath, Maine, on June 2, 1936, the son of George “Dewey” Richardson, a commercial fisherman, and Irish immigrant, Teresa “Tree” Senier Richardson, a cook and professional baker. George grew up on Westport Island, attended the island’s one-room schoolhouse, and graduated from Morse High. He attended Maine Maritime Academy in Castine, then served a two-year deployment in the U.S. Navy before returning to Westport Island to pursue a career as a commercial fisherman. In 1959, George married Marcia Kelley, the beautiful girl next door. They were married for 67 years.
During many decades on the water scalloping, groundfishing, dragging for shrimp in the winter, and fishing for bluefin tuna in the summer, George participated in various research projects, working with scientists on the F/V Marcia Ann sharing his knowledge and experience. Projects included monitoring changes in fish populations and behavior, the effect of overboard septic discharge on fisheries, and the impact of the Maine Yankee Nuclear Power Plant on the Sheepscot River. After 6 decades at sea, he retired and handed the baton to his youngest son, Lincoln.
George was also a passionate and respected public servant and community leader. He served as a Selectman of Westport Island for over three decades, was on the Maine Municipal Association Policy Committee, Lincoln County Budget Committee, Chairman of the School Board, Harbor Master, Select Committee of Marine Resources, Westport Island Shellfish Committee, and was a longstanding board member of the East Coast Tuna Association. In recognition of his commitment to municipal service, George was awarded the Maine Municipal Association Ethel Kelley Memorial Award in 2006.
During his 32 years of service as town Selectman, George’s proudest achievements included his advocacy for constructing a town office building, the development of the Ferry Landing, a food pantry, the Westport Island History Center, and keeping property taxes low to help local island residents retain long-held lands for future generations.
George is survived by Marica Ann Richardson, his wife of 67 years, his five children, George “Chuck” D. Richardson, Corinne (Tom Elliott) Richardson, Gary (Tonya) Richardson, Stacy (Mike) Baxter, and Lincoln Richardson; grandchildren James Richardson, Caleb Richardson, Brad Richardson, Alisyn Richardson, Cameron West, Kayla West, and Mathias Richardson; sister, Deidre Dunlop and her three children Tom Dunlop, Terri Dunlop, Andrew Dunlop; and sister Dianne Roberts and son, Brian Roberts; and great granddaughter, Rosalie West.
A graveside burial with family will take place at the Richardson-Jewett Cemetery on Friday, Oct. 23, and a celebration of life will be held at the Westport Island Old Town Hall on Sunda, Nov. 1 from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m.
In lieu of flowers, donations may be made in George’s memory to the Friends of Westport Island History (fowih.org).
Condolences can be made online at www.daiglefuneralhome.com

title: UMaine needs to be focused on dropping the prices, not just the puck
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
EDITORIAL: What does it mean to be a sports fan? For some, it’s watching every game and knowing the roster inside and out. For others, it might mean keeping up with the social lives of the players they think are cute. Can you just be from a place and show up to a bar when the playoffs start? Sure, why not. While all these people may be at different levels of fandom, most of them have one thing in common: they own a jersey. For the University of Maine’s hockey program, this tradition has become too expensive.
The most basic and recognized way of showing your support to a team is owning a jersey; it’s synonymous with fandom. For many UMaine college students, this sign of support has become exorbitantly priced. A standard replica jersey is $129.99. This is the jersey that looks like the ones players wear on the ice.
If you want to save money and get a cheaper option, one that doesn’t look like the one your team wears, you can get one of those for only $20 less, at $109.99. However, if you want one with an actual player’s name on it — you know, something that is pretty normal for a jersey to have — you are looking at around $260.
There are a good number of students who just bite the bullet and buy one because they love their community more than they hate the price tag, but the fact of the matter is, it’s unacceptable.
The college experience, while filled with lots of joy and foundational life moments, has a lot of costs. Tuition, room and board, textbooks and all the other ordinary living expenses are things college students have to think about. I mean, there’s the term “broke college kid” for a reason. To ask students who are already up to their necks in expenses to spend $130 to $250 to purchase a sports jersey is one of clearest examples of greed and exploitation we have seen in our time at college.
While the thought of bringing down prices of UMaine hockey jerseys is completely sound, it’s unrealistic. However, a possible solution for this, one that is at least somewhat feasiable, would be to give every incoming first-year class a one-time discount on a UMaine jersey or any other UMaine apparel item at the bookstore.
This would not be a challenging thing to implement. Giving students coupons is something the university has done before and could easily do again. It would go a long way in showing a sense of care for students and their culture.
The exact percentage of the discount, like the concept as a whole, will be up to the university. However, it would be nice to see it in the 30% to 50% range. We think this is a perfectly reasonable compromise to a ridiculous situation.
We know that prices will never come down, but kids coming into the college experience and the rich traditions of UMaine — hockey games being chief among them — deserve an opportunity to buy a jersey at a reasonable price.

title: PLC raises more than $125,000 for Children's Miracle Network Hospitals
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
COURTESY OF THE PROFESSIONAL LOGGING CONTRACTORS (PLC) OF THE NORTHEAST
The Professional Logging Contractors (PLC) of the Northeast once again demonstrated the logging industry’s commitment to children’s health this summer, raising a combined total of more than $125,000 at its annual Log A Load for Kids golf tournaments in Maine and continuing a long-running effort that has now generated more than $3 million for children’s hospitals since 1995.
Nearly 200 people attended the two tournaments, which were held in southern and northern Maine and brought together PLC members, supporters, sponsors and teams to raise money for children in need.
The fundraising total included a record $55,407 raised at the eighth annual Log A Load for Kids Southern Maine Golf Tournament on Aug. 28 at Lake Kezar Country Club in Lovell. The tournament sold out with 38 teams, surpassing the previous Southern Maine record of $55,360 set the year before.
Three weeks later, PLC raised an additional record $70,000 at its 30th annual Log A Load for Kids Northern Maine Golf Tournament on Sept. 18 at JaTo Highlands Golf Course in Lincoln. The Northern Maine event also sold out, with 41 teams participating.
The Northern Maine total received an additional boost after the tournament when an anonymous donor contributed more than $6,000, pushing the final total to the record $70,000.
Funds raised through the two golf tournaments support Children’s Miracle Network hospitals, including Barbara Bush Children’s Hospital in Portland and Northern Light Eastern Maine Medical Center in Bangor. The money supports research and training, medical equipment, neonatal intensive care and other efforts aimed at improving the lives of children.
The PLC has partnered with Northern Light Health Foundation in the Log A Load effort since 1996, while Barbara Bush Children’s Hospital joined the effort in 2019. The University of Vermont Children’s Hospital became a PLC Log A Load partner in 2024.
The two golf tournaments are part of a much larger annual Log A Load fundraising effort. PLC also raised $134,610 through its live auction at the 2026 Annual Membership Meeting, bringing the organization’s fundraising total since 1995 to more than $3 million. In 2025, PLC’s Log A Load efforts raised $292,746.
Thank you to the sponsors, supporters, and players who made the tournaments a success!

title: Social Security COLA increase to affect 388,000 Mainers in 2027
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
MAINE — The Social Security Administration has released its cost-of-living adjustment, providing a 3.6% increase for 2027.
Starting in January, Mainers will see about $75 more in their monthly Social Security payments or about $900 for the year.
“The Social Security Cost of Living Adjustment, or COLA, is something that’s built into Social Security that makes sure that as inflation goes up, your Social Security payments can go up too,” explains Bill Sweeney, Senior Vice President of Government Affairs for AARP.
How the increase compares
Sweeney notes this is not the biggest COLA increase in recent years. That came in 2023 with an 8.7% raise. It is more than this year’s 2.8% adjustment.
“It’s not a bonus, it’s not extra money” explains Sweeney. “It really is designed to keep up with the higher prices for everything that people are seeing, whether it’s heating fuel, or grocery prices or pharmacy prices.”
About 388,000 Mainers are currently receiving Social Security benefits.
“In the state of Maine, Social Security has lifted 106,000 people out of poverty every single year,” says Sweeney.
Rising costs could offset increase
However, University of Maine Finance Professor Pankaj Agrrawal cautions that the extra money coming in 2027 may not go as far as recipients would like.
“Because of the slighter higher increase in medical costs, health care costs, it will actually be harder for people receiving Social Security benefits,” he says.
National Retirement Security Month
This is National Retirement Security Month.
Age 62 is the average age for retirement. However, many Generation X-ers are now realizing that may not be an option for a while.
“These are folks who are really kind of the first generation who didn’t have a pension as part of their workplace,” says Sweeney. “This is the 401K generation, the folks who had to do all of their own savings for retirement. And what we know is that they’re going into retirement in a really bad spot.”
Retirement age considerations
The earliest age to begin collecting Social Security is 62. Recipients who begin at that age take a 30% cut every month for the rest of their life. Age 70 is the age to collect the maximum amount of money.
Those wondering how much money they currently have in their Social Security account can click here and sign up for a personal account. There, users can see a yearly record of their earnings as well as estimated benefits.

title: Three Portland breweries medal at the Great American Beer Festival

text:
Three Portland breweries recently earned medals at the prestigious Great American Beer Festival.
Orange Bike Brewing Company won two medals, while Bissell Brothers Brewing and Allagash Brewing Company won one medal each.
Orange Bike took home a gold for its Pumpkin Ale in the category of Specialty Gluten-Free Beer. Its Oktoberfest beer also won a silver in the Classic Gluten-Free Ale or Lager category at the event, held earlier this month in Denver.
“This one’s for our brewers, starting with our head brewer, Jason Kissinger,” Orange Bike founder and CEO Tom Ruff said in a news release. “It’s also for our growers and partners, the state of Maine and the Maine Venture Fund, our Mug Club members and community investors, and every gluten-free guest who has walked through our doors and finally felt like they could order anything on the menu.”
Allagash White won a gold medal in the Belgian-Style Witbier catgeory. The iconic flagship beer was also among five “Landmark Craft Beers” in the American Craft Beer Hall of Fame’s second annual induction ceremony in August.
Bissell Brothers’ Precept won a bronze medal in the American Pilsner category.
Judges evaluated 7,267 entries of beer, cider and hop water at the competition from 1,300 breweries and cideries in 49 states, plus Washington D.C. and Puerto Rico. A total of 243 breweries and cideries won medals this year.

title: Meet a man keeping accordion tradition alive through repair and performance
text:
MONTPELIER, Vt. (Aging Untold) — Nathan Longo plays an Italian accordion from the early 1960s, an instrument he said he plays most often.
Longo said performing in front of people gives him stage fright.
Small workshop, growing demand
Longo repairs accordions in a small workshop. He said he is better at fixing the instruments than playing them.
He is one of a handful of people who repair accordions in New England.
“I’m a lot busier than I ever thought I would be,” Longo said.
What began as something to do in retirement has turned into a 30-hour-a-week job.
“There really are more people that are interested in accordion than I ever thought,” Longo said.
Growing up with dyslexia
Longo grew up in Orange County and said he liked to tinker with things.
“It bothers me when something doesn’t work right,” Longo said.
He said he struggled in school as a child and teachers thought he was slow.
“I mean, it took forever for them to teach me how to write my name,” Longo said.
Longo said nobody knew about dyslexia at the time, and he had a poor self-image during that period.
He completed high school and discovered he had a talent for fixing cars. Longo attributed the skill to being dyslexic.
“Dyslexics have a really good three-dimensional visualization,” Longo said.
Longo later made prototypes for high-end machinery in Massachusetts.
From machinery to music
Around age 50, Longo started playing the accordion as a way to keep his brain active.
“Whatever you can, to just stay in the present,” Longo said.

title: A Black Hawk carrying a school bus over a Florida town had residents asking one question: Why?
text:
A Black Hawk carrying a school bus over Florida stunned residents — but there was a good reason for it
"I heard the helicopter loud and clear," said Kelly Vokaty, a resident of Babcock Ranch in the Punta Gorda, Florida, area.
Vokaty watched from her lanai in Babcock Ranch Friday morning as a Black Hawk helicopter hovered over the water. However, what she didn't realize was that it was carrying a school bus!
"Oh, I did see a shadow or something long. It looked like something was being carried, but I couldn't differentiate what it was," said Vokaty.
Residents in the area couldn't help but do a double-take.
"Had I seen that live, I would have just, like, totally been freaking out. Did they take it out of the water or, you know, what happened?" said Babcock Ranch resident Richard Berlin-Velez.
Only sister station WBBH (Gulf Coast News) caught this footage on our live weather cameras Friday morning. Our team reached out to the Charlotte County Sheriff's Office for answers.
The sheriff's office says its dive team is practicing how to save people in the water.
"It's something that you don't see every day. But when you learn what's happening, you're amazed," said Berlin-Velez.
CCSO says its dive team visits Babcock Ranch multiple times a year to practice underwater extractions, using setups like a submerged bus and dummies to prepare for real-world emergencies.
"We're just lucky to live in a community where we have the backdrop for them to learn what they need to do to save lives," said Vokaty.

title: Husband, wife charged in interstate shooting death of 17-year-old: ‘Senseless act’
text:
ST. LOUIS COUNTY, Mo. (KMOV/Gray News) — A husband and wife from Texas are facing charges in connection with the death of a 17-year-old who was shot on Interstate 170 in Missouri.
Willie Herndon, 42, and his wife, Taiya Herndon, 45, were charged in connection with the shooting death of Alyssa Wilson, 17, last Wednesday.
Charges filed against couple
St. Louis County Prosecutor Melissa Price-Smith said Willie Herndon faces charges of first-degree murder and armed criminal action. Taiya Herndon faces a charge of hindering prosecution for driving Willie Herndon to Illinois after the shooting.
Willie Herndon is being held on a $1 million cash-only bond. Taiya Herndon is being held on a $500,000 cash-only bond.
Surveillance video shows shooting
The Major Case Squad of Greater St. Louis said at a news conference Monday that surveillance video showed a white SUV pulling over to the shoulder on southbound I-170 just south of St. Charles Rock Road.
Investigators said Willie Herndon exited the vehicle and stood outside briefly. A gunshot was then fired and he got back into the vehicle before driving away. Investigators said Taiya Herndon was also inside the vehicle.
The car was registered to Taiya Herndon, according to police.
Officers were then called to the southbound lanes of the interstate near Midland Boulevard in Overland for a crash around 7:20 p.m. When they arrived, officers said they found Wilson shot inside the crashed car. She was taken to a hospital, where she later died.
Victim was a high school senior
Wilson was a senior at McCluer North High School. She was a student-athlete and office aide and planned to attend college next year, the school said.
Arrest made in Illinois
Officials said investigators used license plate readers to identify the suspected vehicle and tracked it to a hotel in Caseyville, Illinois.
Law enforcement then arrested the couple from Arlington, Texas.
Investigators found evidence in the hotel room after executing a search warrant, including the gun. Willie Herndon gave details about his involvement in the shooting, as well as information “pertaining to possible ongoing investigations in other areas,” officials said.
Father speaks at news conference
During Monday’s news conference, Wilson’s father, Robert Hickman, thanked law enforcement for working to secure justice. He said Wilson was 60 days from turning 18, and the family planned a vacation to a Disney theme park.
“This was a senseless act, and we ask that everyone take a look at yourselves inside and make sure that next time something happens like this, you think before something happens,” Hickman said.

title: Check Your Fridge: Kayem Products From March Through October Under USDA Recall
text:
What Mainers Need to Know About a Massive Recall of Kayem Meats
A variety of Kayem ready-to-eat meats have been recalled after reports that they may have been stored at the wrong temperature.
Kayem Meats Issues a Huge Recall of Ready-to-Eat Meats
After working in a deli for several years, I'm very particular about the meat I serve. If it's the least bit questionable, I'll throw it out rather than risk making people sick.
So I was very interested when I read about this massive recall of Kayem meats that the USDA says may not be safe.

The products are RTE, or ready-to-eat meats, like hot dogs, bologna, bacon, kielbasa, chicken sausage, and more.
Kayem Meats Recalled After Being Stored at Inappropriate Temperatures
According to the USDA recall, these Kayem products distributed from Chelsea, Massachusetts, were stored in a refrigerator that experienced temperature deviations.
The Kayem products in question were produced between approximately March 31, 2026, and October 7, 2026.
That means if you bought any Kayem products over the summer, it's probably part of this recall.
USDA Has Lists of UPCs and Product Pictures for International Kayem Meats Recall
People are urged to check their refrigerators and freezers for Kayem meats with a UPC that appears on this long list of recalled products.
You can find pictures of the affected meats on the USDA website.
I looked through the pictures and realized the 'Old Tyme Red' hot dogs in my refrigerator may be part of this recall.
Anyone with Kayem products listed in the worldwide recall should throw the meat away or return it to the store for a full refund.
So far, the USDA says no one has reported getting sick from the affected products.

title: Interest in trapping grows in Maine
text:
AUGUSTA — The class gathered in a small clearing, under orange and yellow leaves, and trained their attention on Ronald Fournier. He held a metal cable with a loop on the end, used to trap the paw of a black bear.
“You’re always checking live restraining devices how often?” Fournier asked the group.
“Every day,” nine people said in unison.
“When?” Fournier asked.
“In the morning,” they answered together.
Fournier, recreational safety supervisor for the state Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife, gave a satisfied nod. This class is mandatory for anyone who wants to get a trapping license in Maine. In recent years, the state has seen a surge of interest.
In 2020, Maine had 4,381 licensed trappers, according to department data. By 2025, that number had increased to 5,345.
Fournier surveyed participants to understand the shift and learned that new trappers were less interested in selling fur for profit than they were in decades past. In general, he said, they wanted a trapping license in order to be more self-sufficient, whether they planned to harvest meat for their family or manage pests and predators on their properties.
“The No. 1 choice was to expand on their hunting and outdoor activities and broaden their outdoor skills,” he said. “Right behind that was trapping for personal use to make craft items and garments. People wanted to trap a couple of furbearers to make a pair of beaver mittens or a hat for the family.”
Brian Bernosky, president of the Maine Trappers Association, said trappers used to be more reluctant to share their knowledge because they wanted to guard the tricks that helped supplement their income or they were afraid to encounter people opposed to the practice. Today, he sees a broader culture of mentorship.
“If we don’t share it with everybody and share all the great things we know, we are going to go by the wayside,” said Bernosky, 43, of Bradford.
State rules say that a trapping license is valid from July 1 to June 30 of the following year. Anyone applying for an adult license in Maine needs to prove that they have taken the state course at least once.
Fournier said Maine requires more education than most states in order to get a trapping license. Generally, people need to complete homework in advance and attend a full-day course that includes an exam. The curriculum includes practical and legal information, as well as tips on how to represent trappers well to private landowners and to the general public.
On an overcast Friday in October, Joshua Dostie knelt on the floor of the classroom at the Sportsman’s Alliance of Maine Outdoor Center in Augusta to demonstrate the proper setting of beaver traps. The participants listened as he talked about making ethical choices in the field — how to confirm the presence of beavers in an area, when to move on from a location, how to avoid catching species that aren’t the target and how to make sure the trap will kill the animal immediately so it does not suffer additional stress.
“If we as trappers want to keep our seasons as manageable as they are, we have to make good decisions,” said Dostie, a recreational safety coordinator for the Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife.
Maggie Morgan, 34, of Bowdoinham, joined Dostie and Fournier at the recent course as a volunteer instructor. She used to be a more active hunter, but now prefers trapping in part because it is more flexible around her family’s schedule. She said she is seeing more women and kids in these courses, and her own two children enjoy helping her prepare equipment at home and accompanying her to check traplines.
“If I spend three hours out in the woods deer hunting, I may or may not get a deer,” Morgan said. “Whereas if I spend three hours over the course of a few days tending a trapline, and I get a few beaver, that feeds the family and makes a few hats. I feel like it’s more productive.”
Brooke Blood, of Avon, signed up for the trapper education course because she is interested in becoming a game warden and wanted to build her skills in the outdoors. She was looking forward to learning about species that are less familiar to her, such as beaver or otter.
“I’ve been hunting, but trapping, I don’t have any experience with,” said Blood, 30.
Adam Austin, of Belgrade, got a trapping license more than a decade ago in order to help with animal control at his job, but he hadn’t renewed it or kept up with the practice. One way he plans to use his license is to target the predators that have been killing his chickens for years, but the 51-year-old also wants to spend more time outside after a recent cancer diagnosis and treatment.
“It’s not about the pelts, the money or anything like that,” Austin said. “It’s learning about the animals.”

title: Susan Collins’ math doesn’t add up
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Need some straight data on why it’s time to vote Sen. Susan Collins out? The senator takes credit for bringing money to Maine, but the math doesn’t work.
Her one vote allowing the “big, beautiful bill” is estimated to cost Maine a projected $4.125 billion in cuts over 10 years. Compare that to the $3.45 billion she claims to have brought in over 10 years and we get a loss of $675 million. She could have stopped it. She’s playing us, and it’s costing lives. The real costs of that legislation start in January.
Add on the rising costs of the Iran war, heating oil, gasoline, groceries, health insurance, tariffs and devastating hospital closures from her Trump support, and Troy Jackson is the common- sense choice.
Martha White
Rockport

title: Letter: Remember how Paul LePage gutted healthcare
text:
Letters submitted by BDN readers are verified by BDN Opinion Page staff. Send your letters to letters@bangordailynews.com
For anyone struggling with medical debt, skyrocketing health insurance costs, basic access to medical care, paying for prescriptions, or finding help for a loved one with a substance use problem, please remember Paul LePage’s track record as governor.
LePage gutted the public health system. He left thousands of children without health coverage, refused to comply with court orders to implement a MaineCare expansion that had been enacted, cut financial assistance for medications, and made it harder to access life-saving naloxone. There’s more, but I think this should be enough to convince voters that he’s not the man to help us in Congress.
All of this in the name of saving money. But it’s well documented that early intervention and access to basic care are the cheapest, most cost-effective medical care. Not to mention the fact that they reduce misery, stress, and suffering.
I’ll vote for Matt Dunlap, thank you.
Laura Levenson 
Carmel

title: The luck of the draw
text:
In Maine, the annual chance drawing of a permit to hunt moose is a high-profile event. For most big game hunters, the permit is a ticket to the hunt of a lifetime. The odds of being drawn are formidable. This year about 75,000 residents and nonresident applicants entered the drawing for just 3,343 hunt permits.
Every year, there are many more losers than winners, and a few skeptics who follow the list of winners ask the same questions year after year: “Is the lottery really fair?” “I have been applying for more than 20 years unsuccessfully, yet my neighbor has been drawn three times? How can that be fair.” Or “I know a family that got three permits the same year.”

title: Suspect allegedly attacked man with knife and brass knuckles in Lewiston
text:
A man allegedly attacked another man with a knife and brass knuckles in Lewiston on Saturday afternoon.
Alexander Keith, 18, has been charged with aggravated assault and criminal threatening, according to the Lewiston Police Department.
Keith allegedly stabbed the 20-year-old in the back and then beat him with brass knuckles outside a Dunkin’ on Main Street about 3:30 p.m.
The victim was taken to Central Maine Medical Center, where he was treated for serious but not life-threatening injuries.
Keith was being held without bail at the Androscoggin County Jail in Auburn because he was out on a deferred disposition before the alleged assault.

title: Supreme Court won’t hear challenge to Maine’s 72-hour waiting period to buy guns
text:
Maine’s 72-hour waiting period for gun purchases will remain in place, after the U.S. Supreme Court declined to hear an appeal of an April ruling by the First Circuit Court of Appeals.
Maine enacted the waiting period for certain gun sales after the October 2023 mass shooting in Lewiston, in which 18 people were killed and 13 injured.
The goal of the “cooling off” period was “to decrease suicides and homicides carried out after impulsive firearm purchases,” according to court records.
The law took effect in August 2024 but was quickly challenged.
Andrea Beckwith, who owns an organization that offers gun training to victims of domestic violence, along with a coalition of individuals and businesses, sued Maine Attorney General Aaron Frey to stop the law, which they argued violated their 2nd Amendment rights.
A federal granted a preliminary injunction in the case, Beckwith, et al v. Frey, but the decision was overturned in the First Circuit Court of Appeals. The Supreme Court decision not to hear the case upholds the appellate court’s ruling.

title: 9 Maine events include ‘Cabaret’ in Auburn and Ogunquitfest
text:
7:30 p.m. Thursday-Saturday, 2 p.m. Sunday. Community Little Theatre, 30 Academy St., Auburn, $25, $22 seniors and students, $17 for 13 and under. laclt.com.
Put down the knitting, the book and the broom and head to Auburn for L/A Community Little Theatre’s production of the Tony Award-winning musical “Cabaret.” Set in a 1920s Berlin nightclub, “Cabaret” delves into the the lives of some locals and expatriates as the Third Reich starts to emerge in Germany. Young American writer Cliff falls for English singer Sally Bowles. At the same time, Fräulein Schneider, owner of Cliff and Sally’s boarding house, sparks up a romance with Herr Schultz, a mild-mannered, Jewish fruit seller. Musical numbers include “Willkommen,” “Don’t Tell Mama” and the always enchanting title song.
7 p.m. Thursday. Merrill Auditorium, 20 Myrtle St., Portland, $25-$75. porttix.com.
Canadian modern circus troupe Cirque Alfonse presents a show that celebrates love with circus elements, live music, dance and humor. During every performance of “La Noce D’Alfonse,” a couple in the audience is spotlighted through a special segment featuring aerial straps, roller skating, juggling, tightwire, swing dancing and other flashy displays. With an homage to Québécois folk traditions, you’ll hear music that merges vintage and contemporary sounds into a live, joyful soundtrack.
Thursday-Sunday. Blue Hill locations. wordfestival.org.
Word: Blue Hill Literary Festival celebrates its 10th anniversary over the course of four days. The schedule features appearances by authors, workshops and other literary events. Highlights include a writing workshop and talk with Stephen King scholar Caroline Bicks, a conversation with Kelly Link and Ben Shattuck on the art of the short story and the workshop The Politics of Poetry with Nyamuon “Moon” Nguany Machar, among several other offerings.
7 p.m. Friday, 2 p.m. Saturday, 2 p.m. Sunday, 2 and 7 p.m. Oct. 29. Through Nov. 8. The Public Theatre, 31 Maple St., Lewiston, $42, $15 for 12-18, $25 for 19-35. thepublictheatre.org.
Robert Harling’s “Steel Magnolias” comes to life at The Public Theatre. Set in the late 1980s in the fictional northwestern Louisiana parish of Chinquapin, the play centers on six Southern women who converge weekly at a beauty parlor. Through much laughter and as many tears, the story is full of joyful, comedic and sorrowful moments, and you’ll love every one of them.
7 p.m. Friday. State Theatre, 609 Congress St., Portland, $15 in advance, $20 day of show, $10 students and filmmakers. statetheatreportland.com.
Damnationland is an annual event featuring genre-bucking original works from Maine filmmakers that reinvent what you think you know about thrillers and horror films. You’ll see a variety of short films that pair ghoulishly well with the Halloween season. This year, the festival celebrates its Sweet Sick-Steen anniversary.
Friday-Sunday. Downtown Ogunquit and surrounding areas. ogunquit.org/ogunquitfest.
OgunquitFest is a three-day celebration of autumn that’s been happening for more than two decades. You can partake of several events and activities including a classic car show, Dogtoberfest costume parade, the Frannie Peabody High Heel Dash, artisan craft fair with more than 60 vendors and an array of food trucks. title: Zelenskyy: Ukraine got no early warning from partners as Russia hits the power grid again
text:
Zelenskyy says Ukraine got no early warning from partners as Russia hits the power grid again
Russia used ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones to launch more attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Monday, noting that Kyiv again received no early warning of the attack from partner countries who, in the past, have shared that intelligence.
Related video: Trump temporarily waives Russia sanctions to end war in Ukraine
Zelenskyy is grappling with the implications of recent Washington moves benefiting Russian President Vladimir Putin, including waiving U.S. sanctions on Moscow and signing a deal to import Russian diesel.
In parallel, limits on Ukraine’s use of the military-grade version of U.S. company SpaceX’s Starlink satellite internet service have choked Ukrainian drone operations, according to Zelenskyy. Also, a severe shortage of American-made Patriot air defense systems have made Ukraine more vulnerable.
Western intelligence sharing has helped Ukraine counter Russia’s devastating ballistic missiles and hold back Moscow’s invasion, which began more than 4 ½ years ago.
U.S. President Donald Trump says Washington hasn’t stopped providing intelligence to Kyiv, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio repeated that position Monday.
Rubio said he had no information about the previous night’s Russian attack.
Russian barrage hammers power grid, kills 21-year-old woman
The Russian nighttime barrage damaged more than 10 energy infrastructure facilities across the country, denying more than a half-million people light, heating and running water, Zelenskyy said on social media.
Russia fired 16 ballistic missiles at Kyiv and the region around it, Zelenskyy said, with officials in the capital reporting that a 21-year-old woman was killed.
The Russian Defense Ministry said that it carried out a “massive strike” against targets inside Ukraine, including a data center, a logistics hub storing components for drones and cruise missiles, an industrial facility making drone components, and a locomotive depot where missiles are stored.
Zelenskyy says Ukraine has made every diplomatic effort to end the war
Trump accuses Zelenskyy of not wanting Russia’s invasion to end. Washington's efforts to bring peace, meanwhile, have made no progress. Even a recent truce covering energy infrastructurethat Trump demanded came to nothing.
Western help has been vital for Ukraine’s defense against Russia’s bigger military, but fears have mounted in Kyiv that Trump may be turning his back on Ukraine.
Putin, Western analysts and officials say, believes that he can wait for foreign support for Ukraine to unravel and that Russia’s bigger military will then crush Ukraine’s resistance.
“Ukraine never wanted this war, and we have welcomed literally EVERY attempt by our partners to bring this war to a dignified end. We have responded positively to EVERY ceasefire proposal,” Zelenskyy said Monday on social media.
“The reality is that the war continues, and it continues solely because of Russian strikes and Russia’s desire to drag this war out.”
Ukraine has held back Russia’s bigger army on the front line and has hit back with long-range strikes deep inside Russia that have struck oil refineries and brought fuel shortages.
On Sunday, Ukraine launched more than 1,000 drones at Russia in one of its largest aerial attacks of the war, setting fire to an oil export terminal and a depot in St. Petersburg.
Russia has sought to disrupt daily life in Ukraine and torment civilians with drone and missiles strikes that hit trains, shopping malls, gas stations and supermarkets.
___
Hatton reported from Lisbon, Portugal.

title: 3 injured after horse jumps during wagon ride at popular North Carolina drive-thru zoo
text:
MOORESVILLE, N.C. (WBTV/Gray News) - Three people were injured after a startled horse jumped while pulling a wagon at Lazy 5 Ranch, officials said.
The incident happened Saturday during a horse-drawn wagon ride at the ranch, a popular drive-thru zoo in North Carolina.
According to a social media post, a limb fell from a nearby tree and hit the side of the wagon, causing the horses to jump and three people to fall from the wagon.
All three were taken to a hospital for treatment, but their conditions were not available Sunday morning, officials said.
The other passengers were unharmed or declined treatment, and the wagon driver was uninjured, officials said. The horses were unharmed and were evaluated before returning to work.
“Our thoughts and prayers are with everyone involved in this incident, and we extend our heartfelt concern to those affected and their families,” officials said. “This is the first incident in [Lazy 5 Ranch] history resulting in hospitalizations requiring an overnight stay.”
Lazy 5 Ranch is located in Rowan County, about 36 miles northeast of Charlotte, North Carolina. More than 3 million people have experienced the ranch’s horse-drawn wagon rides, according to officials.

title: More than 60,000 Maine college students, faculty to receive free local news subscriptions
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
More than 60,000 students, faculty and staff at Maine colleges and universities will receive free one-year digital subscriptions to Maine Trust for Local News publications this fall through a new sponsored program.
The subscriptions will provide access to the Portland Press Herald, Sun Journal, Morning Sentinel and Kennebec Journal, among other Maine Trust publications. Funded by Bangor Savings Bank, the program covers Maine’s public universities, the Maine Community College System, Husson University in Bangor and Thomas College in Waterville.
Eligible students, faculty and staff will register using a school email address through a dedicated online page and receive digital access on computers and mobile devices.
Gavin Robinson, senior vice president, community relations manager and public finance officer at Bangor Savings Bank, said in a statement that the initiative is intended to increase access to local news and encourage civic engagement.
“Strong communities depend on people who are informed, connected and engaged,” Robinson said.
The program also aims to give students access to news about communities where they attend school and, in some cases, where they may eventually work.
“Maine’s community college students tend to come from — and ultimately stay and work in — their local communities, so having free access to the local news is a real gift,” said David Daigler, president of the Maine Community College System, in a statement.
Daigler said community college graduates enter fields including healthcare, emergency response, skilled trades and business, making familiarity with current events and local issues useful as they begin their careers.
The program comes after four private colleges — Bates College in Lewiston, Colby College in Waterville, Bowdoin College and The Roux Institute at Northeastern University in Portland — are already paying for Maine Trust digital subscriptions for their school populations.

title: Maine women’s ice hockey earns a road win over RPI
text:
TROY, N.Y. — The University of Maine women’s ice hockey team earned a 5-3 victory over Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute (RPI) on Friday, Oct. 16, at Houston Field House. The Black Bears broke a three-game losing streak with a strong offensive performance, led by second-year forward Mackenzie Podewell, who recorded two goals and an assist. The win improved Maine’s record to 2-5-0 on the season.
Maine came out aggressively in the first period, opening the scoring on the power play at 4:14. Second-year defenseman Lulu Rucinski put the Black Bears ahead 1-0, finishing a play assisted by third-year defenseman Brenna Curl and second-year forward Isabelle Michaud. RPI responded just over two minutes later when fourth-year defenseman Kendal Davidson tied the game at 1-1.
The Black Bears regained the lead at 13:44 when first-year defenseman Oda Bruland Austefjord scored her first collegiate goal. Austefjord found the back of the net unassisted, giving Maine a 2-1 lead. However, RPI answered again at 6:25 in the first period, with first-year forward Barbora Cerna-Proskova tying the game at 2-2 heading into the first intermission.
Maine regained control of the game in the second period, finding the back of the net to take a 3-2 lead into the final frame. With 7:57 remaining in the frame, second-year forward Mackenzie Podewell scored to put the Black Bears ahead. The goal was assisted by second-year forward Sophia Dau and third-year defenseman Kendall Sundby. Maine’s defense kept RPI scoreless throughout the remainder of the period, allowing the Black Bears to carry their momentum into the third.
RPI came out strong in the final period. Just 25 seconds after the opening faceoff, second-year forward Mia Montanari scored to even the game at 3-3, putting pressure on Maine to respond. The Black Bears answered halfway through the period when Podewell scored her second goal of the night at 9:17. Second-year forward Julie Jebousková and third-year forward Stephanie Jacob assisted on the go-ahead goal, giving Maine a 4-3 lead.
With RPI pushing for a comeback late in the game, the Engineers pulled their goaltender in favor of an extra attacker. Maine capitalized on the open net at 19:29 when fourth-year forward Raegan Wurm scored to extend the lead to 5-3. Rucinski and Podewell recorded assists on the insurance goal, sealing the victory for the Black Bears.
Maine finished the game with 24 shots on goal compared to RPI’s 16. The Black Bears converted one of four power-play opportunities and limited the Engineers to zero power-play goals. Ten different Maine players recorded at least one point, highlighting the team’s balanced offensive effort.
Third-year goaltender Madisyn Ryan also made an important contribution in her first start of the season, recording 13 saves. Her performance helped Maine maintain its lead during key stretches of the game as the Engineers continued to apply pressure.
The victory was an important step forward for the Black Bears after three consecutive losses. Maine demonstrated resilience by responding each time RPI tied the game and ultimately finding the go-ahead goal in the third period. Podewell’s three-point performance, Austefjord’s first collegiate goal and contributions throughout the lineup helped Maine secure the road win.
The Black Bears will look to build on the momentum when they face RPI again on Saturday, Oct. 17, at 3 p.m. in Troy, New York, to conclude the two-game nonconference series.

title: Pet dog kills 7-week-old in Livermore Falls, police say
text:
Police say a 7-week-old was killed by a pet dog at a home in Livermore Falls last week.
Livermore Falls police Chief Abe Haroon said he responded to the report at about 11:10 p.m. Wednesday.
“Super, super tragic,” Haroon said Monday.
The child was pronounced dead at the scene.
Maine State Police Major Crime Unit-South is investigating the death, Haroon said.
Haroon said the dog was a Belgian Malinois. He could offer no other details, saying the case is still under investigation.
The family said Monday they were grieving privately and asked for their privacy.
Haroon was assisted at the scene by Jay police and MaineHealth Emergency Services ambulance personnel.
This is a developing story.

title: Maine voters must choose between listener and lecturer
text:
Brenda Power is a retired educator who lives in Ellsworth. She received the UMaine Distinguished Professor award in 1999.
I attended a town hall meeting of Troy Jackson’s in Ellsworth and witnessed a remarkable exchange.
A young woman stood up and said to Troy, “I want to support you. But I am an immigrant. I watch your campaign ads. You talk about the logging blockade in the 1990s, and how you worked so hard to keep foreigners from taking Maine jobs. How do I know you will support and help people like me, and not see me as a foreigner taking a Maine job?”
Her voice was shaky and lightly accented. Everyone could see how much courage it took for her to stand up and ask her question.
Troy paused. You could tell he was as moved as the audience by the question. He responded, “Thank you for speaking up. I’m sorry.”
He then explained how it was never his intention to castigate the Canadian workers. He saw the problem at that time as the same one we face today throughout Maine and the U.S. — large, wealthy corporations in Canada were using their workers as pawns.
He said he would have supported those Canadian workers immigrating to Maine for a better life, and was dedicated to finding pathways for immigrants in Maine, because we desperately need and want immigrants here. He vowed to look at the ad and improve his message, and thanked her for identifying a problem he needed to address.
After the session ended and most everyone left to partake in the pizza provided, Troy made a beeline to that woman for a private conversation. I noticed Troy mostly listened. At the end, he pulled out a contact card and wrote down a personal cellphone number, urging the woman to call if she wanted to continue the dialogue.
I couldn’t help but contrast that exchange with another I read about recently.
The last conversation Sen. Susan Collins had with Maine Planned Parenthood representatives was reportedly almost eight years ago, just weeks before the Kavanaugh vote. Nicole Clegg, the head of the Maine Planned Parenthood Action Fund, flew down with a small group of Maine women to D.C. in early August 2018, all of whom either worked with Planned Parenthood, or had received abortion care.
When they sat down to talk with Collins, they were stunned when she gave them little time to share their stories. As Clegg explained, “Before we could even have these women share their experiences, Senator Collins wanted to share her displeasure at the fact that during Colby [College’s] graduation ceremony, where she was the speaker, many Colby students wore ‘I Stand with Planned Parenthood’ stickers. That set the tone for the meeting. I left deeply regretful that I had asked these women to come down and do this. Because it was clear to me it did not have an impact. I actually communicated to their office to say ‘I can’t bring constituents into this space if I don’t think they are going to be respected.’”
Planned Parenthood of Maine has not had a conversation with Collins since.
These Maine women all showed great courage. One is an immigrant who worries any step outside her Maine home might bring her face to face with ICE. Yet she comes to a town hall to confront a candidate because she wants to understand his views and share her experience. The others flew to D.C. to share deeply personal trauma with a powerful legislator who was supposed to be their voice in Congress. One person listened. The other lectured.
It’s no wonder Troy Jackson has evolved in his views over the past 15 years, leading the Maine Legislature to pass one of the most thoughtful abortion rights laws in the country. And it’s also no wonder Susan Collins has “evolved” to support militant anti-abortion judges.
I hope Maine voters will also show some courage in the coming weeks. We have a choice to vote for someone who shows up and welcomes those who challenge him so that he can become a better representative. Or we can vote for the senator who hasn’t held a town hall in 25 years, preferring to lecture those who challenge her in private. The choice couldn’t be more clear.

title: Maine Savings Amphitheater Brings Over $600 Million To Maine
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The Amount of Money the Maine Savings Amphitheater Has Brought Into the State is Mind-Blowing
It is wild to think about how the Maine Savings Amphitheater has grown over the last 15 years.
When it first opened, it was little more than a grassy hillside with a stage. Now, it is one of New England's premiere concert venues. And, the venue makes new additions each season. For example, there is now rooftop seating.
In it's 16 years of operation, the venue has hosted over 250 concerts and welcomed more than 1.6 million attendees.
Not only is the Maine Savings Amphitheater an amazing venue, it is also a major driver to the economy of Eastern Maine and beyond.
How Much Money Has the Maine Savings Amphitheater Brought to Bangor's Economy?
The number is truly astounding!
According to a recent article on the Bangor Daily News, the amount of money brought into just the Bangor-area economy between 2010 and 2025 is in excess of $600 million.
That figure comes from a recent report done by Professor Todd Gabe, of the University of Maine School of Economics. In the report, he took into account revenue & employment information from Waterfront Concerts and taxable retails sales from the area during the days when concerts happened.
Of course, when you factor in the fact that people are coming from all over New England to see these concerts, and spending money as they travel, the amount balloons even more.
What was the last show you saw at the Maine Savings Amphitheater? Share any pictures of videos with us using our app.

title: For equal rights for LGBT citizens, Collins has been in the room where it happens
text:
Ken Mehlman is a businessman and former chairman of the Republican National Committee (2005-2007). Michael S.C. Soto is the co-leader of the Equality and Fairness for All Americans Coalition.
One of the most memorable songs in “Hamilton” is “The Room Where It Happens.”
It tells the story of a 1790 dinner where Alexander Hamilton, Thomas Jefferson and James Madison struck a deal. Hamilton won federal assumption of the states’ war debts. Jefferson and Madison won a capital on the Potomac. Aaron Burr, who sings the song, is left outside wondering how it all came together.
Washington still works much the same way. Debates happen in public, and public opinion shapes what is possible. But the details are usually settled in smaller rooms, among members of Congress, with the White House and with the advocates and stakeholders who will live with the results.
We have spent our careers in and around those rooms. One of us has worked in Republican politics, the other in progressive politics. We don’t agree on everything. But we have both worked to advance freedom and equal opportunity for gay and transgender Americans, and we have learned that who is in the room matters.
When it comes to gay rights, Sen. Susan Collins has been in that room for a long time.
In 2010, she and Sen. Joe Lieberman led the effort to repeal “Don’t Ask, Don’t Tell,” allowing gay and lesbian Americans to serve openly in the military. She supported federal hate crimes protections and workplace protections. She opposed amendments to ban same-sex marriage, publicly supported marriage equality and signed the Republican brief urging the Supreme Court to recognize same-sex marriages nationwide. In 2019, she joined Democratic Sens. Jeff Merkley, Tammy Baldwin and Cory Booker in introducing the Equality Act.
Some of the most important rooms in Washington are the ones where budgets get written. As chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, Collins secured more than $2.5 billion for the Ryan White HIV/AIDS Program this year, including $525 million that had been slated for cuts. Last year she stopped a proposed $400 million cut to PEPFAR, the global AIDS program that has saved an estimated 26 million lives. That work earned her the 2025 Champion Award from U.S. Business Action to End HIV.
Over time, she has become the Republican that Democratic senators call first when they want to move equality legislation forward. The Respect for Marriage Act shows why.
In 2022, many married same-sex couples worried their marriages were not fully secure under federal law. Congress had a chance to act, but only if a bill could reach 60 votes in the Senate. That meant bringing Republicans along without losing Democrats.
Collins and Baldwin led that effort, working with Sens. Rob Portman, Thom Tillis and Kyrsten Sinema. Much of the work happened quietly. They met with colleagues one at a time, listened to concerns about religious liberty and wrote language that addressed those concerns while keeping the heart of the bill intact. The final law repealed the Defense of Marriage Act and required federal and state recognition of same-sex and interracial marriages.
It passed the Senate 61-36 with support from Democrats, Republicans, equality advocates and religious organizations. President Biden signed it into law.
Some people hear the word “compromise” and worry it means supporters of equal rights must settle for less. That is not what happened here. The religious liberty language did not weaken the protections for married couples. It ensured everyone had a seat at the table and answered honest concerns so the bill could win the votes it needed and stand up in court. Sen. Collins knew the difference. She knew what could change and what could not, and people on both sides trusted her to keep her word.
That kind of legislating rarely makes headlines. It is slow, and it often happens out of view. But it is how lasting protections get written into law.
Washington is more divided today than at any point in our careers. That makes lawmakers who can work across party lines to solve our country’s biggest challenges more valuable and harder to find.
The room where it happens is less glamorous than Broadway makes it look. But for more than two decades, whenever the rights and lives of gay and transgender Americans have been on the table, Susan Collins has been in that room. And the laws that came out of it are stronger because she was there.

title: Correcting the record
text:
To the Editor:
This op-ed is written to correct the record, and provide further citizen updates, on last week’s Islander headline article entitled “Recall of Elected Officials Sought.” Whether due to lack of understanding, deliberate distortion, or simply a sensationalist approach designed to provoke increased attention and readership, I regard this title as unworthy of the usual standards of the news outlet of record for our community.

title: North Korea threatens to restart propaganda broadcasts, deploy weapons along South border
text:
North Korea threatens to restart propaganda broadcasts, deploy weapons along South border
North Korea threatened Monday to resume propaganda loudspeaker broadcasts and deploy more weapons along the border with South Korea, as the rivals remain locked in animosities over last month’s mine blasts that injured three South Korean soldiers.
Related video: Trump temporarily waives Russia sanctions to end war in Ukraine
Earlier this month, South Korea formally blamed North Korea-planted mines for the Sept. 21 blasts at the border, urging the North to apologize and remove other mines. That announcement came after North Korea denied responsibility for the explosions and warned of strong retaliation if provoked.
On Monday, Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, accused South Korea of firing warning shots and issuing warning broadcasts numerous times at the border since August under “such an unreasonable pretext” that North Korean soldiers crossed the border. She said that such provocations “have gone beyond the red line” since the mine blasts.
“A grave situation is prevailing along the southern border due to the reckless behavior of the ROK military gangsters,” Kim Yo Jong said, referring South Korea by its official name, the Republic of Korea.
She said the North Korean military was considering “deploying more tactical strike means along the southern border as a preemptive and suppressive measure to deal with contingency, and of resuming the loudspeaker broadcasting against the ROK.”
In recent years, tensions along the Korean border, one of the world's most heavily fortified, have increased as North Korea added mines, barbed wire fences, anti-tank barriers and other front-line fortifications in line with its policy of terminating ties with South Korea.
South Korea’s military earlier said North Korean soldiers violated the border’s military demarcation line 50 times this year during their fortification works. South Korea’s military said it responded by firing warning shots and making warning broadcasts. It didn’t immediately respond to the latest North Korean warning.
In 2015, mine blasts blamed on North Korea that maimed two South Korean soldiers pushed the Koreas to the brink of an armed conflict, after South Korea resumed front-line loudspeaker propaganda broadcasts for the first time in 11 years.
Loudspeaker broadcasts are one of the old-fashioned, Cold War-era psychological warfare campaigns the two Koreas have occasionally used against each other in times of confrontation.
Since taking office last year, South Korea's liberal government, led by President Lee Jae Myung, halted such broadcasts as part of efforts to improve ties with North Korea. North Korea later stopped its own broadcasts.
North Korea has recently dialed up weapons testing activities in a likely bid to pressure the United States to make bigger concessions, after President Donald Trump renewed his efforts to restore diplomacy with Kim Jong Un.

title: A Maine family bought land on MDI with dreams of building a home. Then a scammer tried to sell it.
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Several years ago, Haley and Michael Walcott of Bucksport bought a nearly 3-acre plot in Bar Harbor to one day build a home on.
So they never expected to see a “for sale” sign on the land when driving by it this spring.
The family’s property nearly fell victim to a fraud scheme in which a scammer impersonated Michael Walcott, and real estate agents unknowingly put it on the market without the rightful owner’s knowledge.
“We got married on that land and it holds a lot of sentimental value,” Haley Walcott said. “It would have been gutting for us if this had gone any further.”
While the scam was caught before money changed hands, it’s a prime example of deed fraud attempts that have become a growing risk to both Maine real estate agents and unassuming prospective buyers. Lawmakers have taken notice and formed a commission to understand the issue further, but passed on enacting recommended rule changes to combat the issue despite real estate agents now receiving fines for falling for the schemes.
The Walcotts learned of the scam after receiving a call from another real estate agent, Laurie Smallidge of Better Homes and Gardens Real Estate The Masiello Group, telling them someone appeared to be targeting their land.
Smallidge knew this because the scammer had also contacted her and asked her to sell it, she said.
Smallidge noticed the scammer’s behavior matched patterns often found in other fraud attempts. For example, they wanted to sell land quickly, preferred to communicate digitally, and contacted her through a third-party listing service, such as Zillow or Redfin.
“One of the red flags for me was that he knew the tax ID number that the town uses,” Smallidge said. “No one ever knows that.”
These scam attempts also usually involve vacant land, as it’s more difficult to verify ownership because “people own land but aren’t doing anything with it and aren’t paying attention to it,” Smallidge said. In some cases, scammers will go so far as to make a fake ID and give title companies a number to wire money to.
“I just had a gut feeling and it didn’t sit right with me,” Smallidge said. “You have to trust your instincts and verify the facts.”
She looked up the property owner’s address in public records and used a verification tool available to real estate professionals to find Michael Walcott’s genuine phone number, then called him.
Shortly after that, the Walcotts checked on the land and found a “for sale” sign on it, signaling that another agent had fallen for the ruse.
In the case of the Walcotts’ land, the scammer sent a message to Eileen McMorrow-Hallock of The Knowles Company in Northeast Harbor on May 8 and the pair communicated primarily via email before she and another associate broker, William Burnett, listed the property later that month, according to consent agreement documents from the Maine Real Estate Commission, which investigated the incident.
In one email to the fraudster, McMorrow-Hallock confirmed she “located your land information on the town tax records,” according to the commission. Bar Harbor Property Tax records for the land include Michael Walcott’s genuine Bucksport mailing address.
Haley Walcott called McMorrow-Hallock on May 27 to inform her that the property is not for sale and demanded the listing be removed immediately.
Michael Walcott filed a complaint with the Maine Real Estate Commission the same day, which resulted in McMorrow-Hallock and Burnett each receiving $4,000 fines for “failing to take steps to confirm the identity of the person who purported to be the owner,” among other things, according to the consent agreements.
McMorrow-Hallock did not return requests for comment about the Walcotts’ case. Claire Dorwart, owner of The Knowles Company, said the agency “responded promptly, diligently, and the matter was resolved before any transaction occurred or anyone suffered a financial loss.”
“We know others have faced more serious outcomes, and we hope greater awareness and shared guidance within our industry will help protect everyone involved in a sale,” Dorwart said.
Burnett said on Friday that he has learned from the experience and the team is “moving forward with a continuous improvement of standard practices” while ensuring colleagues and clients are aware of the growing risk.
Maine law doesn’t require real estate agents to follow a specific process to verify someone owns the property they’re attempting to sell, according to the Maine Real Estate Commission.
However, the Maine Association of Realtors provides methods agents can use to vet sellers, such as requiring them to provide a government-issued photo identification and engage in a face-to-face interaction before listing a property.
Realtors are also encouraged to verify the identity of a property owner by checking the county registry of deeds and municipal tax records. While that’s often how scammers find information to conceal their identities, the association advises agents to go a step further and send a letter to the address listed on a property’s tax bill.
Lastly, real estate agents have access to a security app that allows them to check if the phone number or email address someone is using to contact them is connected to the property they’re looking to sell, Smallidge said.
Title companies are also becoming more familiar with these types of scams and taking additional steps to ensure a seller genuinely owns a property before sending money to them, Smallidge said.
So far this year, the Maine Real Estate Commission has received two complaints in which a licensed agent listed properties by fraudulent sellers, according to Kristina Lunner, deputy commissioner of the Department of Professional and Financial Regulation.
In each case, the hoax was discovered before the property titles changed hands, but three people were disciplined because of those complaints.
These scam attempts arose after the commission received no complaints of such activity last year, Lunner said.
The Legislature formed a Commission to Recommend Methods for Preventing Deed Fraud, which delivered a report late last year that explained deed fraud, especially cases of people attempting to sell properties they don’t own, is “a growing problem nationwide” and has started to appear in Maine.
However, there isn’t much data on how frequently it’s happening in Maine, the methods scammers are using and how each attempt is discovered. That’s because there’s no uniform method for collecting such information, the report found.
“Due to the difficulties of locating and holding responsible the perpetrators of seller impersonation fraud, and the difficulties of unwinding real estate transactions after the fraudulent activity has occurred, it is essential to focus on preventing seller impersonation fraud,” the report said.
The report included a series of recommendations to combat the issue, such as encouraging the Legislature to require real estate professionals to “verify the identity of persons selling property in all real estate transactions” using specific steps.
Another recommendation would require municipalities to ensure the property tax records they keep contain up to date contact information for the owners, as that is a helpful tool for agents to confirm the owner of a property before listing it, the report outlines.
A bill to enact those recommendations was introduced in February, but killed the following month.
The report explained that seller impersonation cases often contain some red flags agents should be vigilant for. Faux sellers also usually contact multiple agents at a time to improve the chances of one taking the bait, Smallidge said.
“As Realtors, we have a responsibility to protect people, not just sell property,” Smallidge said. “We’re trusted and need to do our due diligence from the beginning to make sure this doesn’t happen.”

title: Longtime CNN anchor Christiane Amanpour leaving network after a storied career of 43 years
text:
(AP) - Longtime CNN anchor Christiane Amanpour will be leaving CNN after 43 years at the network.
The network’s chief international anchor will scale back her daily show, “Amanpour,” on CNN International to once a week at the beginning of 2027, and end the show at the end of May, leaving the network the following month. She said in a statement that she looks forward to “interesting new projects down the line.”
Amanpour, 68, also will end her PBS show, “Amanpour and Company,” at the end of the year, she said in her statement, shared by CNN. She will continue her podcast, “The Ex Files,” with her ex-husband, Jamie Rubin, a former U.S. diplomat.
“After many months of thought and a few sleepless nights, I have decided to separate from CNN, my partner of 43 fantastic years!” Amanpour said in the statement.
Amanpour also said she would “always be rooting for CNN and maintaining its history of independent journalism. Remember: always be truthful, not neutral.”
Amanpour’s exit coincides with a new era at CNN as it comes under a new owner, Skydance. After a yearlong process, Skydance-owned Paramount closed its $81 billion buyout of Warner Bros. Discovery on Oct. 6. The merger unites under one roof two giants in TV news — CBS and CNN.
On a personal front. Amanpour has spoken openly about her 2021 diagnosis of ovarian cancer and its later recurrence, calling it “the invisible killer.” She has urged others to “get all the scans that you can.”
