title: Hannaford still offline a week after cyberattack on French supermarkets
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Hannaford supermarkets were still offline Monday, a week after Dutch owner Ahold Delhaize shut down its websites and apps following a “cybersecurity incident.”
The outage began the same day that cyberattacks disrupted supermarket refrigeration systems across France. A spokesperson for Hannaford, which operates 68 stores in Maine, said the company does not believe the issues are related. But some Hannaford locations have recently experienced refrigeration problems.
“The issue impacting some of our stores is specific to the refrigeration equipment itself, not other factors,” spokesperson Caitlin Cortelyou said in an email Monday.
About 700 French supermarkets experienced widespread food loss and some fires on Oct. 12, when hackers forced refrigeration units into continuous defrost cycles and set temperatures as high as 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit), according to The Associated Press.
Ahold Delhaize announced the same day that it had taken “some systems offline to help protect them” as “precautionary measures following (a) cybersecurity incident,” according to the company’s website.
The company said its stores — including Albert Heijn in the Netherlands, Delhaize in Belgium and Hannaford, Stop & Shop, Food Lion and Giant in the United States — would stay open while its websites and apps were offline.
On Monday, Ahold Delhaize announced that its European stores were back online and that e-commerce services at its U.S. stores “are expected to come back in the coming days.”
The company said it had no evidence that suggests any sensitive customer, associate or partner data was taken. It also didn’t note a connection to the cyberattacks on supermarkets in France.
“As the investigation is ongoing, we are not sharing further details that could compromise security measures or interfere with our response efforts,” the company said.
Based in Scarborough, Hannaford operates 188 stores across the Northeast and is Maine’s second-largest employer, with about 9,500 workers in stores from York to Fort Kent.
Hannaford confirmed Monday that it continued to experience a network issue affecting some services, including its website, mobile app, and Hannaford To Go pickup and delivery.
“This is related to a security issue within the network of our parent company, Ahold Delhaize,” Cortelyou said. “While we can’t comment on another company’s issue, we do not have any reason to believe the Ahold Delhaize matter is related to the issue impacting some French retailers.”
She noted that Hannaford stores remain open and continue to welcome customers, and that customers can continue to shop with the store online through Instacart, DoorDash and Uber Eats.
French Finance Minister Roland Lescure told Parliament last week that while the cyberattacks on refrigeration systems posed no risk to France’s food supplies, the attack “touches the heart of our food security,” AP reported.

title: Ex-OpenAI worker accused of bugging conference room planned to fly to Saudi Arabia, prosecutors say
text:
SAN FRANCISCO (AP) — A former OpenAI engineer charged with secretly installing a recording device in a conference room to glean company details had been “mere days” away from absconding to Saudi Arabia before his arrest, federal prosecutors said in new court filings.
Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old Saudi national, was also fired from his job at the ChatGPT maker, according to a government memo filed Sunday. His wife and young son left the country the day after his arrest on a one-way ticket booked and paid for by a Saudi military official, prosecutors said in the filing.
“Ultimately, the defendant has little incentive to remain in the United States to see this case through,” federal prosecutors wrote. “He has ample resources —including his significant compensation from a decade of high-tech employment in the Bay Area and at least two bank accounts in Saudi Arabia — and what appears to be considerable support from a foreign government.”
Prosecutors also noted Saudi Arabia has no extradition treaty with the U.S. as they seek to detain Alfozan until trial. A judge will consider the request Monday in federal court in San Francisco.
Alfozan’s lawyers didn’t immediately respond to an email seeking comment ahead of Monday’s hearing.
But in their own court filings, they argued that Alfozan, who had worked at OpenAI since July 2025, had purchased one-way tickets for his family to Saudi Arabia more than two weeks before prosecutors allege the recording devices were installed. The defense said the couple planned to spend Alfozan’s roughly two-month paternity leave in Saudi Arabia following the birth of their U.S.-citizen son.
Prosecutors say after his arrest, Saudi officials purchased new plane tickets for the wife and son to leave the U.S. sooner than the Oct. 12 flight Alfozan initially booked.
Alfozan’s lawyers also argued that he was on track to become a naturalized U.S. citizen with an interview with federal officials scheduled next month. They said he has been a legal permanent resident since 2020, has lived in the U.S. for 15 years and attended MIT and the University of California, Berkeley.
“This was a long-held dream for the Alfozan family, as it is for so many immigrants,” his lawyers wrote. “His plan was always to return to the Bay Area, where his home, his career, and his community are.”
Rather than remain in federal custody, Alfozan’s lawyers argue he should be confined to his family’s home in the San Francisco suburbs, with GPS monitoring, travel restrictions and a requirement to surrender his passport.
Prosecutors have not said what Alfozan might have wanted to do with the recordings, but say he was in “frequent communication” with a member of the Saudi royal family. They said the royal family member repeatedly tried to recruit Alfozan to an artificial intelligence venture being launched in Saudi Arabia.
Alfozan told the unnamed person in WhatsApp messages that he wouldn’t leave OpenAI until his stock was vested, even as he explored other career opportunities in the Middle Eastern kingdom, prosecutors wrote.
Prosecutors say Alfozan concealed an audio recording device in toilet paper and plugged it into a USB port on the back of a television in an executive conference room he wasn’t authorized to access. They say security cameras captured him entering the room and checking behind the television after installing the device. It remained there for several days before being found Sept. 30.
Prosecutors say the conference room was typically used for meetings involving company leaders, government officials and other executives and “discussions of highly confidential technical, commercial, and strategic information, including proprietary research, as well as nonpublic information.”
OpenAI has said the recording device Alfozan used was sophisticated, designed to evade detection and featured advanced encryption and audio-monitoring capabilities. They also said they had evidence Alfozan planned to place other listening devices elsewhere in the office.
Alfozan has been charged with using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications. If convicted, he faces a five-year prison sentence.
__
Marcelo reported from New York.

title: Medicare Advantage selection system is a disaster
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The Medicare Advantage system is broken. With open enrollment approaching, increasing costs and decreasing benefits are in the news. But a less discussed issue is that the array of charges and benefits is now so complex that a reasonable consumer cannot make an informed decision.
In Kennebec County alone, the 32 Advantage plans that include drug coverage differ in at least 11 respects. Without even considering medications, an informed consumer would have to consider 352 data points in various combinations in order to choose her best plan.
Excluding the plans marketed exclusively to those with special needs, there are still 17 plans requiring the consideration of 187 data points. Dental coverage is particularly vexing, with its disorienting set of copayments, co-insurances, covered and uncovered services, in- and out-of-network coverage and premiums. The result is a mind-boggling array of choices that stultify rather than clarify consumer choices.
In 1990, the federal government simplified the Medigap marketplace by requiring insurers to offer set menus of benefits from which beneficiaries can choose. Insurance companies then compete based on price and service. Applying this framework to the muddle that is Medicare Advantage would turn it into a workable system that allows consumers to make informed decisions.
Eileen Ringel
Oakland

title: Artist Maria de los Angeles explores migration and belonging in COA public lecture
text:
BAR HARBOR — Artist Maria de los Angeles, the fall 2026 College of the Atlantic Kippy Stroud Artist-in-Residence, presents her vibrant, deeply human exploration of migration, identity, and belonging in an evening lecture on Friday, Oct. 23 at 6:30 p.m. in the Thomas S. Gates, Jr. Community Center.
Known for her intricate drawings, mixed‑media works, and wearable sculptures, de los Angeles uses art as a way to illuminate the lived experiences of immigrants and to question the systems that shape our sense of home. Her one-month residence and public lecture offer a chance to engage with an artist whose work is as visually compelling as it is socially urgent.

title: Beautiful Weather Ahead: High Pressure Keeps Us Storm-Free Through the Weekend
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - High pressure will dominate our forecast for the next several days... keeping us storm free at least through the upcoming weekend!
High pressure will build through the area today... giving us a beautiful start to the work week. We’ll see lots of sunshine today with high temperatures mainly in the upper 50s to low 60s although coastal areas will be a bit cooler with highs in the mid to upper 50s due to a southerly breeze off the ocean. A storm centered off the coast of the Carolinas will drift northward a bit... throwing some high clouds into areas closer to the coast this afternoon into tonight otherwise the bulk of this storm will remain well to our south. Expect clear to partly cloudy skies for the night tonight with the bulk of the clouds over areas closer to the coast. Temperatures will be mainly in the 30s for nighttime lows. A cold front will work southward through the state tonight... pretty much unnoticed as the front doesn’t have much moisture associated with it.
Our Tuesday looks great as strong high pressure builds in from the northwest. There will likely be some lingering high clouds... associated with the storm well to our south... to start the day... but those are expected to give way to plenty of sunshine as the day progresses. Temperatures on Tuesday will be in the 50s to around 60°. Strong high pressure will provide us with lots of sun Wednesday. Highs on Wednesday will be in the upper 40s to mid-50s. Thursday looks good with sunshine and high temperatures in the upper 40s to mid-50s. A cold front is forecast to cross the state Thursday night... allowing some cooler air to move in for Friday. At the same time... strong high pressure building in from the west on Friday combined with a storm well to our east will lead to tightening pressure gradient which means we’ll see a breezy day Friday with a northerly wind possibly gusting to 30 MPH or so throughout the day. We’ll see lots of sunshine Friday with highs in the mid-40s to low 50s. The nice weather continues into the weekend as strong high pressure is forecast to build into the Northeast.
Rest of Today: Mostly sunny. Highs between 56°-64°. South/southwest wind 5-15 MPH.
Tonight: Clear to partly cloudy. Lows in the mid-30s to low 40s... warmest along the coast. Light and variable wind.
Tuesday: Partly sunny during the morning then becoming mostly sunny. Highs in the 50s to near 60°. North wind 5-15 MPH with gusts to 20-25 MPH possible.
Wednesday: Mostly sunny. Highs in the upper 40s to mid-50s.
Thursday: Mostly sunny. Highs in the upper 40s to mid-50s.
Friday: Mostly sunny and breezy. Highs in the mid-40s to low 50s.

title: Why experienced nurses are leaving — and what could bring them back
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(Aging Untold) — The emotional weight of nursing can be immense, but burnout is not caused by one factor alone. Workload, staffing shortages, safety concerns, documentation demands and the loss of meaningful connection with patients are all pushing experienced nurses away from the bedside.
The Aging Untold experts are exploring what nurses are facing — and what hospitals and health care systems could do to help them stay in a field they entered to care for people.
Nursing has become more demanding — and less personal
For many nurses, the pressure begins with the number of patients they are expected to care for. When staffing does not keep pace with demand, nurses can feel overwhelmed before they have a chance to provide the personal care that drew them to the profession, the Aging Untold experts say.
“There’s no way you can have adequate care when you have this short staff and you’re not replenishing that. It’s so easy to get burnout,” Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said.
Rogers recalled a time when nurses offered guidance and encouragement to physicians in training, creating a more personal, supportive environment. She said that sense of connection can be difficult to maintain when the system focuses primarily on numbers and patient volume.
Safety concerns add to the strain
Nurses also may face unsafe situations on the job, including violence from patients and the risks that can come with treating people in emergency settings.
Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, said she did not have a difficult time recruiting nurses because they wanted to get out of the hospital.
One nurse told O’Rourke that a patient grabbed her by the throat and shook her during the COVID-19 pandemic.
“She was scared to death and the hospital didn’t seem to take enough action. Well, who could blame her for leaving?” O’Rourke said.
“Sam” Cradduck, a gerontologist, said safety issues can be especially complicated in hospital emergency rooms, where nurses may encounter patients with serious injuries as well as people connected to violent incidents.
Delirium and hyperconfusion among older patients can sometimes lead to combative or violent behavior, which can create another layer of stress for nurses who are already working under pressure, Cradduck added.
When care becomes a transaction
“Care is about a relationship, not a transaction,” Cradduck said. “And unfortunately, the system has created transactional relationship instead of the relationship.”
Nurses often enter the field because they want a meaningful career centered on helping others. But administrative demands and a growing focus on documentation can make the work feel increasingly transactional, the experts say.
Documentation can pull nurses away from patients
O’Rourke described a familiar conflict: A patient needs help getting out of bed or going to the bathroom, but the nurse also has charting requirements to complete. Electronic medical record systems can change, adding new training and documentation demands to an already full workload.
The result can be a difficult choice between being present with a patient and keeping up with the records, forms and insurance-related requirements that surround care.
Nurses need meaningful support after trauma
The COVID-19 pandemic exposed many weaknesses in the health care system, but the underlying problems existed before the pandemic, Cradduck said.
Cradduck said nurses witnessed deaths and worked through sustained pressure — yet the response was not always equal to the trauma they experienced.
Learn more
Oregon is facing a nursing crisis. Registered nurse Heather Sweeney and therapist Amy Ponteri started “Helping Healthcare Heal” to address what they saw as insufficient resources for healthcare workers in intense settings like emergency rooms.

title: Victim of Florida alligator attack remembered as kind, generous
text:
Victim of Florida alligator attack remembered as kind, generous
Steven Hamilton, a 71-year-old man whom people in the area said regularly fished at a retention pond near Florida's Lake Apopka, was killed Friday in an alligator attack. 
Hamilton was well-known to those who frequented the pond in Dr. Bradford Memorial Park in Winter Garden, Florida, which is outside of Orlando.
"Every time it was a, 'Hey Steve, how's it going?' You know, just checking in. He was out there almost every single night fishing," said Connor Kelley.
Jason Handley, another regular at the park, said, "He was a regular that comes out here and fishes."
"My stomach dropped"
Handley arrived at the park Friday shortly after hearing about the attack but did not initially know who was involved. Kelley was also there and recalled the moment he learned it was Hamilton.
"As I was leaving to go home, I heard someone say apparently it was an older gentleman who fishes there every night, and just immediately my stomach dropped because I was so worried it was Steve, and it turns out it unfortunately was," Kelley said.
Kelley, who had fished with Hamilton a few times, described him as kind and generous.
"It just shows that he was a very kind man. Very relatable. I heard from someone else in town that he had helped her kids with fishing down there a few times," Kelley said.
Winter Garden police said Hamilton was fishing when the attack occurred. He did not survive.
Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC) officials said a trapper later removed a nearly 12-foot alligator from the water. Handley witnessed the capture.
"Yeah, he's got him. He's got him," Handley said in a video he took of the capture Friday.
"They are hunting"
Just a few minutes from the pond, Emily Porto, who lives along Lake Apopka, saw a news helicopter overhead Friday and immediately feared the worst.
"I went on live, and it was there, and I said, 'Oh no. That can't be happening.' And I warned them," Porto said.
Porto said she has been calling FWC after her 8-year-old Samoyed dog, Stormi, was killed by an alligator in the lake last month. She shared a photo that she said shows Stormi in the gator's mouth. She also displayed recent phone calls she made to FWC's nuisance alligator program.
She said a trapper was sent out after her dog was killed, but said the gator responsible was not caught. Since then, she said, more alligators have been spotted near her property, and trappers have returned to the area. Porto is calling for more action to remove alligators from the lake.
"They cannot, when I call, they cannot just tell me that, you know, any body of water in Florida, it can have a gator. I understand that. The gator took my dog offshore. The gator took the man yesterday offshore. They are hunting. So they are becoming very aggressive. They are fearless, and we have to care about people," Porto said.
For those who knew Hamilton, his death is a stark reminder of the dangers posed by Florida's waterways.
"He was not someone that, you know, was harassing any alligators or anything like that. It was just a very unfortunate event that happened and a very sober reminder of, you know, how just mindful to be around water in Florida," Kelley said.

title: Chellie Pingree’s Portland office gets suspicious letter, prompting FBI response
text:
U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree’s Portland office received a suspicious letter Monday, the latest in a string of concerning packages that have been sent to members of Congress in recent days.
Starting last week, representatives and senators around the country began getting similar letters, many of which authorities said contained an unknown white powder. The Portland office of Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, received one, her staff said Friday. Sens. Pete Ricketts, R-Nebraska, Ted Cruz, R-Texas, and Chuck Schumer, D-New York, were also among the several dozen recipients, NBC News reported.
The envelope containing the letter addressed to Pingree, D-1st District, had a return address of “DSA” along with the street number for a building in New York City’s financial district. But NBC reported that authorities have yet to trace the letters’ origins.
So far, no injuries have been reported in connection with the mailings.
“We cannot accept threats and intimidation as a normal part of our politics. The people who work in congressional offices and administer our elections are public servants dedicated to helping their communities. They deserve to do that work without fear,” Pingree said in a written statement. “Political disagreement is part of a healthy democracy. Threatening the people who keep it running is unacceptable.”
The statement from Pingree noted that the FBI responded to her office’s call about the letter, as did the Portland police and fire departments.
Pingree is heavily favored to win a 10th term representing Maine’s deep-blue 1st District this fall as she faces Republican Ronald Russell for the second straight election.

title: Former Maine writer John Gould’s Lisbon home destroyed by fire Sunday
text:
A fire early Sunday morning in Lisbon destroyed well-known author John Gould’s hand-built house, which was soon to be a renovated into a recovery home.
According to the Maine Department of Public Safety, a fire broke out at 51 Gould Road around 3 a.m. Firefighters found the residence fully engulfed and beginning to collapse when they arrived. The home was unoccupied and no one was inside, according to authorities.
The property had been recently sold to Lewiston-based An Angel’s Wing Inc., which posted on Facebook Sunday morning the property was planned as a recovery house for those struggling with alcohol and substance abuse disorder.
“This property represented so much hope, hard work, and planning for the future, and seeing it damaged this way is heartbreaking,” the group posted. “We are still processing the loss and determining what comes next.”
The home was built by Maine author and columnist John Gould in 1940. In his book “The House That Jacob Built,” Gould mentions that his great-grandfather, Jacob Gould, built the original house on the lot in the 1780s before it burned down. John rebuilt the house himself.
Gould died in 2003 at the age of 94. He was the author of numerous books and columns on Maine life, including writing a weekly column for The Christian Science Monitor for more than 60 years.
Debra York, executive director of An Angel’s Wing Inc., said that last Friday members of her team brought over three carloads of furnishings to the house such as bedding and cookware, donated by community members, and left it in the home’s livingroom area.
York said she’s waiting to see what their insurance company tells them before making any decisions about the property.
York said the organization was still in the planning process for the home. Leaders were considering using it as a recovery home for eight veterans providing 24/7 care, but nothing was finalized.
An investigation into the fire is ongoing.

title: Meet the Bowdoin Protester Who Interrupted Susan Collins in Senate Debate
text:
Bowdoin sophomore Henry Elgie organized an interruption to the Susan Collins-Troy Jackson debate on Thursday with the Sunrise Movement and Bates YDSA, hoping to speak directly to Senator Susan Collins.
In an edited Instagram video posted by the Sunrise Movement, Elgie’s interruption is shown behind clips of the livestreamed debate. The Student obtained the original video, taken by Bowdoin sophomore Cline McConnell, which captures the entire interruption from the seat next to Elgie.
The video shows Elgie standing up in the Gracie Theatre at Husson University in Bangor, where the debate was held, shouting, “Senator Collins, I’m so sorry to interrupt, but I’m a young person and I’m terrified. I’m terrified. AI data centers are destroying our climate.”
Elgie continued as he was led out by a security member, “They are poisoning our waters. You are taking corporate PAC money to an absurd degree, an absurd degree. 30 years for what? 30 years for what, Susan Collins?”
In an interview with The Student, Elgie shared his rationale and how he got in. “I felt like this disruption was one of my only ways that I could really speak to her, and get my message across as one of her constituents and as a voter in Maine,” he said. Though Collins has six offices in Maine, Elgie shared that he’d never been to one of them because “she’s rarely at them.”
Elgie said he hoped to show Collins that her young constituents “have genuine concern. “We are genuinely afraid and want a livable future for our generation,” Elgie said.
Elgie’s concerns about Collins were “really a combination of AI data centers, the billionaire class having such a tight grip over her, and her continuous support for military intervention.”
Though Collins’ website has a number of contact options, speaking in person was key to Elgie.
“Online presence, you know, she may not see it. Face-to-face is directly coming to terms with your own constituents and coming to terms with your power, your authority,” Elgie said. “And the decisions you make over in D.C. directly impact the students that live here in Maine, and the people that live here.”
As reported by the Portland Press Herald, Elgie is registered to vote in Brunswick, where he attends Bowdoin. While Elgie is originally from Vancouver, British Columbia, he’s a dual citizen and shared, “I have lots of family in Maine.”
Elgie shared that he wore a press badge created on Canva which he printed out and laminated to get in. “That was one of the levers we had to exercise to speak with her face-to-face,” he said. Elgie added that though event organizers told him and his close friend, who had been his roommate their first year, that they weren’t on the list, “then they let us in… it was barbecue chicken from there.”
Portland Press Herald previously reported that event organizers said Elgie presented a press badge from The Bowdoin Orient, the Bowdoin College student-run newspaper. Elgie shared with The Student that the press badge he wore deliberately misspelled “Bowdoin Orient” as “Bowdowin orient.”
For Elgie, this was an opportunity to talk to Collins. “While billionaires, major donors, have Collins on speed dial, young people haven’t really seen the Senator at a public town hall in over 25 years,” he said. “So I want people to know, online at least, that she’s not this untouchable figure… that she has accountability for her constituents.”
The interruption was “primarily organized through the Sunrise Movement,” including involvement from Bates students, according to Braedon Parker ’27. Parker, who is both an intern for the Sunrise Movement and a co-chair of Bates Young Democratic Socialists of America (YDSA), shared that the two organizations “have been collabs…as far as planning an event, coming up with ideas, facilitating basically anything that might need to be done.”
According to Parker, Bates YDSA provided “practical and logistical support for the disturbance.” Parker also said he was involved in a lot of planning and execution of the event.
Despite not being in the room when the interruption happened, Parker also had “a lot of excitement about the fact that Henry was able to actually yell at Susan Collins about her destroying our planet.”
Elgie and Parker seemed to share views on Collins’ accessibility.
“They [people] have no way of communicating their positions, their ideas, their beliefs, their desires for the state of Maine to their representative in the highest legislative body in the country,” Parker said. “I think that’s a little concerning… The [Collins] offices are great, but that’s not the same thing as Susan having to hear from actual Mainers themselves.”
In response to the interruption, Collins was heard on the broadcast saying, “So this is obviously one of Troy’s supporters,” to which Jackson responded, “Oh, shut up. I don’t even know that kid.”
While Elgie confirmed, “He’s right. I don’t know Troy Jackson,” he also shared his thoughts on Collins’ response. “I think it goes to show that she… sees it in partisan lines.” Elgie’s speech made no mention of a political party besides Collins herself. Elgie said to The Student, “I didn’t want the message to be clouded by party affiliation on partisan lines. I just wanted to speak the facts that were in my mind about AI data centers, I didn’t [even] get to billionaires.”
Going forward, Elgie said he doesn’t anticipate having many more opportunities to speak with Collins face-to-face. “I think that now is all about getting out the vote,” Elgie said. “If you’re not registered to vote in Maine, vote where you’re registered to vote… And yeah, pull up to the polls and let’s get authoritarianism off the ballot.”
Parker said, “I think it went down perfectly… The message got out for sure.”

title: Medicare Advantage selection system is a disaster
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The Medicare Advantage system is broken. With open enrollment approaching, increasing costs and decreasing benefits are in the news. But a less discussed issue is that the array of charges and benefits is now so complex that a reasonable consumer cannot make an informed decision.
In Kennebec County alone, the 32 Advantage plans that include drug coverage differ in at least 11 respects. Without even considering medications, an informed consumer would have to consider 352 data points in various combinations in order to choose her best plan.
Excluding the plans marketed exclusively to those with special needs, there are still 17 plans requiring the consideration of 187 data points. Dental coverage is particularly vexing, with its disorienting set of copayments, co-insurances, covered and uncovered services, in- and out-of-network coverage and premiums. The result is a mind-boggling array of choices that stultify rather than clarify consumer choices.
In 1990, the federal government simplified the Medigap marketplace by requiring insurers to offer set menus of benefits from which beneficiaries can choose. Insurance companies then compete based on price and service. Applying this framework to the muddle that is Medicare Advantage would turn it into a workable system that allows consumers to make informed decisions.
Eileen Ringel
Oakland

title: Doing it for the shirt: The appeal of intramural sports at UMaine
text:
Like many things, sports are forced upon us for our own well-being in our younger years. When we get to college, the gap left in their place may feel vacuous. The effort required to get back into sports can seem like too much for the benefits we receive out of it, but if you had a really cool shirt to look forward to, things might be different.
“At the end of the day, everyone is just there to have fun” was the message echoed by both Will Young, a third-year chemical engineering student, and Brady LaForge, a fourth-year economics student. Young played in the league throughout his first two years and is only taking a hiatus now because of the co-op he will be a part of in the spring. LaForge played for a few years before being presented with an opportunity to referee.
“One day an employee came up to us and said that they were looking for refs,” LaForge recounted. “I thought, ‘I enjoy playing so why not fill my evenings when I don’t do much else being around people playing sports.’” After some time, LaForge became a program assistant and was recently featured on the intramural sports Instagram page as the supervisor of the month.
“Coed volleyball was my first time ever playing the sport,” LaForge said. “I had no knowledge and neither did most of my teammates. But we played with someone who knew the game and with his help and our experience in other sports, we somehow became pretty good.” LaForge talked about how his ragtag team made it all the way to the championship only to have an unfortunate loss in the third set. “I had never played volleyball before but now I think it’s my favorite sport,” LaForge said.
“Sometimes people get a little serious,” Young said. “Usually I was like, come on, let’s just have fun and get the most amount of playtime. That’s what I’m here for, to play an organized sport.” Young was grateful for the experience of organized play because it is something fleeting after high school, with college being one of the few real opportunities left.
Young talked about how other athletes wanted more action than just the season of their chosen sport. “I joined what is basically the ‘tennis club team’ for softball. It’s just a bunch of people who get other tennis players to join their groups.” He felt that the softball season was unfortunately short.
“As a supervisor,” LaForge said, “I just check up on people during the games and make sure things are going smoothly. We are all first-aid trained, so I help with any injuries that occur. The best part is there are usually enough people to cover, so getting in on games during your shift is not only allowed but encouraged.” It is not a bad deal, considering it is a paid position at the New Balance Recreation Center.
“I think the hype has definitely gone up recently,” said LaForge. “This year men’s and coed soccer both have 16+ teams; those are crazy numbers that I haven’t seen before.” Despite the hype, LaForge said that there is always room for more. “There’s plenty of brackets going around for everyone and every bracket has a shirt, so try a sport you’ve never played before.”
The shirt is certainly the focus of the entire ordeal. Not only is the intramural sports website emblazoned with “Become a Champion / Do it for the shirt!” but LaForge remembers numerous seniors in their final semesters approaching him to say they didn’t have a team yet, but wanted to do whatever they could for that illustrious prize. Similarly, Young ended the interview saying, “Senior year, I’m getting a T-shirt for every season.”
